papers.abstract: End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models achieve strong planning performance but remain largely opaque, limiting observability and trust. We apply mechanistic interpretability to E2E driving by training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on the internal activations of a simple, single-camera end-to-end path planning model. Unsupervised clustering of SAE latents reveals interpretable structure aligned with route intent, vehicle speed, and braking behavior, recovering route intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision. Through paired counterfactual image edits, we further show that specific SAE features are visually grounded and systematically respond to scene changes such as traffic light state and stop sign presence. Steering individual SAE latents produces predictable, monotonic changes in planner outputs including lateral displacement, curvature, and braking. Finally, we demonstrate a practical application of these representations: we build a lightweight adapter trained on SAE latents that reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, outperforming an equivalent adapter that omits SAE latents, confirming that the sparse representation captures useful information for interpretability. Code and visualizations are available at https://mgagvani.github.io/mechanistic-interpretability-for-e2e-driving/
bullets: The study targets the opacity of end-to-end autonomous-driving models, which limits observability and trust.
SAEs are trained on activations from a simple single-camera path-planning model; clustering reveals interpretable latent structure.
SAE latents recover route intent with 98.3% accuracy without supervision and respond to visual changes such as traffic lights and stop signs.
Intervening on individual latents causes predictable changes in lateral displacement, curvature, and braking.
An adapter using SAE latents reduces trajectory selection error by 3.44%, indicating the representations are useful beyond explanation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Model Architecture. Our Simple Monocular Trajectory Scorer (SMTS) uses only the front camera, past ego state, and route intent as input. Past state and intent initialize a query token, which attends to adapted visual tokens through four transformer blocks. The final query predicts candidate control sequences, rolls them out into future trajectories using a kinematic motion model, and scores each trajectory with a learned proposal scorer. A supervised depth head is used as an auxiliary training output.

(c) Visible edit, weak trajectory change: a clear stop sign is added, yet the predicted path shortens only slightly relative to the original. Note that blue/red curves are the selected planner proposals before/after the edit and the dashed green curve is the ground truth future trajectory.

Features are ordered by connected components, revealing four major clusters. papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis offers formal safety guarantees for control systems, but training accurate neural certificates remains difficult, particularly when unsafe regions are hard to characterize. We propose a verification-guided training framework that addresses this by using probabilistic enumeration of safety constraints to detect forward-invariance violations, i.e., states where the learned certificate incorrectly classifies unsafe behavior. This produces a compact, targeted set of counterexamples that more precisely captures the failure boundary than inputs generated by standard adversarial attack methods. Crucially, using this representation to fine-tune a pretrained HJ value function yields larger certified regions and reduces certification time across all tested benchmarks. We further introduce a shielding mechanism based on the refined certificates to enforce safety constraints at deployment time. We evaluate the proposed safety filter in a realistic, physics-based Isaac Sim environment and through real-world autonomous racing experiments, achieving zero safety constraint violations compared to a nominal controller and a backup policy based on Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed shielding mechanism in ensuring safe operation under high-speed, safety-critical conditions.
bullets: Targets forward-invariance violations to identify where learned certificates misclassify unsafe behavior.
Uses probabilistic constraint enumeration to generate compact, focused counterexamples instead of standard adversarial inputs.
Fine-tuning a pretrained HJ value function produces larger certified regions and reduces certification time across tested benchmarks.
Introduces a certificate-based safety shield evaluated in Isaac Sim and real-world autonomous racing.
The shield achieved zero safety constraint violations against a nominal controller and an LQR backup policy in the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose ThinkLocoManip, an agentic harness for legged loco-manipulation designed to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks in large-scale environments. Existing approaches typically follow either direct action generation or a plan-then-act paradigm, both of which can struggle with the generalization and error-recovery capabilities required for extended task execution. In contrast, ThinkLocoManip adopts an interleaved reasoning-and-acting paradigm, allowing the agent to continuously reason about its current state, execute actions, observe their outcomes, and adapt its strategy accordingly. Building on this paradigm, our agentic harness orchestrates a suite of specialized tools for perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion, enabling flexible composition of heterogeneous capabilities. Unlike existing robotic agentic harnesses, ThinkLocoManip explicitly incorporates locomotion as a tool domain for agent reasoning and execution. We further design a set of skills that explicitly account for both tool usage within each functional domain and coordination across domains, supporting effective execution of complex behaviors over long horizons. To tackle task failure during long-horizon interactions, we develop keyframe thinking mechanism to preserve critical execution context and support efficient error recovery. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that ThinkLocoManip substantially outperforms representative methods based on both direct action generation and plan-then-act paradigms across challenging long-horizon legged loco-manipulation tasks. Notably, ThinkLocoManip achieves a success rate of 77%, more than twice that of the strongest plan-then-act baseline (37.1%). Our experiments further validate the effectiveness of interleaved reasoning and acting, tool orchestration, and coordinated skill execution.
bullets: Targets the limited generalization and error recovery of direct-action and plan-then-act approaches.
Continuously reasons, acts, observes outcomes, and adapts its strategy during execution.
Orchestrates perception, navigation, manipulation, and locomotion tools, explicitly treating locomotion as a reasoning domain.
Uses coordinated cross-domain skills and keyframe thinking to preserve context and recover from failures.
Real-world experiments report a 77% success rate, versus 37.1% for the strongest plan-then-act baseline.

papers.abstract: Passive-wheel quadrupedal robots offer energy-efficient locomotion through leg-driven propulsion and momentum-driven gliding. However, navigation requires coordinating steering with intermittent propulsion and adapting push-glide timing to task demands. Velocity-tracking objectives may suppress the speed variations inherent in skating, discouraging efficient gliding. To address these challenges, we propose SkateNav, a unified skating-navigation framework based on reinforcement learning. A time-budgeted goal-reaching objective allows the policy to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their temporal allocation. An adaptive skating cycle structures gliding, pushing, and recovery, while frequency modulation at every control step adjusts phase durations to navigation demands. Simulation experiments demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner-controller baselines, with ablations confirming the contributions of cycle structure and frequency adaptation. Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer from simulation to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor spaces, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces. Supplementary videos are available on the project page: https://ktw1404.github.io/SkateNav/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of navigating with intermittent leg propulsion and momentum-driven gliding.
Uses a time-budgeted goal-reaching objective to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their timing.
Introduces an adaptive skating cycle with per-step frequency modulation for gliding, pushing, and recovery.
Simulation results show higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than evaluated planner-controller baselines.
Transfers zero-shot to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor areas, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces.

papers.abstract: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.
authors: Michael Baumgartner, Dario Mylonopoulos, Sammy Christen, Markus Gross, Moritz Bacher
bullets: Builds a dense reference memory by sampling and offline-rendering views from a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan.

Works with one classical and four learned localizers across simulated and real dynamic scenes.
On real data, reduces position RMSE by 15–60% in nine of ten backend/split combinations.
Runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz and supports hallway navigation amid people and rearranged objects.

papers.abstract: Simulation is essential for marine robotics, yet existing platforms often trade off between visually realistic worlds, high-throughput experimentation, and ocean-condition realism grounded in real data. We present OneOcean, a data-grounded simulation suite and benchmark built around a unified spatiotemporal ocean-environment product that harmonizes bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields for cleanup-related evaluation. On top of this environment representation, OneOcean defines a task ladder spanning navigation and station-keeping under currents, waypoint and route following, depth-profile tracking, area scanning, pipeline inspection, and multi-agent coordination, including formation transit, fish protection and patrol (herding), and surface pollution localization, containment, and cleanup. The suite supports multi-agent settings with 2-10 vehicles. Our simulator supports three to six Degrees of Freedom (DoF) and produces standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests, enabling consistent aggregation across tasks, difficulties, and scaling settings. Experiments across dataset variants and scenes systematically stress planning and control under data-grounded disturbances and reveal trade-offs among heuristic baselines, Behavior Cloning (BC), and a Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner.
authors: Shuaijun Liu, Qifu Wen, Xingwei Chen, Xinwen Hu, Feiyang You, Sijia Chen, Ningxin Su
bullets: Combines bathymetry with data-driven currents and tides, with optional pollution fields.

Uses standardized metrics and reproducible run manifests across tasks, difficulty levels, and scaling settings.
Experiments compare heuristic, Behavior Cloning, and LLM-based planning under data-grounded disturbances, exposing planning–control trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) enable robots to reason about semantic and spatio-temporal context, verify task-relevant objects, and guide sensing and navigation. Persistent memory can reduce redundant search for field robots, but when should a memory continue to guide behavior? Repeated misses may suggest that a memory is stale. Our experiments show why this evidence can remain ambiguous under VLM-based perception. Using a Boston Dynamics Spot with four fixed cameras and a persistent spatio-temporal visual memory, we measure negative-verification behavior across targets, viewpoints, language queries, and repeated revisits. False-negative rates vary substantially across objects, nearby revisits often reproduce the same detector outcome, and some matched target-present and target-removed experiments yield identical miss histories. This ambiguity persists under changed observation geometry, identity-preserving query reformulation, and conditioning on a previously verified target image. These findings raise two questions: is the object still there, and is this memory still useful for navigation? We introduce a dependence-aware, reversible memory-update mechanism that avoids double-counting correlated misses and stops using unsupported memories as direct navigation goals without claiming that the object is absent. Later positive evidence can restore a memory's use for navigation. One resident onboard VLM is shared across memory verification, semantic frontier reasoning, and in-motion perception. In three matched real-robot decision contexts, an episode-local baseline selected a stale memory as its navigation objective in every case, whereas our method selected semantic frontiers in all three. A complementary trial re-verified the target during motion and promoted fresh memory. These results support revising memory actionability rather than interpreting failed detection as object absence.
authors: Sumukh Shrote, Shenbagaraj Kannapiran, Eric Eaton, Camillo Jose Taylor
bullets: VLM-based negative detections are ambiguous: false-negative rates vary, repeated nearby views can reproduce misses, and target-present and target-removed scenes may look identical.
The proposed dependence-aware, reversible updates avoid double-counting correlated misses and stop unsupported memories from serving as direct navigation goals.
Semantic frontiers become alternatives when memory confidence is insufficient; later positive evidence can restore navigation use.
On a Spot robot in three matched decision contexts, the baseline chose a stale memory every time, while the proposed method chose semantic frontiers in all three.
A motion-time recheck demonstrated that fresh positive evidence can promote memory again.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Persistent semantic-navigation system architecture. The robot combines four fixed cameras, persistent CLIP/FAISS visual memory, semantic frontier exploration, and a shared resident VLM. Historical observations are retrieved and strictly reverified before they can influence navigation. Negative evidence updates memory actionability from VERIFIED ACTIVE to SUSPECT and eventually DORMANT UNTRUSTED, while later strict positive evidence can restore navigation authority. When no trusted memory remains, the system selects a semantic frontier instead. A single resident Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct instance is shared across target verification, memory verification, frontier reasoning, and asynchronous perception during motion.

Fig. 1. Memory is not ground truth. A previously verified object can fail current VLM verification either because the environment has changed or because perception has failed. An episode-local policy forgets earlier failed verification and can repeatedly revisit the same remembered location. Our method instead revises the memory’s navigation authority without asserting that the object is absent, redirects search toward a semantically selected frontier, and preserves the memory for future positive evidence. The inset in (c) shows frontier candidates in the deployed 2-D navigation representation.

Fig. 3. Repeated VLM misses are redundant and can be ambiguous with respect to physical object state. In E2, Spot repeatedly leaves and returns to human-visible target viewpoints; nearby revisits frequently preserve the previous verifier outcome, with 90.0% of adjacent observations producing the same result. In E3, the corresponding objects are physically removed and the same anchor regions are revisited. For the three blue-chair anchors C1-C3, both target-present and target-removed conditions produce the identical six-observation history MMMMMM. Thus, the deployed detector observations alone cannot distinguish the two physical states.

papers.abstract: When a robot navigates an unfamiliar grid, noisy sensor readings can make it hard to tell whether the cells along its next move are free. Additional scans can reduce that uncertainty, but a fixed scan count spends the same sensing effort at every position. In a static-grid simulation, a sequential rule uses a Gaussian likelihood ratio to determine when the cells newly covered by the robot's footprint have enough evidence of free space. On 324 held-out scenarios from 18 public maps, the sequential gate and a four-scan reference chosen on validation data both completed every mission without an observed collision. With their respective validation-selected routing weights, the gate averaged 123.15 scans per episode versus 224.13 for the reference, a reduction of 45.05% (95% map-stratified bootstrap interval: 42.21--48.95%). In a retrospective check on the same scenarios with routing weights held equal, the reductions were 43.91% and 43.37% at the two tested weights, with all missions completed. On 216 scenarios from 12 previously unused maps, allocating more of the same certification error budget near the initial start--goal rectangle cut the sequential gate's scan count by a further 11.58%. The spatial variant completed 206 missions versus 208 for the original gate and increased computation time. The collision bound depends on the assumed observation model and footprint geometry. In a stress test with persistent per-cell bias, the original gate completed 0 of 54 missions.
bullets: Problem: Fixed scan counts waste sensing effort because perception uncertainty varies across positions during navigation.
Method: A Gaussian likelihood-ratio rule adaptively scans newly covered footprint cells until evidence supports that they are free.
Result: Across 324 scenarios on 18 maps, the gate used 123.15 versus 224.13 scans per episode—a 45.05% reduction—with no observed collisions.

Extension: Reallocating the certification error budget near the initial start–goal region reduced scans by a further 11.58% on previously unused maps, but slightly reduced mission completions and increased computation time.
Limitation: Collision guarantees rely on the observation model and footprint geometry; persistent per-cell bias caused the original gate to complete 0 of 54 missions.

papers.abstract: Generative driving planners may produce trajectories that appear feasible at their reference points but violate environmental constraints over the full vehicle body. We propose FeaXDrive2, an end-to-end generative planning framework that enhances vehicle-embodied spatial feasibility (VESF) through body-scene spatial grounding. The proposed method constructs spatial queries from actual vehicle-body corners and dynamically updates visual sampling locations using evolving trajectory estimates across Flow steps. Retrieved local visual features condition subsequent Action Flow-DiT velocity predictions, allowing trajectory generation to guide spatial information retrieval. Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning (RC-F) combines high-risk trajectory supervision with reference behavior preservation, followed by planning-supervised VLM-Action Alignment. Vehicle-geometry counterfactual analysis reveals safety differences under identical trajectories but varying vehicle geometry. On NAVSIM, FeaXDrive2 reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% relative to the base planner and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8. Under NAVSIM v2 evaluation, EPDMS increases from 86.5 to 88.3. Ablation and body-clearance analyses further demonstrate the safety benefits of body-scene spatial grounding.
authors: Bo Leng, Baoyun Wang, Wenxin Wen, Ming Liu, Weiqi Zhang, Ran Yu, Chongfeng Wei, Zhuoren Li, Lu Xiong
bullets: Addresses collisions caused by evaluating feasibility only at trajectory reference points rather than across the vehicle body.
Builds spatial queries from vehicle-body corners and updates visual sampling locations as trajectory estimates evolve during Flow steps.
Uses retrieved local visual features to condition Action Flow-DiT predictions, enabling trajectory-guided spatial retrieval.
Adds Rollout-Consistent Safety Fine-Tuning and planning-supervised VLM–Action Alignment.
On NAVSIM, reduces at-fault collisions by 36.5% and improves PDMS from 87.0 to 88.8; NAVSIM v2 EPDMS rises from 86.5 to 88.3.

papers.abstract: Dexterous mobile manipulation is essential for robots to perform useful tasks in complex, unstructured environments. However, existing systems face two challenges. First, navigation remains too coarse for downstream manipulation, which often requires a precise base position and approach orientation rather than merely reaching a meter-scale goal region. Second, navigation and manipulation are commonly trained in isolation, lacking a feedback loop that enables the two capabilities to co-evolve. These limitations prevent current systems from reliably executing long-horizon dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks in real-world environments. To address them, we introduce Nav4Manip, a bidirectionally coupled co-evolution system for long-horizon dexterous mobile manipulation. It comprises two complementary architectures: Nav4Manip-N learns long-horizon navigation and refines its policy through manipulation feedback, while Nav4Manip-M trains a world-action model (WAM) for downstream dexterous manipulation. We train Nav4Manip-N in three stages: multi-task co-tuning learns navigation behavior and manipulation-aware affordance prediction; rejection sampling fine-tuning (RFT) rejects low-quality policy-generated paths and fine-tunes the model on retained trajectories; and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF) uses counterfactual preferences to further improve navigation decisions. To support this framework, we establish the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and construct Nav4Manip-Pairs from benchmark rollouts, providing large-scale paired navigation--manipulation trajectories and affordance supervision. Extensive experiments on public vision-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, while real-world evaluations show that Nav4Manip completes diverse dexterous mobile-manipulation tasks. Project website: https://nav4manip.github.io/.
authors: Yusen Feng, Zixi Kang, Zhijun Yin, Changxiao Liu, Tianhong Gao, Jiazhao Zhang, Jiahang Liu, Libin Liu, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Targets navigation that must achieve manipulation-ready base positions and orientations, not just coarse goal regions.
Uses two coupled components: Nav4Manip-N for manipulation-aware navigation and Nav4Manip-M with a world-action model for dexterous manipulation.
Trains navigation through multi-task co-tuning, rejection-sampling fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from AI feedback.
Introduces the Nav-N-Manip benchmark and paired navigation–manipulation trajectories with affordance supervision.
Reports state-of-the-art results on public VLN benchmarks and Nav-N-Manip, plus successful real-world task execution.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models introduce language reasoning into end-to-end autonomous driving. They output a language decision together with a trajectory, which makes the planner more interpretable. However, in existing methods the language decision is either an independent output or an index that selects among similar candidate trajectories, and its annotations are not verified against the trajectory. As a result, the language decision and the trajectory are often inconsistent in closed-loop driving. To address this, we propose Commit2Drive, a framework that imposes the language decision as a consistency constraint on trajectory planning. The decision is a commitment, a maneuver class with a continuous parameter that one deterministic rule reads from any trajectory, and it is grounded in facts reported by the perception of the model itself. A Maneuver Bank maps the commitment to a code with a kinematic meaning, and consistency losses train the planner to execute every admissible decision of a scene, so that the trajectory follows the decision. An automatic data pipeline supplies the supervision. Decisions are labeled from the future motion of the expert, counterfactual executions train the decision and the trajectory together, and rule-based functions with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) generate, review and refine the language annotations. The code is a lookup that involves no hidden state of the language model, so Commit2Drive is extensible to rule-based decisions, which the same planner executes without retraining. Commit2Drive uses a 0.5B language model and runs closed-loop inference online on a single consumer graphics card. On Bench2Drive, Commit2Drive reaches a Driving Score (DS) of 78.50 and a Success Rate (SR) of 55.91% with a lightweight model, which is competitive with the state of the art, and greatly reduces the language-action inconsistency. Code will be released soon.
authors: Zikai Zhang, Hubert P. Shum, Toby Breckon
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies between language decisions and trajectories in vision-language-action driving models.
Represents each decision as a maneuver class plus a continuous parameter grounded in the model’s perceived scene facts.
Uses a Maneuver Bank and consistency losses so trajectories execute every admissible decision in a scene.
Automatically generates supervision from expert motion, counterfactual execution, rule-based checks, and VLM-refined annotations.
With a 0.5B language model, it runs online on a single consumer GPU and substantially reduces language-action inconsistency on Bench2Drive.

papers.title: Commit2Drive: Perception-Grounded Language Decisions as Commitments for Trajectory Planning in Vision-Language-Action Driving Models

papers.abstract: We present $\mu$MPC, a fast model predictive control (MPC) framework that reduces online computation using learned Koopman-linearized dynamics. By precomputing finite-horizon control-to-output maps, $\mu$MPC eliminates lifted-state trajectories, yielding an action-only Koopman-Compiled QP (KC-QP) with $Hn_u$ decision variables, independent of lifted dimension. A fixed, precomputed primal operator enables efficient primal-dual iterations using only matrix-vector products and projections, accommodating changing goals and constraints without refactorization. This efficiency also enables control-aware dynamics learning through differentiable KC-QPs in the training loop and batched DAgger-style data aggregation. $\mu$MPC achieves solve times as low as $23\mu$s on a desktop CPU and 24 ms onboard a 168 MHz Crazyflie microcontroller. It scales to 4096D quadruped control in under 5 ms, visual planning with 2048D world models in 0.4 ms, and collision-aware planning for 200 quadrotors at over 30 Hz on the GPU. Across these benchmarks, $\mu$MPC achieves up to $108\times$ faster constrained MPC and $1907\times$ faster visuomotor planning than competing methods.
bullets: Precomputes finite-horizon control-to-output maps, removing lifted-state trajectories and making optimization size depend only on the control horizon and input dimension.
Uses a fixed primal operator for fast primal-dual iterations with matrix-vector products and projections, while supporting changing goals and constraints without refactorization.
Enables differentiable KC-QPs for control-aware dynamics learning and batched DAgger-style data aggregation.

papers.abstract: Latent world models plan in a compact latent space by predicting the outcomes of actions. Their planners judge a plan by the latent distance between its predicted end state and the goal image. We show that this distance fails in two distinct ways. First, it loses directional signal a few steps from the goal, causing distant goals to fail. Second, it weighs the robot arm over the manipulated object, causing manipulation to fail at contact. We measure both failures directly on recorded data by asking whether a lower latent distance corresponds to true progress toward the goal. Across five environments, six visual representations (including raw pixels and V-JEPA 2), and nine Meta-World tasks, this ranking test cleanly separates the two failures, and the graph distance to a goal predicts where closed-loop planning breaks down. Both failures share a single remedy: replacing the distant goal with a nearby target that lies on a recorded trajectory. We realize this principle with Graph Anchors, a training-free planner for frozen latent world models. It builds a sparse graph once over the model's own training frames and aims each planning step at a node a few moves ahead along the shortest path to the goal, keeping paths on recorded transitions wherever contact matters. On goals up to 400 steps away, Graph Anchors raise LeWM's success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, from 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and from 5% to 71% on Push-T, where stronger search toward the goal fails and where prior training-free planners break down under missing step horizons, subsampling shortcuts, or fragmented contact.
authors: Syed Nazmus Sakib, Abdul Monaf Chowdhury, Peizhen Li, Nafiul Haque, Chandak Chakma, Md Mehedi Hasan, Zehong Cao, Shifat E. Arman
bullets: Latent goal-distance planning fails because it loses directional guidance near distant goals and overweights the robot arm during object contact.
A ranking test on recorded data diagnoses these failures across five environments, six visual representations, and nine Meta-World tasks.
Graph Anchors build a sparse graph over training frames and guide each step toward a nearby node on a shortest recorded path to the goal.
The training-free method raises LeWM success from 13% to 85% on PointMaze-Medium, 8% to 87% on PointMaze-Large, and 5% to 71% on Push-T.
The approach targets goals up to 400 steps away and preserves recorded transitions where contact dynamics matter.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySercher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.
authors: Giacomo Vianello, David Morilla-Cabello, Juan Dendarieta Serrano, Ruggero Carli, Eduardo Montijano
bullets: Targets large outdoor scenes without dense 3D reconstructions or continuous cloud connectivity.
Uses high-altitude VLM observations to identify targets or location-relevant semantic cues.
Projects semantic information onto the ground through the camera frustum, leveraging the wide elevated field of view.
Maintains a probabilistic query-belief map and task-driven memory to guide information-driven exploration.
Simulations report improved success rate, flight time, and navigation precision over baselines; onboard drone deployment demonstrates feasibility.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. System Overview. A ground-station LLM parses the user query Q into the target, semantic cues, and their expected co-occurrence distance, and variability. NBV optimization fuses this geometric and semantic evidence to select the next viewpoint, until visual servoing approaches the target detection and confirms (or rejects) it.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving powered by neural network models lacks safety guarantees. We propose a state-level policy editing technique that guarantees closed-loop safety under recoverable disturbances while reusing the model's existing driving capabilities. Closed-loop safety means that the vehicle remains free of collisions at all future times. We introduce the concept of policy recoverability to characterize whether a vehicle can safely return to the original policy's feasible set in finite time. Our method identifies states that are unsafe in the long term under the original policy but recoverable, and selectively edits policy outputs within this region. The vehicle corrects its actions upon entering this region and resumes the original policy upon recovery. Closed-loop simulations on nuPlan urban driving scenarios show a 48% reduction in safety incidents under the original policy while largely preserving its driving performance.
bullets: Targets the lack of safety guarantees in neural-network autonomous driving.
Defines policy recoverability as the ability to return safely to the original policy’s feasible set in finite time.
Edits actions only in states that are unsafe under the original policy but still recoverable.
Resumes the original policy after recovery, retaining existing driving capabilities.
Closed-loop nuPlan simulations report 48% fewer safety incidents while largely preserving driving performance.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The concept of a policy's recoverable set. The feasible set of a given neural policy (blue region) guarantees the vehicle's closed-loop safety. However, disturbances whose evolution differs from the training environment, such as an unexpected vehicle running a red light, can force the vehicle outside this set. Without policy intervention, the vehicle will eventually enter an unsafe state (red region). While preserving the original policy's capabilities, our method first identifies the set of states that are recoverable to the original policy's feasible set (yellow region) and those that are not (grey region). It then incrementally edits the original policy's outputs in recoverable states, guiding the vehicle back into the original policy's range of capabilities and thereby ensuring closed-loop safety.

papers.abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.
authors: Jonas Pech\'e, Dmitry Matveev, Vladimir Ciric, Lizaveta Sakalova, G\"unter Wallner
bullets: Addresses coordinated task allocation under adversarial actions, spatial constraints, and changing battlefield conditions.
A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals such as survival, local superiority, interaction, travel time, and objective contribution.
Rule-based terms and a constrained minimum-cost-flow solver produce globally coordinated assignments.
Evaluated with predictive metrics, offline diagnostics, online A/B tests, and latency measurements.
Results suggest stable, feasible, and inspectable allocation under strict real-time constraints; the system remains an R&D prototype, not a shipped-game deployment.

papers.abstract: In 2D-3D localization, a camera estimates its pose by matching an image to a 3D map. A camera held in a hand or mounted on a robot can often choose its viewpoint before it takes the image. In this work, we ask whether an image detectability field is a useful viewpoint utility when the planner reads only the geometry of the map. The field can be queried at any 3D point near a surface. From the local geometry around the point, it predicts how likely a 2D image detector is to fire at the projection of the point. We use the trained field as it is, without fine-tuning it for view selection. A fixed SuperPoint and EPnP-RANSAC localizer then estimates the pose from the chosen view. We answer in two settings, each with a test registered before the runs. On synthetic ShapeNet objects with sparse point maps, summing the field over the visible landmarks beats counting them by +2.0 points of localization success rate (object-clustered 95% interval [+0.7, +3.2]). It also beats summing Harris-3D ranks by +2.2 [+0.8, +3.5]. On real indoor scenes from SceneFun3D, our adaptation of the learned view scorer LWL falls below counting on the test rooms. We therefore add the field to a learned per-landmark planner. On the test rooms with sparse maps whose landmarks the field also selects, the planner with the field beats the same planner without it by +1.8 points. It beats the planner with Harris-3D or curvature in its place by +1.0 and +0.8 points. All three room-clustered intervals lie above zero. In both settings, the field helps in sparse maps and is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.

bullets: The goal is to choose camera viewpoints using only map geometry before capturing an image.

Benefits are observed in sparse maps; performance is on par with Harris-3D in dense maps.

papers.abstract: Tool-using large language model (LLM) agents raise safety risks that are not captured by text-only refusal behavior, especially when tools can trigger high-impact actions. This concern is salient in military settings, where autonomous weapons raise the possibility of delegating force decisions to software agents. In this work, we study whether a drone agent's action boundary is stable under changes to the target descriptor. We evaluate recent and popular LLMs in a simulated perception-action pipeline over real-world drone imagery, where models can localize requested targets and invoke a simulated lethal tool. We find two concerning failure modes. First, some LLM agents invoke the lethal tool for ordinary generic descriptors such as \emph{people}, requiring no jailbreak at all. Second, an agent that initially appears conservative under protected descriptors can become unsafe under a simple semantic target shift.

bullets: Studies whether target-descriptor changes alter an agent’s decision to invoke a simulated lethal tool.
Evaluates popular LLMs in a perception–action pipeline using real-world drone imagery.
Some agents trigger lethal action for generic descriptors such as “people.”
Agents that appear safe for protected descriptors may become unsafe after a simple semantic shift.
Highlights safety risks for autonomous weapons that text-only refusal tests may miss.

papers.abstract: Open-world aerial object search methods often rely on persistent spatial maps, learned world models, or task-specific policy training. To examine how far a minimal, training-free design can go, we introduce SimpleUAV, an agent built around a frozen, off-the-shelf vision-language model (VLM). SimpleUAV separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection, combining fresh candidate evidence with lightweight search context. Local geometry converts visual selections into bounded straight-line movements, depth-based checks halt blocked segments, and measured execution feedback guides subsequent decisions. This closed loop sustains search without persistent spatial maps or task-specific training. SimpleUAV achieves 41.61% Success Rate (SR) on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, compared with 23.80% and 3.20% for the strongest prior baselines, respectively. With limited benchmark-specific adaptation, the same core agent transfers to aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across all three splits under L1 assistance. These results establish a strong baseline for evaluating when additional architectural complexity benefits aerial search.
authors: Jitai Hao, Liangxing Yang, Zhenyang Li, Fan Liu, Qiang Huang, Jun Yu
bullets: Addresses whether a minimal, training-free agent can handle open-world aerial search.
Separates current-view target assessment from history-conditioned action selection.
Uses local geometry, depth checks, and execution feedback to produce bounded movements and avoid blocked paths.
Achieves 41.61% SR on UAV-ON and 11.98% on AerialDojo-200K, outperforming reported prior baselines.
Transfers to aerial VLN on TravelUAV, improving Full SR by at least 19.66% across three splits with L1 assistance.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Architecture of SimpleUAV. Given a language goal and four RGB-D views (front, left, right, and downward), SimpleUAV executes three stages without persistent maps or task-specific training. (1) Select (Section 3.2): A frozen VLM detects candidate boxes (ℬ𝑡 ) from current RGB views. Depth and camera calibration provide 3D candidate locations to construct (𝒞𝑡 ), and a second VLM query selects an action (𝑎𝑡 ) using this catalog and lightweight interaction history. (2) Fly Straight (Section 3.3): The selected region or candidate determines a 3D waypoint (𝑤𝑡 ) for exploration (Exploreℎ , Explore𝑣) or Approach, and the UAV moves from 𝒙𝑡 along a bounded straightline segment. (3) Check & Halt (Section 3.4): Throughout motion, local depth checks test upcoming segments using a 3D safety capsule and halt the current segment when an obstacle is detected. Execution feedback guides the next observation and decision cycle.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation asks a robot to reach the viewpoint of a target photograph without a map or goal pose. In three dimensions, this requires not only recognizing the goal but also estimating 3D displacement and generating continuous control actions to approach and settle at the target view. This is difficult because the same visual difference between current and goal image can require very different actions depending on the robot's velocity, yet monocular images alone reveal neither metric scale nor body motion. As a result, existing image-goal policies are limited to planar action spaces and rely on a state estimator for flight control. Policies that map directly from images to low-level control commands have been demonstrated for agile flight, but not toward goal images in unseen environments. We present the first image-goal navigation policy that directly commands thrust and angular rates for agile quadrotor flight in unseen 3D environments, without relying on state estimation (e.g., SLAM, VO, or SfM) or a separate velocity controller. We train a recurrent vision-based policy through a four-stage pipeline that combines geometric and motion supervision with privileged-teacher distillation and end-to-end reinforcement learning fine-tuning. On 1000 held-out flights in unseen environments, the policy achieves an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10m across successful flights. Deployed zero-shot on a real quadrotor, the policy reaches an 84% success rate over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.
authors: Simone Nascivera, Ismail Geles, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation, where identical visual differences may require different actions due to the quadrotor’s motion and velocity.

Directly controls low-level thrust and angular rates, avoiding SLAM, visual odometry, structure-from-motion, and separate velocity control.
Achieves 82.3% success over 1,000 simulated held-out flights, with 0.10 m mean terminal position error on successful flights.
Transfers zero-shot to a real quadrotor, achieving 84% success over 25 trials in an unseen indoor environment.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies increasingly operate without explicit HD maps at inference, raising the question of what road knowledge they actually internalize. To probe this knowledge through model outputs, we introduce Road-KSU, a framework that automatically converts HD maps and actor annotations into a road-centric scene graph. From this, we derive road-focused question answering and reasoning targets, complemented by map-based trajectory compliance metrics. Pairing Road-KSU with geographically disjoint splits yields a $2 \times 2$ evaluation crossing output modality (language vs. action) with place familiarity (seen vs. unseen roads). On NAVSIM, 95% of test samples lie within 10m of a training sample, and scores of 13 published planners on turns rise steeply with the number of training drives through the test location, pointing to memorized road geometry. Retraining on geographically disjoint splits and probing with Road-KSU confirm that action-space performance degrades most on unfamiliar turns, with failures dominated by geometric compliance. Language accuracy, however, drops on road-centric VQA on straight and curved roads alike, and remains stable on dynamic scene content. Scaling the training data further reveals a double dissociation: more drives through the same places improve driving on unseen roads but leave road question answering unchanged, whereas spreading a fixed data budget over more places increases road question answering with little change in driving performance. These findings show that improved driving scores need not imply broader road understanding on unseen roads, and identify geographic diversity as key to transferable road knowledge.
authors: Lena Wild, Christian Helten, Katie Z Luo, Jakob Thumm, Rafael Valencia, Patric Jensfelt, Marco Pavone

papers.abstract: Computing per-player feedback strategies in $N$-player adversarial differential games is challenging as the associated coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman system is high-dimensional and generally lacks classical solutions. We address this by approximating viscosity solutions using physics-informed neural networks within a policy iteration scheme with a vanishing-viscosity annealing schedule. Theoretically, we establish an explicit $\varepsilon$-Nash guarantee by bounding per-player regret via computable residuals and prove our method reaches this stopping criterion in finite time. For two-player zero-sum games, we further establish a computable bound on the approximation error of the value function. Numerical experiments on pursuit-evasion scenarios illustrate the tightness of these computed bounds and the framework's scalability to high-dimensional environments.
authors: Takuma Adams, Andrew C. Cullen, Tansu Alpcan
bullets: Targets coupled, high-dimensional Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman systems that may lack classical solutions.
Uses physics-informed neural networks with policy iteration and vanishing-viscosity annealing to approximate viscosity solutions.
Provides an explicit ε-Nash guarantee by bounding each player’s regret through computable residuals.
Proves finite-time attainment of the stopping criterion and derives a computable value-function error bound for two-player zero-sum games.
Pursuit–evasion experiments demonstrate tight computed bounds and scalability to high-dimensional environments.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon diffusion-based planning for kinodynamically constrained systems requires both scalability and feasibility, yet existing diffusion planners typically sacrifice one for the other. We present DFLAT, a diffusion-based planning algorithm that operates directly on a differentially flat trajectory representation. Instead of diffusing over time-discretized controls, DFLAT denoises a compact set of Hermite curve parameters in the flat-output space, consisting of intermediate waypoints together with the endpoint tangents of each segment. Every denoised sample maps to a dynamically consistent trajectory, so feasibility holds by construction rather than being restored afterward. Experiments on challenging tractor-trailer planning benchmarks show that DFLAT matches or exceeds the success rates of existing baselines at consistently lower planning times, particularly on long-horizon problems requiring multiple forward-reverse maneuvers. In cases where kinodynamic RRT requires over 100 seconds, DFLAT plans in subsecond time, enabling practical deployment.
authors: Ege Yuceel, Taekyung Kim, Keyvan Majd, Hideki Okamoto, Bardh Hoxha, Sayan Mitra, Georgios Fainekos
bullets: Targets the scalability–feasibility tradeoff in diffusion planning for kinodynamically constrained systems.
Diffuses over Hermite curve parameters—intermediate waypoints and segment endpoint tangents—instead of discretized controls.
Maps every denoised sample to a dynamically consistent trajectory, making feasibility hold by construction.
Matches or exceeds baseline success rates with consistently lower planning times on tractor-trailer benchmarks.
Achieves subsecond planning in cases where kinodynamic RRT takes over 100 seconds, especially for multi-maneuver horizons.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of DFLAT. At each reverse diffusion step i = N, . . . , 1, candidates are drawn by perturbing the waypoint poses and the segment-local Hermite parameters, lifted through the inverse flatness map into dynamically consistent trajectories, and scored under the planning cost. The score-weighted mean seeds the next step, refining the coarse prior into a low-cost trajectory for the downstream tracking controller.

Fig. 4. Sample trajectories from DFLAT. Green slots mark the start pose, orange slots mark the goal. DFLAT produces a collision-free trajectory respecting the dynamic limits in every case, at low latency. Right: DFLAT Playground, an interactive web-based demo in which all maps can be tried with different start and goal poses and custom obstacle placement, with DFLAT replanning in the browser.3

papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci

papers.abstract: Safety-critical interactions are rare in recorded driving data, leaving end-to-end driving planners with limited exposure to evasive behaviour during training. This lack of critical supervision can lead to unsafe behaviour and, in rare instances, collisions. To address this gap, we introduce CriticalScenes, a reconstruction-based framework that transforms ordinary recorded driving scenes into photorealistic safety-critical interactions with corresponding collision-avoidance supervision. Across 53 reconstructed source scenes, 979 of 1,060 attempted interactions yield feasible threat trajectories (92.4\%), while the inserted threat actors remain detectable in more than 95\% of non-occluded observations within 5--35\,m. Experiments with two structurally different end-to-end planners show that the generated supervision improves critical-scenario planning, while closed-loop transfer varies across planner architectures. SparseDrive achieves a 46.5\% relative reduction in collision rate on an independent photorealistic closed-loop benchmark, whereas UniAD shows only a modest closed-loop improvement despite substantial open-loop gains. The results further highlight the importance of closed-loop evaluation, as improvements in open-loop trajectory prediction do not necessarily translate into equivalent safety gains.
authors: Alexandros Theocharous, Holger Caesar, Ziqi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of safety-critical interactions and evasive-behavior supervision in recorded driving data.
Reconstructs scenes by inserting threat actors with collision-avoidance supervision.
Across 53 scenes, 979/1,060 attempted interactions produced feasible threat trajectories; inserted actors remained detectable in over 95% of non-occluded observations.
Improved critical-scenario planning for two different end-to-end planners, but closed-loop benefits varied by architecture.
SparseDrive achieved a 46.5% relative collision-rate reduction, while UniAD showed only modest closed-loop improvement despite open-loop gains.

papers.abstract: Safe-mode events causing thrust outages are common in missions with electric propulsion. To demonstrate mission feasibility in such an event, missed-thrust margin studies are performed where thousands of outage scenarios need an exact re-plan solved. We train a neural operator that maps a nominal trajectory with an outage profile to a re-planned trajectory and to the probability that the recovery exists, for 270 low-thrust near-rectilinear halo orbit (NRHO) to distant retrograde orbit (DRO) transfers, at an allowed slip of up to 10 days. On unseen transfers and zero slip, its median control error on the severe half of outages is 1.20% compared to 14.0% for the best cheap re-planner benchmark. With the arrival slip as an input, the error is 1.67% against 23.2%. It also predicts the recoverability of an outage for a given arrival slip with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.997, while the minimum recoverable slip prediction is optimistic by more than half a day on only 6 of the 84 checked outages needing slip. At the original arrival, the ensemble spread of an operator variant with solver inputs has a rank correlation of 0.91 with the actual error, and performing exact solves on the 31% most uncertain severe outages reduces the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%. A query takes milliseconds without a solver, making this a useful tool for large outage studies where the cost of thousands of exact solves outweighs the time to train the operator.
bullets: Addresses mission-feasibility studies requiring thousands of exact re-plans after electric-propulsion outages.
Maps a nominal trajectory and outage profile to a recovered trajectory and recovery probability for NRHO-to-DRO transfers with up to 10 days of arrival slip.
On unseen transfers, median control error was 1.20% at the original arrival and 1.67% with arrival slip, outperforming the reported cheap re-planner benchmarks.
Recoverability prediction achieved AUC 0.997; uncertainty-guided exact solves reduced the 90th-percentile error from 8.5% to 2.3%.
Millisecond queries support large outage studies; results are demonstrated for 270 low-thrust NRHO-to-DRO transfers and the stated slip range.

papers.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation and stale points caused by append-only mapping in dynamic scenes.
Updates each point’s confidence using multi-view temporal evidence from segmentation, depth, and visibility consistency.
Combines point refinement with object tracking and re-identification to maintain identities through motion and relocation.
Improves mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet.
Supports downstream object navigation and embodied question-answering, with reported success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed dynamic semantic mapping framework. Given posed RGB-D observations, openvocabulary detections are generated and associated with object instances in the 3D semantic map. For each association, we perform a visibility-based point confidence update. Points supported by current detections, such as the green points on the table, receive higher confidence. In contrast, inconsistent outlier points, such as red points mistakenly fused into a bed instance due to previous segmentation errors, are down-weighted when later observations identify them as pillows. Points belonging to removed objects are identified through visibility reasoning, assigned lower confidence, and eventually pruned. Unobserved points in the current frame, shown in gray, remain unchanged until more evidence is collected in later frames. The semantic map is updated online in this frame-by-frame manner, while periodic instance-fragment merging reduces duplicate instances and re-identification preserves object identities when objects are relocated and re-observed at new locations.

Fig. 6: Example of handling under-segmentation. A pillow is initially fused into the chair instance due to undersegmentation. Once the pillow is correctly segmented in later frames, our method adds it as a separate instance and gradually removes the corresponding points from the chair instance through confidence updates.
Fig. 7: Example of in-view object tracking. Our method tracks the moving bowl in images and updates its location in the semantic map while preserving the same instance ID.

Fig. 5: Example of object fragment merging. A table is initially reconstructed as two separate instances due to temporally disconnected partial observations at 1s and 10s. As more observations become available at 12s, our method merges the fragments into a complete object instance.

Fig. 1: Dynamic open-vocabulary semantic mapping. Our method maintains a refinable object-centric 3D semantic map through point-level probabilistic updates. It handles dynamic objects that newly appear, move within the robot’s view, or are relocated out of view and later re-identified.

Fig. 9: Examples of object navigation and EQA tasks executed on the Spot robot. Our semantic map serves as an online memory that helps the LLM localize target objects, plan embodied skills, and answer questions.

Fig. 4: Example of handling incorrect detections. A plastic bag is mistakenly detected as a pillow, creating a false instance in the map. Our confidence update mechanism accumulates positive evidence for consistently detected objects and negative evidence for unsupported instances, eventually removing the false pillow while preserving the true one.

papers.abstract: This work demonstrates the use of a fast simulation-based training framework to learn control policies using reinforcement learning. The hardware requirements are minimal and the simulation-learned policies transfer reliably to the real world. With this setup, we show that a quadruped robot can learn to traverse diverse real-world terrains reliably---including in a lunar-analog facility---after less than 20 minutes of training on a single consumer-grade GPU. These results provide a glimpse of a future where reinforcement learning is a crucial tool in developing more capable and robust space robotic systems. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/vUFJiZdJaQ0.
bullets: Motivation: make reinforcement learning practical for capable, robust space robotics.
Method: train control policies in fast simulation with minimal hardware requirements, then deploy them on a real quadruped.
Result: the robot traverses diverse real-world terrains reliably, including a lunar-analog facility.
Training uses less than 20 minutes on a single consumer-grade GPU.
Scope: demonstrates promising real-world transfer for quadruped locomotion in space-robotics-relevant environments.

papers.abstract: A small ground robot can carry one camera and a few watts of compute, but the depth foundation models that could turn that camera into a range sensor are vision transformers sized for GPUs. We bring one to a Raspberry Pi 5 with the Hailo-8L, an accelerator that runs every layer in integer arithmetic, attention included. Quantised for it, Depth Anything V2 loses large parts of the scene, and we measure why: at 449 tokens, 91% of softmax weights fall below one int8 step while carrying 17-33% of the attention mass. Our answer is to distil, not quantise. An attention-free ResNet-34 U-Net student of Depth Anything V2-Large (24.5M parameters) runs at 27.1 FPS on the chip, its int8 output matches its float twin (Pearson 0.99993), and on held-out scenes of its simulated yard it is the most accurate depth network on the chip (AbsRel 0.269 against 0.354-0.530). On 1,000 stereo-verified points of a real outdoor drive it is not resolvably different from the vendor's Depth Anything V2-Small build, while running faster (27.1 vs 21.6 FPS). Ranging obstacles by where they meet the floor needs only the camera height, so mapping, hybrid-A* planning and SLAM run on the Pi's own CPU. In real-time hardware-in-the-loop tests in a Gaussian-splat reconstruction of a real yard, the stack reaches the goal without contact in 7.9$\pm$1.1 of 10 scenes, against 9.2$\pm$0.4 with exact obstacles, and in 7.7$\pm$0.7 on its own pose with simulated wheel odometry (ten seeds each; 8.2$\pm$0.4 with the real Pi and Hailo-8L in the loop, five seeds). The source code, pre-trained models and data are available at https://github.com/itaim18/DANIEL.
bullets: Quantising the transformer-based Depth Anything V2 directly causes severe information loss because many attention weights fall below int8 precision.
The proposed ResNet-34 U-Net student, distilled from Depth Anything V2-Large, runs at 27.1 FPS using 24.5M parameters.
Its int8 predictions closely match its float version (Pearson 0.99993) and achieve the best held-out simulated-yard accuracy among tested onboard models (AbsRel 0.269).
On 1,000 stereo-verified real-drive points, it performs comparably to the vendor’s Depth Anything V2-Small while running faster (27.1 vs. 21.6 FPS).
Integrated with mapping, planning, and SLAM, the system reaches goals without contact in most hardware-in-the-loop yard trials, though less often than with exact obstacle maps.

papers.title: Seeing to Drive on a Single Board: Attention-Free Depth for Onboard Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: An attention-free, distilled depth model enables real-time monocular obstacle ranging and navigation on a Raspberry Pi 5 with Hailo-8L hardware.

papers.abstract: We were surprised to find that leading end-to-end driving models across major paradigms, despite scoring close to human drivers on NAVSIM, cannot reliably make a simple 90-degree turn in photorealistic closed-loop simulators. To investigate why, we build LaWanle, a benchmark of turns drawn from three such simulators. Driving each turn from several starts, we find that the same model passes it from one start and fails it from another, and that the two drives look alike until they enter the junction. Rotating the car by a few degrees at the junction entry can fail a turn it otherwise passes. Conversely, a slight heading correction to the plans can rescue about half of the failed turns we tested. Such errors arise when a model drives by itself, so we post-train an open-source lane-keeping model with closed-loop DAgger on its lateral path. Training 5% of its parameters is enough to raise its turn pass rate from 19% to 76%. The gain transfers to the two other benchmarks, where the policy also scores among the leading models. Further fine-tuning on recovery data repairs the deviations it is trained on but, against a control trained equally long, improves turns on none of the three benchmarks, and every variant stays far below a human driver.
authors: Chengzhi Gao, Junzhe Gao, Yongzhi Liu, Weichao Zhuang, Weilong Hu, Taonian Liang, Guodong Yin
bullets: Models that score near humans on NAVSIM often fail simple turns in photorealistic closed-loop simulators.

papers.abstract: Dynamic obstacle avoidance is essential for safely deploying humanoid robots in real-world environments, where rapidly approaching objects require immediate evasive responses. Recent advances in reflexive evasion have focused primarily on quadrupeds, which typically rely on large-scale whole-body maneuvers. In contrast, humanoids can exploit their rich body articulation to evade through small, localized body adjustments. By moving threatened body regions without repositioning the entire body, these responses may require less execution time and less surrounding free space. However, local adjustments can alter mass distribution or support conditions, making it challenging to achieve rapid evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. To this end, we propose BARE (Body-Aware Reflexive Evasion), a humanoid reflexive evasion framework guided by human motion priors that enables rapid local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability. A risk-guided motion adapter is designed to select reference motions from a retargeted human evasive motion library based on the threatened body region and to adjust their temporal phases based on collision urgency, allowing the robot to reach evasive postures before potential contact. Conditioned on the adapted reference and link-level collision risk, a reflexive evasion policy learns through reinforcement learning to coordinate local body adjustments with whole-body stabilization. We validate BARE in simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating its ability to perform targeted local evasion while maintaining whole-body stability.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of fast, stable evasion for humanoids, whose local adjustments can disturb balance.

A reinforcement-learning policy coordinates localized evasive movements with whole-body stabilization using adapted references and link-level collision risk.
Validated in simulation and real-world experiments for targeted local evasion with maintained stability.

papers.abstract: Multi-vehicle collaborative perception can use observations from different perspectives to alleviate the problems of occlusion and limited sensing range. However, missing echoes and false echoes caused by bad weather will reduce the quality of single-vehicle features and affect collaborative detection. LiDAR provides richer geometric information, and 4D Radar has strong weather adaptability. The complementarity of the two provides the possibility to improve perception under degraded observations. However, how to adjust cross-modal repair according to the current observation conditions and how to reasonably integrate multi-vehicle features whose reliability still differs after repair are still problems that need to be solved. To this end, we propose CoReQ, a condition-aware repair and quality-guided collaborative perception framework. For the former, the condition-guided bidirectional cross-modal repair module (CBCR) extracts vehicle-level observation conditions from point cloud occupancy, density and feature statistics, and adjusts the bidirectional correction of LiDAR and Radar features accordingly. For the latter, we combine local reliability assessment with collaborative weighting: first, the task-aware quality estimation module (TaQE) uses the classification and positioning information of the EMA teacher to construct a supervision target and predict the spatial quality of the repaired features; then, the condition and quality guided fusion module (CoQF) matches the quality information with the content, and the observation conditions of both parties are jointly used for multi-vehicle feature weighted fusion. Experiments on V2X-R and V2X-Radar-C show that the framework is competitive under a variety of observation conditions, achieving significant gains in AP@0.7 on V2X-R under snowy conditions, and achieving the highest AP among the compared V2X-Radar-C methods.
authors: Ziwei Guo, Lingzhi Li, Jin Wang, Yunjiang Xu, Yupeng Ouyang, Benyuan Yang, Yujun Shi
bullets: Addresses missing and false echoes that degrade single-vehicle features and collaborative detection in adverse weather.

On V2X-R and V2X-Radar-C, CoReQ is competitive across conditions, with significant snowy-condition AP@0.7 gains on V2X-R and the highest AP among compared V2X-Radar-C methods.

papers.abstract: Socially-aware robot person following (RPF) requires a mobile robot to follow a designated person in dynamic human environments while maintaining target identity, avoiding obstacles and pedestrians, and preserving socially comfortable formations. Existing benchmarks only partially evaluate this coupled problem: embodied visual tracking benchmarks emphasize target visibility with limited social interaction, person re-identification benchmarks study perception without closed-loop control, and motion-planning benchmarks often assume ground-truth target and pedestrian states. We introduce Follow-Bench 2.0, an end-to-end 3D benchmark for evaluating socially-aware RPF under coupled perception--planning challenges. Built in Unreal Engine, Follow-Bench 2.0 provides difficulty-leveled scenarios with diverse pedestrian flows, lighting and weather conditions, cluttered layouts, bottlenecks, queueing behaviors, distractors, and temporary target occlusions. The benchmark supports modular perception--planning pipelines, end-to-end visual policies, and foundation-model-based active trackers under a unified closed-loop protocol. It further evaluates both back- and side-following configurations and reports safety--comfort metrics covering task success, target visibility, target recovery, social-space intrusion, following formation, and motion smoothness. Experiments show that RPF-oriented modular pipelines substantially outperform current end-to-end visual policies on close and socially comfortable following, but also reveal that socially-aware RPF remains far from solved in interaction-heavy environments and especially in side-following. Follow-Bench 2.0 therefore provides a diagnostic platform for studying how perception errors, occlusions, crowd interactions, and following configurations jointly affect robot person following.
authors: Hanjing Ye, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Yanci Wen, Yuchen Zhou, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
bullets: Evaluates target identity, obstacle and pedestrian avoidance, and socially comfortable following formations in closed loop.
Provides difficulty-leveled Unreal Engine scenarios with crowds, clutter, bottlenecks, queues, distractors, occlusions, varied lighting, and weather.
Supports modular perception–planning systems, end-to-end visual policies, and foundation-model-based active trackers.
Measures task success, target visibility and recovery, social-space intrusion, formation quality, and motion smoothness in back- and side-following.
Experiments find modular RPF pipelines outperform end-to-end visual policies, while side-following and interaction-heavy settings remain difficult.

papers.abstract: Learned driving planners keep being updated after deployment as new logs arrive, yet continual learning evaluations rarely ask whether an update improves on the deployed model, and their verdicts rest on unstated evaluation choices. We present ContinualDrive, a deployment-anchored benchmark for post-deployment continual learning of driving planners. It updates a deployed planner on real-world nuPlan logs one scenario-type group at a time, evaluates the same checkpoints in open and closed loop, makes four measurement axes explicit (evaluation loop, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation and stream protocol), and anchors a three-valued release verdict to the deployed checkpoint. We study two planners (PlanTF and Diffusion Planner) under full fine-tuning and adapter or LoRA updates, with and without replay or gradient projection, in three task orders. Verdicts can reverse or vanish when one axis changes: open-loop ADE ranks the final PlanTF model above the deployed one in half of its core-suite runs, whereas every closed-loop score ranks it below; backward transfer misses this loss, which on average is already present when each group has just been learned; and regime rankings vary far less across training seeds than across task orders. In the core suite of full and adapter updates, no regime measurably improved on the deployed planner in closed loop; on a panel more than ten times larger every evaluated final checkpoint trails it, and joint training on all groups recovers much of the loss without exceeding its nuPlan closed-loop score. We distill these findings into a reporting contract and will release the code and all checkpoints.
authors: Zirui Li, Zhiqi Mao, Yangang Ren, Heye Huang, Haohan Yang, Qihang Huang, Zhan Chen, Chen Lv
bullets: Benchmarks continual updates on real-world nuPlan logs, processing scenario-type groups sequentially.
Makes evaluation choices explicit across loop type, reference checkpoint, temporal aggregation, and stream protocol.
Evaluates PlanTF and Diffusion Planner with full fine-tuning, adapters/LoRA, replay, gradient projection, and multiple task orders.
Open-loop and closed-loop verdicts can disagree; backward transfer may miss degradation that appears immediately after learning each group.
No tested update regime improved on the deployed planner in closed loop; task order affected rankings more than training seed.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) delivery is an important application of the low-altitude economy, enhancing the flexibility and accessibility of last-mile logistics. Existing UAV delivery methods generally rely on precise terminal coordinates, predefined terminal specifications, or task-specific localization procedures, limiting the scope and flexibility of delivery. As UAV logistics becomes more intelligent, open-ended semantic descriptions offer a new paradigm for specifying terminal destinations. However, conventional aerial navigation methods have limited ability to generalize to delivery scenarios that require open-vocabulary terminal navigation. To enable this broader delivery paradigm, we propose CoFiNav, a VLM-guided coarse-to-fine UAV semantic navigation framework that progressively grounds relation-defined terminal destinations through hierarchical semantic search and active 3D observation. Given a task description, a coarse prior map from OpenStreetMap (OSM), and accumulated observations, CoFiNav uses a vision-language model (VLM) to determine which unresolved entity or spatial relation should be verified next. A geometry-aware module converts the semantic observation request into feasible viewpoints using RGB images and LiDAR, while conventional motion planning handles safe execution. Experiments across multiple urban environments show that CoFiNav outperforms representative adapted baselines in success rate while requiring shorter flight paths and fewer observations.
