papers.abstract: Large language models can write competent robot navigation code, but not only does the research on the topic advance, a model may also, due to the volume of findings, fail to recall relevant findings and apply them to the task at hand. In this work, we test whether providing particular research papers as context improves the LLM-written navigation code for the Go2 quadruped, with the LLM (Claude Opus 5) and locomotion policy frozen. Specifically, we compare the navigation controllers the LLM writes when provided with and without particular papers across three settings: behavior trees, navigators edited from a shared base, and controllers written from scratch. When a maze's shortest route is blocked mid-episode, 2 of 8 controllers written with the context of an incremental-replanning paper complete all four trips under Isaac Sim physics, against 7 of 8 without it (two-sided Fisher's exact test, p = 0.041). This difference appears only under physics: in an idealized kinematic simulator, the controllers written with and without the paper are indistinguishable. We hypothesize that an LLM provided research papers as context tends to overweight both their content and their goals -- in this case, the efficiency of incremental replanning -- negatively affecting the fulfillment of the main task and leading to less robust code.
bullets: The study tests whether selected research papers improve LLM-written quadruped navigation code with the model and locomotion policy fixed.
Controllers are compared with and without paper context across behavior trees, shared-base edits, and from-scratch implementations.
With an incremental-replanning paper, fewer context-conditioned controllers completed all blocked-maze trips under Isaac Sim physics: 2/8 versus 7/8 without context.
This difference was absent in an idealized kinematic simulator, suggesting sensitivity to physical realism.
The authors hypothesize that paper context can cause the LLM to overemphasize the paper’s objectives, such as replanning efficiency, at the expense of robust task completion.

papers.abstract: Visual world models enable goal-directed planning by predicting action outcomes. Gradient-based planners optimize actions to lower predicted goal cost, but continued optimization can exploit prediction errors after execution stops improving. Comparing plans requires informative relative scores; improving them also requires reliable update directions. Exact-state execution reveals that a frozen hierarchical world model ranks goal-conditioned proposals even when its rankings among outputs of prolonged gradient search are uninformative. Effective planning pairs goal-directed candidates with predictions that distinguish their outcomes. We introduce CriticJEPA, which learns goal-conditioned flow proposals from reward-free trajectories and uses frozen rollouts to select among them at every hierarchy level. Forward selection forms a complete planner; short anchored updates refine candidates before selection. Across visual navigation and manipulation, CriticJEPA increases success at a fraction of the planning compute, transferring shared settings across independently trained models, hierarchy depths, and unseen tasks while keeping every world-model weight fixed.

papers.abstract: Memory-augmented large language model (LLM) driving agents can reuse past experience, yet previously learned corrections often fail to transfer when traffic conditions change. A key limitation is that existing memories mainly record observed outcomes, providing little evidence about alternative actions. We introduce XMind, a training-free framework that enables LLM-based driving to "Think Twice" through cross-memory reasoning. XMind integrates working memory of recent traffic states with episodic memory of critical risk events. The agent first makes an initial decision from the current context and then cross-checks it against retrieved historical experience. If a conflict arises, it makes a second decision guided by the retrieved evidence. To construct reliable episodic memory, XMind evaluates alternative actions through counterfactual rollouts under perturbed traffic conditions and stores the verified outcomes as structured risk capsules. These capsules are retrieved by jointly matching spatial risk patterns and scenario semantics. Across closed-loop highway simulations, XMind achieves success rates of 83.3-93.3%, exceeding the strong baseline by 6.6 percentage points on average. Evaluation on K-Risk further demonstrates lower decision risk on unseen real-world high-risk interactions. Ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of working memory, risk-text retrieval, and counterfactual verification. Code is available at https://github.com/xiangxiangliuwo/XMind

papers.abstract: LiDAR reconstruction supports closed-loop autonomous driving simulation, but hours of per-scene optimization make large asset libraries costly to build and maintain. We present Instant LiDAR, a feed-forward pipeline that reconstructs multiple LiDAR scans as reusable Gaussian assets in minutes without per-scene optimization. LiDAR measurements provide strong geometric priors, but directly initializing Gaussians from them yields poor reconstruction due to nonuniform sampling and a limited field of view. Sparse returns leave surface gaps, while combining scans expands coverage but introduces redundant primitives. To address these challenges, Instant LiDAR combines measurement-anchored Gaussian prediction, sampling-aware Gaussian scales, and multi-frame consolidation. The predictor refines attributes anchored to recorded returns, while the scales adapt spatial support to LiDAR sampling. Multi-frame consolidation merges overlapping predictions into a compact asset spanning the driving log. Compared with NuRec, Instant LiDAR reconstructs scenes approximately 46 times faster on Physical AI (PAI) and 70 times faster on Waymo. It also achieves comparable downstream 3D detection accuracy on Waymo.

bullets: Eliminates costly per-scene optimization, reducing reconstruction to minutes.

papers.abstract: A driving planner needs both scene semantics, which vision-language models (VLMs) provide, and spatial structure, which geometric foundation models recover from visual history. We present VLG-Drive, which keeps both models frozen and trains only a fusion interface and a planner from trajectory labels. At each camera-grid cell, the interface fuses the paired VLM and geometry features into one joint token through a geometry-anchored residual, and a command-conditioned planner reads these tokens to predict the ego trajectory. VLG-Drive achieves 31.78 EPDMS on NavHard under perturbed initial states, the highest among the compared methods, and 88.27 PDMS on NavTest from cameras alone. Pointwise fusion outperforms independent VLM and geometry streams on both benchmarks. In closed-loop driving on 420 HUGSIM scenarios, VLG-Drive outperforms all compared planners. These results indicate that a lightweight planner trained on fused features of frozen vision-language and geometric foundation models is an effective alternative to adapting either model for planning.

papers.abstract: Released autonomous-driving models achieve strong benchmark performance, yet deploying them on a new real vehicle remains challenging. We study this deployment gap and find that released models can remain coupled to assumptions from their source sensing, data, and execution processes even after conventional adaptation. We introduce Released-to-Real (R2R), a deployment-localization methodology that identifies such source-system coupling and corrects only the affected components while preserving the released model. For data and behavior adaptation, we find that the mismatch between trajectory-level optimization and receding-horizon execution enters through the ego state rather than the observation, and introduce Human-Anchored Reinforcement Learning (HA-RL), which corrects it on recorded target driving without the costly rollouts of generative closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). For physical sensor adaptation, R2R localizes and corrects source-dependent spatial and temporal representations with frozen perception weights, requiring neither target annotations nor retraining. HA-RL improves the closed-loop success rate of a released diffusion-based planner from 82.2% to 95.2%, while sensor adaptation across multiple released detectors and three real sensor rigs improves the vehicle mean average precision (mAP) of a released multi-camera detector from 0.041 to 0.420 on a five-camera target rig. These results provide a practical path for preparing released models before deployment on new real vehicles. Our project page is publicly available at https://released-to-real.github.io.
authors: Morui Zhu, Deyuan Qu, Qi Chen, Qing Yang

Sensor adaptation corrects source-dependent spatial and temporal representations with frozen perception weights and no target annotations or retraining.
HA-RL raises closed-loop success from 82.2% to 95.2%, while sensor adaptation improves detector mAP from 0.041 to 0.420 on a five-camera target rig.

Deploying a driving model on a new vehicle requires both adaptations: sensor adaptation keeps perception valid on the target rig, and behavior adaptation keeps planning safe under target driving. When the planner acts on detected objects, sensor adaptation is a precondition for behavior adaptation.

papers.abstract: Although radiance fields provide detailed scene representations for robotics, they remain underexplored for trajectory planning, without a widely agreed-upon way to translate learned spatial primitives into reliable collision criteria. To bridge this gap, we introduce Collision Rendering, the first trajectory planning framework on sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR), which supports GPU-accelerated, risk-bounded collision checking and a differentiable collision cost. Our key insight is that the structured volumetric density of SVR allows its rendering pipeline to serve as a fast numerical approximator of collision probability. We approximate the robot with collision spheres and place a coinciding spherical camera at each sphere. Under a probabilistic collision model, we derive an upper bound on each sphere's maximum directional collision probability from the camera's rendering pipeline. Evaluating this bound on the GPU yields a modular collision checker that integrates with established sampling-based planners without an auxiliary geometric map or changes to the learned representation. We further compute a collision cost and its gradients from rendered opacities through the same pipeline, extending the framework to trajectory optimization. Experiments demonstrate millisecond collision checking time on a consumer-grade GPU and collision-free trajectories in all queries, outperforming other radiance field-based planners.
authors: Byoungkwon Yoon, Han Gyeom Lee, Hojun Lee, Yuseop Sim, Daniel Sungwoo Bae, Martin Byung-Guk Jun

Reports millisecond-scale checking on a consumer GPU and collision-free trajectories across all queries in experiments.

papers.abstract: Vision-based rover autonomy requires integrating perception, localization, planning and platform-specific control under limited sensing and computing resources. We present an open-source ROS 2 stack for following directional arrows, reaching a terminal cone and returning autonomously to the start. It connects YOLOv8n detection and geometric direction, range and bearing estimation with RGB-D SLAM, wheel-inertial state estimation, kinematics-aware planning, behavior-tree mission management and STM32 actuation. Standard interfaces separate reusable autonomy from the hardware layer; a proportional path-following plugin supports low-speed rover motion. Public resources include software, configuration, a labeled dataset, trained weights and evaluation logs. On 478 held-out images, the detector achieves mAP@0.5 of 0.720 under the Ultralytics evaluator and outperforms a classical OpenCV baseline under a shared evaluation protocol. The reported perception latency is 25 ms on a Jetson Orin NX. Three missions, one indoor and two outdoor, demonstrate marker-guided navigation and autonomous return without operator motion commands or reported collisions. Field results document integration failures and corrective choices; repeated instrumented trials remain necessary to quantify physical navigation errors and reliability.
bullets: Addresses autonomous rover navigation under limited sensing and computing resources.
Combines YOLOv8n-based arrow detection, RGB-D SLAM, wheel-inertial estimation, kinematics-aware planning, behavior-tree mission management, and STM32 actuation.
Uses standard interfaces to separate reusable autonomy software from platform-specific hardware; public code, data, weights, configurations, and logs are provided.
The detector reaches 0.720 mAP@0.5 on 478 held-out images with 25 ms reported perception latency on a Jetson Orin NX, outperforming a shared-protocol OpenCV baseline.
Three indoor/outdoor missions demonstrate autonomous marker-guided navigation and return; repeated trials are still needed to quantify physical navigation errors and reliability.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving can extend a vehicle's awareness beyond its own sensors, but existing cooperative end-to-end methods inject shared information into the planner and rely on cooperative driving demonstrations to learn how to use it. The moments in which shared information should change a driving decision are rare in such data, providing limited supervision for learning this behavior. We argue that cooperation need not be learned by the planner. Instead, reacting to shared information requires predicting how surrounding agents will move and selecting a response from the candidate trajectories of an ego planner. We introduce CoSel, a cooperation-as-selection framework that leaves the planner and its ego-only input unchanged. A separately trained cooperative predictor uses observations from the ego vehicle, roadside units, and connected automated vehicles to predict surrounding agents and their future motion. CoSel evaluates the planner's candidate trajectories against these predictions, preserves the planner's choice when it remains safe, and selects the closest safe alternative when shared information reveals additional risk. Each safety intervention is traceable to the shared evidence that triggers it. In closed-loop evaluation, CoSel achieves a driving score of 70.7 on V2Xverse, outperforming the best compared cooperative method by 7.5 points, and the highest average driving score of 85.8 on MDrive. Under missing ego detections, the collision count of CoSel increases only from 17 to 19 in 72 scenarios, compared with 19 to 32 for an existing cooperative end-to-end model.
authors: Yiping Li, Haohua Que, Zhipeng Bao, Wenjie Zhao, Qianwen Li
bullets: Cooperative driving methods often receive little supervision for learning when shared information should alter decisions.
CoSel keeps the ego-only planner unchanged and uses a separately trained predictor to forecast surrounding agents from ego, roadside, and connected-vehicle observations.
It evaluates candidate trajectories for safety, preserving the planner’s choice when safe and otherwise selecting the closest safe alternative.
Interventions are traceable to the shared evidence that reveals additional risk.
In closed-loop tests, CoSel scores 70.7 on V2Xverse and 85.8 on MDrive; with missing ego detections, collisions rise from 17 to 19 across 72 scenarios.

papers.selection_reason: Cooperative driving with learned prediction and trajectory selection fits autonomous navigation and planning without language conditioning.
papers.title: CoSel: Cooperation as Selection for End-to-End Driving
papers.tldr: CoSel adds cooperation to end-to-end driving by selecting safer ego-planner trajectories using shared predictions, rather than retraining the planner to consume cooperative data.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved significant milestones, yet its reliance on the i.i.d. assumption renders it vulnerable to real-world distribution shifts. While Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm for on-the-fly enhancement, its application to driving is hindered by two barriers: (i) multi-task adaptation dependency, where updates to upstream perception also affect downstream planning, while perception confidence alone does not directly assess these downstream effects; and (ii) continuous adaptation instability, where recursive online updates over long horizons cause compounding parameter drift. To address these challenges, we propose P2-TTA, a plug-and-play TTA framework for the continual adaptation of end-to-end driving models. P2-TTA coordinates adaptation through a joint objective combining perception entropy minimization with a retrospective temporal planning consistency objective derived from observed ego motion. To stabilize online updates, we use an EMA teacher as a moving parameter reference and reject candidate updates that increase historical planning loss. Extensive experiments across multiple models demonstrate that, by updating an average of 0.11 per mille of parameters with an average adaptation time of 19.9 ms on different backbones, P2-TTA achieves average recovery rates of 36.4%, 30.0%, and 9.3% for L2, collision rate, and PDMS, respectively, under severe distribution shifts. Under a shared perception-planning objective, P2-TTA achieves the highest L2 and collision recovery among the compared TTA baselines on UniAD.
authors: Shiyu Fang, Yiming Cui, Qihang Huang, Zhan Chen, Collister Chua, Wenhui Huang, Peng Hang, Chen Lv, Jian Sun
bullets: Addresses two challenges: perception–planning adaptation dependencies and instability from continual online updates.
Combines perception entropy minimization with a temporal planning-consistency objective based on observed ego motion.
Uses an EMA teacher and rejects updates that worsen historical planning loss to limit parameter drift.
Across multiple backbones, updates only a very small parameter subset with low adaptation latency and recovers performance under severe distribution shifts.
Reports the strongest L2 and collision recovery among compared TTA baselines on UniAD under a shared perception–planning objective.

papers.abstract: Coordinating vessels through the shared waterways of busy ports grows more challenging as vessel traffic increases. Port authorities need realistic simulations to assess how arrival schedules, anchorage assignments, and routes affect vessel throughput and navigation safety. Existing AIS-based trajectory models predict a vessel's track from its past trajectory in an open-loop fashion. They do not simulate step-by-step responses to other ships or test whether a vessel collides or reaches its goal. To address this problem, we introduce JaxNaviSim, a data-driven simulator and learning benchmark coupling Automatic Identification System (AIS) data with fast, controllable traffic simulation, in which learned models steer vessels through recorded traffic. First, we release a dataset of ~141 million AIS records from over 30K vessels across eight high-density regions of the Singapore Strait, among the world's busiest waterways, with ~6.7 million vessel-hours. Unlike several existing AIS datasets which mostly cover open seas, ours captures close-quarters vessel traffic in the narrow strait. Second, we define a navigation task for each recorded vessel trajectory. A model steers that vessel every 10 s from its recorded state to its anchoring point or region exit, while surrounding ships follow their recorded tracks or are steered by the model. We implement a JAX simulator that runs these tasks in large batches on a GPU. We also incorporate multiple vessel dynamics models and sea surface currents. Finally, we benchmark imitation learning (IL), offline and online RL, and include Predictive Action Refinement (PAR) as a safety baseline that cuts collision rates to 1-3%. The comparison shows that low tracking error does not ensure arrival, and learned policies can reach most destinations yet collide in 20-45% of episodes.
authors: Quang Anh Pham, Janaka Chathuranga Brahmanage, Hue Tse Leong, Akshat Kumar, Tien Anh Mai, Siu Loon Hoe, Venky Shankararaman
bullets: Provides approximately 141 million AIS records from over 30,000 vessels across eight high-density Singapore Strait regions, covering close-quarters traffic.
Defines step-by-step navigation tasks in which vessels steer every 10 seconds toward anchorage points or region exits while interacting with surrounding traffic.
Implements large-batch GPU simulation in JAX with multiple vessel dynamics models and sea-surface currents.
Benchmarks imitation learning, offline and online reinforcement learning, and Predictive Action Refinement as a safety baseline.
Policies reach most destinations but collide in 20–45% of episodes; Predictive Action Refinement reduces collision rates to 1–3%.

Figure 12: The forward law of each dynamics model, as a vector sum. From the position pk, the commanded displacement is blue and the commanded turn green, while the drift δk contributed by the sea current is red. Their result, grey, is the step over ground the model produces, ending at the solid hull; the dashed ray is the bow f(ψk). Delta commands displacement on both axes and turns independently of it. Port-glide instead takes its heading from the AIS recording rather than choosing it, and can only push along that bow. Any sideways motion in the recording is therefore out of reach, so the vessel ends up somewhere other than the recorded pk+1, drawn as a dashed hull, indicated in pale red (Equation 27). The other three reproduce the recorded step ∆pk = pk+1 − pk exactly. Water-track turns first and defines the bow as the direction of travel through the water, and Nomoto does the same with a first-order lag, so that its commanded turn aψk (dotted) and the turn ∆ψk actually applied (grey) differ.

Figure 6: The JAXNAVISIM pipeline. Recorded AIS trajectories supply offline demonstrations and the replayed traffic of each scenario. Policies are trained offline from demonstrations or online from closed-loop rollouts, in which one or more controlled vessels act among replayed traffic, optionally through a test-time layer. Policies receive only current local observations; only the simulator accesses future replay samples. Section 3.4 defines the metrics.

papers.abstract: This report presents a comprehensive pipeline for developing an end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving model for the Physical AI AV Track. The framework consists of data curation, HD map auto-labelling, data-driven imitation learning, and simulator-based reinforcement learning. To ensure safety in the closed-loop setting, we introduce a selection-based E2E planning approach that leverages object detection and BEV segmentation to filter out trajectory candidates likely to cause collisions or off-road driving. Trained on NVIDIA NuRec and the NVIDIA PAI-AV dataset, our method scores a fixed vocabulary of trajectory candidates for collision, drivable-area compliance, and progress learned from simulated rollouts, and selects the best candidate that passes the filter. This design highlights the effectiveness of combining E2E planning with perception-based trajectory filtering for safe and reliable closed-loop autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) does not change the optimal policy, but how much it speeds up learning depends on the potential and on effects outside this guarantee. We analyse how PBRS changes the one-step reward while it preserves the discounted return: a per-step $(\gamma-1)\Phi$ term, the terminal-state rule, a constant shift of the potential, and positive cycles in a bonus that is not potential-based. We then measure these consequences in pre-registered experiments with a PPO agent. The agent has a limited egocentric view and is tested on two MiniGrid navigation tasks (160 runs, 10 seeds per condition). On LavaCrossing, a geodesic (BFS) potential learned faster than both the sparse baseline and a Euclidean potential with a 7x7 and a 5x5 view (AUC difference +0.27 to +0.39, Holm p between 0.007 and 0.0499). The Euclidean potential did not differ from the baseline. In 20 runs with a non-potential bonus, none of the agents learned the task. The Euclidean potential caused more than twice as many deaths in lava during early training. View size did not detectably change the benefit of shaping. With a 5x5 view on SimpleCrossing, some BFS runs got stuck in loops and never learned; shifting the potential did not remove this, so the per-step term alone does not explain it.
bullets: Analyzes per-step reward effects, terminal-state handling, constant potential shifts, and failures from non-potential bonuses.
In PPO navigation with limited egocentric views, a BFS/geodesic potential accelerated learning on LavaCrossing versus sparse and Euclidean shaping.
Euclidean shaping matched the sparse baseline and caused more than twice as many early lava deaths.
Non-potential bonuses failed completely in the tested runs, while view size did not detectably change shaping benefits.
On SimpleCrossing, some BFS agents became stuck in loops; shifting the potential did not resolve this.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models have made substantial progress, yet reliable closed-loop driving in complex traffic remains challenging. Beyond improving individual models, system-level orchestration offers a complementary approach by coordinating driving capabilities and computation. We introduce ROSE-Drive (Runtime Orchestration and System Evolution), a model-agnostic framework that jointly orchestrates driving execution and computation. It coordinates frozen driving models with driving skills, perception tools, and feedback controllers. A distilled vision-language model (VLM) proposes driving tasks and scene relations. Shared physical state and persistent tasks support capability composition, task continuity, and adaptive scheduling. The orchestrator combines model and skill outputs across control channels, maintains task responsibility through handover, and uses execution feedback to select controllers, reuse valid motion references, and schedule model inference. Offline revisions use execution records to refine skills and their coordination through a stable task interface. Successive system stages inherit these revisions while model, perception, and VLM weights remain fixed. Evaluations with four driving models on Bench2Drive v0.0.3, Bench2Drive v0.0.4, and Fail2Drive show accumulated capability and transfer before target-benchmark revision. On held-out Longest6, driving score (DS) rises from 25 to 52 for AutoMoT and from 22 to 47 for SimLingo across system stages, while both systems skip new model inference on over 71% of control steps.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of reliable driving in complex traffic through system-level orchestration rather than model retraining.

Refines skills and their coordination from execution records while keeping driving, perception, and VLM weights fixed.
Across multiple benchmarks and four driving models, held-out Longest6 driving scores improved substantially across system stages.
More than 71% of control steps skipped new model inference for both reported systems, reducing runtime computation demand.

papers.abstract: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. The relative-capability principle guides these choices by relating the benefit of additional computation or intervention to its cost. After open-loop initialization, dual-loop evolution trains the Router, agent, and self-scheduler from closed-loop experience while failure-driven updates refine skills and execution feedback. AgentMoT achieves state-of-the-art results on Bench2Drive v0.0.3 and v0.0.4, with 94.48/92.33 driving score and 85.45/82.73% success rate, respectively. With skills disabled, learned routing improves over the strongest fixed pathway by 1.79 driving-score points and 4.09 percentage points of success rate on v0.0.3. Ablation studies further show gains from closed-loop agent learning, two-view queries, and event-triggered wake-up.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot embodied systems are typically designed to collaborate by coordinating actions, sharing trajectories, or learning joint policies. We ask a complementary question: can collaboration emerge before decision-making, by first building a shared understanding of the environment? We introduce Shared Environmental Understanding, a policy-agnostic representation that aggregates partial egocentric observations from multiple robots into a shared latent world model. This shifts collaboration from the policy space to the representation space, enabling decentralized decision-making with shared environmental context. To this end, we propose Shared Environment Encoding and Retrieval (SEER), a framework that organizes multi-robot observations into a shared memory, retrieves relevant context via spatio-temporal similarity, and encodes it using a predictive latent world model. The resulting representations are injected into downstream navigation agents as tokens. Experimental results demonstrate that SEER captures action-relevant environmental structure and consistently improves navigation performance across both specialized VLN agents and general vision-language model agents, while preserving single-agent capabilities.

papers.abstract: Adversarial object attacks pose a threat to BEV-based 3D object detectors in autonomous driving. Existing attacks typically target a single modality, coordinate camera and LiDAR observations at the current timestamp, or model temporal persistence mainly in camera streams. Without a unified construction of current and historical observations, attacks can leave part of the detector's accumulated evidence unsuppressed, limiting their effectiveness. In this paper, we propose AdvMTO, a 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) framework for suppressing detection of persistent adversarial objects. Its oriented surfels encode appearance, geometry, and opacity in one object state, from which camera images and scanline LiDAR returns are generated. AdvMTO then constructs current and historical inputs through detector-native processing, regenerating LiDAR returns in each native source sweep for fusion detectors. We optimize bounded appearance perturbations for each detector, propagating gradients through historical BEV memory for temporal camera detectors. For fusion detectors, bounded geometry refinement along local normals further perturbs both sensing modalities. Experiments on nuScenes demonstrate effective suppression of traffic-cone detection across three BEV detectors. Temporal ablations further highlight the importance of detector-native history modeling for both attack construction and optimization.

bullets: Targets a gap in attacks that fail to jointly suppress current and historical camera–LiDAR evidence.
Represents objects with oriented surfels encoding appearance, geometry, and opacity, enabling camera and scanline LiDAR generation.
Builds detector-native current and historical inputs, including native-source LiDAR sweeps and temporal BEV memory.
Optimizes bounded appearance perturbations, with additional local-normal geometry refinement for fusion detectors.
Experiments on nuScenes show effective traffic-cone suppression across three BEV detectors; temporal ablations emphasize native history modeling.

papers.title: AdvMTO: Multimodal and Temporal Adversarial Object Attacks via 2D Gaussian Splatting for BEV-Based 3D Object Detection
papers.tldr: AdvMTO uses 2D Gaussian Splatting to create multimodal, temporally consistent adversarial objects that suppress persistent-object detection in BEV 3D detectors.

papers.abstract: A UAV that flies without GNSS has to estimate its absolute position and heading without any external signal. Most existing methods for UAV-to-satellite cross-view geo-localization (U-S CVGL) treat the task as image retrieval: they compress the UAV image and each satellite tile into separate descriptors, rank the tiles by their similarity, and return the center of the best tile. The output can therefore only lie on a pre-defined grid, its accuracy is limited by the tile size, and no heading is produced. Regressing the pose in a single pass removes the grid, but it leaves no chance to correct the estimate afterwards. We observe that satellite tiles are not independent samples. They are laid on the map at a fixed spacing, scale and orientation, so neighboring tiles join into one continuous satellite block with a consistent metric, and a nadir UAV view of that block differs from it by a planar rigid transform only, i.e. a 2D translation plus an in-plane rotation. We therefore reformulate U-S CVGL as solving for this transform between two images of different sizes. Position and heading then become parts of one geometric quantity, and the accuracy is no longer limited by the tile grid. We propose RigidAnchor, which solves the transform iteratively. The network encodes the two images and builds a multi-level correlation pyramid between them. At each iteration, it indexes the pyramid with every aerial cell carried through the current estimate, pools the descriptors of all cells into one hidden state, and lets two decoupled heads predict a translation increment and a rotation increment, the latter being composed rather than added. On Bearing-UAV-90K, the cross-view mean errors are 78.6% lower in position and 69.7% lower in heading than Bearing-UAV, and HSR@15 increases by 19.06 points. Code is available at https://github.com/wwsource/RigidAnchor.
authors: Bo Wang, Dekang Zhu, Jian Li, Zhipeng Meng, Bo Wang, Dewen Hu
bullets: Addresses GNSS-denied UAV localization, where retrieval methods are grid-limited and typically do not estimate heading.
Models a nadir UAV view and a continuous satellite-image block as related by a 2D translation and in-plane rotation.
Uses a multi-level correlation pyramid and iterative updates, with separate translation and composed rotation prediction heads.
On Bearing-UAV-90K, reports 78.6% lower position error, 69.7% lower heading error, and a 19.06-point HSR@15 increase versus Bearing-UAV.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of RigidAnchor. A UAV view Iu and the satellite block Ib that contains it are encoded by two independent branches and correlated into a four-level pyramid C1, . . . , C4, so that one volume serves every candidate pose. At each iteration the pyramid is indexed at the current estimate, the descriptors of all aerial cells are reduced by a motion encoder and a GRU to one hidden state hk, and two heads predict a single rigid increment. After K iterations the estimate is read out as localization and heading.

Figure 6: Convergence of the iterative pose estimate. Each row is one test query: the UAV view on the left, followed by the same 512× 512 satellite block, on which the footprints of the estimates at iterations 1, 2, 3 and 12 are accumulated over the four panels. The footprint is a square of the same side length as the aerial coverage, drawn at the estimated offset and heading, so its displacement and tilt with respect to the ground truth are the errors of that iteration. Light yellow marks the starting pose (block center, nose pointing north), green the ground truth, and red darkens from iteration 1 through 2 and 3 to 12. The legend below each row gives the position and heading errors of the four iterations.

Figure 3: Error distributions on Bearing-UAV-90K. Errors of Bearing-UAV (top) and RigidAnchor (bottom) over the 9000 queries of the UAV-view setting. From left to right: histograms of the localization error and of the heading error, and the per-sample localization and heading errors. Dashed and dash-dotted lines mark the mean and the median. The Bearing-UAV row comes from a separate run of that baseline under the same protocol, so its mean errors differ slightly from the Bearing-UAV row of Table 1.

Figure 4: Number of refinement iterations, with and without rotation normalization. On the UAV-view split of Bearing-UAV-90K (9000 queries) the same weights are run with K swept from 1 to 32: (a) localization and (b) heading error on a logarithmic axis, with (blue) and without (red) renormalizing the rotation to unit length after each update, and (c) the recall of the normalized variant at 5 and 10 m. Both conditions share the first iteration, where the normalization is an identity, and they separate from the second on. Without it the error bottoms out at iteration 8 and then rises; with it the minimum (1.84 against 2.01 m) holds through 32. The dashed gray line marks the training setting K = 12.

Figure 2: One iteration of the pose update. The correlation features of all s2u aerial cells are encoded and average-pooled into one motion vector mk. It is concatenated with the context vector g and the current estimate (cos θk−1, sin θk−1, t̃k−1) to drive a GRU from the hidden state h0 given by the context encoder. Two separate heads read the resulting state hk: one predicts the translation increment ∆t̃k, and the other the rotation increment as the pair (cos∆θk, sin∆θk), which is composed with the previous rotation instead of being added to an angle.

Figure 5: Success rate versus the orientation gap. papers.selection_reason: Proposes RigidAnchor for UAV cross-view geo-localization. This addresses autonomous navigation and pose estimation for UAVs, fitting Robot Navigation.
papers.title: RigidAnchor: Cross-View Geo-Localization for UAV via Iterative Planar Rigid Alignment
papers.tldr: RigidAnchor reformulates UAV-to-satellite geo-localization as iterative planar alignment, jointly refining position and heading beyond the satellite tile grid.

papers.abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/
authors: Tianle Zeng, Hanjing Ye, Bingyi Xia, Yuchen Zhou, Zibo Zhang, Yufei Huang, Yonggen Ling, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling route execution with continuous follower- and scene-aware adaptation.
Uses a structured multimodal policy with an explicit Path, learned Pace for route progress, and Residual for local adaptation.
Introduces LeadInfra for closed-loop Unreal Engine data generation and LeadBench with 108 held-out episodes.
Trains on an approximately 4M-sample corpus and reaches 39.6% task success, the highest among evaluated policies on LeadBench.
Transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning.

papers.title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading

papers.abstract: Millimeter-wave radar offers weather-resilient sensing for 3D occupancy prediction. Existing radar occupancy methods mainly model geometry, with limited joint modeling of semantics and motion. Cascaded imaging radar provides fine spatial detail but has a limited unambiguous velocity range, whereas single-chip radar offers a wider range but coarser spatial resolution. We propose RadarOSV, to our knowledge the first radar-only framework that jointly predicts occupancy, dynamic object semantics, and ground-relative velocity from raw radar data in unified voxels, by exploiting complementary measurements from both radars. Its Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry (PCG) backbone maps polar imaging-radar features into Cartesian voxels through fixed and deformable sampling, guiding cross-radar fusion for geometry and attribute prediction. Single-chip detection outputs provide class evidence, while raw Doppler spectra supply motion features and radial-velocity candidates. The velocity readout selects from these candidates using fused features to resolve aliasing, then combines the selected radial estimate with learned motion. Ego-motion compensation uses radar-estimated velocity, so inference requires no external odometry or other sensors. On K-Radar, single-frame PCG achieves 40.7% mIoU within 12.8 m, compared with RadarOcc's reported 34.3%. On the BRIDGE-Liv dataset, compared with a cascaded-radar baseline predicting the same outputs with external ego velocity, RadarOSV improves macro-averaged accuracy across four dynamic object classes within annotated object regions from 63.1% to 75.5% and reduces object radial-velocity MAE against manual Doppler annotations from 1.03 to 0.51 m/s, while maintaining geometric occupancy mIoU.
authors: Yuan Fang, Long Zhuang, Xijia Wei, Jingqi Jiang, Fangzhan Shi, Simon Julier, Kevin Chetty
bullets: Addresses the limited joint modeling of geometry, semantics, and motion in existing radar occupancy methods.
Uses a Polar-to-Cartesian Geometry backbone with fixed/deformable sampling to fuse radar features into unified voxels.
Combines single-chip class evidence with raw Doppler spectra and candidate selection to handle velocity aliasing.
Performs ego-motion compensation using radar-estimated velocity, without external odometry or other sensors.
Reports improved occupancy, dynamic-class accuracy, and radial-velocity error on K-Radar and BRIDGE-Liv.

RGB images are shown for reference only. LiDARderived voxels and manual SC labels provide training supervision.

papers.title: RadarOSV: Unified 3D Scene and Motion Perception from mmWave Radars
papers.tldr: RadarOSV unifies radar-only 3D occupancy, dynamic semantics, and ground-relative velocity prediction by fusing complementary imaging- and single-chip-radar measurements.

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration is widely used to map unknown environments, yet maintaining both path efficiency and low online computation remains difficult as environment scale increases. Hierarchical planners reduce global search through coarse regional representations but often rely on handcrafted local viewpoint-selection rules. Graph-based reinforcement learning can improve local decisions, but its inference cost grows with the exploration graph and global direction is usually represented only implicitly. To address these limitations, we present HERO, a hierarchical framework that assigns distinct responsibilities to global planning and learned local decision-making, enabling each level to focus on the function it is best suited to perform. To reduce the growing inference cost of graph-based policies, HERO restricts learned target selection to reachable candidates within the current region while using region-level planning to provide long-horizon guidance. To avoid informative targets causing excessive deviation from this global direction, the proposed Dual-Branch Graph Policy balances Frontier Utility with guidance toward the next region, improving both local exploration and global progress. Experiments on unseen 2D maps show the lowest overall mean path length and target-decision cost among the evaluated methods. MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites further demonstrate the framework's applicability with LiDAR-based mapping and chassis dynamics.
authors: Xulin Xiao, Shengyi Liang, Mingjie Zhang, Chengkai Wu, Chen Chen, Zhigang Li, Jinni Zhou, Jun Ma, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Targets the trade-off between path efficiency and online computation as exploration environments grow.
Uses hierarchical planning: global regions provide long-horizon direction, while learned decisions select reachable targets within the current region.
Introduces a Dual-Branch Graph Policy balancing frontier utility with progress toward the next planned region.
Achieves the lowest reported mean path length and target-decision cost among evaluated methods on unseen 2D maps.
MARSIM simulations and deployments at three real-world sites demonstrate applicability with LiDAR mapping and chassis dynamics.

Bottom: The Dual-Branch Graph Policy separately encodes Frontier Utility and the Guidance-Distance Feature, fuses the resulting representations through cross-attention, and selects a target from the feasible neighbors.

papers.title: HERO: Hierarchical Region-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Exploration
papers.tldr: HERO combines region-level planning with a guidance-aware graph policy to enable efficient, low-cost autonomous exploration in large unknown environments.

papers.abstract: Residual world models forecast a driving scene through its temporal change, so feature components that stay constant over time vanish from the residual pathway. We ask whether evidence with weak temporal change, such as a waiting pedestrian or a stopped vehicle, can be used more effectively for planning, and introduce MOVER, a complementary event-routing mechanism. A training-time teacher measures how each spatially grounded event query responds when a past frame is removed from shared history and contrasts that sensitivity with the event's pooled temporal residual, prioritizing events that depend on history but receive weak residual evidence. A student predicts the resulting priorities from unperturbed history, so the teacher adds no inference cost. Under fixed total routing mass, one distribution scales a low-rank future bird's-eye-view update and biases trajectory-conditioned event reading. On nuScenes, MOVER reduces ResWorld's UniAD-style average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and its collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12% without direct planner ego status (0.50 m and 0.09% with it), adding 4.1 ms per frame. Matched controls show that the complementary teacher outperforms either signal alone and that the allocation acts mainly during training. Adapted to BridgeDrive-LEAD, MOVER reaches a 96.52 +/- 0.65 driving score over three seeds on the 220-route Bench2Drive closed-loop benchmark, exceeding matched controls in each paired seed by a margin within seed variation.
authors: Xiangyu Li, Yu Jiang, Tianyi Wang, Liang He, Qixing Huang, Zhaomiao Guo
bullets: Residual world models may underrepresent static or slowly changing evidence, such as waiting pedestrians and stopped vehicles.
A training-time teacher identifies events that depend on past frames but receive weak temporal-residual evidence; a student predicts their routing priorities at inference.
The priorities allocate a fixed routing budget between low-rank future bird’s-eye-view updates and trajectory-conditioned event reading, adding no teacher cost at inference.
On nuScenes, MOVER reduces average L2 from 0.65 to 0.55 m and collision rate from 0.23% to 0.12%, with 4.1 ms/frame overhead.
On Bench2Drive, adapted MOVER achieves a 96.52 ± 0.65 driving score across three seeds and exceeds matched controls within paired-seed variation.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of MOVER. A residual driving world model predicts future BEV features from ego-aligned history, and MOVER adds a complementary event-routing branch. We discover current-frame events once, pool the corresponding regions across aligned history, and enrich them with shared history cross-attention. During training, a history-occlusion teacher produces complementary priorities from history sensitivity and residual evidence; a single-view student router distills these priorities. At inference, the learned allocation writes a low-rank update to the future BEV representation and provides a prior for trajectory-conditioned event reading. The base predictor supplies the future BEV baseline while MOVER routes supplementary evidence.

Figure 9. A turning scene with a pedestrian. The left-front camera view is paired with the model’s ten-point planned route in ego coordinates and its executed event allocation at the same observation.

Figure 10. Three interactive driving scenarios. Original camera views show a parked obstacle, a turn with a pedestrian, and a blocked intersection. Each is paired with the model’s ten-point planned route at the same observation, expressed in ego coordinates.

Figure 6. Planning accuracy across forecast horizons. The matched uniform-routing and MOVER models are evaluated on 5,119 observations with a complete 3-second future. The panels display endpoint L2 and collision-rate summaries for the two routing strategies.

Figure 4. The complementary routing module. We discover current-frame event masks on the current BEV and reuse them to pool aligned history. papers.abstract: Explicit reasoning enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to interpret complex traffic interactions and support trajectory planning, but introduces additional computational demands. Determining when explicit reasoning can improve planning accuracy remains a key challenge, as its benefits vary across driving scenarios. To address this challenge, this study proposes Scene-Adaptive Gating of Explicit Reasoning for Driving (SAGE-Drive), a benefit-aware adaptive reasoning framework for autonomous driving planning. First, paired planning outcomes with and without explicit reasoning are analyzed to measure the reasoning benefit, i.e., the reduction in planning error achieved by explicit reasoning, which serves as the supervision label. SAGE-Drive then learns to predict these benefits using geometric features of the initial trajectory planned without reasoning and multimodal scene information, and invokes explicit reasoning only for the scenarios with the highest predicted benefits under a predefined reasoning budget. Experiments on 1,497 paired driving scenarios reveal that explicit reasoning improves planning accuracy in 53.5% of cases while degrading it in 46.5%, yielding a near-zero average benefit. On the test set, with a 20% reasoning budget, SAGE-Drive achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 1.5191 m, compared with 1.5252 m for random selection. At a 35% budget, it achieves an ADE of 1.5148 m, close to the 1.5141 m obtained when reasoning is applied to every scenario. These findings establish the predicted reasoning benefit as an effective criterion for reasoning selection, allowing explicit reasoning to be invoked where it improves planning accuracy at a fraction of its computational cost.
authors: Donglei Rong, Wenbin Yao, Congcong Bai, Xi Gao, Qiaoqiao Ren, Sheng Jin, Cheng Xu
bullets: Explicit reasoning is not uniformly helpful: it improves planning in 53.5% of scenarios and degrades it in 46.5%, producing near-zero average benefit.
The framework defines reasoning benefit as the reduction in planning error from using explicit reasoning versus not using it.
A predictor uses initial trajectory geometry and multimodal scene information to estimate this benefit.
Explicit reasoning is allocated to the highest-benefit scenarios under a predefined reasoning budget.
With 20% and 35% reasoning budgets, SAGE-Drive approaches the accuracy of reasoning on every scenario while outperforming random selection at 20%.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators operating in homes and other complex environments must coordinate their base and arm over long horizons, navigating around obstacles, through narrow passages, and between constrained workspaces. Neural motion planners can provide fast closed-loop planning from partial observations, but scaling them to room-sized environments is difficult because generating high-quality training trajectories is itself a challenging motion-planning problem. To address this, we introduce MoMa-DemoSmith, a demonstration-generation pipeline that separates the problem into global path discovery for large complex scenes and local motion refinement for collision avoidance. This key separation enables the generation of millions of challenging whole-body trajectories across our procedurally generated scenes. We train MoMa-NMP on these demonstrations through behavior cloning (BC) followed by privileged on-policy distillation, achieving 87.0% success on our simulation benchmark and 77.5% across 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes. See video results at https://adamhkan.com/moma-nmp/.
authors: Adam Kan, Jason Jingzhou Liu, Jiahui Yang, Kenneth Shaw, Deepak Pathak
bullets: Targets long-horizon navigation and manipulation in complex, obstacle-filled environments with partial observations.
MoMa-DemoSmith separates global path discovery from local collision-avoidance refinement to generate challenging trajectories at scale.
MoMa-NMP is trained with behavior cloning followed by privileged on-policy distillation.
Achieves 87.0% success in simulation and 77.5% over 80 trials in unseen real-world scenes.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the challenge of scene-level memory design for efficient navigation across sessions and successive object goals. Recent methods commonly represent a scene using scene graphs or image--text records. However, dense scene-graph representations impose substantial reasoning and context overhead on multimodal large language models, while image--text records cannot be directly converted into executable geometric routes. To address these limitations, we propose SuperNav-1.5, an agentic navigation system equipped with a structured spatial memory constructed by the agent. The memory consists of an area-segmented occupancy map annotated with agent-maintained, map-grounded memory nodes. This map guides the agent toward unvisited areas and provides executable routes to known locations. For multi-session navigation, we introduce agent-guided relocalization, whereby the agent infers an area prior from current observations and stored memory records to constrain geometric matching and localize the robot within the stored map. Together, these designs enable efficient navigation across session and successive object goals. Experiments show that our method outperforms baselines on single-object, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation benchmarks, with particularly strong gains in path efficiency. Multi-session evaluation demonstrates that the constructed memory can be reused, while deployment on a real quadruped robot further shows the system's applicability.

bullets: Addresses the overhead of dense scene graphs and the non-executable nature of image–text scene records.

Introduces agent-guided relocalization to match current observations against stored memory and localize within prior maps.
Outperforms baselines across several navigation settings, with especially strong path-efficiency gains, and transfers to a real quadruped robot.

papers.abstract: Service robots that share corridors and lobbies with people must keep moving without endangering them. Reactive planners can stop indefinitely in dense crowds (the freezing robot problem), whereas the attention-based learned navigators that dominate the standard crowd benchmark assume holonomic motion or emit discrete actions unsuited to a differential-drive base. This paper presents TASC, a navigation system for a non-holonomic service robot that integrates an attention-based crowd encoder, an anticipatory collision feature, and a continuous-control policy. We adapt the dual-selection attention module, originally developed for discrete-action value learning, to proximal policy optimization for continuous velocity control, and add a closing-speed time-to-collision feature, a conservative estimate of the time to contact that serves as both an observation and a reward term. The policy is trained on a high-fidelity 3D robot model in NVIDIA Isaac Lab with 10,000 parallel environments, social-force-model pedestrians, and randomized crowd sizes. In 30,000 evaluation episodes, each run to its end, the policy timed out in fewer than 0.5% at every tested crowd density. This liveness comes at a cost: pedestrian collisions rise from 4.5% with five pedestrians to 17.4% with ten. In an ablation with four seeds per variant, policies retrained without the time-to-collision feature succeed 4 to 7 percentage points less often. The policy runs in Gazebo without retraining and on a commercial differential-drive service robot through a ROS 2 package with an inference latency below 10 ms, verified in a hardware-in-the-loop test with virtual pedestrians.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable planning from images, but their predictions do not directly establish whether a robot will satisfy physical constraints. We present JEPA-Shield, which connects a frozen action-conditioned Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world model to task-space safety enforcement. Two downstream models predict relative motion from imagined latent rollouts and decode unsafe geometry from the current image. Split conformal prediction turns end-to-end motion-prediction errors into multi-horizon uncertainty tubes. A backup-based shield checks these tubes against physical constraints and screens both candidate trajectories and final proposals in diffusion-inspired sampling-based model predictive control. Under the stated exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, we establish probabilistic constraint satisfaction at action-block boundaries for a returned plan executed without replanning. We also introduce VParkBench, with geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks and a editable photorealistic Gaussian-splatting environment. In closed-loop evaluation, JEPA-Shield achieves success rates of 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, respectively, with no observed constraint violations. Ablations show complementary benefits from shielding and uncertainty calibration. The results demonstrate the importance of grounding latent world-model predictions in task-space quantities and explicitly accounting for prediction uncertainty in safety-critical planning.
authors: Taekyung Kim, Ege Yuceel, Steven Hong, Georgios Fainekos, Dimitra Panagou, Bardh Hoxha
bullets: Motivation: Image-based latent predictions alone do not guarantee that robot plans satisfy task-space safety constraints.
Method: A frozen action-conditioned JEPA predicts imagined rollouts, while downstream models estimate motion and unsafe geometry; split conformal prediction forms multi-horizon uncertainty tubes.
Safety mechanism: A backup-based shield checks candidate and final diffusion-inspired MPC trajectories against physical constraints.
Guarantee: Under exchangeability and initial-backup assumptions, the returned plan satisfies constraints probabilistically at action-block boundaries without replanning.

Evaluation: On geometric car and tractor-trailer parking tasks in VParkBench, success rates were 84.4%, 82.3%, and 99.0%, with no observed constraint violations; shielding and calibration provided complementary benefits.

papers.abstract: Existing Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) autonomy frameworks lack human contextual awareness, limiting real-time adaptability in unstructured Search and Rescue (SAR) environments. To address data availability, we propose a Robot Operating System (ROS2)-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) framework that translates human directional gestures (left/right) into UAV navigation commands using RGB-Depth (RGB-D) sensing and YOLOv11 (You Only Look Once). The deprecation of ROS1 necessitates migrating to ROS2, prioritising real-time communication, scalability, and long-term maintainability. Unlike approaches optimised for peak accuracy under ideal conditions, the proposed system prioritises robustness and real-time deployment in degraded SAR environments. Our system achieves 89% confidence in depth estimation under occlusion and varying environmental conditions in Gazebo-PX4 simulations. In foggy conditions, RGB-D fusion consistently provides more informative cues than RGB alone, with an average improvement of 46.7% across all scenarios and distances. The framework demonstrates superior occlusion handling (+15%), adaptive RGB-D fusion, temporal consistency modelling, and real-time deployment via a ROS2 data distribution service (DDS), with end-to-end latency below 50 ms. We evaluate the modified YOLOv11 and the depth-weighted pose estimation on a held-out simulated test set and on real people from the public UAV-GESTURE dataset, in clear air and in Koschmieder fog. Without retraining, the framework reads the gestures of real people with 80% accuracy, depth keeps 77% at a visibility of 10 m where RGB drops to 24%, and the modified YOLOv11 reaches 91% in simulation and 99% on held-out real people when trained on real data. The open-source ROS2 implementation eases the transition of SAR-UAV platforms from ROS1, enabling UAVs to act directly on operator gestures without complex path planning.

In simulation, RGB-D fusion improved cues over RGB alone by 46.7% on average in fog; depth retained 77% gesture accuracy at 10 m visibility versus 24% for RGB.
The open-source implementation supports migration from ROS1 and enables direct operator control without complex path planning.

papers.abstract: Time-to-Transit (TTT) is a perceptual cue, proxy for depth, that can be computed in the visual cortex, allowing animals to estimate the time remaining to move past features in the environment. We show how TTT can be estimated and used for bio-inspired navigation of a mobile robot equipped with a monocular camera. The paper describes a lightweight neural network estimation method, named MobileNeTTT, that (1) uses the full field of view and provides a rich array of visual feature TTT estimates; (2) is relatively insensitive to camera rotation; and (3) automatically adjusts to the geometry of the path and the presence of obstacles. Because TTT is a coarse visual cue, it is far simpler to use for robot navigation than current large visual depth foundation models. Our navigation model uses a 1.95M-parameter network that is two to three orders of magnitude smaller than well-known large vision foundation models, making it able to run in real time on edge hardware. Simulation and actual laboratory experiments validate the proposed approach in dynamic and spatially complex environments. Code, data, and video are available.
authors: Chiara Boretti, Philippe Bich, Manuel Morteo, Roberto Tron, John Baillieul
bullets: Uses the full camera field of view to produce rich visual time-to-transit estimates.
Is relatively robust to camera rotation and adapts to path geometry and obstacles.
Employs a 1.95M-parameter network, substantially smaller than large vision foundation models.
Enables simpler navigation from a coarse depth-related cue rather than full visual depth estimation.
Validated in simulation and laboratory experiments involving dynamic, spatially complex environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Overview of MobileNeTTT, which estimates Time-To-Transit from sequential RGB images I(t−1) and I(t) using a DNN-based depth estimator. Instead of predicting a dense per-pixel depth map, the network outputs a coarse depth map and a binary validity map indicating reliable values. Coarse depth values are then divided by the robot’s speed v, with a small constant ϵ added to prevent division by zero, to compute TTT values.

papers.selection_reason: Learning-based visual navigation for a mobile robot using a lightweight time-to-transit estimator, fitting robot navigation.
papers.title: MobileNeTTT: a Lightweight DNN-based Time-To-Transit Estimator for Visual Navigation
papers.tldr: MobileNeTTT is a compact monocular-vision network that estimates time-to-transit across the visual field for real-time, bio-inspired robot navigation on edge hardware.

papers.abstract: Cooperative perception with roadside LiDARs (RSLs) extends the sensing range of autonomous vehicles and resolves onboard-sensor occlusions, particularly at curves and intersections. Because infrastructure deployment is costly, existing work optimizes RSL configurations once, against road geometry and aggregated traffic statistics, and treats them as fixed thereafter. Traffic flow, however, is inherently dynamic, and a placement optimal on average can be far from optimal at any given moment. We introduce RSLaA (Roadside LiDARs as Agents), a framework in which each RSL adaptively adjusts its pose to the evolving traffic scene over decision-time windows. Since ground truth is unavailable at decision time, the framework centers on surrogate metrics computed solely from a probabilistic occupancy grid of historical observations, which predicts the next-window perception performance of candidate poses. We construct a co-simulation benchmark pairing five candidate surrogates with detector-agnostic ground-truth perception labels at every decision window, identifying the multi-view coverage metric J_mv as the most reliable predictor. Upon this validated surrogate we build two adaptive configuration methods, a receding-horizon (MPC) optimizer and a lightweight MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning scheme with centralized training and decentralized execution. Across 10 sites and 89 six-hour traffic scenarios (890 evaluation runs), adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment. Our results indicate that RSLs could be benefitted from being treated as agents.
authors: Yang Ma, Yichen Sun, Yubing Zheng, Zhongxiang Feng, Zeyang Cheng, Said M. Easa
bullets: Static roadside LiDAR placements may become suboptimal as traffic flow changes, especially near curves and intersections.
The framework predicts candidate-pose performance using surrogate metrics derived only from historical probabilistic occupancy grids.
A benchmark identifies the multi-view coverage metric, J_mv, as the most reliable surrogate among five candidates.
Two adaptive strategies are proposed: receding-horizon model predictive control and MAPPO-based multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Across 10 sites and 89 traffic scenarios, adaptive configuration consistently improves the composite perception score over static deployment.

papers.abstract: In difficult driving scenes, a learned scorer can select a poor trajectory from a fixed pool even when a better candidate is available. Nearby vehicles and road boundaries can also leave only a narrow range of high-scoring maneuvers. These constraints vary with the scene and are difficult to cover exhaustively during training. We introduce DriveTTO, a training-free method that searches around native proposals and checks each proposed refinement against a retained trajectory. A frozen scorer evaluates completed paths at the endpoints they actually reach, guiding resampling in progressively smaller neighborhoods. From a shared reference, one branch draws on planner proposals and another perturbs vehicle controls. DriveTTO blends their poses at matching times and accepts a branch or fusion update only when both frozen scorers predict a gain. On Navtest, DriveTTO recovers nonzero predictive driver model scores (PDMS) in 51.35% of native zero-score cases on average. Accounting for new failures, the zero-score rate falls from 1.63% to 1.13%. Benchmark-specific configurations achieve 95.54 PDMS and 92.30 extended PDMS (EPDMS) on Navtest, 57.10 EPDMS on Navhard, and 40.1 HD-Score on HUGSIM under observed commands. With a single frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on both Navtest and Navhard.
authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Zheyuan Lai, Liuxuan Sun, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
bullets: Addresses difficult scenes where a learned scorer selects a poor trajectory despite better candidates being nearby.
Searches around native planner proposals and vehicle-control perturbations using progressively smaller neighborhoods.
A frozen scorer evaluates completed trajectories, while updates are accepted only when both branch scorers predict improvement.
Recovers nonzero PDMS in 51.35% of native zero-score cases and lowers the zero-score rate from 1.63% to 1.13% on Navtest.
With one frozen scorer, DriveTTO-S improves all six evaluated planners on Navtest and Navhard.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces DriveTTO, a training-free method for trajectory optimization in end-to-end driving. It fits Robot Navigation and Test-Time Learning by adapting trajectory selection at inference time.
papers.title: DriveTTO: Understanding Search and Selection in Test-Time Trajectory Optimization for End-to-End Driving
papers.tldr: DriveTTO is a training-free test-time search method that refines driving trajectories to reduce failures caused by poor selection from fixed proposals.

papers.abstract: World-action models learn from future prediction, but accessing their future representations directly at test time can require costly frame generation. Methods that generate future frames before planning incur additional forward passes, while future co-training methods omit explicit future predictions at inference. We introduce \method, a planner that reads the hidden states of masked future tokens without decoding future frames. We pretrain MMaDA-Parallel-M on driving video using frame-level masked world modeling, which predicts a masked suffix of future frames and explicitly includes inputs with all future frames masked. Learned planning queries attend to these masked positions and the observed context, and a continuous head predicts the trajectory in the same forward pass. With a single front camera, \method reaches 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with an end-to-end latency of 60.3\,ms.
authors: Ziyu Zhao, Casey Sun, Zeyu Wang, Shicong Ma, Emily T Zhang, Cheng Lu
bullets: Addresses the inference cost of generating future frames before planning.
Pretrains a masked world model on driving video, including inputs where all future frames are masked.
Uses planning queries over masked future states and observed context, with a continuous trajectory head in one forward pass.
Achieves 92.0 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 89.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 using a single front camera.
Runs with 60.3 ms end-to-end latency.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based planners capture the multimodality of human driving behavior well, yet covariate shift in closed-loop driving can lead them to generate trajectories that result in collisions or road departures. Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning offers a promising way to tackle this issue, but applying it to diffusion-based planners is complicated by their iterative denoising process and receding-horizon execution. We find that small adjustments to the planned trajectories can prevent many of these unsafe outcomes. Motivated by this observation, we propose PlanNudge, which preserves the learned planning capabilities of a pretrained diffusion-based planner by freezing it and trains a lightweight policy that we call the nudge policy. At each planning step, the nudge policy outputs a nudge, a two-dimensional adjustment of the speed and curvature of the plan from the frozen planner. The nudge policy is a multilayer perceptron that predicts the nudge in a single forward pass, and both dimensions directly change the motion of the vehicle, so standard off-policy RL can train it in closed-loop simulation. We evaluate PlanNudge on nuPlan, a large-scale autonomous driving benchmark based on real-world driving data. In all six settings, PlanNudge matches or exceeds the final scores of the previous state-of-the-art RL finetuning method while using about one sixth as many environment steps and less than one fifth as much model compute. We also provide guidelines for reward shaping, value learning, and exploration when using off-policy RL to post-train autonomous driving planners. Our results are reported with means and standard deviations over six training runs. Project page: https://zerlinwang.github.io/plannudge/
authors: Zilin Wang, Guozheng Ma, Saeed Rahmani, Jiong Yang, Antyanta Bangunharcana, Yiluan Guo, Jakob Nicolaus Foerster, Shimon Whiteson
bullets: Diffusion planners model diverse driving behavior but can fail under closed-loop covariate shift, causing collisions or road departures.
The method freezes the pretrained planner and trains a lightweight MLP nudge policy to adjust each plan’s speed and curvature in one forward pass.
These direct trajectory adjustments make standard off-policy RL practical despite iterative denoising and receding-horizon execution.
On nuPlan’s six settings, PlanNudge matches or surpasses the prior RL fine-tuning method using roughly one-sixth the environment steps and less than one-fifth the model compute.
The paper also gives guidance on reward shaping, value learning, and exploration for off-policy RL planner post-training.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of PlanNudge. Starting from random noise, the frozen pretrained diffusion-based planner samples a base plan with K denoising steps. The nudge policy reads the ego state, the pooled scene features, and the beginning of the base plan, and outputs a bounded 2-D action, which the plan transform converts into a speed offset and a curvature offset of the base plan. The simulator follows the nudged plan for one replanning interval ∆t before it returns the next scene observation and the planner replans. Each transition is stored in a replay buffer. The diffusion-based planner is a part of the environment and is never called during RL agent updates.

papers.abstract: Marine robots face partial observability, non-stationary dynamics, and sparse communication, motivating WMs that learn compact predictive states for planning. This review develops a functional taxonomy of WMs for ocean engineering, focusing on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) and AdaJEPA's test-time adaptation within model predictive control, mapping them to navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring, and separating demonstrated evidence from prospective applications. The synthesis identifies key Gaps: benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, safe adaptation and proposes a research agenda for physics-informed, deployment-adaptive marine WMs validated through simulation and field missions.
authors: Basma Dokkara, Esteban W. G. Cluab, Luiz M. G. Goncalves, Paolo Spagnolo, Cosimo Distante
bullets: Marine robots must operate under partial observability, changing dynamics, and limited communication.
It provides a functional taxonomy spanning navigation, adaptive sampling, digital twins, and biodiversity monitoring.
The review focuses on JEPAs and AdaJEPA-style test-time adaptation integrated with model predictive control.
It distinguishes demonstrated evidence from prospective applications.
Key gaps include benchmarks, uncertainty calibration, and safe adaptation; it proposes physics-informed, deployment-adaptive validation in simulation and field missions.

papers.title: World Models for Ocean Engineering: A Critical Review of Maritime Autonomy, Adaptive Latent Prediction, Digital Twins, and Biodiversity Monitoring
papers.tldr: This review maps world models for ocean engineering, emphasizing predictive latent representations and safe adaptation while identifying gaps needed for reliable maritime autonomy.

papers.abstract: Searching from high altitude and navigating to a target instance specified by a reference image is a common application for UAVs. In such tasks, high-altitude observations provide broad ground coverage for efficient search, but targets occupy fewer pixels, making instance verification and action selection more difficult. We present AERIN, a visual world model that uses action-conditioned prediction to guide the UAV toward the target while adjusting its viewpoint to obtain higherquality observations for subsequent instance verification. Highaltitude navigation requires fine-grained target details and scene context relevant to visibility, but repeatedly predicting dense visual representations of this information is computationally expensive. AERIN addresses this challenge with a compact, fixedsize, target-conditioned latent state that separately represents both for efficient action evaluation. Experiments demonstrate that AERIN outperforms the evaluated baselines in target approach and observation quality, while requiring substantially less decision time than similar world models.
authors: Zhenzhen Jiao, Rui Tian, Zhineng Chen
bullets: High-altitude UAV search offers broad coverage but makes target recognition and action selection harder because targets appear small.
The model predicts action-conditioned outcomes to guide target approach and select viewpoints that improve subsequent observations.
AERIN uses a fixed-size latent state that separately encodes fine-grained target details and visibility-relevant scene context.
Experiments show better target approach and observation quality than evaluated baselines, with substantially lower decision time than similar world models.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of AERIN. Reference-conditioned visual features are aggregated into a compact state for action-conditioned prediction. Predicted observation gains guide action selection, followed by execution and replanning from the new observation.
