papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned visual world model for aerial instance navigation; directly fits learned navigation and interactive world modeling.
papers.title: AERIN: Aerial Instance Navigation with a Visual World Model
papers.tldr: AERIN uses a compact target-conditioned visual world model to help UAVs search from high altitude, approach image-specified targets, and adjust viewpoints for better verification.

papers.abstract: How much interaction experience is needed to distill a capable visual agent? We study learning from few tasks and recorded interaction histories. Our framework selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity. On-policy distillation (OPD) learns through fresh interaction on selected tasks or fresh student responses at fixed histories. Across Navigation, Sokoban, and spatial mapping, even one online training task supports transfer to other tasks. Four fixed trajectories raise a 4B student's success from 49.17% to 82.08% on standard Navigation and from 60.16% to 85.55% on Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured gap to a 27B teacher on these panels. On an independent Navigation panel, replay improves success from 45.83% to 76.67%, retaining 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new interaction during optimization. Training repetitions, matched supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and a 9B extension further support the value of compact experience.
authors: Siyu Zhou, Jing Jiang, Chengqi Zhang, Guodong Long
bullets: Studies how few tasks and recorded histories are needed to distill capable visual agents.
Selects representative trajectories using skill-context coverage and ordered visual-decision similarity.
Uses on-policy distillation with either fresh task interaction or student responses on fixed histories.
Four fixed trajectories substantially improve a 4B student on Navigation and Sokoban, recovering over 90% of the measured teacher gap on those panels.
Replay on an independent Navigation panel retains 91.36% of the same-task online gain without new optimization-time interaction.

papers.selection_reason: Distills visual navigation agents from limited interaction trajectories, directly relevant to embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Distilling Visual Agents from Limited Interaction Experience
papers.tldr: Compact, carefully selected interaction trajectories can distill strong visual-agent behavior from large teachers, enabling substantial cross-task gains with little or no new interaction.

papers.abstract: Mobile embodied agents continuously alter their observations through their own motion, while external dynamics further shape future interactions. Different mobile embodied tasks therefore capture complementary patterns of state evolution, yet jointly learning world dynamics across such interactions remains less explored. We investigate this problem through Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) and Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT), which respectively involve navigation toward a stationary goal and interaction with a moving target. We propose WorldWeave, a cross-task world model that couples shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation. Instead of conditioning state transitions on heterogeneous physical actions, WorldWeave learns latent actions from observed state changes via inverse-forward dynamics, establishing a shared transition representation across tasks. The resulting future-state predictions are adaptively integrated into task-specific representations for downstream decision making. Experiments across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over specialized baselines.
authors: Xuan Yao, Jiahao Zhang, Rongjunchen Zhang, Kaixuan Huang, Junyu Gao, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses underexplored cross-task world modeling for embodied agents whose actions and environments continually change future observations.
Uses inverse-forward dynamics to learn latent actions and a shared transition representation instead of relying on heterogeneous physical actions.
Combines shared predictive dynamics with task-specific adaptation for downstream navigation and tracking decisions.
Evaluations across multiple VLN and EVT benchmarks show consistent improvements over specialized baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of WORLDWEAVE. (b) Naive representation sharing creates cross-task trade-offs, which WORLDWEAVE mitigates through shared predictive dynamics and task-specific adaptation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a cross-task world model for embodied navigation that learns latent actions from state changes, bridging VLN and Embodied Visual Tracking.
papers.title: WorldWeave: Rethinking Embodied Navigation through Cross-Task World Modeling
papers.tldr: WorldWeave jointly learns transferable world dynamics from navigation and tracking tasks by inferring latent actions from observed state changes.

papers.abstract: This paper introduces LoKiTO, a 3D local kinodynamic trajectory optimizer that combines a Chebyshev polynomial parameterization with an online neural Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) representation for aerial robotics. While current gradient-based planners often struggle with the high memory requirements of explicit volumetric maps or fail to strictly enforce dynamic limits, LoKiTO embeds kinodynamic constraints directly into a modular cost function and exploits the numerical conditioning properties of the Chebyshev basis. Collision awareness is provided by a continuous, memory-efficient neural ESDF updated online from LiDAR measurements, which drastically reduces map memory consumption to approximately 1.0 MB. Benchmarking in highly cluttered simulated environments against state-of-the-art baselines (Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner) demonstrates the superiority of our approach. Experimental results show that LoKiTO achieves over 99.4% dynamic feasibility compliance, significantly outperforming the baselines, and maintaining higher median clearance from obstacles. By coupling a well-conditioned continuous parameterization with explicit kinodynamic reasoning, LoKiTO provides a practical and extensible basis for local replanning in aerial robotics.
authors: Guillermo Gil-Garcia, J. A. Cobano, L. Merino, F. Caballero
bullets: Addresses the memory demands of volumetric maps and weak enforcement of dynamic limits in gradient-based local planners.
Uses Chebyshev polynomial trajectory parameterization with kinodynamic constraints embedded in a modular cost function.
Maintains an online neural ESDF from LiDAR for continuous collision awareness with approximately 1.0 MB of map memory.
In cluttered simulations, achieves over 99.4% dynamic-feasibility compliance and higher median obstacle clearance than Fast-Planner and EGO-Planner.
Provides a practical and extensible framework for local UAV replanning; results are reported in simulation.

papers.selection_reason: Local kinodynamic trajectory optimization using a learned neural ESDF, fitting learning-based local planning and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: LoKiTO: Local Kinodynamic Trajectory Optimization for UAVs based on Memory-Efficient Neural Distance Fields
papers.tldr: LoKiTO enables memory-efficient, collision-aware UAV trajectory optimization with explicit kinodynamic constraints and strong feasibility in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: A policy that transfers from simulation to a lab robot often fails in the field. Calibrating a simulator from real-world data typically targets only a few hand-picked parameters, and even calibrated simulators fail to capture unmodeled dynamics, while environments reconstructed via onboard perception inherit sensing noise and artifacts. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), a framework based on conditional flow matching that infers online, directly from a robot's execution data, both simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity - the remaining dynamics discrepancy and the gap between perceived and true environment geometry. A simulation-trained anomaly detector determines when recalibration or fine-tuning is required using onboard sensory signals alone, while an exploration policy actively modulates posterior uncertainty using optimism in the face of uncertainty. Across five robot platforms with up to 39 calibrated parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain map, NFC achieves the most accurate posterior distributions compared to established simulation-based inference baselines. In physical outdoor experiments with a wheeled robot suffering an axle failure across snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC increases rough-terrain navigation success from 26% to 70% while reducing orientation jerk by 88%.
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real failures caused by incomplete dynamics models and noisy environment reconstruction.
Uses conditional flow matching to estimate physical parameters plus residual fidelity, including dynamics discrepancies and geometry errors.
A simulation-trained anomaly detector triggers recalibration, while uncertainty-driven exploration improves information gathering.
Across five robot platforms, NFC produced the most accurate posterior distributions among evaluated simulation-based inference baselines.
In outdoor tests with an axle failure, rough-terrain success rose from 26% to 70% and orientation jerk fell by 88%.

Only NFC singles out the front-left wheel with near-zero damping.

Figure 1: NFC-driven adaptation. (a) Residual fidelity: colored trajectories are calibrated-simulator rollouts, black is the real execution, their difference the residual dynamics; the circled terrain region marks uncertain perception, where NFC samples residual environments to reconstruct terrain variants. (b) Simulator calibration: flow matching infers physical parameters matching the real trajectory. (c) Informative adaptation: policy and NFC are pretrained in simulation and fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected.

papers.selection_reason: Online sim-to-real calibration for robot navigation using flow matching, directly fitting learning-based navigation and test-time adaptation.
papers.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration: Turning Field Anomalies into Simulation Fine-Tuning
papers.tldr: Neural Fidelity Calibration uses online execution data to jointly infer simulator parameters and unmodeled reality gaps, substantially improving robot navigation under changing terrain and hardware conditions.

papers.abstract: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.
authors: Mark Zhao, Pengcheng Wang, Rui Yang, Jiarui Yao, Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Bingxuan Li, Hanyang Chen, Ke Yang, Manling Li, Tong Zhang, Huan Zhang
bullets: Real-time games expose a harness limitation: agents may fail because the game continues while the model is deciding.
AutoPILOT supports primitive actions, open-loop macros, and closed-loop controllers that act until control is returned.
The authors introduce AFK-Bench, a suite of 120 diverse browser games playable with either real-time or paused clocks.
With GPT-6.1 Sol, AutoPILOT achieves 68.6% real-time success versus 38.3% for VISTA and matches VISTA’s final success at one-fifth the API cost.
Results across models suggest that converting model outputs into temporally extended actions is a central part of agent design.

papers.selection_reason: Presents AutoPILOT, a visual agent harness that enables models to generate actions, open-loop macros, and closed-loop controllers within a single call, significantly improving real-time performance in games.
papers.title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay
papers.tldr: AutoPILOT improves multimodal game-playing agents in real-time settings by letting each model call produce sustained, screen-based controllers rather than only one action.

papers.abstract: In NAVSIMv1, the standard benchmark for end-to-end driving, $89.6\%$ of the test scenes lie within 4m of a training scene. We show that this geographic overlap inflates the reported scores. We propose a geographically disjoint split of NAVSIMv1 and an evaluation that compares models trained on either split on the same scenes, which neither has seen in training. All sensor-based models we test, DiffusionDrive, Latent TransFuser, and DrivoR, lose 3.4 to 6.1 PDMS points on these scenes, mainly by leaving the road and coming close to other objects, against 1.5 points for a baseline without sensors. The loss concentrates where a training drive of the original split passed the same place. At all other places, models trained on the original split are no better than those trained on the geographic split. Models trained on the original split predict road geometry that no camera can see. The gap persists when the auxiliary map loss is removed, so the models memorize locations even without being supervised to. On nuScenes, the geographic split cuts SparseDrive's mapping accuracy by $59\%$ and also degrades its planning. Driving scores on logged scenes thus partly measure how well a model remembers the test locations. We release the split to evaluate generalization to new places.
authors: Willi Poh, Kevin R\"osch, Christoph Stiller
bullets: 89.6% of NAVSIMv1 test scenes are within 4 m of a training scene.
A geographically disjoint split evaluates models only on places unseen during training.
Sensor-based models lose 3.4–6.1 PDMS points on disjoint scenes, mainly due to road departures and near-collisions.
The performance gap is concentrated where the original training data passed the same locations; elsewhere, the splits perform similarly.
Models infer unseen road geometry and retain location memorization even without auxiliary map supervision; similar degradation appears for SparseDrive on nuScenes.

papers.selection_reason: Exposes geographic overfitting in end-to-end driving benchmarks, directly relevant to learned navigation and planning.
papers.title: Don't Test Where You Trained: Geographic Overlap Inflates End-to-End Driving Scores
papers.tldr: Geographic overlap between training and test scenes substantially inflates end-to-end driving scores by enabling models to memorize locations rather than generalize to new places.

papers.abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.
authors: Binay Kumar Singh, Niels Da Vitoria Lobo
bullets: Formalizes USR and five desiderata, relating it to representations including BEV features, occupancy, maps, neural fields, scene graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents.
Provides a sensor-to-decision taxonomy covering sensing platforms, cross-view matching, fusion, geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models.
Compiles 26 urban datasets and simulators spanning ego, V2X, aerial, trajectory, and language settings, alongside metrics, benchmark results, trends, and coverage gaps.
Introduces USR-5, a proposed five-test protocol and aggregate score for evaluating whether representations are genuinely shared across platforms and tasks.
Highlights open problems in cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance.

papers.abstract: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.
authors: Shahab Salehi, Luca Lusvarghi, Miguel Sepulcre, Javier Gozalvez
bullets: Evaluates five interaction-aware Transformer trajectory prediction models under noisy position, heading, and speed estimates.
Prediction accuracy can degrade by up to 6× as noise increases, exposing a deployment–training mismatch.
Retraining on realistic noise-augmented data is more effective than adding input denoising modules.
Noise-augmented retraining limits degradation to below 1.5×.
The augmented dataset is released openly for further research.

papers.abstract: When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next. We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner. A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route. We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction. We compare four interfaces. The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes. The third is an outcome model that predicts the feasibility and travel time of each route. The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the chance of success and the travel time of the robot on each terrain and composes them along a route. All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard. Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard. At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7-8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35-36% on H1 compared with the plain policy. Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target. Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
bullets: Robot damage changes which routes are feasible and how much risk is acceptable per mission.

papers.abstract: Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains. To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch. However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch. To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective. Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other's latest update. Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion. Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines. Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.

bullets: Addresses mismatch between nominal and actual vehicle dynamics during on-track racing.

papers.abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models' general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR's HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.
authors: Yun Yan, Shizhi Hu, Zhichao Li, Yang Guan, Shiqi Liu, Jiaxin Gao, Xiangteng Zhang, Wenbo Ding, Jiuhua Zhao, Hui Guo, Xintao Yan, Keqiang Li, Shengbo Eben Li

papers.abstract: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner's facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner's facts remains unresolved.
authors: Gautam Kumar Jain, Atharva Mahindrakar, Shubham Phoolari, Ignacio Alvarez, Carsten Markgraf, Constanze Hungar, Christoph Lauer, Julian Staehler

papers.abstract: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.

bullets: TDMA communication delay grows with swarm size and causes collisions through stale neighbor estimates at the safety filter.
Without delay, up to 100-agent swarms remain collision-free; delays beyond roughly 125–175 ms, or 75–100 ms with held measurement noise at 100 agents, can break safety.
At the mean-field layer, delay mainly increases density noise and reduces throughput by at most about one tenth, without biasing local density.
Lightweight neighbor-position predictors restore safety and extend tolerated communication periods by about 1.4–2.3×, depending on predictor and noise conditions.
Prediction should be enabled only beyond the uncompensated safety limit, because its estimation errors can otherwise introduce collisions; widening safety margins performs worse in bottlenecks.

papers.abstract: Human driving logs record only one trajectory per scene, leaving other feasible driving choices without explicit trajectory targets or quality labels. This limits supervision for end-to-end planners that generate and refine multiple candidate trajectories. Meanwhile, conditioning refinement on a large vision-language model adds substantial online inference cost. We propose DriveSTA, which extends autoregressive proposal generation and proposal-conditioned residual flow refinement with scored trajectory alternatives. For each training scene, we generate alternatives offline through smooth deformations of the recorded trajectory and evaluate their simulated execution against logged traffic. Diverse, high-quality alternatives supervise distinct proposals and define residual targets for quality-guided denoising, while candidates spanning the full score range train a scorer to assess driving quality. A shared joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), adapted through masked video-feature prediction, encodes observed frames once and provides temporal context for both refinement and scoring. On NAVSIM v1 Navtest, DriveSTA ranks first among the compared planners trained on NAVSIM data alone. With expanded training data, DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art results among the compared methods on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, while reducing mean planner forward-pass latency by 73% relative to ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.
authors: Xinyao Rao, Zecheng Tang, Liuxuan Sun, Zheyuan Lai, Minjun Yu, Xun Cao, Wei Li
bullets: Addresses the lack of quality-labeled alternative trajectories in single-trajectory human driving logs.
Generates alternatives by smoothly deforming logged trajectories and scoring their simulated execution against traffic.
Uses scored alternatives to supervise proposal generation, residual-flow refinement, and trajectory-quality scoring.
A shared JEPA-based video encoder provides temporal context for refinement and scoring without costly online vision-language-model conditioning.

Ranks first among compared NAVSIM-only planners; DriveSTA-Scale achieves state-of-the-art compared results on Navtest and closed-loop HUGSIM, with 73% lower mean forward-pass latency than ChainFlow-VLA in matched evaluations.

papers.abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.
authors: GiHyun Kim, JinMo Yang, Hyung-Sin Kim
bullets: Addresses the tradeoff between light collection and motion blur in robot-camera depth sensing.
Uses a frozen depth model and a learned predictor of reference-relative disagreement to score candidate camera settings without ground truth at deployment.
A contextual Gaussian-process controller selects subsequent exposure and gain using recent scores plus motion, camera, and illumination context.
Evaluated across nine scene-illumination conditions, it reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned Abs_rel by 14.6% versus built-in auto-exposure and 10.0% versus the best evaluated prior controller.
Demonstrates online control on a mobile robot with the affine-invariant Depth Anything v2 variant.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models have recently attracted increasing attention in motion planning due to their ability to model high-dimensional and multi-modal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion-based planners still struggle to reliably satisfy geometric feasibility in unseen cluttered environments with complex obstacle layouts. To address this challenge, we propose GeoSDF-Diff, a geometry-aware diffusion planner that incorporates multi-scale SDF conditioning into trajectory denoising. The key idea is to provide the denoiser with both route-level geometric context and fine local clearance evidence, enabling generated trajectories to better adapt to unseen complex obstacle layouts. Specifically, a Geometric Encoder extracts multi-scale SDF features and injects them into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention. We further introduce a trajectory-level training objective that combines SDF clearance, violation emphasis, smoothness, and path-length regularization, so that local infeasibilities are penalized during training rather than corrected only at inference time. Experiments on held-out cluttered environments show that, without post-hoc trajectory repair or sampling-time guidance, GeoSDF-Diff achieves a 65.2% average success rate across diverse test scenarios, outperforming strong diffusion baselines by 25.4% to 28.5%.
authors: Yueming Li, Zhanjiang Yang, Yang Shen, Meng Li, Lijun Sun
bullets: Addresses unreliable collision-free planning in complex, unseen obstacle layouts.
Encodes route-level and local geometric information using multi-scale signed distance fields (SDFs).
Injects SDF features into a DiT-X denoiser through cross-attention.
Uses a trajectory-level objective combining clearance, violation, smoothness, and path-length terms.
Achieves a 65.2% average success rate without post-hoc repair or sampling-time guidance, outperforming diffusion baselines by 25.4–28.5%.

papers.abstract: A planner deciding whether to turn left or continue straight needs to inspect different parts of the scene for each maneuver. Yet many end-to-end driving planners evaluate every candidate trajectory against the same compressed scene representation. We let each candidate select the visual evidence used to refine and score it. A global glance first produces trajectory hypotheses from shared scene features. We then project a corridor around each trajectory into the camera views and use the resulting mask to attend to patch features at the backbone's native resolution. After refinement, the scorer projects each final proposal again and ranks it using evidence along its own path. This geometric selection requires only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration. On three planners with different scene representations (learned registers, a perception-supervised bird's-eye-view grid, and a coarse image-token grid), adding this gaze improves planning scores. In ablations, path-aligned patches outperform both a matched number of randomly selected patches and attention over all patches. Using the gaze for ranking yields larger gains than using it for refinement alone. With a ViT-S backbone and no perception labels, GGDriver achieves a rater feedback score of 8.110 on the WOD-E2E test set, 94.2 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1, 48.6 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, and a closed-loop Driving Score of 72.18 on Bench2Drive.
authors: Jiawei Sun, Maosen Li, Jiamin Shi, Xiaoxu Zheng, Jiun Tian Hoe, Yechao Bai, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of scoring all trajectories from the same compressed scene representation.
Generates trajectory hypotheses from shared features, then uses trajectory-aligned camera corridors to select native-resolution patch features.
Refines and ranks each proposal using visual evidence specific to its path, requiring only the predicted trajectory and camera calibration.
Across three planner representations, path-aligned gaze improves planning scores and outperforms random or all-patch attention.
Ranking with gaze provides larger gains than refinement alone; the method operates without perception labels and reports results on WOD-E2E, NAVSIM, and Bench2Drive.

papers.abstract: Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $\gamma$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.
authors: Xiaotao Zhang, Lin Qian, Hao Zhang, Xuanrui Cui, Yuehao Huang, Yunzi Wu, Yucheng Deng, Jiankun Dong, Hujun Yin, Xinhai Li, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li

Enables program refinement and policy learning from tool traces, with shared task-goal criteria for evaluation.
Benchmarks representative agents and demonstrates contact-data collection and trace-informed program revision; the abstract does not report quantitative results.

papers.abstract: Driving world-action models generate planned trajectories through iterative action denoising, with each update depending on the preceding state. This sequential dependency incurs substantial inference latency, limiting timely planning. Speculative inference offers an opportunity to reduce this latency by predicting future denoising states for parallel target evaluation, but requires efficient proposal generation and suitable verification for continuous actions. We present Trailblazer-F, a speculative action-flow inference framework in which a lightweight drafter acts as a trailblazer, charting a candidate denoising path through the compact, structured waypoint space so that the target model can verify multiple steps in parallel and advance with fewer sequential updates. Our method maintains planning quality while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.Across all 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, Trailblazer-F maintains near-baseline planning performance, with PDMS changes of +0.04 and -0.08 points for SimWAM and DriveWAM, respectively. Paired inference measurements on an NVIDIA L20 GPU yield 2.31x and 1.55x speedups. Real-vehicle experiments on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin further demonstrate 1.96x and 1.37x speedups, together with close qualitative trajectory agreement with native sampling. our code is here https://github.com/DanileHaibo/Trailblazer-F
authors: Haibo Hu, Lianming Huang, Qiao Li, Nan Guan, Chun Jason Xue

Uses a lightweight drafter to predict candidate paths in compact waypoint space while keeping the pretrained target model frozen.
Enables the target model to verify multiple denoising steps in parallel.
Across 12,146 NAVSIM v1 navtest scenes, PDMS changed by only +0.04 for SimWAM and −0.08 for DriveWAM.
Achieves 2.31×/1.55× speedups on an NVIDIA L20 and 1.96×/1.37× on Jetson AGX Orin, with close qualitative trajectory agreement.

papers.abstract: Vision-model-based robotic navigation has gained increasing popularity, yet existing approaches still struggle to deliver effective and efficient navigation performance, \textit{e.g.}, diffusion-based policies that require costly iterative denoising. In this work, we propose three improvements to bridge these gaps. First, we adopt a rectified flow framework to reduce the required inference steps to one while achieving comparable or even superior performance. Second, we leverage a bidirectional Mamba-based visual encoder that employs selective state-space modeling to more effectively capture bidirectional temporal dependencies across observation frames, even with longer input sequences. Most importantly, we find that na\"{i}vely combining these two components to balance accuracy with inference speed yields no further performance gains or even produces inferior results. Upon extensive analysis, we realized that the root cause lies in the fact that the Hydra-derived temporal context is shared unchanged across all flow timesteps, and timestep information is introduced only within the velocity network. This weak coupling limits the model's ability to adaptively exploit temporal visual features at different flow states. To address this, we propose a feature-wise timestep conditioning design that explicitly conditions the visual embedding on the flow timestep, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation, thereby restoring a meaningful gradient pathway and enabling coherent interaction between the rectified flow and the temporal encoder. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms both baseline and competitive methods.
authors: Xiaogang Wang, Debasish Mishra, Jia Hao Toh, Wangsheng Liu, Yash Shah
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of diffusion-based robotic navigation policies that require iterative denoising.
Uses rectified flow to reduce inference to one step and a bidirectional Mamba-based encoder to capture temporal dependencies across observations.
Finds that simply combining these components can hurt performance because temporal features are shared unchanged across flow timesteps.
Introduces feature-wise timestep conditioning of visual embeddings, enabling noise-level-aware trajectory generation and stronger interaction between the encoder and flow model.
Experiments across multiple datasets show consistent gains over baseline and competing methods, though specific metrics are not reported.

papers.abstract: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0x/1.25x speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return -- not blind IMU drift suppression - and uncover a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.
bullets: Position-dependent dark zones require active probing, unlike timed outages where hovering is effective; the two appear identical when vision is first lost.

The module interfaces with an unchanged host controller and combines loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height correction, and an optional prior-map branch.
On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark with 1,920 flights, the full configuration achieved 88.5% worst-condition completion and outperformed the reported baselines.
Attached to SimpleFlight without retraining, it improved worst-condition completion to 86.5% and achieved 90% completion across tested speed conditions with no hard failures.
Diagnostics indicate that recovery depends primarily on asymmetric visual-inertial re-acquisition at vision return, with a bias-drift map crossover confirmed on held-out EuRoC windows.

papers.abstract: Language models may enable general autonomy in robot planning, but onboard their reasoning can run for most of a minute while the robot and nearby pedestrians keep moving. The robot must then decide how long to follow a plan that the pending answer may overturn. Here we present staleness deadlines, which hand that decision to the robot's clock. Calibrated prediction regions for pedestrians and deviation tubes for the robot set the deadline. When the language model answers, a graph planner rebuilds the route, which the robot adopts only after it passes the same clearance check against walls and predicted pedestrians. Exact binomial tests determine which prespecified budget-selection policies keep close calls, wrong decisions and late arrivals below their targets at each inference profile. Candidate policies either fix one budget or set each query's budget from how long the robot can continue its plan before it must brake. We study corridor signs that close routes and delivery requests whose destination the language model must infer. In 81,000 simulated missions with recorded Qwen3-4B answers, full reasoning cuts wrong decisions about twentyfold, and tracking until the deadline cuts late arrivals by up to 64%. The robot never collides while it moves, although pedestrians who never yield still walk into the stopped robot in 23% of offline and 32% of live missions. On a Jetson AGX Orin under perception load, short budgets fail the wrong-decision target, and full reasoning the lateness target. Between these extremes, a fixed-budget policy passes for corridor signs and per-query policies pass for deliveries. Live Orin runs match offline replay on all three losses in 24 of the 32 missions where either run records a loss. The deadline turns slower reasoning into measurable mission outcomes, which let designers test how much reasoning each inference profile can support.
bullets: The problem is that onboard language-model inference can take nearly a minute while the robot and pedestrians continue moving.
Calibrated pedestrian prediction regions and robot deviation tubes define when the current plan becomes unsafe to keep following.
After the model responds, a graph planner rebuilds the route and accepts it only after checking clearance from walls and predicted pedestrians.
Across 81,000 simulated missions, full reasoning reduced wrong decisions about twentyfold, while deadline-based tracking reduced late arrivals by up to 64%.
Fixed budgets worked for corridor-sign tasks, whereas per-query budgets worked for delivery tasks; stopped robots were still entered by non-yielding pedestrians in some missions.

papers.abstract: Kinodynamic motion planning in large-scale, cluttered environments remains challenging, as dynamically feasible, collision-free trajectories must be computed efficiently over long horizons. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) can strategically explore long-horizon alternatives but faces large branching factors in continuous control spaces and often relies on random default-policy rollouts, whereas Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) efficiently optimizes local trajectories yet remains susceptible to obstacle-induced local minima. To overcome these challenges, we propose Search-Informed MPPI (SI-MPPI), a unified framework that embeds MPPI trajectory optimization within MCTS-based tree search. The core concept is to fuse the expansion and default-policy simulation stages of MCTS into a single MPPI expansion stage guided by structured intermediate targets, termed baits. During each expansion, an adaptive bait-handling rule retains geometrically valid baits as local targets for GPU-batched MPPI optimizations that generate dynamically feasible candidate motion segments. Feasibility gating then checks these candidates for collision safety and sufficient progress, and top-$k$ selection admits the lowest-cost accepted candidates as tree edges, yielding sparse, directed tree growth; thereafter, effective sample size (ESS)-guided adaptation warm-starts subsequent expansions, while cost-based backpropagation updates tree statistics. Extensive simulations across four large-scale, cluttered 2D occupancy-grid maps demonstrate that SI-MPPI consistently produces the smallest search trees and smoothest angular control profiles compared with three kinodynamic baselines, while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths. Ablation results further highlight the importance of GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and retaining multiple expansion candidates for planning efficiency and robustness.
bullets: Addresses MCTS’s continuous-control branching and random rollouts alongside MPPI’s vulnerability to obstacle-induced local minima.
Uses structured intermediate targets (“baits”) to guide GPU-batched MPPI expansions within an MCTS tree.
Applies feasibility gating and top-k selection to create sparse, directed tree growth, with ESS-guided warm starts and cost-based backpropagation.
Across four large 2D occupancy-grid maps, it produced smaller trees and smoother angular controls than three kinodynamic baselines while maintaining competitive planning times and path lengths.
Ablations identified GPU batching, adaptive bait handling, and multiple retained candidates as important for efficiency and robustness.

papers.abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by $29$ and $50$, sampling-based planners by $35$ and MPPI by $7$ percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4\% of MPPI.
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath, Anindita Ghosh, Uttaran Bhattacharya, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of long-horizon planning, where sampling methods struggle and gradient methods can get trapped in local minima.
Uses Sequential Monte Carlo to evolve action-sequence populations through intermediate target distributions with importance weighting and resampling.
Combines SMC population updates with gradient-based plan optimization in learned latent world models.
Introduces a PDE-derived cost-to-go to guide sampling using latent-state-space structure.
On visual and proprioceptive navigation/manipulation tasks, improves average success rates over gradient-based, sampling-based, and MPPI planners, with competitive iteration counts.

papers.abstract: Active geo-localization (AGL) asks an agent to navigate a small aerial search grid and reach a target specified by an aerial image, a ground-level photograph, or text. Existing methods align the goal modalities well, but they keep the navigation state inside a large sequential Transformer and train with a dense distance reward that uses the hidden goal location. This paper proposes EAGLE, an Explicit spatial-belief Agent for Geo-Localization and Exploration. Offline training jointly optimizes a teacher-conditioned Swin branch and a context-free Swin student from the same randomly masked partial mosaics. The teacher branch attends to frozen full-scene context extracted by Qwen2.5-VL-7B, both branches receive masked-cell aerial-feature reconstruction and uncertainty supervision, while the student additionally distills stop-gradient feature predictions from the teacher. After distillation, Qwen, its cached context, and the teacher-attention branch are discarded. The retained student predicts cell-level aerial-feature embeddings and predictive uncertainty from partial observations alone. These predictions are combined with the modality-aligned goal embedding and a trajectory-derived visitation mask to construct the spatial belief tensor. The student is then frozen while a compact CNN actor-critic is optimized with PPO. EAGLE achieves state-of-the-art average success rates of 78.1%, 76.4%, and 76.8% on MASA, xBD zero-shot transfer, and the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split, respectively, without using a VLM or cached visual tokens at inference. Code will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses AGL state representation by replacing implicit sequential Transformer memory with explicit cell-level spatial beliefs.
Trains a Swin teacher–student system on masked aerial mosaics using reconstruction, uncertainty supervision, and feature distillation from frozen Qwen2.5-VL context.
Combines student predictions, the aligned goal embedding, and visitation history into a spatial belief tensor.
Freezes the student and trains a compact CNN actor–critic with PPO for navigation.
Reports average success rates of 78.1% on MASA, 76.4% on xBD zero-shot transfer, and 76.8% on the MM-GAG zero-shot aerial-goal split; inference uses no VLM or cached visual tokens.

papers.abstract: Large-scale applications of lifelong multi-agent path finding (LMAPF) call for computationally inexpensive movement decisions under changing traffic conditions and across varied layouts. We propose a navigation policy in which a convolutional network computes a shared spatial field over the map once per timestep and a compact goal-conditioned operator derives agents' movement preferences. The complete policy is trained end-to-end using average-reward reinforcement learning with throughput as the reward, without planner demonstrations or a separate online path planner. For structured and unstructured layouts, we train one policy per class on pools of small maps and deploy each without retraining on larger, unseen layouts and agent populations. Across six layouts with 10,000 agents, our policies achieve throughput comparable to or higher than the strongest evaluated baselines. The proposed method has an average execution time below 10 ms per step, more than an order of magnitude faster than several established planners.
bullets: Targets scalable movement decisions under changing traffic and varied map layouts.
Computes one shared convolutional spatial field per timestep, then derives compact goal-conditioned movement preferences for each agent.
Trains end-to-end with average-reward reinforcement learning using throughput, without planner demonstrations or a separate online planner.
Policies trained on small-map pools transfer to larger unseen layouts and populations; across six layouts with 10,000 agents, throughput is comparable to or better than evaluated baselines.
Runs in under 10 ms per step on average, though policies are trained separately for structured and unstructured layout classes.

papers.abstract: Policy representations in reinforcement learning have expanded beyond Gaussian policies to diffusion and flow-matching based generative policies. However, existing RL methods remain representation-specific, lacking a unified optimization interface for emerging generative policies. In particular, extending likelihood-based objectives to multi-step generative policies couples optimization to their internal generation process, where accumulated likelihood ratios can weaken the update signal. Meanwhile, generative-policy-specific methods often rely on multi-candidate generation and critic-based selection, improving overall return while providing limited improvement to the policy itself. We introduce DR-APO (Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization), which decouples policy improvement from policy representation through advantage-guided target improvement and representation-compatible direct action fitting, providing a shared optimization principle for Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies. Across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks, DR-APO remains competitive with SAC for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for both diffusion and flow-matching policies. NavDP post-training improves the Success Rate (SR) from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation. These results demonstrate a unified policy-improvement principle across Gaussian, diffusion, and flow policies, from continuous-control learning to embodied-policy post-training.
bullets: Addresses weakened update signals and representation-specific objectives in multi-step generative policies.
Uses advantage-guided target improvement with representation-compatible direct action fitting.
Matches SAC competitively for Gaussian policies and achieves the best aggregate policy-only performance for diffusion and flow policies across five MuJoCo-v5 tasks.
Post-training NavDP raises navigation success from 70.33% to 89.55% in simulation and from 25% to 65% in real-world navigation.
Demonstrates applicability from continuous control to embodied-policy post-training.

papers.abstract: This paper addresses the finite-budget exposure-aware informative path planning (IPP) problem for a fleet of mobile sensing agents. The agents map an unknown scalar field while limiting exposure to high field intensity. Existing IPP methods optimize informativeness under motion or resource constraints, but do not address field exposure constraints. We formulate exposure-aware IPP (EA-IPP) as a scalarized bi-objective belief-state Markov decision process that trades the normalized Gaussian-process (GP) information gain against a normalized measurement-derived fleet exposure index. A parameter-shared proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework with decentralized actors and a centralized fleet critic is trained offline and evaluated on unseen fields. Across the radar, plume, and wildfire field families, the EA-IPP agent achieves the lowest GP reconstruction RMSE among the evaluated baselines while retaining D-optimal information within $10\%$ of the non-learning information baseline. The minimum field exposure is approximately $34.6\%$, $20.1\%$, and $27\%$ below the non-exposure-aware baseline for radar, plume, and wildfire, respectively.
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi, Yihui Mao, James W. Cross, Kyle Volle, Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
bullets: Formulates exposure-aware informative path planning as a scalarized bi-objective belief-state MDP.
Uses parameter-shared PPO with decentralized actors and a centralized fleet critic, trained offline and tested on unseen fields.
Balances normalized Gaussian-process information gain with a measurement-derived fleet exposure index.
Across radar, plume, and wildfire fields, achieves the lowest reported GP reconstruction RMSE among evaluated baselines while retaining D-optimal information within 10% of a non-learning baseline.
Reduces minimum field exposure by approximately 34.6% for radar, 20.1% for plume, and 27% for wildfire relative to a non-exposure-aware baseline.

papers.abstract: We ask how far a driving model can get with one camera and real-time latency. BADAS-3.0 is a 1B-parameter video encoder with four small heads. From two seconds of one forward camera, it predicts the current speed, the metric path just driven, a collision-risk score and six candidate futures over 6.4 seconds, in under 50 ms. Given the car's current speed, BADAS-3.0 has 44% lower minADE$_6$ over five trajectory benchmarks than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, which reads six cameras and runs over 100x slower. The gain comes from camera rigs that neither model was trained on. On the rig they share, the two are on par. Existing benchmarks are mostly nominal driving, so we add two open-loop safety benchmarks, one of real dashcam collisions and near-misses and one of Euro NCAP scenarios. On both, BADAS-3.0 has a higher pass rate than every published planner we tested.
authors: Roni Goldshmidt, Hamish Scott, Lorenzo Niccolini
bullets: Uses two seconds of video to predict speed, past metric path, collision risk, and six 6.4-second future trajectories.
Runs in under 50 ms with a 1B-parameter encoder and four lightweight heads.

Introduces two open-loop safety benchmarks covering real dashcam incidents and Euro NCAP scenarios.
Achieves a higher pass rate than every tested published planner on both safety benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Off-road vision-language-action (VLA) models generate scene-conditioned plans, but frequent trajectory updates can repeatedly invoke expensive multimodal inference. Reusing a prediction reduces this demand while leaving its commands exposed to changes in vehicle motion. FastRoverVLA addresses this mismatch by decoupling visual plan generation from motion-conditioned execution. Its training-free interface maintains decoded plans between visual predictions. A speed-curvature action buffer is aligned with measured motion at each update, integrated into a local trajectory, and advanced by consuming the current action. The corrected remainder is written back to the buffer, preserving motion corrections across successive updates. A bounded refresh rule normalizes speed and curvature variations within a newly decoded plan and assigns a short or long reuse budget according to the resulting plan-roughness score. The interface requires neither backbone features nor an additional learned driving policy. Over a 3 s horizon, independent real-request evaluation achieves average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) of 0.328/0.596 m on ORAD-3D and 0.266/0.526 m on RELLIS-3D, reducing FDE by 18.0% and 36.7% at request rates of 6.0% and 4.8%, respectively. These runs retain lower errors across four backbones and both datasets and reduce Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by factors of 16.6 and 20.8 under serial replay, while mechanism and motion-only controls identify persistent state correction as the main source of the observed accuracy benefit. The source code and evaluation materials are publicly available at https://github.com/ADEPT-ORG/FastRoverVLA.
authors: Changtao Zhao, Yingxue Guan, Li Wang, Shijie Zhao, Yuhang Zhang, Shengkai Zhang, Qing Wang, Ziying Song
bullets: Addresses the cost of frequent multimodal inference and the risk that reused commands become misaligned with vehicle motion.
Uses a training-free action buffer that aligns speed-curvature commands with measured motion, advances execution, and preserves corrections across updates.
Refreshes plans using a bounded rule based on plan roughness, without backbone features or an additional learned driving policy.
Over a 3 s horizon, it reports lower trajectory errors across four backbones on ORAD-3D and RELLIS-3D, with FDE reductions of 18.0% and 36.7% at the evaluated request rates.
Reduces Qwen3-VL request-processing cost by 16.6× and 20.8× under serial replay; controls attribute the accuracy gains mainly to persistent state correction.

papers.abstract: Tight-space navigation requires a robot to clear obstacles and stop inside its goal despite uncertainty. We present GeoDiff, a motion-program planner coupling original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, and factored proof compilation. An exact feasible-translation characterization guides repair; request-local reuse reduces repeated geometric work. We establish conditions for compiler equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness. Across 11,440 floorplan-derived jobs, GeoDiff certifies 61/139 tasks at 5-cm tolerance within 15 s, versus 44/139 for the stop-set baseline. The strongest observed external certificate adapter certifies 13/139 tasks from 119/139 native routes, separating route availability from certification. On tasks derived from public BARN maps, GeoDiff certifies 202/270 at 5-cm tolerance for a Jackal-shaped body, versus 3/270 for the portal baseline. Development analyses distinguish emitter savings from solver coverage, and 1,420 route-tracking episodes characterize the execution interface. These results show how terminal reasoning and proof reuse increase finite-budget certification coverage while preserving the original physical task and goal.
authors: Runtian Zheng, Congpeng Zhang, Ying Liu
bullets: Addresses navigation under uncertainty where a robot must both clear obstacles and stop within its goal.
Combines original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, exact feasible-translation characterization, and request-local proof reuse.
Establishes compiler-equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness conditions.
Certifies 61/139 floorplan-derived jobs versus 44/139 for a stop-set baseline, and 202/270 BARN-derived tasks versus 3/270 for a portal baseline at 5-cm tolerance.
Results focus on finite-budget certification coverage and distinguish route availability from external certification.

papers.abstract: Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) requires trajectories that avoid environmental obstacles and collisions between robots in a shared workspace. Diffusion-based planners often address obstacle avoidance through sampling-time guidance, while some conditioned approaches aggregate map geometry into a global representation. We present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a map-conditioned trajectory generator for multi-robot planning. SCTD retains multiple position-aware occupancy tokens accessed through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net, with hard endpoint inpainting enforcing start and goal states. One model trained on single-robot demonstrations across procedural environments generates obstacle-aware trajectories without sampling-time obstacle-cost guidance. High-level Conflict-Based Search (CBS) coordinates these trajectories through constrained replanning, retaining inter-agent guidance during sampling and reusing the model across workspace layouts and team sizes. Experiments assess single-robot success and trajectory quality, generalization to unfamiliar layouts with added obstacles, and coordinated multi-robot planning. On 15,000 held-out tasks, SCTD achieves higher success than the evaluated guided diffusion baseline, with the largest gains on hard-detour tasks, while trajectory-quality comparisons show smoother trajectories. Conditioning ablations show higher success with spatial tokens than with a global map embedding, and map-replacement tests demonstrate dependence on the supplied geometry. The resulting multi-robot system achieves higher team success than the compared diffusion baselines, with experiments covering teams of up to 15 robots.
authors: Yefim Nudelman, Dor Atzmon, Tom Tirer
bullets: Targets multi-robot motion planning with obstacle avoidance and collision-free coordination.
Uses position-aware occupancy tokens throughout a temporal U-Net and hard inpainting for start and goal states.
Trains on single-robot demonstrations and reuses one model across layouts and team sizes; CBS handles inter-robot conflicts.
Outperforms the evaluated guided diffusion baseline in held-out success, especially on hard-detour tasks, while producing smoother trajectories.
Ablations support spatial conditioning and map dependence; experiments cover teams of up to 15 robots.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Training and inference of the map-conditioned trajectory diffuser. During training, the temporal U-Net predicts noise added to normalized expert trajectories, conditioned on spatial occupancy-map tokens and the diffusion timestep. Endpoints are fixed by inpainting and excluded from the loss. During single-agent inference, map tokens depend only on the map and are therefore identical at every reverse step; endpoints are restored after every update. The raw trajectory is converted back to world coordinates without static-obstacle-cost guidance or a separate smoother; this describes the single-agent pipeline, not the multi-agent system. Start/goal markers on the maps are illustrative only.

Figure 4: Trajectory examples for MPD and SCTD on selected tasks in MMD’s Conveyor (a) and Highways (b) environments. The map-conditional model (SCTD) handles new obstacles better than a model that relies on guidance (MPD).

Figure 2: The occupancy encoder Eϕ and its two-stage training. A binary occupancy map is converted into 256 position-aware, 64-dimensional tokens. These tokens condition the denoiser through cross-attention and retain spatial structure instead of compressing the map into a single global vector. In Stage 1 (bottom), the convolutional stem is pretrained to predict clipped analytic signed distances at sampled workspace points using an auxiliary head and an L1 loss. The head is then discarded, and the stem is finetuned jointly with the denoiser in Stage 2 (top). Analytic SDF supplies supervision only; occupancy is the planner’s only learned environmental input. Token and SDF illustrations are schematic; ⊕ denotes concatenation. Additional head and sampling details appear in Appendix A.

papers.abstract: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.
authors: Xiaoxin Mi, Zhen Cao, Chong Liu, Yuhao Li, Zhen Dong, Bisheng Yang, Yang Jia, Shengwu Xiong
bullets: Addresses gaps in existing datasets, including limited semantic richness, modality diversity, and scenario complexity.

Supports research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction, road mapping, topology reasoning, map updating, and street-scene generation.

papers.abstract: A collision-free detour can still bring a legged robot to the next stair or ledge a few centimetres or degrees off, and a fixed locomotion skill, factory or learned, can stall or fall. Existing methods prevent this with a robot model or extensive trial and error, but on a new site with unknown skills neither is available, so they cannot be used. We find that a single 27-minute teaching session already supplies what these methods have to derive or learn: for every stair and ledge, one crossing the skill has completed. Our method, passage-conditioned navigation, makes the route remember how each transition was entered, not only where the path went. It stores each taught crossing as an event and, without training or a robot model, enforces it after every local replan: before each ledge, an entry gate makes the robot turn or back up and retry if it is more than 10 cm or 10{\deg} off the taught crossing. Under localization noise, with path, gait schedule, and sensing unchanged, this raises the share of disturbed ledge crossings that stay within these limits from 24.1% to 88.6%. In contact simulation with our learned policies, a robot pushed off course before stairs never falls in 180 climbs, against 9 falls when the stored direction is ignored; pushed 1.2 m away, it rejoins the route, ending on average 0.14 m from it (1.10 m without rejoining), and finishes as often as an undisturbed robot. This suits any robot with fixed skills that repeats a route over terrain transitions, as in inspection and patrol, where one wrong entry can end the task. We deployed it in competition on a real wheeled-legged robot: over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain spanning 7.0 m of elevation, it completed all six runs, won third place at the 2026 Global Open-source AI Challenge, which drew 2,999 submissions, and was the only finalist in its task to finish fully autonomously.
authors: Wai Ka Sun, Waiyiu Pong, Bowen Wang
bullets: A collision-free route can still fail when the robot approaches a stair or ledge with the wrong position or heading.
A 27-minute teaching session records one successful crossing for each terrain transition as reusable route events.
Before each transition, an entry gate triggers turning or backing up when the robot is more than 10 cm or 10° from the taught approach.
Under localization noise, compliant crossings increased from 24.1% to 88.6%; simulation and real-robot tests also showed improved recovery and reliable completion.
The method was demonstrated over 271 m of multi-obstacle terrain, with six autonomous successful runs in competition.
