papers.abstract: AutoE2E is an open-source end-to-end driving model developed by the Autoware Foundation Robotaxi Working Group. It introduces a temporal bird's-eye-view (BEV) architecture that combines multi-camera perception, HD-map information and route conditioning to predict future vehicle motion. The evaluated model uses a pretrained camera-BEV backbone, temporal feature fusion and a lightweight recurrent trajectory planner. It contains approximately 79.9 million parameters, of which approximately 1.45 million are trainable in the evaluated configuration. The v1.0 release provides model checkpoints, training and evaluation code, and DataModelConsole, a dashboard for visualizing and inspecting model experiments. On the KITScenes validation benchmark, the fine-tuned checkpoint achieves an average displacement error (ADE) of 0.745 m and a final displacement error (FDE) of 2.020 m at a three-second prediction horizon. The paper also reports preliminary real-vehicle research conducted with the Technical University of Munich's EDGAR platform, alongside ongoing collaboration with the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology. AutoE2E v1.0 is an early open research release. Its quantitative evaluation is open-loop, and the model has not yet demonstrated validated closed-loop autonomous driving. The release is intended to provide the autonomous-driving community with an inspectable baseline for further research, experimentation and collaborative development.
authors: Muhammad Zain Khawaja, Zaynab El Mawas, Ryota Yamada, Gabriela Cordova, Arseni Lysak, Intisar Chowdhury, Bharat Jayaprakash, Apostolos Georgiadis, Shri Harsha Adapala, Jatin Gautam, Christoph Bank, Alejandra Solarte Uscategui, Atanasko Boris Mitrev, Hassan Ali Ansari, Nishad Sahu
bullets: Targets real-time end-to-end autonomy across advanced driver assistance and robotaxi research.
Uses a temporal bird’s-eye-view architecture with multi-camera perception, HD-map data, route conditioning, temporal fusion, and a recurrent trajectory planner.
The v1.0 release includes checkpoints, training/evaluation code, and an experiment-visualization dashboard.
On KITScenes validation, it reports 0.745 m ADE and 2.020 m FDE over a three-second horizon.
Includes preliminary real-vehicle research, but remains an early release with open-loop evaluation and no validated closed-loop autonomy.

papers.abstract: Lifelong embodied navigation requires agents to accumulate experience through continuous interaction and reuse it for subsequent goal searches. Existing memory-enhanced methods typically retain historical observations or construct structured scene representations. However, storing observations or high-dimensional semantic embeddings incurs growing storage costs. Meanwhile, structured representations support retrieval and semantic reasoning but do not explicitly evolve accumulated experience into environment-specific knowledge. To address these limitations, we propose Experience-Evolving Memory (EvoNav), a novel two-timescale memory framework. It organizes semantic observations, spatial relations, and task-feedback cues into sparse experience atoms. During online operation, experience atoms continually consolidate repeated observations and form dynamic links based on transitions. At the slower timescale, EvoNav distills accumulated category co-occurrences and feedback signals into environment-specific structural knowledge without relying on predefined object--room relations. For each new goal, EvoNav combines direct goal evidence from experience atoms with learned structural knowledge to guide goal-directed search on the current traversability map. Experiments on single-goal, sequential multi-floor, and multimodal navigation demonstrate effective experience reuse and improved path efficiency with compact persistent memory, together with successful transfer to a real robot.
authors: Weitao An, Chenghao Xu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Addresses the growing storage costs and limited knowledge evolution of observation- and embedding-based navigation memories.

Demonstrates experience reuse, improved path efficiency, compact persistent memory, and real-robot transfer across multiple navigation settings.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based end-to-end autonomous driving models have shown strong potential in generating multimodal planning trajectories. However, their performance still depends heavily on trajectory initialization, mode evaluation, and supervision quality. Weakly constrained noisy initialization may introduce infeasible proposals and increase the burden of denoising. Moreover, selecting the optimal mode remains challenging when candidate trajectories are geometrically similar but differ in safety, interaction risk, and progress. To address these issues, we propose FIRE-Drive, a feasibility-informed risk evaluation framework for end-to-end autonomous driving. FIRE-Drive improves diffusion-based planning through dynamic feasible anchor initialization, candidate-specific bird's-eye-view risk evidence, and compact high-quality candidate supervision with lightweight refinement. This design aligns the initial support, risk-aware scoring, and multimodal supervision of trajectory modes under a unified planning objective. It enables the diffusion decoder to focus on refining plausible trajectories while the scorer distinguishes modes using local risk evidence. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 show that FIRE-Drive achieves a Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 with a ResNet34 backbone. Additional closed-loop evaluation on 220 Bench2Drive routes yields a Driving Score of 71.43 and a Success Rate of 42.73%. Component ablations and a scorer comparison under matched candidate inputs support the contributions of feasible initialization, auxiliary supervision, and risk-informed selection. Our code is available at https://github.com/Latte00/FIRE-drive.
authors: Qifeng Xie, Kai-Yuan Feng, Wenkang Wan, Yue Wu, Maoguo Gong, Kai Sheng
bullets: Addresses infeasible noisy proposals, difficult mode selection, and weak supervision in diffusion planning.

Adds lightweight refinement and compact high-quality supervision to align multimodal planning.
Reports a NAVSIM v1 Predictive Driver Model Score of 91.5 and closed-loop results on 220 Bench2Drive routes, with ablations supporting its components.

papers.abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl

papers.selection_reason: Learning-based region-of-attraction estimation for path-following control of unicycle and quadrotor fits robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.
authors: Lihao Zheng, Ying Wu, Chen Jiang, Randy Freeman
bullets: Addresses the limitation of binary safety constraints in safety-critical navigation.
Estimates kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal risks for objects and people.
Combines risk factors into continuous object-level risk scores.
Uses a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as an online safety filter.
Demonstrated in a simulated restaurant scene; broader real-world performance is not established in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Visual place recognition (VPR) in forest environments remains challenging because repetitive vegetation, and changes in illumination, season, and viewpoint can make distinct places appear similar and revisited places appear substantially different. In this paper, we investigate whether temporal, linguistic, structural, and geometric context can improve on an appearance-only descriptor, and what limits each representation when it does not. Using MegaLoc as the appearance-based baseline on the WildCross benchmark, we evaluate score-space and descriptor-space sequence matching, vision-language captions and reranking, scene-graph representations, and depth-derived stem graphs across same-direction revisits, extended routes, and reverse traversals. On a same-direction revisit, both sequence matching strategies reach similar Recall@1 (94.1% vs. 91.5%), but recall at 100% precision rises from 50.9% (single-frame MegaLoc) to 71.6% in score space and falls to 36.5% in descriptor space. The remaining context representations provide no consistent improvement over the appearance-based baseline. Same-place captions show limited place-specific discrimination, reranking is constrained by the initial candidate shortlist, and stem-graph matching remains weak even with LiDAR depth.
authors: Blake Matheson, Ben McShanag, Isabella Moffat, Michael Milford, Peyman Moghadam, Dana Kuli\'c, Somayeh Hussaini, Kavindie Katuwandeniya
bullets: Forest VPR is challenged by repetitive vegetation and changes in lighting, season, and viewpoint.

papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.
bullets: Addresses adapting automatic tractor guidance when the machine or steering actuator changes, without gradient descent or an optimiser.
GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable edited a 253-parameter controller using natural-language guidance and limited simulated feedback.

The generated controllers were sparse and classically cascaded, and all operated the real tractor without intervention with errors comparable in order to pure pursuit.
Gradient descent achieved higher accuracy but required substantially more simulation; unsupported or limited cases include Fable’s occasional success without simulation.

papers.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
papers.tldr: Large language models can directly write neural-network weights to create or adapt tractor-steering controllers that work in simulation and on a real tractor.

papers.abstract: We use neural networks to optimize trajectories by modeling the position as a function of time and minimizing the thrust with respect to the network parameters. This corresponds to an unsupervised training procedure in which physical laws are incorporated directly into the optimization objective. In standard physics-informed neural networks, initial and terminal states are enforced through additional weighted loss terms, resulting in a multi-objective optimization problem that is highly sensitive to the choice of loss weights and can lead to poor convergence and reduced accuracy. To address this challenge, we construct a simple transformation, exploiting the mathematical structure of trajectory optimization problems, to enforce boundary conditions exactly a-priori. This transformation can be interpreted as a reparameterization of the solution space that embeds the boundary conditions directly into the function. This converts the original constrained optimization problem into an unconstrained one over admissible trajectories. I.e. the transformation eliminates the boundary condition penalty terms and reduces the problem to a single-objective optimization. Crucially, trajectory optimization comes with a low-dimensional boundary, which allows particularly simple and stable constructions of distance functions compared to general domains in partial differential equations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach meaningfully improves convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
authors: Samuel Sch\"onherr, G\"unther Waxenegger-Wilfing, Sascha Ranftl
bullets: Standard PINNs enforce initial and terminal states with weighted penalties, making training sensitive to loss-weight choices.
The method embeds boundary conditions directly into the trajectory representation through a simple transformation.
This converts constrained, multi-objective training into unconstrained single-objective thrust minimization over admissible trajectories.
Numerical experiments show improved convergence behavior and solution accuracy.
The approach leverages the low-dimensional boundary structure of trajectory optimization problems.

papers.abstract: Bird's-Eye-View (BEV)-conditioned large language models (LLMs) enable language-interactive driving, but onboard deployment requires efficient perception and continuous planning alongside autoregressive language generation. We present GridDriver, an efficient BEV-conditioned LLM framework combining trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, natural-language navigation, driving explanations, and scene question answering. Lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception and spatially structured tokens provide scene context to a shared LLM, while frame-wise scheduling interleaves trajectory prediction with asynchronous language generation. GridDriver achieves competitive performance on public benchmarks, reaching 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM and 57.6% accuracy on nuScenes-QA with a shared planning and QA checkpoint. Spatial representation analyses demonstrate improved geometric information retention and trajectory prediction compared with Q-Former compression. The system achieves 32.7 ms standalone planning latency and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline. We further evaluate planning on our own data recordings and demonstrate open-loop onboard operation on a research vehicle. Across public benchmarks and real-world evaluations, we identify strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.
authors: Katharina Winter, William Engel, Zain A. Alishammat, Fabian B. Flohr
bullets: Addresses the challenge of running autoregressive language generation alongside real-time onboard driving planning.
Uses lightweight spatio-temporal BEV perception, spatially structured tokens, and frame-wise scheduling to interleave planning with asynchronous language generation.
Supports trajectory prediction, structured driving indicators, navigation instructions, driving explanations, and scene question answering.
Reports 87.9% PDMS on NAVSIM, 57.6% nuScenes-QA accuracy, 32.7 ms standalone planning latency, and 9.4 plans/s in an onboard ROS 2 pipeline.
Evaluations include public benchmarks, proprietary recordings, and open-loop operation on a research vehicle; the abstract notes both strengths and limitations of the BEV-based approach.

papers.abstract: This paper presents FlowRRT, a kinodynamic planner for agile monoped hopping on discrete terrain. Steering for kinodynamic RRT on complex dynamical systems currently relies on motion primitives or closed-loop policies, limiting the diversity of motions or the planning speed. Distilling a trajectory optimizer avoids both, but existing methods regress a single solution per query, which fails on monoped hopping, where the feasible action set is narrow and disconnected. Our key insight is to treat steering as set-valued and predict the distribution of feasible actions instead. A multi-start MPPI expert collects the entire feasible set of each query offline, and conditional flow matching distills it into a generative sampler. With this sampler, FlowRRT coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and finds non-greedy maneuvers that are hard for reactive policies to discover. Benchmarks across different terrains show higher success rates and substantially shorter planning times than sampling-based baselines. On terrains with inclined platforms, FlowRRT reaches $80\%$ success within $1$~s, versus $24$~s for RL-RRT and $77$~s for SST. Sim-to-sim tracking in MuJoCo confirms accurate execution under full-order dynamics.
authors: Yue Qin, Denglin Cheng, Jingyu Liu, Yanran Ding
bullets: Addresses kinodynamic planning challenges caused by narrow, disconnected feasible action sets in monoped hopping.
Uses multi-start MPPI to collect feasible action sets offline, then applies conditional flow matching to learn a generative steering sampler.
Coordinates successive jumps over long horizons and discovers non-greedy maneuvers beyond reactive policies.
Outperforms sampling-based baselines in terrain benchmarks, including 80% success within 1 s on inclined platforms versus 24 s for RL-RRT and 77 s for SST.
MuJoCo sim-to-sim tracking confirms execution under full-order dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Kinodynamic planning with distilled MPPI steering for agile legged hopping, a learned planner for robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Birds are modeled as environmentally sensitive agents whose movement reflects real-world air quality conditions, where AQI serves as a measurable world feedback signal representing pollution-driven consequences. Instead of relying on human preference or synthetic rewards, the system uses environmental outcomes as the primary training signal, enabling policy learning grounded in ecological impact. We propose a multi-instance reinforcement learning simulation in which agents navigate a 2D grid representation of India integrated with a precomputed AQI matrix and geographic state boundaries. The framework combines bird call metadata from the Xeno-canto dataset, spatial discretization, and real environmental data to learn adaptive navigation strategies under pollution constraints. To ensure scalability and efficiency, repeated real-time API queries are replaced by a structured AQI mapping that enables fast lookup during training and execution. Multiple baselines, including Monte Carlo, Q-Learning, and Value Iteration, are evaluated for comparison. Deep Q-Network demonstrates stronger stability, adaptability, and cumulative performance across varying environmental conditions, establishing a scalable foundation for world-feedback driven ecological decision modeling.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.
authors: Baiting Luo, Shatadal Mishra, Ahmadreza Moradipari, Nejib Ammar
bullets: Addresses the cost of repeated history encoding and iterative video generation in driving-oriented video foundation models.
Uses causal autoregressive temporal modeling to incrementally update visual context from a single front camera.
Computes future features in one forward pass to condition trajectory generation, avoiding iterative video generation.
Applies reinforcement learning to optimize driving rewards and improve the policy.
Achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1; it also performs well in continuous dynamic driving while retaining visual history.

papers.abstract: Monitoring oil spills with fleets of Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) requires mapping a heterogeneous pollutant field from sparse, noisy measurements under tight time and energy budgets. Informative Path Planning (IPP) addresses this problem by coupling a reconstruction model, which infers the field and its uncertainty, with a planner that decides where to sample next. Prior work has focused on planning strategies and has largely relied on Gaussian Processes (GPs), leaving the calibration of the model's uncertainty underexplored. We study how uncertainty calibration conditions multi-vehicle IPP with a fleet of ASVs that coordinates online through a shared uncertainty map. We introduce Evidential Deep Learning (EDL) as an uncertainty-calibrated information model. We benchmark EDL, Monte Carlo Dropout and Deep Ensembles against a GP in closed loop with five planners on physics-based oil spill simulations. Across 60 maps, the choice of model dominates the outcome, explaining 80\% of the variance of the final reconstruction error, against 1\% for the planner among the deep models. EDL achieves the lowest error and the highest IoU under every planner, is the best calibrated model and runs at 3.9 ms per step. With 50 cells per vehicle it reconstructs the spill better than MC Dropout and Deep Ensembles with 150. Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error grows, whereas EDL is unaffected. Robustness of the information model to the data its own planner collects is therefore a requirement of uncertainty-aware IPP.
authors: Alejandro Casado-P\'erez, Marija Popovi\'c, Daniel Guti\'errez-Reina, Sergio L. Toral., Samuel Yanes
bullets: Multi-ASV monitoring must reconstruct heterogeneous oil-spill fields from sparse, noisy measurements under time and energy constraints.
The study evaluates Evidential Deep Learning, Monte Carlo Dropout, Deep Ensembles, and Gaussian Processes within closed-loop IPP using five planners.
Across 60 physics-based maps, the information model explains 80% of final reconstruction-error variance, compared with 1% for the planner among deep models.
EDL achieves the lowest error and highest IoU under every planner, is best calibrated, and runs in 3.9 ms per step.
Deep Ensembles become more confident as their error increases, highlighting the need for uncertainty models robust to planner-collected data.

papers.abstract: Hybrid solid-state LiDAR sensors are making their way into production vehicles, yet the data they produce differs structurally from that of the established spinning mechanical sensors behind today's autonomous-driving datasets: it is ring-free, dense, cluttered, and concentrated in a frontal field of view. The classical geometric methods that autonomous vehicles rely on for drivable space computation and navigation assume the ordered ring-and-column structure of a 360-degree spinning LiDAR and degrade or fail on this data, while learned alternatives are computationally heavy, hard to certify, and trained almost exclusively on spinning-LiDAR data. We demonstrate that the same dense, per-curve geometry is instead an opportunity to close the divide between the industry's preferred sensors and autonomous-driving research. We present GHySSeg, a purely geometric method that segments ground and drivable road from a single hybrid solid-state LiDAR frame by tracing each scan curve and reading two geometric signatures, a step in height and a fold-back in range, with no training and no graphics processing unit. To evaluate it, we release HySoLiD-Drive, the first public benchmark dedicated to ground and road segmentation on an automotive hybrid solid-state LiDAR, comprising 100 manually labeled and 7000 unlabeled frames recorded by two vehicles in real driving. On this benchmark, GHySSeg surpasses both geometric and learned state-of-the-art baselines across ground and road segmentation, reaching an intersection-over-union of 0.907 for road and 0.896 for ground at over 0.96 precision, while running in real time at about 22 milliseconds per frame on a single core.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between ring-free, front-facing hybrid solid-state LiDAR and methods designed for spinning 360° LiDAR.
Traces each scan curve and detects two geometric cues: height steps and range fold-backs.
Introduces HySoLiD-Drive, a benchmark with 100 labeled and 7,000 unlabeled real-driving frames from two vehicles.
Reports 0.907 road IoU and 0.896 ground IoU, with over 0.96 precision and roughly 22 ms per frame on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Formation maneuver control enables a multiagent system to cooperatively navigate through constrained environments in collective motion. While various formation controllers exist, they rely heavily on high-quality and dynamically feasible reference trajectories provided a priori, making formation motion planning (FMP) essential. To address the computational challenges for high-dimensional joint trajectories faced by conventional constrained optimization-based solutions, this paper introduces a hybrid optimization-generative framework with a focus on affine formations, which provide the necessary spatial flexibility. By formulating the planning task as a constrained Maximum-a-Posteriori estimation, we decouple multiagent objectives to leverage pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors for dynamic feasibility, obstacle avoidance, and smoothness. We then interleave the generative process with projected gradient descent (PGD) to strictly enforce affine geometric constraints with safety guarantees. Simulations demonstrate that our framework generates highly smooth, collision-free plans that are readily trackable by common distributed controllers and outperforms state-of-the-art planners in various metrics.
authors: Zhonggang Li, Hongyu Zhou, Raj Thilak Rajan
bullets: Targets the computational difficulty of planning high-dimensional joint trajectories for formation motion.
Formulates planning as constrained maximum-a-posteriori estimation using pre-trained single-agent diffusion priors.
Interleaves diffusion sampling with projected gradient descent to enforce affine formation constraints and safety.
Simulations show smooth, collision-free, controller-trackable plans with strong performance across multiple metrics.
Scope: focuses on affine formations and simulation-based evaluation.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available at https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill
authors: Shiyu Fang, Sheng Zhao, Jiarui Zhang, Chengkai Xu, Xiaocong Zhao, Peng Hang, Jian Sun
bullets: Targets coordination, exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability in cooperative driving.
Uses a potential-game planner for fixed-path longitudinal guidance and a residual MARL policy for acceleration, timing, and lateral corrections.
Focuses training on hard interactions unresolved or delayed by the potential-game planner.
Selects actions by comparing learned corrections with potential-game outcomes through comparative rollouts.
Across merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios, it improves success and reduces delay versus the potential-game baseline, with no observed collisions.

papers.abstract: Autonomous monitoring and intervention in semi-structured agricultural environments, such as orchards and vineyards, require mobile robots to navigate to locations across diverse field configurations. This entails performing navigation behaviors including in-row driving, row turning and skipping, and inter-row traversal. Recent learning-based approaches have enabled robust in-row navigation from onboard perception, but navigation across rows typically requires a priori knowledge of field geometry to specify and tune row-transition maneuvers, preventing arbitrary transitions between rows. We address this challenge by framing navigation in these environments as a goal-directed navigation task, where a long-horizon goal is expressed relative to the robot and a planner generates local paths based on the goal and the robot's perceptual observations. We present FlowRow, a flow-matching-based local planner which models the distribution of diverse agricultural navigation behaviors as $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ paths using the long-horizon goal and depth perception. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce RowNavBench, a navigation benchmark for semi-structured agricultural environments developed in Isaac Sim, comprising 900 episodes across grape vineyards, lemon orchards, and apple orchards with varying row lengths, row and plant spacings, plant positions, and weed growth. FlowRow achieves 87% success, compared to 44% for the strongest generative behavior cloning baseline retrained on the same demonstrations. We will release our benchmark, data, and code upon acceptance.
authors: Utkarsh Bajpai, C\'{e}dric Pradalier, St\'{e}phanie Aravecchia

papers.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.
bullets: Temporal inconsistency between modalities can corrupt fused representations and cause driving-policy failures.
STA jointly optimizes when to delay observations and which modality to attack, using historical states instead of modality-specific noise.
The method uses clean policy actions to identify sensitive decision patterns and includes theoretical analysis of distribution shift and modality selection.
In CARLA, STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest PPO baseline with 17.8% fewer attack attempts and also generalizes to a VLM-based policy.
The results emphasize temporal consistency and robustness as important for safe autonomous driving.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed Split Temporal Adversary (STA). At each time step, the adversary observes the current state and driving policy information, then decides whether to attack based on the attack budget and policy awareness. If activated, it selects which modality to manipulate (visual or numerical) and replaces the selected modality with a delayed observation from the history buffer. This creates cross-modal temporal misalignment that leads to erroneous control decisions by the driving policy.
TABLE II: Results on the VLM-based driving policy in Town02 dense traffic (mean ± variance over five seeds).

papers.title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
papers.tldr: STA adaptively evaluates multimodal driving-policy robustness by introducing realistic, budget-constrained temporal misalignments across selected sensors.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Place Recognition (PR) can improve robustness, but most systems rigidly read and process every sensor for every query, even when the primary sensor is sufficient, with implications for energy consumption, second sensor update rate, and domain-specific considerations such as passive stealth. We introduce selective, controllable sensor acquisition, where a user specifies a desired second sensor usage rate and the system acquires the additional sensor only when the primary sensor's estimated performance is sufficiently poor. An online threshold adjustment achieves the requested usage rate by adapting to recent primary sensor performance, directing additional sensing towards queries where fusion is most likely to help without calibration specific to sensor modality, PR method, or environment. The approach requires only a PR method that produces a match score and applies to both single-frame and sequence-based PR. Our system, across multiple datasets, PR descriptors, and sensor combinations, recovers 55% of the available PR performance gain while using the second sensor on only 25% of queries, and 81% while using it on 50%. We further analyse alternative acquisition decision mechanisms and usage-rate control methods, and examine performance when the second sensor is stronger than, comparable to, or weaker than the primary sensor.
authors: Margaux Edwards, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford

papers.abstract: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.
authors: Gibran Fathoni Belva, Mansur Arief, Ahmad Alfan Alfian Irfan

papers.abstract: Existing autonomous driving datasets and benchmarks provide extensive resources for routine driving, yet real-world data covering safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions remain limited. To address this gap, we present ExtremeDrive, a real-world dataset and benchmark covering emergency maneuvers, complex traffic interactions, and adverse conditions such as slippery or snow-covered roads, alongside routine driving. The dataset comprises 589 driving scenes curated from a larger pool of real-world driving recordings, with calibrated and aligned multisensor data and reviewed annotations of road structure and traffic participants. We further establish a benchmark to evaluate planned trajectories through simulated vehicle execution, measuring safety-related metrics and driving performance. Experiments at equal training set sizes show that incorporating critical driving data reduces trajectory prediction errors and improves mean critical-success rates in critical scenarios. ExtremeDrive provides a unified resource for learning and evaluating autonomous driving in safety-critical scenarios and extreme environmental conditions.

Covers both critical and routine driving, enabling unified training and evaluation.

papers.abstract: Language-guided navigation enables mobile robots to interpret natural language commands and navigate toward user-specified targets in unstructured environments. However, integrating open-vocabulary visual perception with classical robotics pipelines for mapping and navigation remains a challenging problem. In this work, we present a complete ROS2-based system that combines frontier-based exploration, open-vocabulary object detection using Grounding DINO, depth-based 3D localization, and semantic mapping to enable end-to-end vision-language grounded navigation in simulation. The system accepts natural language commands such as ``go to the yellow box,'' detects candidate objects from RGB images using text prompts, estimates their positions in the world frame, and generates navigation goals executed by the Nav2 stack. In a Gazebo-based indoor environment with a TurtleBot3 robot, the system autonomously explored the room, detected three of the five target objects, and successfully executed both natural language navigation commands tested, without task-specific training. The results indicate that open-vocabulary grounding models can be integrated into classical navigation pipelines, though performance is limited by detection uncertainty, depth-based localization error, and incomplete exploration coverage. These findings highlight both the feasibility and current limitations of deploying vision-language grounded navigation systems using lightweight, CPU-only architectures.

papers.abstract: Proposal-conditioned scene predictions can lack a common object-level reference across candidate trajectories. Aggregate planning scores also leave the objects and times associated with violations implicit. We present WTR-Drive (World-Task-Risk Driving), a Drive-JEPA-based planner that separates shared scene estimation from proposal-conditioned reasoning. A proposal-independent World Memory estimates object states, map structure, and future motion by re-reading the original visual features at each refinement round. Proposal feedback updates a residual Task branch without writing back to World Memory. This branch guides refinement through candidate-specific retrieval and gated visual feedback. A final Task readout supplies candidate-conditioned features for scoring. We derive structured risk targets from existing candidate-scoring rollouts without additional simulator calls. For at-fault collision and time-to-collision violations, the targets encode event existence, association with shared object slots, and the first violation time bin. On the NAVSIM navtest split, WTR-Drive achieves 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2 (expert-frame sequential evaluation). These scores are 0.96 and 0.44 points above the published Drive-JEPA values, respectively. Candidate-level analysis shows that higher best-candidate scores can coexist with lower selected-trajectory scores, revealing a gap between candidate quality and selection effectiveness.
authors: Haoyu Xing, Shaobing Ding, Guanglei Zhao, Guanhua Zhao, Nawu Peng, Mingyang Hou
bullets: Addresses missing shared object references and implicit violation details in proposal-conditioned planning.

Supervises collision and time-to-collision risks using event existence, object association, and first-violation timing.
On NAVSIM navtest, reports 94.66 PDMS on v1 and 88.24 EPDMS on v2, above published Drive-JEPA scores; analysis exposes a candidate-selection gap.

papers.abstract: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.
bullets: They build on SuperMimic, using a learned robot world model and analytic policy gradients through imagined short rollouts.
The training loop, including MuJoCo Warp simulation, is compiled with JAX and parallelized across up to four GPUs.

XSoma learns rough-terrain locomotion with a one-second horizon, no critic, and exact computation of non-dynamics quantities such as foot terrain height.
The reported speedups are 3.7× over BlinkMimic and 12.3× over FastSAC, with XSoma using one-eighth as many environment steps as FastSAC.

papers.abstract: Continual robot navigation requires reinforcement learning policies to continuously adapt to new environments while retaining previously acquired knowledge. Meanwhile, explainable reinforcement learning aims to learn meaningful behavioral representations through policy interaction. However, these objectives are inherently conflicting, as continual learning emphasizes policy stability whereas explainable behavior learning requires adaptive exploration. Existing methods rarely address both simultaneously. To resolve this issue, this paper proposes a Fuzzy Explainable Continual Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (FECHRL) method. A two-stage behavior cloning strategy is introduced to balance rapid policy adaptation and explainable behavior evolution by progressively transitioning from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning. Furthermore, a fuzzy critic based on a Takagi--Sugeno fuzzy inference system is proposed to alleviate value extrapolation errors during the transition between imitation-guided learning and autonomous exploration, thereby improving continual training stability. Experimental results on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks demonstrate that the proposed method effectively unifies continual learning capability and policy explainability within a single reinforcement learning framework, achieving stable knowledge retention and meaningful behavioral explanation.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between stable knowledge retention and adaptive, explainable exploration in continual robot navigation.
Uses two-stage behavior cloning to transition from strong imitation guidance to autonomous reinforcement learning.
Introduces a Takagi–Sugeno fuzzy critic to reduce value extrapolation errors during this transition.
Experiments on sequential multi-scenario navigation tasks show stable retention and meaningful behavioral explanations.
The abstract reports effectiveness in the tested sequential navigation setting, without specifying broader generalization limits.

papers.abstract: An autonomous vehicle must foresee the consequences of its actions, especially in the rare, time-critical situations where crashes happen. A world model offers this foresight, but only within the coverage of its training data, which poses an exploration-exploitation dilemma. Within this coverage a planner can hardly improve on the data, and beyond it the model's errors mislead it. Logs of competent driving rarely contain the failures that would widen the coverage, and agents that learn from interaction gain them only by failing themselves, without being shown what to do instead. We propose SAFER, a framework that learns offline from failures that others make, judged by an expert, and keeps learning online from its own driving. Offline, partially trained agents and scripted, recoverable perturbations Stage failures in simulation, and an expert Annotates every visited state with its action and value, so that much of what the planner explores is covered before it drives. In planning, a chunked latent world model Foresees the consequences fast enough for real-time use, and a risk-aware sampling-based planner Evaluates candidate maneuvers by their return minus a bounded collision penalty. Online, a loop continuously Refines the model wherever this driving leaves the coverage of the offline data. In closed-loop evaluation against the compared methods, SAFER reaches the highest route completion and reward per step on the CARLA Leaderboard routes, 0.95 and 0.77 from a privileged bird's-eye view, and the highest episode reward in MetaDrive, 53.4 in regular and 49.0 in safety-critical traffic. Project page: https://ys-qu.github.io/safer-website.
authors: Yansong Qu, Zilin Huang, Zihao Sheng, Sikai Chen, Samuel Labi
bullets: Addresses the exploration–exploitation dilemma caused by limited world-model training coverage and scarce failure examples in driving logs.
Stages recoverable failures in simulation and uses an expert to label visited states with actions and values before deployment.
Uses a chunked latent world model with a risk-aware sampling-based planner that penalizes collisions.
Continuously refines the world model online when driving encounters situations outside offline coverage.
Achieves the best reported route completion and reward per step on CARLA routes, plus the highest episode reward in MetaDrive among compared methods.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Technical overview of SAFER, illustrated with its CARLA instance. The numbered badges link each part to its scene of the analogy in Fig. 2. (a) Stage and Annotate: the expert, weaker Roach checkpoints and scripted hold and late-brake events drive until the first violation, and the expert labels every visited state with its action and value (Section 3.2). (b) Foresee: from the context Mt of the past BEVs, the dynamics imagines the 16 latents of a candidate chunk in one pass, and heads read them as the behavior-cloned prior, the reward and its five factors, survival, value and collision risk (Section 3.3). (c) Evaluate: every 0.1 s, the planner scores 135 candidate chunks on their imagined futures (Eq. (28)), refits its sampling distribution to the 16 best in each of two iterations and executes the first action (Section 3.5). (d) Refine: the planner’s own driving fine-tunes the dynamics, the reward and the risk head online, while the encoder, the prior and the value stay frozen and the planner scores with slowly moving EMA copies (Section 3.6). The crash frame in (a), the context frames in (b) and the candidates and risk curves in (c) are from a recorded collision of the corpus (Fig. 5a); the other two BEV frames are illustrative.

Figure 2: An everyday analogy for SAFER (top) and the corresponding stages of the method (bottom, detailed in Fig. 3); the numbered badges link each stage to its scene. (1) Parents praise what works and point to negative examples, so that the child need not fail first. (a) Likewise, weaker drivers and scripted perturbations stage failures in simulation, and the expert labels every visited state with its action and value. (2) The child learns what each choice leads to. Hard work (action) brings good grades (reward), a far goal is worth pursuing (value), and staying out all night is risky (risk). (b) Likewise, the world model foresees these quantities for each candidate action chunk, and (c) the planner scores the candidates by their return minus a price on risk. (3) Away from home, school and work keep reshaping the beliefs while the core ones stay. (d) Likewise, the planner’s own driving refines the dynamics and the reward and risk heads, while the prior and the value, whose targets only the expert provides, stay fixed.

Figure 7: The imagined reachable set and its risk area in two closed-loop decisions of the full system. Left: a front camera added for visualization, which the agent does not observe. Middle: (a) the BEV that the agent observes; (b) a top-down view drawn from the simulator state, with CAT’s opponent (magenta) and the trajectory that CAT generates for it (dashed), which the planner does not know. In both views the 270 candidate chunks that the planner scored at that step are drawn as in Appendix B, as the paths that they trace under a kinematic bicycle model at the speeds that the world model predicts, colored by the predicted reward of each imagined step; together they sample the reachable set. Red: the risk area, i.e. the risk head’s probability of a priced safety event (CARLA: collision; MetaDrive: vehicle contact plus leaving the road, object contact staying at zero), averaged at each place over the imagined states of all candidates that pass there and drawn with an opacity that grows with the probability; it is the same field in both views. Orange: executed plan; dotted: behavior-cloned prior. Right: the same probability along the horizon for every candidate (gray), the plan (orange) and the prior (dotted), with their risk terms Wρ̄ of Eq. (26).

Figure 1: Learning paradigms for autonomous driving, compared by where the experience beyond competent driving comes from. The glyph under each paradigm shows the coverage of its data (gray) and how the paradigm treats it. Exploiting (blue) spreads the candidates over the coverage and takes the best one up to its edge, but no further. Exploring (orange) grows the coverage at the price of failures (red crosses), the paradigm’s own or, for SAFER, failures that others make, labeled by the expert (teal). A step out of the coverage that does not grow it is misjudged (?). (a) Imitation learning copies expert demonstrations and never observes a failure; reinforcement learning discovers consequences by failing in the environment. (b) A world model learned online (Hafner et al., 2020; Li et al., 2024) still explores by failing. A world model learned from logged expert driving (Wang et al., 2024b; Zheng et al., 2025) covers competent driving only, and a planner that searches beyond this coverage favors the actions that the model misjudges. (c) SAFER broadens the coverage offline with staged failures that an expert annotates, plans with a fast chunked world model that prices collision risk, and extends the coverage online from the planner’s own driving. The BEV frames, candidates and risk curves in (c) are from a recorded collision of the corpus (Fig. 5a).

Paths: the 270 candidate chunks scored at that step, sketched with a kinematic bicycle model at the predicted speeds and colored by the predicted reward of each imagined step; orange: executed plan; dotted: behavior-cloned prior; crosses: the first imagined step at which the predicted collision probability reaches 0.5. (a) Straight road with oncoming traffic; (b) right turn at a T-junction; (c) junction where the route turns right while a few chunks, the prior among them, continue straight towards a red light.

papers.abstract: We present Lao Siji, an end-to-end driving policy that ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge, ahead of most entries built on foundation models. Instead of training from scratch on a general-purpose vision backbone, we adapt openpilot, an open-source L2 production model. We freeze its vision encoder and fine-tune the policy layers with an ego-state adapter and a route memory. On closed-loop rollouts in neural-reconstructed scenes, we supervise the policy with a privileged map teacher for lateral self-correction and a body-extent loss for road and obstacle clearance, while distilling the base model's remaining outputs to retain car following. Ablations show that self-correction samples carry the gain, while the clearance loss substitutes for them where no teacher exists. Longitudinal safety instead rests on the base model's lead-vehicle estimate behind a rule-based speed layer. Longer training, imitating human logs, and human-log speed targets yield either no measurable gain or adverse effects. Without further training, Lao Siji also places among the leaders on HUGSIM and Odyssey. The final training takes only one GPU-hour and shifts the weights by 3.9% from the shipped model. Code will be released after review.
authors: Chengzhi Gao, Yongzhi Liu, Jinchang Xu, Weichao Zhuang, Guodong Yin
bullets: Ranks third in the 2026 NVIDIA AlpaSim E2E Driving Challenge and performs competitively on HUGSIM and Odyssey without additional training.
Freezes openpilot’s vision encoder while fine-tuning policy layers with an ego-state adapter and route memory.
Uses privileged-map supervision for lateral self-correction, a body-extent clearance loss, and output distillation to preserve car-following behavior.
Ablations identify self-correction samples as the main source of gains; clearance loss helps when teacher supervision is unavailable.
Training takes one GPU-hour and changes only 3.9% of the shipped model’s weights; several longer-training and human-log strategies provide no benefit or hurt performance.

papers.abstract: Agentic navigation must maintain goals and adapt actions from incomplete evidence despite execution failures and delayed inference. We present AgenticJevNav, which links goal-directed planning, evidence memory, event-triggered verification, and bounded execution. The Agent plans from RGB, odometry, memory, and feedback, retaining goal ownership while authorizing a bounded action set. Jev reviews structured evidence after blocked/failed execution or two consecutive low-progress segments. Version, freshness, and once-only checks govern decision application. A single executor and independent RGB reflex constrain motion. Goal revisions revoke obsolete requests and actions before replanning. Across six simulated task families, AgenticJevNav achieves 73.33% SR over 60 trials, 21.67 percentage points above the next-best Agent-only aggregate control under differing historical protocols. A real-world GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment achieves 70.0% success over 30 trials, including bounded search reporting. Together, the simulation and physical-robot results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed architecture, while remaining failures highlight opportunities to improve grounding, approach planning, and runtime.
authors: Shuning Zhang, Shuli Zhang, Yunheng Wang, Wei Lu, Jiaxi Zhang, Yihang Kang, Tao Wang, Xiangyu Chen, Yixiao Feng, Kai Sheng, Renjing Xu

Achieves 73.33% success across six simulated task families and 70.0% success on a real GENISOM L1 quadruped deployment.
Remaining failures point to grounding, approach planning, and runtime limitations.

papers.abstract: Most robot navigation stacks implicitly bind mapping, localization, planning, and control to specific representations and data flows, yielding architectures hard to extend, compare experimentally, or reason about end-to-end timing. This is critical in heterogeneous scenarios, where multiple spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames coexist and evolve at different rates. This paper presents a navigation architecture centered on an explicit, shared navigation state that serves as the sole interaction interface between modular components. Constraining mapping, localization, planning, and control to operate over this shared state enables interchangeable, representation-agnostic pipelines under explicit compatibility and timing contracts. We realize this architecture as EasyNav, an open source ROS 2 framework, and validate it through real-robot experiments, including indoor navigation with laser sensing and large-scale indoor-outdoor navigation with GPS and 3D LiDAR across multi-level routes. Compared with Nav2 under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency from 377 to 33 ms indoors and from 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while also using less CPU and memory.
authors: Francisco Mart\'in Rico, Francisco Miguel Moreno, Juan Sebasti\'an Cely Guti\'errez, Esther Aguado, Miguel \'Angel De Miguel Para\'iso, Jos\'e Miguel Guerrero
bullets: Existing navigation stacks tightly couple mapping, localization, planning, and control, making them difficult to extend, compare, and analyze for timing.
EasyNav uses an explicit shared navigation state as the sole interface between components, with compatibility and timing contracts.
The architecture supports interchangeable pipelines across spatial representations, sensing modalities, and coordinate frames.
Real-robot experiments cover indoor laser navigation and large-scale indoor-outdoor GPS/3D LiDAR navigation across multi-level routes.
Under matched conditions, EasyNav reduces reaction latency versus Nav2 from 377 to 33 ms indoors and 71 to 8 ms outdoors, while using less CPU and memory.

papers.abstract: In 2025, there was a total of 358 weather-related disasters worldwide affecting millions of people. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to autonomously aid these people, they need to be able to navigate around complex obstacles and reach their destinations to deliver supplies or quickly locate survivors in disaster-stricken areas. Our research addresses this need by providing a method to compute minimum-time trajectories in real time while providing guarantees of obstacle avoidance along the trajectory. Previous approaches treat the problem of computing time-optimal trajectories without considering obstacle avoidance. Our work not only includes obstacle avoidance constraints, but also improves overall mission time for navigation. We define mission time as the sum of planning time and traversal time. In time-sensitive emergencies, rapid trajectory planning is essential to ensure the prompt delivery of critical medical aid. As such, we consider the combined planning and traversal time as the key metric for how quickly the vehicle can reach a survivor. We show a sample mission in Fig. 1 where the quadrotor navigates through multiple canyon-like obstacles to deliver aid; during most of this trajectory, it is applying the near-maximum thrust.
authors: Pranav Nedunghat, Jeffrey Mao, Praveen Merumugumala
bullets: Targets autonomous drone navigation through complex obstacles to deliver supplies and locate survivors.
Optimizes mission time, defined as planning time plus trajectory traversal time.
Incorporates obstacle-avoidance constraints into time-optimal trajectory computation.
Demonstrates a sample quadrotor mission through multiple canyon-like obstacles, often using near-maximum thrust.
The abstract does not report quantitative evaluation results or specific limitations.

papers.abstract: Experiments near vehicle handling limits must keep three questions apart: what a maneuver requests, what the closed-loop system executes, and whether the task is completed. We present DynLimit, a simulation platform that organizes this process end to end. Scenarios are composed from road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects; planners and controllers attach through a shared observation and control interface; a vehicle adapter runs either a license-free four-wheel model or an external dynamics solver; and synchronized records feed task evaluation, replay, and response inspection. The platform carries a task-oriented evaluation method that pairs a prescribed reference demand with a sampled passing set and event-aligned diagnosis. Across eight task families, three friction environments, and three reference-assisted baseline chains we executed 450 runs: 360 nominal, 18 locally refined, and 72 with prescribed initial offsets. Method differences depend on the task family, equal aggregate pass counts arise from different passing cells, and local refinement narrows two sampled transitions without locating a continuous boundary. Two case comparisons show why sideslip or tire-utilization peaks cannot replace task constraints. The three views therefore stay distinct in every reported run: an outcome can be traced from the prescribed demand, through the executed response, to the task rule that decided it. Code is available at https://github.com/Yang2581/dynlimit
authors: Yang Xiao, Yongzhi Liu, Sunan Zhang, Kang Wang, Guodong Yin, Weichao Zhuang
bullets: Supports composable scenarios with road, friction, obstacle, and reference objects.
Connects planners and controllers through a shared interface to either a four-wheel vehicle model or an external dynamics solver.

Across eight task families and three friction environments, it found that methods with equal aggregate pass counts can differ in which task conditions they pass.
Shows that sideslip and tire-utilization peaks alone cannot substitute for task-specific success criteria.

papers.abstract: Water--land cross-domain robots require continuous localization across land, transition and underwater phases, where sensor characteristics and availability change abruptly. Existing datasets and conventional metrics are not designed to capture transition-induced degradation and failures. We present \textbf{M-CROSS}, to the best of our knowledge, the first multisensor simulation dataset and benchmark for SLAM across continuous water--land transitions. It provides synchronized LiDAR, sonar, stereo camera, IMU, DVL, and depth measurements; 6DoF pose ground truth; sensor-wise medium-state annotations; and medium-dependent sensor degradation models. We establish a transition-aware protocol comprising the Trajectory Completion Rate (TCR), Piecewise Absolute Pose Error (PW-APE), Transition End Error (TEE), and Transition Survival Period (TSP), which measure trajectory completion, single-domain accuracy, transition-induced error, and localization survival under prolonged partial immersion, respectively. Experiments with 6 representative SLAM systems show that existing methods fail to maintain both localization accuracy and trajectory continuity across the full set of water--land transitions, exhibiting transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures. M-CROSS is publicly available https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MCross-Dataset
authors: Yan Dong, Tianyi Wu, Junyu Yang, Shaoqiang Qiu, Zefeng Yan, Tao Zhang, Bin Han
bullets: Addresses localization degradation and failures caused by abrupt changes in sensor characteristics and availability during water–land transitions.

Introduces medium-dependent sensor degradation models and four metrics: TCR, PW-APE, TEE, and TSP.
Evaluation of six representative SLAM systems reveals transition-induced drift, trajectory discontinuities, and tracking failures.
Dataset and benchmark are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Progress in autonomous navigation in off-road environments requires not only advances in algorithms, but also robust and capable physical platforms suited to both development and deployment. Today, off-road autonomy is typically developed and tested at one of two extremes of vehicle scale, each with different drawbacks. Full-size vehicles are capable but expensive, require large logistic infrastructure for deployment and maintenance, and expensive when pushed beyond their limits. RC-scale vehicles are small and inexpensive, but limited in the terrain they can traverse and the payload that they can carry, which includes their sensors and compute. We present the AlphaTruck platform, which leverages recent advances in compact sensing and compute to integrate multimodal sensing, embedded CPU-GPU compute, and an onboard autonomy stack for high-speed, off-road navigation, all integrated into a large-scale, 1/5th RC vehicle chassis. AlphaTruck is designed as both a research testbed and a field-deployable platform for commercial and defense missions such as survey, search and rescue, and agriculture, with the capacity to carry task-specific payloads. At 1/5 scale, the autonomy stack, sensors, and batteries all compete for the same mass, power, and cooling budget, so the platform must balance five needs: mobility over rough terrain, rich sensing, onboard computation, payload capacity to carry the autonomy stack while leaving room for task-specific equipment, and practical operation and repair. Thus, AlphaTruck navigates off-road environments autonomously at 6-10 m/s using only onboard sensing and compute.

papers.abstract: Accurate and timely air pollution monitoring and tracking are critical for protecting public health and supporting effective environmental management. This paper presents an adaptive Density-Driven Control (D$^2$C) framework for coordinating multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to track and map dynamically evolving pollutant distributions. The proposed framework extends the D$^2$C strategy to guide UAV trajectories based on predictive pollutant propagation and dynamically updated reference densities. A sensor-driven surrogate plume update mechanism is employed, in which reference samples are propagated using locally sensed concentration gradients and wind estimates through gradient attraction, wind advection, inter-sample repulsion, and stochastic diffusion, enabling UAVs to maintain an accurate spatio-temporal representation of the pollution field. The framework utilizes a coordinated structure where individual UAVs share their local measurements with a central coordinator to maintain a unified set of reference samples, facilitating systematic target allocation and trajectory planning. Simulation results under both mild and strong wind conditions demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of Sinkhorn distance. Specifically, in scenarios where the plume drifts beyond a fixed monitoring domain under high-velocity, time-varying wind fields, the tested baseline methods fail to maintain tracking, whereas the proposed D$^2$C framework successfully adapts to the evolving distribution. These findings highlight D$^2$C as an efficient and resilient solution for atmospheric monitoring in dynamic environments.
authors: Julian Martinez, Ruchika Singh, Mohammad Afrazi, Kooktae Lee

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based driving planners can generate multiple trajectories for the same scene, but these candidates vary in quality. Can their internal states reveal which candidate will be better before denoising is complete? We systematically study this question in three pretrained planners: Alpamayo, ReCogDrive-IL, and HDP, using linear probes to predict final trajectory quality from intermediate states and evaluating candidate ranking and selection on held-out scenes. Across all three planners, we observe that states from the first denoiser evaluation already support informative selection, while further denoising does not consistently improve selection quality. Further analyses show that readout depends on the representation and reader, and that selection can coexist with limited overall ranking accuracy. These findings motivate an early-selection method that selects after the first denoiser evaluation and completes only the chosen candidate. This reduces computation relative to fully denoising every candidate and improves open-loop trajectory quality over random selection across all three planners. In particular, it reduces Alpamayo's average displacement error by 17.8% and 13.4% in one- and four-camera configurations, respectively. Closed-loop evaluations also show higher mean driving scores and progress.
authors: Xiang Zhang, Ziyang Leng, Yuxin Bao, Zhihao Zhao, Bolei Zhou, Xugui Zhou

papers.abstract: Effective planning requires representations that preserve task-relevant geometry and object identity while ignoring visual variation that does not alter the task. Existing evaluations of visual generalization often change several factors simultaneously, making the source of a failure difficult to identify. We introduce a controlled evaluation of object-goal navigation (ObjectNav), the task of reaching an instance of a named object category, in procedurally generated ProcTHOR houses. Training and evaluation houses share floor plans, object locations, goals, and start states, while visual factors are changed individually or in combination. Across model-free reinforcement learning (RL), model-based RL, and agents using frozen pretrained visual representations, our results show that appearance changes impair navigation, but their effects differ sharply by factor. Surface material changes account for most of the average change in success, whereas clutter and lighting have little effect. The magnitude of a global image statistics shift does not reliably predict performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially impair an end-to-end agent despite a small image-level change. We found that a model based agent that plans over frozen features from the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder achieves the highest success (0.83) under the full shift, but remains sensitive to surface appearance. Our experiments reveal an important requirement for planning representations: they must separate invariant spatial task structure from appearance.
authors: Aarav Srivastava, Vishwas Sathish, Rajesh P. N. Rao
bullets: Evaluates visual generalization by changing one or more factors while keeping ProcTHOR layouts, objects, goals, and starts fixed.
Surface material changes cause most of the average success degradation; clutter and lighting have comparatively little effect.
Global image-statistics shifts do not reliably predict navigation performance: changing only the goal object's appearance can substantially hurt end-to-end agents.
A model-based agent planning over frozen DINOv2 features achieves the highest reported full-shift success (0.83), but remains sensitive to surface appearance.
Results span model-free RL, model-based RL, and frozen-visual-representation agents, highlighting the need for appearance-invariant planning representations.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a depth-aware path planning and collision avoidance framework for the safe navigation of robotic nursing assistants in cluttered environments with low-height obstacles. Conventional LiDAR-based navigation systems, while accurate for mapping and localization, fail to detect transparent or low-height obstacles, whereas vision-based systems are prone to noise and occlusion. The proposed framework integrates RGB-D depth sensing, rule-based obstacle avoidance, and the NavfnROS global path planner to drive the robot from an initial point to a goal point. The proposed approach is implemented on the Husky A200 robot, equipped with a Kinova Gen3 arm, to form a complete setup for a robotic nursing assistant. This system features a multi-layer architecture for global planning, perception fusion, and real-time control in the ROS-Gazebo environment. Experimental evaluations in a simulated cluttered environment demonstrate up to 40\% higher success rate and 35\% improvement in minimum clearance compared with single-sensor baselines. Furthermore, real-world experimental results validate the proposed approach as a computationally efficient and safety-aware navigation solution for autonomous healthcare robots.

papers.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.
bullets: Addresses safety constraints that sampling-based planners handle only by scoring or rejecting action sequences.

On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks, it had fewer violations than MPPI and CEM under the reported equal-time comparison, with higher return at longer horizons.
Planning converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models and reports whether a feasible first-order KKT point was found nearby.
