papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive priors over trajectories, but adapting these priors to test-time constraints requires maintaining feasibility and consistency across successive control decisions. We introduce Persistent Particle Planning (P3), a sequential Monte Carlo framework for diffusion control that maintains a weighted population of candidate plans across replanning steps. At each control step, P3 shifts and partially re-noises the candidate trajectories, refines them under the latest observation, and uses constraint-aware weighting and resampling to select among alternative continuations without retraining the diffusion model. We consider denoising and replanning as one Feynman--Kac particle system and analyze it under an idealized repair. We prove that the re-noising depth controls how reliably a kept plan stays on its route, and that keeping a rare, well-separated route takes far fewer plans than rediscovering it by sampling from scratch. Experiments under multiple test-time constraint configurations show that population reuse reduces route switching and improves success without constraint violations. Because P3 refines earlier plans instead of redrawing them, it also needs fewer denoising iterations per replan. On maze-navigation tasks, it plans faster than both regenerated populations and methods that correct a single sampled plan by constrained optimization. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/p3-username/p3-anon.
bullets: Maintains weighted candidate trajectories across replanning steps using shifting, partial re-noising, constraint-aware weighting, and resampling.
Unifies denoising and replanning as a Feynman–Kac particle system and analyzes route retention under an idealized repair.
Theoretical results link re-noising depth to route persistence and show efficient preservation of rare, well-separated routes.
Experiments find less route switching, higher constraint-compliant success, and fewer denoising iterations than regenerating plans or correcting one plan by optimization.
On maze navigation, P3 plans faster than the compared baselines; scope is demonstrated under multiple test-time constraint configurations.

papers.abstract: Emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, satellite inspection, and active debris removal require trajectory design methods that are adaptable to a variety of mission scenarios. We present a diffusion-based trajectory generation approach for rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) that enables flexible configuration of mission constraints. First, individual energy-based diffusion models are trained to satisfy distinct constraints such as approach cone and sensor line-of-sight from a set of optimized trajectories. Then, at inference time, the learned energy models can be composed with one another, or with an analytically defined energy field, to enforce specific constraint combinations. We validate this framework with the composition of a learned approach cone model and a learned sensor line-of-sight model, as well as a learned approach cone model and synthetic obstacle avoidance model, both of which yield constraint satisfaction rates that are within 1 percentage point of the single-constraint models or higher. These results indicate that our compositional diffusion framework can provide a modular approach to RPO trajectory design and enable reconfiguration for new constraint combinations without requiring model retraining.
bullets: Targets adaptable trajectory design for rendezvous and proximity operations, including servicing, inspection, and debris removal.
Trains separate energy-based diffusion models for constraints such as approach cones and sensor line-of-sight.
Composes learned constraint models at inference time, including with analytical obstacle-avoidance energy fields.
Combined models achieve constraint satisfaction within 1 percentage point of, or better than, corresponding single-constraint models.
Scope is demonstrated on approach-cone, line-of-sight, and synthetic obstacle-avoidance constraint combinations.

papers.abstract: In recent years, humanoid loco-manipulation has progressed to whole-body grasping, lifting, and transport. A basic requirement underlying these tasks is carrying the object to its destination, which depends on the locomotion controller accurately executing velocity commands from the navigation policy. However, carrying an object in one hand introduces a persistent asymmetric upper-body load that can degrade velocity tracking. Persistent tracking biases can accumulate into position and heading deviations, increasing the risk of collisions and navigation failure. To address this problem, we present ReACT, a framework for accurate velocity tracking under asymmetric upper-body loads. Reflection-consistent disturbance modulation uses the estimated wrench to modulate actor features for load compensation while preserving action correspondence under reflected observations. Cross-load tracking consistency training compares loaded and unloaded conditions under the same velocity commands to promote consistent velocity tracking across loading conditions. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot show improved velocity tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads. Real-world experiments demonstrate collision-free goal reaching in all 40 tested navigation trials under unilateral hand loads with a fixed mapless navigation policy.

bullets: Addresses persistent velocity-tracking and directional biases caused by carrying an object in one hand.
Uses estimated-wrench modulation of actor features to compensate for asymmetric loads while preserving reflected-action correspondence.
Trains consistency between loaded and unloaded conditions under identical velocity commands.
Simulation results show improved tracking and reduced directional bias under varying asymmetric loads.

papers.abstract: Motion planning for stochastic systems aims to find a sequence of control inputs that drives a system to a goal set while avoiding unsafe states with high probability. Existing approaches, however, are either restricted to linear dynamics with perfect knowledge of the underlying distributions or lack formal correctness guarantees. To address these limitations, we propose \emph{Learn-To-Propagate Distributionally-Robust Forest (L2P-DR-Forest)}, a distributionally-robust sampling-based planning algorithm for \emph{nonlinear} stochastic systems with \emph{unknown} initial state and process noise distributions. Our approach leverages recent advances in optimal transport to learn ambiguity sets that contain the true system distributions with high confidence. We develop an efficient method for propagating these sets through the system dynamics and for verifying their safety. We then integrate these techniques into a novel sampling-based planning algorithm to grow a forest of search trees in the system's state space while accounting for and mitigating the growth of ambiguity-sets radii. We prove that the algorithm is correct, i.e., every returned plan satisfies the specifications with the prescribed confidence, and, under some feasibility and distributional assumptions, is probabilistically complete. Evaluations on several robotic benchmarks demonstrate that our algorithm significantly outperforms existing methods while providing formal guarantees with high confidence.
authors: Eduardo Figueiredo, Adrien Banse, Qi Heng Ho, Raphael Jungers, Morteza Lahijanian, Luca Laurenti
bullets: Targets high-probability goal reaching and unsafe-state avoidance under nonlinear dynamics and distributional uncertainty.
Uses optimal transport to learn high-confidence ambiguity sets containing the true system distributions.
Efficiently propagates and safety-checks these sets while growing a sampling-based forest of search trees.
Proves correctness with prescribed confidence and probabilistic completeness under feasibility and distributional assumptions.
Demonstrates strong performance on several robotic benchmarks while retaining formal guarantees.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems increasingly rely on generating multiple trajectory candidates and selecting one for execution. In this setting, a central challenge is no longer only candidate generation, but how to evaluate candidates according to their long-horizon consequences under uncertainty. Existing methods still mainly use deterministic point scores, heuristic subscores, or single-outcome evaluations, which makes it difficult to capture delayed failures, tail risk, and ranking instability under plausible future perturbations. We present RiSE-Drive, a framework for risk-sensitive long-horizon candidate evaluation in end-to-end autonomous driving. RiSE-Drive first performs candidate-conditioned latent future rollout, then estimates long-horizon outcome distributions instead of single scalar scores, and finally ranks candidates using a tail-risk-aware and perturbation-robust decision criterion. This reformulates candidate scoring from deterministic oracle-style evaluation into distributional outcome assessment with explicit risk control. As a result, the evaluator is encouraged to prefer candidates that are not only strong under nominal conditions, but also reliable under long-horizon rollout and safety-critical deviations. Experiments on the NAVSIM-v1 and NAVSIM-v2 benchmarks, as well as the closed-loop HUGSIM benchmark, show that RiSE-Drive achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly improves the robustness of candidate selection.
authors: Yu Zhao, Hongyi Duan, Ming Yin, Hongyuan Zhang, Fan Yang, Hongzhi Wang, Xiubo Liang
bullets: Addresses delayed failures, tail risk, and unstable candidate rankings in end-to-end autonomous driving.
Uses candidate-conditioned latent future rollouts to estimate distributions of long-horizon outcomes.
Ranks candidates with a tail-risk-aware, perturbation-robust decision criterion rather than deterministic point scores.
Evaluated on NAVSIM-v1, NAVSIM-v2, and closed-loop HUGSIM, where it reports state-of-the-art performance and more robust candidate selection.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the RiSE-Drive pipeline. Multi-view observations are encoded, and the proposal generator produces 𝐾 ego-trajectory candidates. A future-condition generator predicts 𝐿 branch-specific condition codes that parameterize plausible downstream evolutions. For each candidate–condition pair, RiSE-Drive initializes a latent consequence state, propagates it along the trajectory, and decodes one branch-level long-horizon outcome sample. The resulting branchwise consequence traces are pooled over time and across branches and mapped to ordered outcome quantiles by a distribution head. The final ranking score combines the mean estimate, lower-tail CVaR, and cross-condition instability, thereby favoring candidates that remain reliable under plausible future deviations rather than merely optimal under a single nominal forecast.

papers.abstract: Monocular depth foundation models make it tempting to replace depth sensors on mobile robots with a single RGB camera. We show that, used off the shelf, this is unsafe: in a simulated indoor navigation benchmark, a standard Nav2 stack driven by Depth Anything V2 (metric) collides in 63\% of 120 episodes, because the model systematically over-estimates the distance to nearby obstacles. We propose a lightweight plug-in module that turns predicted depth into \emph{safe depth}. A 0.58\,M-parameter head on top of the \emph{frozen} depth model predicts, per pixel, a log-depth correction $\mu$ and an uncertainty $\sigma$, trained with a $\beta$-weighted Gaussian negative log-likelihood. The navigation stack consumes the one-sided bound $\hat d_{\text{safe}}=d\,e^{\mu-k\sigma}$, where $k$ is set by conformal calibration on a held-out world, and uncertainty also decides which pixels may be treated as floor. The correction halves the depth error (AbsRel $0.262\rightarrow0.134$) and reduces near-range over-estimation from 59.8\% to 12.0\%. In navigation, safe depth raises the success rate from 37\% to 70\% and lowers collisions from 63\% to 3\%, close to the 2\% of ground-truth depth. A constant safety margin calibrated to the same pixel coverage reaches only 30\% success because it freezes the robot; uncertainty-aware safety wins 52 of 56 discordant paired episodes against it. Gains hold on glass, texture-less walls and dark regions.
bullets: Off-the-shelf Depth Anything V2 depth caused collisions in 63% of 120 simulated navigation episodes, mainly by over-estimating nearby obstacle distances.
A lightweight 0.58M-parameter head predicts per-pixel log-depth corrections and uncertainty while keeping the depth model frozen.
Conformal calibration converts predictions into a one-sided safe-depth bound, with uncertainty also guiding floor-pixel selection.
Safe depth reduced AbsRel from 0.262 to 0.134 and collisions from 63% to 3%, while raising navigation success from 37% to 70%.
The approach outperformed a constant safety margin and retained gains on glass, texture-less walls, and dark regions.

papers.abstract: Photorealistic and metrically consistent world representations are a primary requirement for LiDAR--inertial--visual SLAM systems that serve robots over continuous operation. 3D Gaussian splatting makes such representations attainable by supplying an explicit, renderable, and queryable scene model. We present GEMOR-GS (Global Extrinsic-calibration-refined Mapping and Online Relocalization for 3D Gaussian-Splatting SLAM) to make the Gaussian map geometrically accurate, globally refined, and re-enterable, providing a better appearance for robot perception and decision-making. To improve the 3DGS map, the LiDAR--camera extrinsic is first estimated offline by direct-method alignment over dedicated calibration segments and reused by all following online and offline processes. Under the calibrated geometry, keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters are refined alternately under a gated differentiable-rendering and LiDAR--projection objective. The final global reconstruction is then rebuilt from the refined keyframe schema with all online constraints lifted. For the robot SLAM lifecycle, the method recovers the pose from the 3DGS map after tracking loss through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP coarse localization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement. Experiments on one self-collected and five public sequences quantify each element: the offline reconstruction wins all paired keyframes against the online map by 14.3--19.9 dB, improves PSNR by approximately 9 dB over Gaussian-LIC2, and achieves 86--100% held-out relocalization success tied to extrinsic quality. The results show that GEMOR-GS improves the geometric accuracy, appearance fidelity, and re-enterability of the 3DGS map, serving as a dependable robot world model for SLAM and downstream tasks.
authors: Yuchen Yang, Ming Ding, Xinyu Wu, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Targets photorealistic, metrically consistent world models for continuous LiDAR–inertial–visual SLAM.
Calibrates LiDAR–camera extrinsics offline, then jointly refines keyframe poses and Gaussian parameters using rendering and LiDAR projection objectives.
Reconstructs a globally optimized map from refined keyframes without online constraints.
Relocalizes through an XFeat bypass map, RANSAC-PnP initialization, and Gaussian RGB-D warp refinement.
Across one self-collected and five public sequences, reports 14.3–19.9 dB gains over the online map, about 9 dB higher PSNR than Gaussian-LIC2, and 86–100% held-out relocalization success.

The online track 1O runs an IESKF over LiDAR, inertial, and visual measurements against a compact Gaussian tracking reference, and keyframes accumulate under the five-channel contract into the shared keyframe schema. The offline track 2O consumes the keyframe schema: joint optimization refines keyframe poses and map, after which global reconstruction reinitializes the Gaussians into the final 3DGS model. The calibration refinement 3O is an independent process: the extrinsic is estimated once per sensor rig by direct-method calibration and reused by both tracks. papers.abstract: End-to-end navigation in cluttered environments relies on compact visual representations to support collision avoidance and goal-directed motion. Existing methods typically learn these representations jointly with the policy or through observation reconstruction, which does not explicitly specify what information the representation should preserve. Moreover, they are usually evaluated with a single downstream policy learner, although the benefit of a representation may depend on how the policy is learned. It therefore remains unclear how different representation-learning objectives affect downstream navigation performance and robustness. This work proposes DeRep, a navigation-oriented representation-learning method that combines local bird's-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction. To compare representation objectives under controlled conditions, we pretrain encoders with a common architecture and freeze them during downstream learning. We evaluate the representations using a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and reinforcement learning with PPO. DeRep achieves the lowest linear policy probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction alone across all six tested PPO conditions. In imitation learning, both reachability-based objectives achieve higher mean success rates than reconstruction alone, with similar mean success rates between the reachability-only and joint objectives. These results demonstrate consistent benefits of incorporating reachability supervision into depth representation pretraining across different downstream learning methods and evaluation conditions. We further deploy the PPO policy with the frozen DeRep encoder in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor without fine-tuning, demonstrating its capability for zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.
bullets: Addresses the unclear relationship between representation-learning objectives and downstream navigation robustness in cluttered environments.
Combines local bird’s-eye-view reachability supervision with depth reconstruction; encoders are pretrained with a shared architecture and frozen during evaluation.
Tests representations with a linear policy probe, flow-matching imitation learning, and PPO reinforcement learning.

DeRep has the lowest linear-probe prediction error and outperforms reconstruction-only pretraining across all six PPO conditions; reachability-based objectives also improve imitation-learning success.
A PPO policy using the frozen DeRep encoder transfers without fine-tuning in Gazebo and on a physical quadrotor, demonstrating zero-shot sim-to-sim and sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Existing cooperative end-to-end driving works at Class A (status-sharing) of the SAE J3216 classes of cooperative driving automation (CDA): vehicles exchange what they perceive, not what they intend, so each plans alone when to go, which limits cooperation and leads to deadlock when both vehicles yield or to collisions when both go. We present When2Go, a cooperative end-to-end driving system that learns when to go by sharing intent under CDA Class B or higher. Each vehicle broadcasts its LiDAR detections with forecast motion as instance tokens, together with its plan and intended trajectory. The receiver draws the fused detections, forecasts and partner plans into a route-time conflict map, the occupancy along its route over the planning horizon, on which a planner scores candidate speed profiles. Where two intended trajectories conflict, an order gate, a precedence network distilled from a right-of-way rule, decides who goes first; both vehicles evaluate it on the same messages and so reach the same order. When2Go imitates the rule-based expert of V2Xverse, which sees the simulator's ground truth; stops that When2Go cannot observe within its 2 s planning horizon are relabelled, so that it does not learn to wait without an observable cause. For our runs only, the benchmarks' PID controller steers by When2Go's waypoints instead of the route, and its forced push of long-waiting vehicles is off. With one model, When2Go sets the state of the art on three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks: 97.8 and 90.7 driving score on InterDrive without and with traffic (best published 90.1 and 78.9), 70.0 on the public V2Xverse protocol (best of sixteen rerun methods 59.1) and 88.2 on MDrive (best rerun 85.1), with 95.0% of its vehicles collision-free (87.7%).
authors: Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Tianle Zhu, Zhipeng Bao, Yiping Li, Handong Yao
bullets: Addresses the limits of perception-only cooperation, which can cause mutual yielding deadlocks or collisions when vehicles proceed simultaneously.
Vehicles share LiDAR detections, predicted motion, plans, and intended trajectories as instance tokens.
A route-time conflict map represents predicted occupancy along the ego route; a planner evaluates candidate speed profiles.
An order gate based on a distilled right-of-way precedence rule gives vehicles a consistent crossing order.
Achieves reported state-of-the-art driving scores across three closed-loop CARLA benchmarks, with 95.0% of vehicles collision-free.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of When2Go. Each vehicle runs the same network on its LiDAR and broadcasts its detections, forecasts and plan. papers.abstract: A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.
authors: Rumi Loghmani, Bozhang Song, Victor Alvarado, Aliyah Redding, Amir Barati Farimani
bullets: Reads experiment steps from a photo of a printed protocol.
Identifies identical containers by reading labels from multiple camera views, without fixed positions or fiducial markers.
Relocates target containers before every step and adapts execution settings, including speed, to the handled material.
Completed 5/5 runs of one protocol and 4/5 of another without human intervention; correctly identified all containers in 160 localization trials.
Demonstrated on a Franka Panda arm and two children’s chemistry-kit protocols, so scope is limited to the tested setup and procedures.

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent Barrier Steering (LBS), a hierarchical semantic-to-path framework for safe flow-matching-based generative planning. Existing control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filters for diffusion and flow-matching planners act locally on generated samples, either during sampling or after prediction. Such repair is effective for small violations, but can struggle when a new constraint blocks the whole selected behavior mode rather than merely perturbing it locally. LBS decouples behavior selection from path certification through two coordinated interventions: it first steers the generator's behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margin, then decodes the steered latent and applies a path-space CBF quadratic program (QP) only for residual violations. We show that latent steering increases the margin available to the path-space corrector, yielding finite-time recovery guarantees and reduced correction burden. Experiments across navigation and robot end-effector planning tasks show that LBS preserves safety while improving goal reaching and reducing correction burden compared with path-level safety filters.
authors: Renhao Zhang, Mingzhe Li, Bruno Castro da Silva
bullets: Addresses the failure of local safety filters when constraints invalidate an entire behavior mode.
Steers the generator’s behavior latent toward rollouts with larger safety margins.
Uses a path-space control-barrier-function quadratic program to correct only residual violations.
Provides finite-time recovery guarantees and reduces the burden on path-level correction.
Experiments in navigation and robot end-effector planning show preserved safety, better goal reaching, and less correction than path-level filters.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Experimental domains and test-time safety constraints. Each row shows one planning domain: 2D point-navigation, Maze2D, and Franka 3D end-effector planning. The first column visualizes the original scene and multimodal demonstration dataset, where multiple behaviors can reach the same goal. The remaining columns show three test-time safety constraints imposed on the same pretrained planner. Green circles denote starts, orange stars denote goals, and red shaded regions denote unsafe sets. These constraints test whether a method can preserve safety and goal reaching when certification requires more than local path repair.

Figure 3: Latent steering provides the warm start needed for path-space repair. Stage I performs behavior-level selection by steering the latent and changing the decoded rollout before certification; Stage II then applies path-level CBF repair to remove residual violations. The second row removes Stage I and applies the same path-space correction directly, corresponding to SAFEFLOWMATCHER. Without the latent-steered warm start, the local corrector remains tied to the original rollout and fails to produce a goal-reaching safe path. With Stage I, the corrected trajectory starts from a better behavior and Stage II only needs to repair the remaining local violation.

Figure 1: Latent Barrier Steering separates behavior selection from path repair. A vanilla flow-matching planner may generate a goal-reaching but unsafe rollout under a new constraint. A path-space CBF corrector such as SAFEFLOWMATCHER can enforce safety locally, but may produce a trajectory that is safe while no longer reaching the goal when the selected behavior mode is blocked. LBS first steers the behavior latent from z0 to z+ toward a safer rollout, then applies path-level CBF repair only for residual violations, yielding a trajectory that is both safe and goal-reaching.

papers.abstract: Learning-based decentralized collision avoidance must remain reliable under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics. Existing methods typically address these factors through training-domain variation or by exposing uncertainty and capability estimates to the policy at runtime. However, both leave the policy to infer how these quantities should alter the physical separation required for safe interaction, which can couple collision-avoidance behavior to relationships learned from the training distribution. We introduce the Dynamic Oriented Bounding Box (DOBB), an online geometric representation that maps the current state estimate, uncertainty, and agent-specific response characteristics into a dynamic, direction-dependent safety margin. We derive geometric features that jointly characterize the relative configuration and severity of interactions between agents' DOBBs, along with a reward function that preserves the physical interpretation of those interactions. Across four evaluation environments, DOBB achieves the lowest mean total failure rate of 2.6%. This performance persists under out-of-distribution shifts in actuation dynamics and state-estimation uncertainty, with collision-based failure remaining at or below 2.3% in every tested condition. We attribute this robustness to the geometric abstraction of the safety margin, which is less coupled to the specific uncertainty and actuation regimes encountered during training.
authors: Pedro Antonio Alarcon Granadeno, Jane Cleland-Huang
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance under state-estimation uncertainty and heterogeneous agent dynamics.

Across four environments, reports a 2.6% mean total failure rate and collision-based failure of at most 2.3% under tested distribution shifts.
Scope: robustness is demonstrated for the evaluated environments and out-of-distribution actuation and uncertainty conditions.

papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.
authors: Jiajun Chen, Shicheng Fang, Jiahao Lu, Yuxin Wang, Xipeng Qiu

A task generator creates parameterized 3D and image-based environments with automatic rewards and termination signals for RL.
LoRA RL on generated navigation tasks improves in-domain and cross-category performance, raising native GTA V task performance from 15% to 23%.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANAV, a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action-video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANAV outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors in long-horizon navigation and the limitations of failure-insensitive imitation learning and costly physical RL.
Alternates world-model refinement and policy improvement in a recursive self-improvement loop.
Uses imagined action outcomes for group-relative policy optimization and behavioral novelty/prediction error to build a grounded self-curriculum.
Experiments report gains over training baselines and prior methods, with real-world trials supporting practical applicability.

papers.abstract: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of translating distant navigation goals into coherent local decisions in large, complex environments.
Maintains persistent medium-horizon subgoals and relevant experience through a navigation memory module.
Uses an action-conditioned world model to predict candidate movement outcomes in a visual sandbox.
A vision-language reasoner evaluates predictions, while real observations update memory and revise actions or subgoals.
Evaluations report stronger gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

papers.abstract: Safe robot control often requires combining long-horizon performance optimization with hard state and input constraints, but existing approaches tend to address this tradeoff partially. Sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) methods such as model predictive path integral (MPPI) are effective in handling nonlinear and nonconvex environments, yet their finite-sample rollouts and unconstrained weighted-average update can return an unsafe control. Deterministic nonlinear MPC can explicitly incorporate constraints, but its real-time safety and performance depends strongly on warm starts and local convergence. Hamilton--Jacobi reachability (HJR) provides rigorous safety certificates, but offline value-function computation remains practical only for reduced-order models. We propose ReSQ-MPPI, a reachability-informed generation--refinement architecture that combines these complementary strengths. An HJR value function computed offline for a reduced-order model guides online MPPI sampling toward safe, promising trajectory candidates. The MPPI solution is then refined by a small number of sequential quadratic programming (SQP) iterations in a full-order MPC problem. A key observation is that the standard MPPI inference step is an unconstrained weighted least-squares problem; ReSQ-MPPI replaces it with a constrained MPC refinement that recovers the MPPI update when it is feasible and minimally modifies it otherwise. Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing environments demonstrate that ReSQ-MPPI improves safety and performance over standalone MPPI, MPC, and reachability-filtered sampling-based control baselines.
bullets: Targets the tension between long-horizon optimization and hard state/input constraints in safe nonlinear control.
Uses an offline Hamilton–Jacobi reachability value function from a reduced-order model to guide online MPPI sampling.
Refines MPPI’s weighted-average update with a few sequential quadratic programming iterations in a full-order constrained MPC problem.
The constrained refinement preserves the MPPI update when feasible and minimally changes it when necessary.
Simulations in cluttered navigation and autonomous racing show improved safety and performance over several baseline controllers.

papers.abstract: For ground robots operating in outdoor environments, understanding the properties of the underlying terrain is essential for ensuring reliable operation. In most perception-based studies, this problem is formulated as categorical classification with a fixed number of classes defined during training. We propose an approach that enables new surface classes to be added as trainable vectors, which can subsequently be used to address higher-level tasks. By employing a learning paradigm based on predicting the robot's next state in time and using attention blocks, we improved classification accuracy to 98.56% on the Belyaev-Kushnarev dataset and 94.8% on BorealTC.
bullets: Targets reliable outdoor ground-robot operation through improved surface understanding.
Uses next-state prediction as the learning objective, combined with attention blocks.
Represents newly introduced surface classes as trainable vectors rather than requiring a fixed class set.
Reports classification accuracies of 98.56% on Belyaev-Kushnarev and 94.8% on BorealTC.
The abstract does not specify how well the approach handles classes beyond the reported evaluations.

papers.abstract: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.
bullets: Targets multi-drone coordination in both cooperative and adversarial settings.
Combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints, and trajectory-tracking interfaces.
Compares cooperative game solvers for finding feasible conflict-resolving trajectories.
Evaluates how drone count, prediction horizon, and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance.
PyBullet simulations and a physical-drone flight validate the planner and tracking interfaces; timing tests identify practical real-time limits.

papers.abstract: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.
bullets: Targets fleet management with minimized completion time and priority-dependent tardiness.

papers.abstract: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of maintaining progress across successive goals while producing stable, natural whole-body motion in confined spaces.
Coordinates three asynchronous roles: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body control.
Uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and execution.
Introduces a physics-grounded data engine for collision-aware, route-faithful motion demonstrations paired with visual observations.

In simulation, LHNav improves success and smoothness while reducing collisions and falls; it reaches 75.56% long-horizon success using only single-goal training, and transfers to real-world zero-shot execution on a Unitree G1.

An action buffer supplies the latest motion-token chunk to the Brainstem’s frozen SONIC controller, which combines it with proprioception to produce joint targets at 50 Hz for PD control. The independent arrival-verification VLM updates the results buffer at up to 1 Hz. Geometric supervision encourages waypoint traversability during training.

papers.abstract: Traversability prediction is a core component of autonomous navigation, yet most vision-based methods operate frame-wise and produce temporally inconsistent predictions. We present SAM-VTP (Video Traversability Prediction), which fine-tunes SAM2's video memory pathway for dense, prompt-free traversability segmentation, conditioning each frame on a persistent memory of prior observations. Rather than inferring terrain geometry from appearance, we measure it: slope, roughness and height are computed from depth and fused into the image features. We also introduce an offline continuous supervision pipeline that generates dense per-pixel traversability targets in [0,1] from depth-derived geometry and semantic priors, requiring no robot deployment and no per-pixel annotation, capturing conditional feasibility that binary labels cannot represent. On TartanGround, a large-scale synthetic ground-robot dataset, SAM-VTP improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924 and binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886 over SAM-TP, a frame-wise SAM2 baseline, against a seed-to-seed spread below 0.001, and cuts frame-to-frame flicker by 31%. In closed-loop trials at two field sites, driving the same planner and controller, the baseline's dropouts leave the planner without a feasible path 3.3x more often on a paved course and 6.9x on rough ground, while SAM-VTP runs at 21.4 FPS on the Orin Nano the robot carries.
bullets: Addresses frame-wise vision models that produce inconsistent traversability predictions for autonomous navigation.
Fine-tunes SAM2’s video-memory pathway and fuses depth-derived slope, roughness, and height with image features.
Generates dense continuous traversability targets without robot deployment or per-pixel annotation.
On TartanGround, improves fuzzy Jaccard from 0.908 to 0.924, binary IoU from 0.854 to 0.886, and reduces flicker by 31% versus SAM-TP.
In closed-loop field trials, reduces planner dropouts and runs at 21.4 FPS on an Orin Nano.

At t2 SAM-TP loses roughly half of the traversable surface and recovers it at t3, while SAM-VTP holds a coherent region across all three frames (fuzzy Jaccard, fJacc, 0.69 against 0.92 on this window). SAM-VTP’s output is also traversability-scaled, whereas SAM-TP’s is dominated by binary confidence.

papers.abstract: Cross-view image sequence geo-localization aims to determine the geographic location of a sequence of ground images by matching it against geo-tagged satellite imagery. Although sequential observations provide complementary scene information, substantial overlap between adjacent images introduces feature redundancy, while conventional fusion strategies may weaken spatial relationships essential for cross-view matching. Therefore, we propose a cross-view image sequence geo-localization method via Attention-guided Sequence fusion and Metric Learning (ASML). Specifically, a Sequential Content Fusion (SCF) module models cross-image feature correlations to suppress redundant content and adaptively preserve geographically informative non-overlapping regions. Next, a Spatial Feature Aggregation (SFA) module is used to capture and aggregate the spatial and semantic information of local features, so as to maintain the spatial layout of the image sequence. Finally, a Geo-InfoNCE loss function is proposed, which comprehensively considers the feature distance and geographic distance for mixed-space metric learning, thus improving the ability of the model to distinguish hard negative samples. A new cross-view image sequence dataset CrossRoad-66K is established to provide more complex scenarios. Extensive experiments and visualizations on the SeqGeo and CrossRoad-66K datasets demonstrate that compared to state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods, the proposed method ASML achieves an improvement of 3.37% and 2.10% at R@1, respectively.
bullets: Addresses feature redundancy from overlapping adjacent ground images and weakened spatial relationships in sequence fusion.
Uses Sequential Content Fusion to suppress redundant content while retaining informative non-overlapping regions.
Uses Spatial Feature Aggregation to combine local spatial and semantic information while maintaining scene layout.
Introduces Geo-InfoNCE loss for mixed-space metric learning that incorporates feature and geographic distances to handle hard negatives.
Reports R@1 improvements of 3.37% on SeqGeo and 2.10% on the newly established CrossRoad-66K dataset versus SOTA methods.

papers.abstract: Navigation in dynamic environments requires mobile robots to make progress toward their goals while respecting motion limits and avoiding surrounding obstacles. Learned subgoal policies can guide model predictive control beyond its local prediction horizon, but a geometrically suitable subgoal does not necessarily lead to a successfully solved control problem. This paper proposes OASIS, a hierarchical navigation framework that incorporates recent optimization outcomes into reinforcement learning-based subgoal generation. A high-level policy trained using Soft Actor--Critic generates local subgoals, while a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks them subject to motion limits, geometric collision-avoidance constraints, and embedded high-order control barrier function constraints. The outcomes of controller optimizations over each subgoal interval are summarized and provided to the policy at its next decision, without requiring additional optimization calls. The framework is evaluated in five navigation scenarios with static and moving obstacles, including dense interactions and sensing uncertainty. Comparisons with hierarchical and direct-goal control variants show that OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success. Matched comparisons across three training seeds further show a consistent success advantage over the otherwise identical hierarchy without optimization-status input. The selected-policy comparison also shows fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.
bullets: Targets the gap between geometrically appropriate subgoals and subgoals that yield successfully solvable control problems.
Combines a Soft Actor–Critic subgoal policy with nonlinear model predictive control, motion and collision constraints, and high-order control barrier functions.
Feeds summarized optimization outcomes from each subgoal interval back to the policy without extra optimization calls.
Across five static and dynamic-obstacle scenarios, OASIS achieves the highest aggregate navigation success and consistently outperforms the same hierarchy without optimization-status input.
Selected-policy comparisons show fewer primary optimization failures with similar mean controller time.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object-goal navigation requires autonomous agents to explore unseen environments and locate target objects without task-specific training, posing challenges in perceptual reliability under observation uncertainty and physically grounded goal termination. Although foundation-model-based approaches improve generalization, they remain vulnerable to unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-induced directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect stopping decisions. To address these limitations, we propose CSG-Nav, a zero-shot navigation framework centered on confidence-aware multimodal information fusion. CSG-Nav integrates three complementary fusion mechanisms. First, semantic-source fusion integrates open-vocabulary detection results, detection confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning to produce more reliable direction-level semantic scores and suppress hallucination-induced directional bias. Second, spatial-confidence fusion weights multi-view semantic evidence using a Gaussian decay function, suppressing unreliable distant observations while accumulating spatially consistent exploration preferences. Third, semantic-geometric decision fusion combines semantic target detection with depth-based 3D localization to support physically grounded stopping decisions. Experiments on HM3Dv1, HM3Dv2, and MP3D demonstrate competitive zero-shot performance, achieving success rates of 58.9%, 71.6%, and 44.3%. Fusion-level ablations and real-world deployments in indoor and outdoor environments further verify the effectiveness and practicality of CSG-Nav for robust navigation under uncertain perception. Code is available at https://xr-ui.github.io/CSGNav.github.io/
bullets: Targets unreliable long-range perception, hallucination-driven directional bias, and semantically plausible but geometrically incorrect termination.
Fuses open-vocabulary detections, confidence, scene observations, and relational reasoning for more reliable directional guidance.
Uses Gaussian spatial-confidence weighting to downweight distant observations and accumulate consistent exploration preferences.
Combines semantic detection with depth-based 3D localization for physically grounded goal stopping.
Reports success rates of 58.9% on HM3Dv1, 71.6% on HM3Dv2, and 44.3% on MP3D, with ablations and real-world deployments supporting practicality.

papers.abstract: Underwater leader-follower formation control requires continuous relative-pose estimation despite degraded sensing conditions and limited onboard computation. This paper presents a reliability-adaptive multimodal perception framework for six-degree-of-freedom relative-pose tracking between two moving underwater robots. The framework integrates complementary visual, acoustic-ranging, and hydrodynamic measurements while accounting for their distinct physical characteristics and time-varying reliability. It adaptively weights modality contributions and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity, enabling efficient pose estimation on embedded hardware. Extensive experiments were conducted using a custom-built AUV platform, with 648 pool trials spanning two leader vehicle types, three illumination conditions, and nine trajectory patterns. Evaluation yields an average translational error of 3.8 cm and an average orientation error of 2.4°. On an onboard NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the fusion network achieves an inference latency of 17.62 ms, providing a 2.69-fold speedup over the evaluated Transformer-based fusion baseline. Closed-loop experiments further demonstrate stable formation maintenance with a moving leader under onboard computational constraints. A multimodal dataset containing measurements from all 648 trials will be made publicly available.
bullets: Addresses continuous pose estimation under degraded underwater sensing and limited onboard computation.
Adaptively weights modalities according to their time-varying reliability and models temporal dependencies with linear computational complexity.
Across 648 pool trials, achieves 3.8 cm average translational error and 2.4° average orientation error.
Runs at 17.62 ms inference latency on a Jetson AGX Orin, reported as 2.69× faster than the evaluated Transformer-based baseline.
Closed-loop tests show stable formation maintenance; a dataset from all trials is planned for public release.

The modality-specific encoders incorporate relevant physical and statistical structure, while the fusion module adjusts modality contributions according to their estimated reliability. The fused relative-pose estimate is provided to a sliding mode controller, supporting real-time formation control on resource-constrained AUV hardware.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based planners such as MPPI and CEM query a learned world model thousands of times per control step, so low-bit world models are an obvious way to make model-based control cheaper on a robot. With round-to-nearest activation quantization and no calibration, we find that planning can collapse, by up to 100 points of success, while the world model's latent one-step prediction error stays no larger than that of a stochastic rounding scheme that plans well. At the same bit width, what decides the outcome is not the size of the rounding error but whether it persists across planner iterations and is shared across candidates. Round-to-nearest leaves an error that persists, and an iterating planner drifts toward the candidates that this error favors; in TD-MPC2, holding the same dither fixed within a step or an episode brings the drift back. Dither shared by all candidates and redrawn at every iteration removes most of the damage at the same bit width and without training: at least half of it in all 19 affected Meta-World cells (task $\times$ bit width) of TD-MPC2 (median 95%), in 4 of 5 DINO-WM cells, and in all 8 affected tasks of a 317M-parameter multi-task TD-MPC2. Captured as CUDA graphs on an Ampere GPU, a W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model runs its planning rollouts 1.9-3.3$\times$ and the whole planning step 1.3-1.5$\times$ faster than FP32, though not faster than BF16 with pre-converted weights; shared dither adds at most 2.3% latency. In TD-MPC2, block-scaled NVFP4 removes most of the damage and MXFP4 part of it, which ties the failure to coarse grids with a shared scale. Hypotheses, thresholds and analysis code were fixed before the data that test them, and the hypotheses that failed are reported.
bullets: Round-to-nearest activation quantization can severely degrade planning despite one-step prediction error comparable to stochastic rounding.
The key issue is error persistence and sharing across planner candidates, not simply rounding-error magnitude.
Redrawing common dither each planner iteration removes most of the degradation without retraining across tested TD-MPC2 and DINO-WM settings.
An W8A4 integer TD-MPC2 world model speeds planning rollouts by 1.9–3.3× and full planning steps by 1.3–1.5× versus FP32; dither adds at most 2.3% latency.
Block-scaled NVFP4 largely avoids the problem, while fixed dither within a step or episode restores planner drift.

papers.abstract: Generative models can support both state estimation and control in robotics. For control, a common approach is to use the model as a policy that directly samples actions conditioned on observation histories. However, models that jointly represent states, actions, and observations can also predict how the robot state and its environment evolve. We investigate whether these predictions can improve state estimation and control through a change in inference procedure, without modifying the pretrained model. To this end, we use particle filtering to maintain competing hypotheses about state histories. A single pretrained diffusion model generates these hypotheses along with their predicted observations and associated action proposals. As new measurements arrive, particles are reweighted according to how well their predicted observations match the measurements. While particle filtering conventionally uses these weights only for state estimation, we also use them to guide action selection, favoring proposals associated with hypotheses that better explain the observations. Simulation experiments in partially observed navigation and vision-based manipulation demonstrate improvements in both state estimation and task performance compared to action generation without filtering, using the same pretrained model and no additional test-time information.
bullets: Addresses partially observed robotics, where uncertainty about state can hinder control.
Maintains competing state-history hypotheses using particles generated by one pretrained diffusion model.
Reweights particles by agreement between predicted and observed measurements.
Uses these weights for both state estimation and action selection, without modifying the model or adding test-time information.
Simulation results in navigation and vision-based manipulation show improved estimation and task performance over unfiltered action generation.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have achieved significant progress in locomotion and manipulation, enabling traversal over rough terrain and richer interaction with the environment, such as moving obstacles. However, most traditional navigation methods assume non-interactive environments and focus only on traversal. While Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) approaches relax this assumption, prior efforts have largely focused on flat environments and reactive interaction, rather than predicting object movability and planning ahead. These limitations become critical in outdoor rough-terrain scenarios, where robots must jointly reason about terrain traversability and object movability. In this work, we address NAMO for humanoid robots in cluttered outdoor rough terrain by proposing a hybrid planning framework that combines semantic priors from a Vision-Language Model (VLM) with embodied robot interaction data through a Gaussian process (GP) residual model. The GP corrects the VLM-derived movability prior to produce embodiment-grounded probabilistic movability estimates, which are then incorporated into hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning. The proposed approach allows humanoids to jointly leverage locomotion and manipulation for efficient and safe navigation, representing the first solution to NAMO in rough terrain through predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.
bullets: Addresses Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) for humanoids in cluttered outdoor rough terrain.
Combines VLM semantic priors with a Gaussian process residual model trained from embodied interaction data.
Produces probabilistic estimates of whether objects can be moved, while accounting for robot-specific capabilities.
Uses hierarchical uncertainty-aware planning to jointly coordinate locomotion and manipulation.
The abstract presents it as the first rough-terrain NAMO approach based on predictive movability reasoning and probabilistic VLM integration.

papers.abstract: Autonomous SaR requires robots to explore unknown or partially known environments, avoid hazards, coordinate team activities, and guide discovered victims to safety. Improving individual capabilities of robots does not necessarily improve mission outcomes: safer motion can restrict the exploration behavior, faster discovery can increase the rescue demand, and effective guidance depends on victim responses. We introduce PA-SaR, a mathematical and architectural framework for coordinating heterogeneous local control, learning-based exploration, supervisory task allocation, and adaptive approach-lead victim guidance around mission-level objectives. PA- SaR distinguishes environmental ground-truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior. This provides a common basis for integrating complementary mechanisms and analyzing their interactions across mission stages. We demonstrate the framework through single- and multi-robot simulation studies incorporating model-predictive and learning-based exploration, perception-based safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive victim guidance. The results show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion, indicate that supervisory allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone, and demonstrate that increased exploration does not necessarily yield more rescues. Adaptive guidance increases rescues relative to continuous leading, without a detected improvement in mean or final victim trust or a reduction in mortality. These findings support evaluating local control, team coordination, and evacuation as related but distinct aspects of autonomous SaR within the considered simulation environments.
bullets: Models environmental ground truth, robot-specific perceptions, and simulated victim behavior as distinct components.
Integrates model-predictive and learning-based exploration, safety shielding, event-driven task allocation, and adaptive guidance.
Simulation studies show trade-offs between collision avoidance and search completion.
Supervisory task allocation improves search completion beyond information sharing alone.
More exploration does not necessarily produce more rescues; adaptive guidance increases rescues versus continuous leading but does not improve measured trust or mortality.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.
bullets: Builds an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose to provide explicit geometric memory.
Conditions the world model, actor, and critic on the map and uses mapped geometry for geodesic progress and wall-contact signals.
Adds a forward-cone penalty to discourage motion outside the forward-facing camera’s view.
In Isaac Sim, it achieves 96.3% success and 3.6% collision across 1,560 episodes, outperforming AirDreamer under the same interaction budget.
Removing the forward-cone penalty raises collisions to 9.9%, highlighting its role in perception-aware navigation.

papers.abstract: A driving foundation model must learn reusable decision knowledge from rare critical events and apply it under strict runtime constraints. We introduce DriveFoundry, a closed-loop framework improving iteration efficiency under data and computation budgets by coupling structured causal data refinement with adaptive inference. The Data Engine builds traceable scene-candidate records linking scene evidence and factor-decision relations to candidate trajectories and outcome assessments. Candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations clarify how scene factors affect behavioral feasibility and preference. Verified model failures guide VLM-assisted annotation and expert correction, refining training data and annotation systems. The model engine, Xiaomi-Drive-o1, unifies Perception, Causation, Action, World, and Value within a shared vision-language backbone to enable cross-task knowledge transfer. Block-wise latent refill passes candidate-specific evidence and predicted visual consequences between task blocks, connecting scene understanding, planning, and evaluation. A learned value-of-computation head selects tasks and allocates latent tokens based on expected benefit and cost, adapting inference to each decision. On PhysicalAI, the 9B model achieves the lowest ADE@1 across evaluated splits and horizons among tested models. In AlpaSim, it outperforms Alpamayo 1.5 across all metrics and achieves lower close-encounter and off-road rates than the 34B Alpamayo 2 Super, while trailing in progress and AlpaSim scores. For the 0.8B variant, joint training reduces 5 s minADE@6 by about 54% without altering the inference path or token budget. Adaptive inference matches full reasoning performance using only 28% of tokens. Real-vehicle tests confirm runtime feasibility, supporting a unified paradigm for learning from critical experience and dynamically allocating computation.
bullets: Builds traceable scene–factor–decision records with candidate comparisons and counterfactual annotations to refine training data from critical events and verified failures.
Uses Xiaomi-Drive-o1, a shared vision-language model integrating perception, causation, action, world modeling, and value estimation.
Connects task blocks through candidate-specific latent evidence and predicted visual consequences, while a value-of-computation head allocates inference effort adaptively.
Reports strong benchmark results, including the lowest ADE@1 among tested models on PhysicalAI and broad metric improvements over Alpamayo 1.5 in AlpaSim.
Joint training improves 5 s minADE@6 for the 0.8B model by about 54%, and adaptive inference reaches full-reasoning performance with 28% of the tokens; real-vehicle tests support runtime feasibility.

papers.abstract: Robots that travel long distances through public outdoor spaces must do more than avoid obstacles: they must remain on terrain suited to their mobility and decide when to proceed, yield, or detour around pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, traffic signals, and temporary restrictions. These decisions are difficult because their correctness often depends on how a scene evolves, such as whether an approaching car is slowing or a cyclist will cross the robot's path. Vision-language models (VLMs) can interpret such cues, but they reason over images that lack metric geometry and motion. Supplying this evidence at every step is too slow for real-time navigation, and hand-crafted triggers cannot anticipate the open-ended variety of outdoor situations. We present MOSU2, a long-range navigation system with two-stage trajectory selection, in which first-stage contextual reasoning determines when additional evidence is needed and what to retrieve. Only when an interaction remains unresolved does the first stage trigger the second stage to retrieve geometric and dynamic information and align it with scene context to make navigation decisions. Building on MOSU, MOSU2 follows routes from GPS-based route planning and filters candidate trajectories through multi-modal traversability analysis before selecting a trajectory to move the robot. In real-world experiments spanning stop gestures, construction sites, crosswalks, and roads shared with vehicles, cyclists, and pedestrians, MOSU2 raises mean navigation success from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4% over its single-image predecessor, at about 2.2 times its mean decision latency. Project website: https://jinggm.github.io/mosu2/
bullets: Addresses evolving outdoor interactions involving pedestrians, cyclists, vehicles, signals, terrain, and temporary restrictions.
Uses two-stage trajectory selection: contextual reasoning decides when and what additional evidence to retrieve.
Retrieves and aligns geometric and dynamic information only for unresolved interactions to support real-time decisions.
Follows GPS-planned routes and filters candidate trajectories through multimodal traversability analysis.
Real-world success increased from 61.8% to 94.2% and condition-detection accuracy from 72.2% to 91.4%, with about 2.2× higher mean decision latency.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the MOSU2 architecture. Building on MOSU’s routing and traversability framework, GPS-based routing provides subgoals, while LiDAR and robot-velocity observations support candidate trajectory generation. RGB-based semantic segmentation provides complementary traversability assessments. MOSU2 introduces a VLM-retrievable local map and two-stage trajectory selection: the first stage screens the current scene and determines if more analysis is required, and the second stage, when invoked, combines recent images with retrieved geometric and dynamic information to select a trajectory and velocity mode. The motion planner converts the selected motion into linear and angular velocity commands (v, ω).

Figure 7. Qualitative Evaluation: Each column illustrates one of the three components in our trajectory generation pipeline, (a) CVAE-based multiple trajectory generation, (b) semantic segmentation for traversability analysis, and (c) VLM-based trajectory ranking in the outdoor scenarios with various social conditions. In (a) and (b), lighter colors indicate higher scores, confidence scores in (a) and traversability scores in (b). In (c), the VLM ranks trajectories based on social cues. The top example shows a ranking of [3, 0, 1, 2, 4]. The bottom example shows a ranking of [4, 5, 0, 1, 2, 3].

Figure 1. MOSU2 supports long-range outdoor navigation across wheeled-legged, wheeled, and legged robot platforms (bottom row). The satellite view illustrates a route from the start (yellow star) to the goal (green circle). The left-side examples highlight traversability challenges: (a) distinguishing sidewalks from off-road terrain, (b) accounting for differences in robot mobility, and (c) identifying crosswalks for street crossing. The right-side examples highlight social and traffic challenges: (d) interacting with moving agents, such as pedestrians, (e) interpreting traffic signals, including pedestrian signals with countdown displays, and (f) resolving conflicting traffic cues when vehicles violate traffic rules and obstruct the robot’s path. MOSU2 combines global route guidance and robot-specific traversability assessment with two-stage reasoning that retrieves local geometric and dynamic information to interpret these conditions and select appropriate motion.

Figure 6. Geometric and Semantic Analysis: Both geometric trajectory generation and semantic segmentation perform well in most cases, but there are also failure cases, as marked in yellow circles in (c) and (d). When the elevations of the lawn and sidewalk are similar, the geometric model struggles to perform accurately. Additionally, segmentation fails in out-of-distribution scenarios.

Figure 3. Routing and subgoal transformation. OpenRouteService routing uses the robot’s GPS location and the destination to obtain a global route, from which an intermediate GPS waypoint ĝ is selected. The waypoint is converted to the odometry frame with metric coordinates by aligning the GPS and robot motion, yielding the subgoal g. This subgoal provides directional guidance for trajectory selection.

Figure 8. Representative social, traffic, and irregular navigation scenarios used to evaluate MOSU2: (a) responding to a pedestrian’s stop gesture, (b) navigating a construction area with warning and directional signs, (c) crossing at a signalized intersection, (d) sharing the road with moving agents, illustrated by a cyclist, (e) intersecting with a vehicle, requiring the robot to analyze the car’s velocity to determine if it is yielding, and (f) navigating in sidewalk baseline without any social or traffic situation. Panels (d) and (e) both belong to the shared-road group (Road + Vehicles/Bikes/Peds) in Table 2. These scenarios require interpreting contextual cues and, where relevant, considering the geometry and motion of surrounding road users to determine appropriate robot behavior.

The corresponding LiDAR points are then used to construct a 2D local map that provides the geometric information of the semantic objects and to calculate the motion information of the objects. papers.abstract: Disturbances encountered during autonomous navigation generally vary across space, often discontinuously, as obstacles redirect wind and changing terrain alters traction. Tracking controllers typically assume sufficient control authority to mitigate disturbances and maintain safety; the regime where this assumption fails remains underexplored. We present Belief-guided Residual Adaptive Control (BRACE), a hierarchical reinforcement learning (RL) framework for reach-avoid navigation under unknown, bounded, spatially varying disturbances. BRACE infers a disturbance belief from model prediction errors and uses that to condition a high-level policy that adapts the reference trajectory. The policy combines a nominal and a belief-guided residual term, trained jointly with a likelihood-ratio advantage reweighting heuristic. We evaluate BRACE in three simulated quadcopter environments with abruptly switching wind fields, and validate it on Crazyflie hardware with fan-generated disturbances. Across these settings, BRACE improves reach-avoid performance over model predictive control and RL baselines.
bullets: Targets navigation settings where disturbances can vary abruptly and exceed the assumptions of tracking controllers.
Infers disturbance beliefs from model prediction errors to condition a high-level trajectory-adaptation policy.
Combines nominal control with a belief-guided residual, trained using likelihood-ratio advantage reweighting.
Evaluated in three simulated quadcopter environments and on Crazyflie hardware with fan-generated disturbances.
Improves reach-avoid performance over model predictive control and RL baselines across the reported settings.
