papers.abstract: Real-time cooperative perception (CP) in multi-agent traffic environments is highly resource-intensive, which posing scalability challenges for large-scale deployment. Efficiency can be significantly improved by selectively performing CP only in safety-critical scenarios and for key occluding objects. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are well-suited for complex reasoning in dynamic and uncertain environments, making them a promising tool for this selective CP task. This study proposes a VLM-driven agentic framework for blind spot reasoning and dialogue-based CP. A mixed-model architecture is designed that integrates conventional object detection for stable perception, vision-language reasoning for identifying impactful occlusions, and a physics-based geometric module to align reasoning with real-world visibility constraints. The framework also incorporates a Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting mechanism to enhance interpretability and intent-aware decision-making. We collect real-world data from connected vehicles operating in urban traffic and compare the driving-critical blind spot identification and dialogue performance of four state-of-the-art VLMs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing. This work provides a scalable, interpretable, and bandwidth-efficient alternative to conventional CP pipelines, and offers new insights into agentic communication design for future connected traffic systems.
bullets: Targets the scalability and resource costs of continuous cooperative perception in multi-agent traffic.
Combines conventional object detection, VLM-based occlusion reasoning, physics-based visibility constraints, and Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Uses real-world connected-vehicle data and evaluates four state-of-the-art VLMs for blind-spot detection and dialogue-based sharing.
Achieves over 80% accuracy in driving-critical blind-spot detection and over 90% success in dialogue-driven perception sharing.
Designed as an interpretable, bandwidth-efficient approach for connected traffic systems.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (H-JEPA) enable long-horizon visual control but rely on costly test-time gradient descent for planning. Our analysis reveals that iterative optimization consumes up to 97.7% of episode runtime and that low predicted rollout costs do not necessarily translate into successful control. We further identify a planning-horizon asymmetry between long-horizon top-level composition and short two-step subordinate planning. To address these challenges, we propose WARP-JEPA, a hierarchical amortized planning framework that replaces online gradient optimization with learned multi-candidate trajectory proposers while keeping the world models frozen. WARP-JEPA combines a lightweight world-model-in-the-loop causal Transformer at the top level with parallel residual MLPs at subordinate levels. The proposers are trained using model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, enabling efficient candidate selection without test-time gradient optimization. Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models on four benchmarks, WARP-JEPA achieves 9.6-18.8x faster episode inference on long-horizon tasks (2.9-3.0x on Cube) and improves task success by up to 33.3 percentage points. These results demonstrate that amortized planning can substantially improve both inference efficiency and control performance without retraining the world models. Code is available at https://github.com/hideinsewer/WARP-JEPA.
bullets: H-JEPA planning can spend up to 97.7% of episode runtime on iterative optimization, and low predicted rollout costs may not ensure successful control.
The method uses a hierarchical planner: a causal Transformer for top-level composition and parallel residual MLPs for short-horizon subordinate planning.
Proposers are trained with model-based rollout costs and best-of-K behavior cloning, while the underlying world models remain frozen.
Across 30 frozen H-JEPA models and four benchmarks, inference is 9.6–18.8× faster on long-horizon tasks and 2.9–3.0× faster on Cube.
Task success improves by up to 33.3 percentage points, demonstrating gains in both efficiency and control without world-model retraining.

papers.abstract: Agent harnesses -- runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM's reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory -- have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision -- leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM-planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9-4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS
bullets: Targets the tension between LLM reasoning flexibility and millisecond-level trajectory-planning requirements.
Grounds LLM outputs in a learned variable-level dynamics model, then verifies them with calibrated predicates and forward rollout.
Consolidates verified decisions into indexed rule memory, enabling O(log n) lookup without repeated LLM calls.
Reported results include 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9–4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks.
As memory matures, familiar scenes increasingly bypass the LLM, reducing invocation frequency.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly adopted as end-to-end driving planners, yet they suffer from cross-city domain shift. Existing methods treat this shift as a single quantity addressed by uniform alignment or single-site editing. We challenge this view on two counts: (i) domain shift in VLM trajectory planners is inherently structured across modality and layer, and (ii) a locate-then-repair recipe matched to this structure outperforms every uniform-objective baseline. We analyse domain shift via activation patching and uncover two regularities. (F1) Modality axis. Image and text tokens exhibit distinct shift patterns in each VLM. (F2) Layer axis. The layer-wise shift partition is architecture-dependent and dataset-stable. These findings recast domain shift as a two-dimensional tensor indexed by modality (image vs. text tokens) and layer, motivating a simple principle: locate where shift occurs, and repair only there. We instantiate this principle in MoLaRx (Modality-Layer Repair), a locate-then-repair framework. The Causal Importance Score (CIS) estimates the domain shift as a modality-layer tensor and partitions the layers into functional zones. CIS-Guided Selective Repair (CISR) then applies a matched operator (Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) / low-rank adaptation (LoRA) / freezing) to repair each zone, with the composition adapting automatically to each architecture. We evaluate MoLaRx on three architecturally distinct VLMs (LFM2-VL-1.6B, Qwen2-VL-2B, and PaliGemma2-3B) across two cross-city benchmarks (nuScenes and Argoverse 2). MoLaRx attains the lowest cross-city trajectory-error gap among adaptation methods in all six main-table settings, while using 50-60% fewer trainable parameters and 8.4-10.9 ms lower inference latency. In contrast, uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses in all six settings, highlighting the importance of structure-guided repair.
bullets: Domain shift is structured across image versus text tokens and across model layers, rather than being a single uniform discrepancy.
Activation patching reveals architecture-dependent but dataset-stable layer-wise shift patterns.
MoLaRx estimates a modality-layer shift tensor with the Causal Importance Score and partitions layers into functional zones.
CISR applies zone-specific MMD, LoRA, or freezing operations to match each region’s needs.

Across three VLMs and two cross-city benchmarks, MoLaRx achieves the lowest trajectory-error gap in all six settings, with fewer trainable parameters and lower inference latency; uniform MMD-only adaptation collapses.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable visual control by planning action sequences in compact representation spaces, but a gap remains between how latent dynamics are learned and how they are used for planning. First, teacher-forced training does not expose the dynamics model to the recursively predicted latent states encountered during planning. Second, sampling-based planners typically initialize action search from goal-agnostic proposals, without exploiting the action-conditioned dynamics learned by the world model. We introduce Dynamics-Informed Action Learning (DIAL) to bridge these two gaps. During training, rollout alignment exposes the forward model to its own autoregressive latent predictions, while multi-step inverse supervision trains a lightweight inverse dynamics head to infer actions from latent-state transitions. We further apply the inverse head to model-generated transitions with its parameters held fixed, encouraging predicted rollouts to retain action-relevant information. At test time, DIAL autoregressively couples the inverse and forward dynamics to construct a dynamics-informed action sequence toward the goal, which initializes the mean of the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) proposal distribution. The subsequent CEM search then refines this initialization using the standard sampling and updating procedure. Experiments across four visual control benchmarks demonstrate that DIAL outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines in both standard and long-horizon scenarios.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between teacher-forced latent dynamics training and recursive planning, plus goal-agnostic action proposals.
Uses rollout alignment to train on the model’s own predicted latent states.
Adds multi-step inverse dynamics supervision and applies the fixed inverse head to model-generated transitions to preserve action-relevant information.
At test time, couples inverse and forward dynamics to initialize Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) planning, which then refines the action sequence.
Outperforms existing latent world models and planning baselines across four visual-control benchmarks, including long-horizon settings.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DIAL. (2) Multi-step inverse supervision trains the inverse-dynamics head Gψ on observed latent state pairs and uses a frozen inverse head Gψ̄ to encourage model-generated states to preserve action-relevant information. (3) Dynamics-informed planning autoregressively couples Gψ and Fθ to generate a goal-directed action sequence, which initializes only the mean of the CEM proposal.

papers.abstract: Reliable navigation with a single monocular limited field-of-view camera is challenging because the lack of depth measurements and limited spatial awareness complicate collision checking. Existing approaches to tackle these challenges fall into two categories. Model-based planners can incorporate explicit collision-avoidance guidance which leads to better generalization but are often computationally expensive and require manual tuning of the algorithmic parameters. In contrast, end-to-end approaches trained by imitation learning can be flexible but typically encode safety only implicitly and thus can suffer from high collision rates in novel scenarios. In this paper, we present a middle ground through model-based imitation learning. The model-based part is a learned collision model that can map a sequence of past images and a candidate control sequence to a distribution of worst-case obstacle clearance. This predictive distribution in turn is used to define a collision-risk cost in a trajectory optimization formulation. The imitation component uses human demonstrations to learn scene-dependent balancing of collision risk with other task costs such as goal progress. We also use it to learn the algorithmic parameters (e.g., a warm start) of our optimizer to accelerate the solution process. We show that our approach can demonstrate highly reliable navigation in cluttered environments on robots with different embodiments. We also demonstrate a substantial reduction in collision rate over recent end-to-end and model-based baselines.
bullets: Addresses limited depth and field of view, which make collision avoidance difficult with a single camera.
Learns a model that predicts worst-case obstacle-clearance distributions from image histories and candidate controls.
Uses predicted risk in trajectory optimization, while demonstrations learn how to balance safety with task objectives such as goal progress.
Learns optimizer parameters, including warm starts, to improve solution speed.
Reports highly reliable navigation across different robot embodiments and lower collision rates than end-to-end and model-based baselines.

papers.abstract: We introduce Latent-WAM++, a representation-centered World Action Model (WAM) for end-to-end autonomous driving. Existing WAMs are primarily trained to predict future states or final actions, leaving the intermediate world and action representations that connect prediction to planning only indirectly constrained. Latent-WAM++ matches the supervision of each representation to its role in planning. World Representation Construction combines scene-ego future prediction, SIGReg-based distribution stabilization, and frozen geometric priors to learn a temporally predictive, non-degenerate, and geometry-aware world representation without an EMA target encoder. Trajectory MeanFlow Planner directly predicts multimodal trajectory proposals while being optimized with an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective, enabling one-step sampling. Visual-Action Representation Alignment further aligns the resulting pre-output action features with a stop-gradient target derived from current visual semantics. Latent-WAM++ achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v2 and under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM, reaching 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 47.0 average RC and 30.1 average HD-Score on HUGSIM. Training the planner end to end costs 190 GPU-hours for Latent-WAM++ versus 1,600 for Latent-WAM, a reduction of 88.1%.
bullets: Addresses weak supervision of intermediate world and action representations in existing World Action Models.
Learns a temporally predictive, geometry-aware world representation using future prediction, SIGReg stabilization, and frozen geometric priors.
Uses a MeanFlow-based planner for multimodal trajectory proposals with one-step sampling.
Aligns pre-output action features with current visual semantics through visual-action representation alignment.
Reports 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, zero-shot results on HUGSIM, and 88.1% lower planner training cost than Latent-WAM.

papers.abstract: SLAM failures remain difficult to avoid in autonomous robotic systems, and undetected failures can propagate to unsafe planning, control, and mission-level decisions. Existing monitoring strategies often depend on prior maps, estimator-internal variables, or redundant sensing, which limits their applicability to deployed and resource-constrained robots. This paper presents a scene-geometry consistency monitor for detecting geometry-manifested SLAM failures using only the geometric output of the SLAM backend. The targeted failures include cumulative drift-induced failures, abrupt misregistration failures, and backend map corruption when they become observable as inconsistency in reconstructed scene geometry. The proposed method represents revisited local regions with recursive latent voxel geometry and evaluates each current observation against a trusted continuation explanation and a weak non-propagated reference explanation. The resulting voxel-wise evidence contrasts are aggregated into a fixed-boundary monitoring signal for online failure declaration and downstream safety response. Experiments on self-collected sequences, GEODE benchmark sequences, multiple robotic platforms, and different SLAM backends show that the monitor responds to failures when they are manifested in backend scene geometry. It achieves 4/4 valid post-onset declarations with no pre-onset alarms on four self-collected sequences, detects geometry-manifested failures in all five corrupted GEODE runs while remaining alarm-free in five geometrically consistent runs, adds only 0.1--0.2\% absolute CPU load, and supports a closed-loop UAV detect--isolate--recover workflow.
bullets: Targets cumulative drift, abrupt misregistration, and backend map corruption that become geometrically observable.
Uses recursive latent voxel representations of revisited regions and contrasts trusted continuation evidence with a weak non-propagated reference.
Aggregates voxel-level evidence into a fixed-boundary online signal for failure declaration and safety response.

Reported experiments achieved 4/4 post-onset declarations without pre-onset alarms on self-collected sequences and detected all five corrupted GEODE runs while staying alarm-free on five consistent runs.
Adds only 0.1–0.2% absolute CPU load and supports a closed-loop UAV detect–isolate–recover workflow.

papers.abstract: In real homes, assistive robots must repeatedly locate targets from large furniture to tiny tabletop items, as people move objects between household surfaces. Uniformly instantiating detections at different scales as 3D objects can be brittle for small on-surface items; without explicit object-state validation, stale entries may persist after scene changes. Our key insight is to separate persistent 3D furniture entities from revisable surface-object hypotheses, retaining their visual evidence without requiring independent object geometry. We formalize this design as the Hypothesis Scene Graph (HSG), which preserves small-object evidence and supports local revision without rebuilding the stable entity topology. Building on HSG, HSGNav uses this separation for multi-scale lifelong navigation: retrieval selects entity or hypothesis evidence according to target scale, exploration acquires additional surface observations, and verification confirms target presence or invalidates contradicted hypothesis records. Because existing lifelong benchmarks such as GOAT-Bench rarely require mid-episode memory invalidation or multi-scale search, we introduce FAROS-Bench (Find And Re-find Objects across Scales) for mid-episode relocation of surface objects and multi-scale find goals. Experiments show that HSGNav performs competitively on GOAT-Bench while substantially outperforming prior methods on FAROS-Bench.
bullets: Addresses stale memories and brittle 3D representations when small objects move between household surfaces.
Introduces Hypothesis Scene Graphs, preserving visual evidence for surface objects while keeping persistent furniture topology stable.
Uses scale-aware retrieval, exploration for new surface observations, and verification to confirm or invalidate hypotheses.
Introduces FAROS-Bench for multi-scale search and mid-episode object relocation with memory invalidation.
Performs competitively on GOAT-Bench and substantially outperforms prior methods on FAROS-Bench.

When retrieval fails, OCE selects a new observation goal; CGN executes the selected goal, and BDV verifies retrieved targets using fresh views. papers.abstract: Predicting where multiple agents will move next is fundamental to autonomous driving, robotics, and any system that must share space with people safely. Modern stochastic predictors read off inter-agent interactions once from the observed past and keep that view fixed throughout the generative rollout, so the reciprocal geometric constraints that emerge as the joint future sharpens are not re-examined. We address this gap with SRA (Spatial Reasoning Adapter), a modular graph denoiser that is integrated into existing diffusion and flow-matching predictors without redesigning their generative cores. At every reverse step, SRA reads the host's current future estimate, builds a sparse Euclidean interaction graph on the predicted trajectories, and returns a residual correction to the host's decoding path. Our adapter consists of three core components: a sparse neighborhood retrieved with a learned query-key score and a geometric bias, a future-conditioned relational feature recomputed on the evolving prediction, and uncertainty-weighted message passing where confident agents act as anchors for uncertain ones. We instantiate SRA on three structurally different hosts (LED, MID, and MoFlow) across four multi-agent benchmarks: SDD, NBA, Soccer, and Football. SRA improves ADE for every host on every dataset, with average gains of 5.8% in ADE and 7.0% in FDE. A cumulative ablation shows that the three components act as one mechanism: only together do they improve every host on every sports dataset, indicating that spatial reasoning over the model's own evolving future, weighted by how far that future can be trusted, is broadly useful across denoising architectures. Code is available at https://github.com/Jaewoo97/SRA.
bullets: Targets predictors that do not re-examine reciprocal geometric constraints as predicted futures evolve.
Adds a modular graph denoiser adapter to diffusion and flow-matching models without changing their generative cores.
At each reverse step, it builds a sparse graph from current predicted trajectories and applies uncertainty-weighted residual corrections.
Combines learned geometric neighbor selection, future-conditioned relational features, and confidence-based message passing.
Improves ADE for all tested hosts and datasets, with average gains of 5.8% ADE and 7.0% FDE; the full component combination is needed for consistent sports-dataset gains.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robot teams deployed in remote, unstructured environments may face changes in the environment, hardware, and team composition that degrade previously effective policies. Shifting mission objectives can be handled by selecting a different solution from an existing Pareto set, but shifting deployment conditions can reorder the set itself, making previously dominated policies competitive or new policies necessary. However, evaluating these policies in new contexts while minimizing risk to the hardware remains an open problem. We argue that, although largely untested in this domain, world models merit investigation for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation. By predicting policy outcomes under updated estimates of current conditions, world models could enable teams to re-evaluate existing policies without physically executing each candidate, provided predicted performance changes reflect those realized on deployed systems. We identify research priorities for model-based policy re-evaluation, validation of predicted against realized performance, and incorporating shared information into world models to support coordinated team adaptation.
bullets: Environmental, hardware, or team changes can reorder the Pareto set, making previously dominated or new policies viable.
Selecting among existing Pareto-optimal policies may address objective shifts but not changing deployment conditions.
World models could predict policy outcomes under updated conditions, reducing the need to physically test every candidate.
Safe adoption requires validating predicted performance against outcomes on deployed systems.
Shared information should be incorporated to support coordinated adaptation across robot teams.

figures.caption: Figure 1: This is a proposed pipeline for maintaining a shared, current representation of the world using world models after deployment. Distributed agents collect local observations, model predictions are tracked against realized performance, and if the context is out of distribution, the model can be updated. The model is used to evaluate policies when objectives change, or possibly even learn new policies with the updated world models.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes using world models for post-deployment multi-objective adaptation in remote robot teams, directly addressing world models for robotics.
papers.title: Multi-Objective Adaptation After Deployment: A Position on World Models for Remote Robot Teams
papers.tldr: World models could help remote robot teams safely reassess and adapt policies after deployment as conditions and objectives change.

papers.abstract: In this work, we train agents to act under uncertainty according to specified, belief-dependent rules. Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can in theory train agents to follow rules if encoded into well-designed rewards, but in practice, RL fails to perfectly optimize these rewards, leading to ineffective or noncompliant agent behavior. Belief-space planners by construction produce behavior in line with developer specification, but require hand-programming online planners and belief-state estimators, adding significant engineering complexity at scale. We combine the two: we plan offline to generate a dataset of sample trajectories and then distill the plans into a policy that acts on raw observations. We propose two changes to planner distillation that address problems specific to history-based policies: Dual Averaging, a loss that combines per-timestep predictive loss and average loss on task changes, and $ρ$-Optimal Reinforcement, a feedback mechanism that reinforces the policy's own successful rollouts when these are near-optimal. We provide a sufficient condition under which static search problems with noiseless observation models is complete, and show that maximum-likelihood-observation planning implies this condition in static search with continuous beliefs. We create a challenging new domain, Scavenger, where an agent needs to gain information in order to succeed. We evaluate our distilled policy in two versions of Scavenger, one where information is provided visually and one where it is provided as a command in natural language. In either case, the learned policy attains a success rate above 90% in Scavenger, compared with at most 5% for RL. We also find that distilled planners transfer with greater than 60% success to following unseen and intentionally vague commands and greater than 75% success to following floorplans larger than those seen in training.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of making RL agents reliably comply with specified, belief-dependent behavior and the engineering cost of hand-coded belief-space planners.
Distills offline belief-space task-and-motion-planning trajectories into a history-based policy operating on raw observations.
Introduces Dual Averaging for combining timestep and task-change losses, plus ρ-Optimal Reinforcement to reinforce near-optimal successful rollouts.
In the new Scavenger domain, the distilled policy exceeds 90% success in both visual- and language-guided settings, versus at most 5% for RL.
Transfers to unseen vague commands with over 60% success and larger-than-training floorplans with over 75% success.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: An overview of the Scavenger domain. (a) The agent starts in a random room for a procedurally generated floorplan, with a set of visual markers, a geometry visualizing connectivity between rooms, and a visual prior denoting a set of possible locations. (b) The robot must search among possible locations for a hint, either represented visually or as a command in natural language. (c) It succeeds when it approaches the marker hinted at, and then takes a relevant “guess” action when it is sufficiently close to that marker. Guessing before it is certain of the correct marker, or guessing the wrong marker, counts as a failure.

Fig. 4: Results of the generalization study. The policy from our method, trained in Figure 3b, transfers to unseen language commands, to intentionally vague commands, and to problems with vastly more rooms than was seen in training. This shows that our policy learns to comply with physical and epistemic constraints reliably, even in floorplans and given language hints that were unseen in training. Each success rate is calculated based on 50 episodes, and the error bars are binomial standard errors.

Fig. 3: Success rates vs. wall-clock time on Scavenger. The dots on the baseline runs refer to the point in baseline runs where as many simulation timesteps are used for training the policies as our method. In all cases, our method attains at least 18 times the success rate of the baseline RL policies, even while giving the baseline RL policies access to at least 50% more simulator steps for training. Our method attains the highest success rate among the ablations for our feedback mechanism. Note: our method and ablations do not all start at 0 wall-clock time, because there is an initial phase of data generation without policy training for each, longer for the No Feedback ablation since it does not get further policy / planner feedback afterward. The ablations attain much stronger performance than the RL baselines, but start to struggle more with parsing language hints. All methods are run with a single seed.

Fig. 1: A worked example, where the robot must obey the epistemic rule: “ensure the user leaves their home, and has what they need when they leave”, while being physically safe. The robot should be confident that the user has what they need before they leave the house. Left: The robot must first search for the user in the house, who may be in one of three locations. Middle: After finding the user, the robot asks them about what they might need for the day. Right: The robot hears the user is planning to go on a drive to see friends on a rainy day, and then brings them their keys and umbrella.
Fig. 5: We evaluate transfer from the 3-6 room problems seen in training, to 18 room problems like those shown above, three times the maximum number of rooms seen in training.

papers.selection_reason: Distills belief-space task and motion planners into compliant robot policies; relevant to embodied robot learning and navigation.
papers.title: Deploying Physically and Epistemically Compliant Agents by Distilling Belief-Space Task and Motion Planners
papers.tldr: Planner distillation produces agents that follow belief-dependent rules under uncertainty far more reliably than direct reinforcement learning while acting from raw observations.

papers.abstract: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.

papers.abstract: Agricultural production faces persistent labor shortages and increasing demand for automation, yet progress in agricultural robotics remains constrained by the limited availability of affordable, flexible, and accessible research platforms. This paper presents Agibot, an open-source, modular, low-cost agricultural robotics platform designed for autonomy research and experimentation, with potential applications in hands-on robotics education. The platform integrates four-wheel independent swerve drive, swappable computing, distributed embedded control, multimodal sensing, and configurable manipulation within a unified sense-plan-act-verify framework supporting perception, control, navigation, manipulation, and autonomous task verification. The platform was evaluated through representative row-crop navigation and manipulation tasks under varying lighting and soil conditions. Experiments demonstrated reliable lane following, autonomous row-to-row navigation, target identification, seed dispensing, plant manipulation, and closed-loop verification of task success. Its modular architecture supports independent testing, modification, and validation of autonomy components for rapid prototyping and experimentation. These proof-of-concept tasks, controller-tuning studies, and integrated trials demonstrate the platform's research capabilities, while its accessible and reconfigurable design supports its use for hands-on robotics education. By combining affordability, modularity, open-source accessibility, configurable manipulation, and end-to-end sense-plan-act-verify autonomy, Agibot provides a practical platform for agricultural robotics research, technology development, and workforce training.

Its proof-of-concept scope and reconfigurable architecture support component testing, rapid prototyping, experimentation, and hands-on training.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid state estimation and language-grounded motion understanding from robot recordings ties training coverage to the robot's motion repertoire. Human motion datasets offer broader coverage, yet transferring this knowledge requires overcoming differences in body geometry, sensing, and physical disturbances. To enable this transfer, we propose a unified inertial encoder whose shared inertial interface uses kinematic IMU synthesis to represent human and humanoid motion at corresponding body sites. Within this common input space, joint training on human and kinematically retargeted humanoid motion combines velocity estimation and motion--text alignment with continuous-time encoding and sensor and motion randomization. The resulting model transfers zero-shot to a physical Unitree G1 without physics simulation, real-robot training trajectories, or fine-tuning, achieving the lowest velocity error among evaluated methods across five datasets, including 0.099m/s on real G1. Its motion-description retrieval also extends to retargeted G1 motion categories observed only in human training, demonstrating how human motion knowledge can support the generalization of humanoid inertial odometry and language-grounded motion understanding.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between human datasets and humanoid robots in body geometry, sensing, and physical disturbances.

papers.abstract: Ensuring high returns while providing strong safety guarantees in offline imitation learning (IL) is a fundamental challenge: existing approaches either rely on explicitly specified cost functions, which are difficult to design for complex real-world safety constraints, or require expert demonstrations that are both safe and high-performing, which are often too costly to collect. We introduce dual-expert imitation learning, which leverages two complementary data sources: (i) safety-compliant demonstrations that faithfully follow safety guidelines but may be suboptimal, and (ii) performance-oriented demonstrations that achieve high returns but may violate safety guidelines. To address this problem, we propose DexDICE (Dual-expert offline imitation learning via stationary DIstribution Correction Estimation). Instead of conventional distribution constraints, DexDICE combines DICE-style offline learning with safe support constraints, enabling agents to exploit high-return behaviors while remaining within safety-compliant regions. We prove that the ideal solution satisfying this constraint exactly has zero unsafe-region visitation with high probability. We evaluate DexDICE on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and validate it on a real-world mobile-robot navigation task trained directly from human teleoperation demonstrations, where it substantially outperforms baselines and remains robust to data scarcity and quality degradation.
authors: Seokin Seo, Sung Kuk Shyn, Minji Seo, Yisoo Lee, Jongmin Lee, Hongseok Yang, Kee-Eung Kim
bullets: Addresses offline imitation learning when safe, high-performing demonstrations are unavailable and explicit safety costs are difficult to specify.

Evaluations on a re-curated DSRL benchmark and real-world mobile-robot navigation show strong baseline performance and robustness to scarce or degraded data.

papers.abstract: Autoware is an open-source autonomous driving software platform widely adopted by researchers and industry developers. Originally developed primarily for public-road applications, including passenger vehicles, taxis, and buses, Autoware is increasingly being extended to off-road environments such as construction and agricultural sites. Construction sites, however, differ fundamentally from public roads and challenge many assumptions underlying conventional autonomous driving systems. They are characterized by unstructured terrain, airborne dust, continuously evolving site conditions, and construction-specific objects. This paper presents lessons learned from ongoing efforts to extend an Autoware-based autonomous driving system to large dump trucks operating at construction sites. We identify gaps between public-road and off-road construction applications across the sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules of the Autoware stack. We then discuss potential solutions for addressing these gaps, with particular emphasis on ongoing LiDAR-based perception pipeline development and findings from field testing. Finally, we propose a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomous driving for construction vehicles.
bullets: Construction sites introduce unstructured terrain, dust, changing conditions, and specialized objects that violate public-road assumptions.
The authors identify gaps across Autoware’s sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules.
Potential solutions are discussed, with emphasis on developing a LiDAR-based perception pipeline.
Field-testing lessons inform the proposed path toward end-to-end autonomy for construction vehicles.

papers.abstract: Inertial odometry is a compelling approach to state estimation for agile quadrotor flight due to its affordability, low weight, and robustness to perceptual degradation. However, relying only on integrated inertial measurements is impractical, as sensor errors and time-varying biases lead to significant pose drift. Although recent advances have enabled inertial odometry for drone racing, existing approaches show limited generalization to trajectories not seen during training. This work improves generalization by adopting a body-frame representation and incorporating body-frame torque dynamics into the learning pipeline. The learned model predicts short-horizon relative displacements, which are fused with IMU measurements in an Extended Kalman Filter. Experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous state-of-the-art learned inertial odometry approach for quadrotor pose estimation on unseen trajectories. An additional evaluation on four public quadrotor datasets, with whole trajectory shapes held out of training, confirms a lower velocity error on every held-out set and shows that the torque input is most informative when it is derived from the rotor signals. Code, data pipeline and trained models are publicly available.
bullets: Addresses pose drift and poor generalization in inertial odometry for agile quadrotors.
Uses body-frame representations and incorporates body-frame torque dynamics into learning.
Predicts short-horizon relative displacements and fuses them with IMU data in an Extended Kalman Filter.

papers.abstract: Autonomous 3D exploration with UAVs requires efficient target selection under limited flight time and onboard computation. In conventional Euclidean-distance-based frontier pipelines, geometric distance may poorly represent the actual collision-free travel cost in cluttered environments, leading to inefficient frontier choices. This paper presents a lightweight path-aware frontier re-ranking method for LiDAR-based UAV exploration. The method first retains a small top-N set of promising frontier candidates using a lightweight utility function and then applies time-bounded RRT* planning to estimate their feasible path costs for re-ranking. The path generated for the selected frontier is further reused for navigation to reduce redundant global planning. Experiments in three warehouse-like environments show that the proposed method consistently produces shorter exploration trajectories than conventional frontier baselines, with traveled-distance reductions of up to 14.1%, while reducing exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments and remaining competitive in the third. The method maintains map detail comparable to the conventional OctoMap-based baseline, demonstrating an effective trade-off between exploration efficiency and mapping quality.
authors: Duc Manh Do, Thanh Nguyen Canh, Ngoc Minh Do, Mai Thanh Thai, Xiem HoangVan
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between Euclidean frontier distance and actual collision-free travel cost.

Reuses the selected path for navigation, reducing redundant global planning.
In three warehouse-like environments, it reduced traveled distance by up to 14.1% and exploration time by up to 9.5% in two environments.
Preserved map detail comparable to an OctoMap-based baseline, with competitive performance in the third environment.

The UAV uses 3D LiDAR measurements together with its pose estimate to construct and update an OctoMap, denoted by (V ), where the current robot position is represented by (prb). The exploration module detects frontier voxels, clusters them into frontier candidates, and selects the best frontier (vbf ) by evaluating candidates according to their estimated collision-free path costs. The reusable-path mechanism stores and reuses the feasible path generated during frontier evaluation (Pbf ), thereby reducing redundant planning and accelerating subsequent navigation.

papers.abstract: Modern object detectors can predict keypoints as per-object geometric features, but keypoints are inherently vulnerable to occlusion and truncation. Object edges can provide complementary information, often remaining observable even when partially occluded or when their defining endpoints leave the field of view. We therefore introduce object keyline detection, the task of predicting a fixed, semantically ordered set of infinite lines per object instance. Unlike the outputs of general line-segment detectors, each keyline is associated with an object instance and identified by a semantic index, providing a line-level analog of keypoints. To solve this task, we extend YOLO with keyline prediction parameterized in continuous Hesse-normal form $[\rho,\cos\theta,\sin\theta]$, and introduce Object Keyline Similarity (OKLS), which serves as an evaluation metric, target assignment signal, and regression loss. We instantiate this formulation on runway perception in vision-based landing, a motivating example containing semantic linear features that remain partially observable throughout the approach. Experiments show that our representation achieves the highest detection accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations, and keylines integrate directly into standard YOLO heads as additional output channels without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.

For runway perception, the proposed representation achieved the best accuracy among four evaluated line parameterizations.
Keyline outputs integrate into standard YOLO heads without degrading keypoint performance or adding meaningful latency.

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.
authors: Etor Arza, Luca Girardi, Gabriel Maquignaz, Javier Paez, Stefan Leutenegger, Stefano Mintchev, Kostas Alexis
bullets: The method jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque–deflection response of two passive folding arms.
Candidate designs are evaluated in contact-based traversal simulations, with success rate guiding iterative improvement.
The prototype narrows from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm opening at a 2 m/s reference speed.
It tolerates approach-angle errors up to 30° and folds through a 40 cm confined passage.
Compared with a rigid twin, it adds only 2 mm position RMSE and under 1% electrical power during contact-free flight.

papers.abstract: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.
authors: Chinmay Mundane, Amith Manoharan, Arun Kumar Singh
bullets: Defines traversability as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair executes a path while satisfying trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements.
Predicts closed-loop trajectory distributions with a latent-space flow-matching model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features, vehicle attitude, and wheel-ground contacts.
In 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT lowers safe-path rejection to 2.2% and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%.
When integrated into a receding-horizon planner, EGT reduces navigation failures and goal-reaching time relative to two baselines.
The simulation-trained model demonstrates zero-shot transfer to real-world outdoor experiments.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT) using latent-space flow matching to predict closed-loop trajectories, improving rough terrain navigation planning and generalization.
papers.title: EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions
papers.tldr: EGT estimates rough-terrain traversability from learned closed-loop trajectory distributions, improving path safety assessment and navigation performance over point-wise terrain metrics.

papers.abstract: Global planners for ground vehicles usually approximate the vehicle by a disk, trading safety against conservativeness, while exact-footprint checking pays for every candidate motion, pose, and footprint edge. We present TPS-A*, a lattice planner whose edges are kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators, built on certified collision checking in trajectory parameter space. A grid precomputed per footprint returns, in one pass over the local obstacles, a certified free distance along every candidate trajectory, so the per-node collision cost is independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count. We prove that this grid never overestimates the free distance of the continuously swept, possibly non-convex footprint, and state the planner's guarantees: collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to its lattice abstraction. Goals with or without heading are reached exactly by Reeds-Shepp shots certified as trajectories of the same generators. An exact independent test finds no collision in its paths. On 300 cluttered worlds, with the true footprint and the same goal pose for all planners, it solves every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of three milliseconds on an AMD Ryzen 7 2700X, on par with hybrid A*, 45\% of whose paths overlap obstacles, and nearly sixty times faster than a state-lattice planner, the only other collision-free one; with position goals, eighty-nine times faster than hybrid A*. It matches hybrid A* in automated parking and on narrow doorways, docks a non-convex fork footprint that no convex model admits, and drove a real robot across a university campus among people.
authors: Jose Luis Blanco-Claraco, Shravan S. Rai, Fernando Ca\~nadas-Ar\'anega, Jos\'e Luis Torres-Moreno, Jos\'e Carlos Moreno-\'Ubeda
bullets: Uses a lattice of kinematically feasible trajectories from parameterized trajectory generators.
A precomputed per-footprint grid certifies free distance for all candidate trajectories in one obstacle pass, independent of footprint complexity and trajectory count.
Provides collision-free paths and bounded suboptimality relative to the lattice abstraction, with exact Reeds–Shepp goal connections.
In 300 cluttered worlds, it solved every query with a collision-free goal pose in a median of 3 ms; an independent test found no collisions.
Supports non-convex footprints, including a fork shape that convex models cannot dock, and was demonstrated on a real robot among people.

papers.selection_reason: Presents TPS-A*, a lattice planner for ground vehicles that uses certified collision checking in trajectory parameter space to handle any-vehicle shape, directly addressing robot navigation challenges.
papers.title: TPS-A*: Path Planning for Any-Shape Vehicles with Certified Collision Checking in Trajectory Parameter Space
papers.tldr: TPS-A* plans fast, collision-free paths for arbitrary vehicle footprints by certifying swept-footprint clearance directly in trajectory parameter space.

papers.abstract: Shielding is a safe reinforcement learning technique that provides safety guarantees while learning, by blocking unsafe actions. Traditional shielding relies on a complete model of the environment to provide long-term guarantees. Probabilistic logic shielding (PLS) lifts the requirement of having such model, but only considers safety in the short term, typically looking only one or few steps ahead. We propose Probabilistic Option Shielding (POS), which extends PLS to the option level, recovering long-horizon safety without reintroducing the need for a complete environment model. POS learns a model-free critic directly from one-step PLS signals, to estimate the probability that an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty. We evaluate POS on safe navigation tasks in the LogiCity environment, and show that it achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of standard step-level PLS and other safety related reinforcement learning baselines.
authors: Gian Luca Ascari, Isidoro Tamassia, Ying Jiao, Luc De Raedt, Giuseppe Marra
bullets: Addresses the lack of long-term safety guarantees in probabilistic logic shielding without requiring a complete environment model.
Learns a model-free critic from one-step shielding signals to estimate whether an entire option will complete safely under uncertainty.
Evaluated on safe navigation tasks in LogiCity.
Achieves considerably safer training while matching the task performance of step-level PLS and other safety-oriented RL baselines.

papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.
authors: Jingjia Teng, Yang Li, Wenjie Huang
bullets: Targets safe cooperative merging in mixed traffic, especially under dense conditions.
Uses latent-context and action-conditioned models to infer directed behavioral influence, with uncertainty-aware interaction graphs.
Shapes cooperation rewards using signed influence and marginal team utility, while assigning responsibility through excess tail risk versus a safe reference policy.
Applies conditional diffusion for future-response risk estimation and trust-region optimization with adaptive, agent-specific safety requirements.
In highway-env experiments across three traffic densities, high-density success increased 66.04% and crash rate decreased 56.23% versus the best evaluated baselines for each metric.

papers.abstract: We focus on the problem of high-speed multi-robot navigation in cluttered spaces with tight spatial constraints. A key challenge is balancing safety with agility, as existing methods often trade one for the other (slowing down near a bottleneck to avoid collisions versus failing to swerve in time at high speeds), especially for car-like systems. Our approach belongs to the family of formation control methods, in which Ackermann-steering agents coordinate while navigating tight spaces. However, current formation control techniques rely on rigid, pre-defined shapes and transitions that depend on initial conditions, the environment, and vehicle dynamics, and are impractical to maintain at high speeds. For example, agents passing through a small gap must first form a square, transform into a line using analytical equations, and then return to a square. In contrast, our approach is inspired by a droplet of water that continuously adapts its shape to the space it flows through without slowing down. We propose a hierarchical algorithm in which, at the high level, a reinforcement learning policy produces a dynamic, blob-like elliptical patch that morphs its shape in real time, squeezing, stretching, and orienting itself around obstacles and through tight spaces. At the low level, the robots are controlled via distributed model predictive control (DMPC) to stay inside the patch, which acts as a soft forcing function, while avoiding collisions with each other. We evaluate our approach, FastFunnels, on simulated F1TENTH racing cars across 14 scenarios with N=1 to N=6 robots, averaged over 20 trials each. FastFunnels achieves an 89% completion rate at 7.73 m/s, while all baselines either fail to complete the track or succeed only at very low speeds (0.07-1.79 m/s, about 40% completion rate).
bullets: Targets the safety–agility trade-off in high-speed multi-robot navigation through tight spaces.
Uses a hierarchical design: reinforcement learning generates a morphing elliptical formation patch, while distributed MPC keeps robots inside it and prevents collisions.
Avoids rigid, pre-defined formations and discrete shape transitions that are difficult to maintain at speed.
Evaluated in simulation with 1–6 F1TENTH cars across 14 scenarios and 20 trials per scenario.
Achieved 89% completion at 7.73 m/s; baselines completed about 40% of trials at only 0.07–1.79 m/s or failed entirely.

papers.title: FASTFUNNELS: Agile Multi Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces via Adaptive Dynamic Funnels

papers.abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
bullets: Dense BEV grids waste computation on regions the vehicle will not traverse.
A coarse scene encoding predicts path-related heat, then selectively refines high-heat cells under a fixed budget.
The mixed-resolution BEV covers the full scene and requires neither an HD map nor a navigation command.
With 10% refinement, it uses 28% of BEV queries and 66% of encoder time versus a full fine grid, while achieving lower reported errors on nuScenes and NAVSIM navtest.
The approach is evaluated on two benchmarks and is intended for path-focused, efficient end-to-end driving.

papers.abstract: Long-term object search requires learning where objects usually appear from repeated but uneven observations of a changing environment. We formulate retrospective open-vocabulary memory as probabilistic inference from censored observations, where the key idea is to reason with evidence per opportunity: a detection or non-detection should influence belief only in proportion to the robot's opportunity to observe the corresponding location. We introduce ECROM, which uses this principle to estimate long-term prevalence for concepts specified only at query time and converts the resulting belief directly into an active-search prior. To evaluate this problem, we introduce a controlled long-term benchmark in ten HM3D homes that independently varies object placement and observation opportunity across repeated traversals. ECROM improves support-level AP on held-out queries by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric. The benchmark, dataset, and code will be open-sourced. Project page: https://jiaming.im/ecrom/
bullets: Addresses learning object-location prevalence from repeated, uneven observations.
Models detections and non-detections as censored evidence weighted by observation opportunity.
Supports concepts specified only at query time and converts beliefs into active-search priors.
Evaluated on a controlled benchmark spanning ten HM3D homes with varied placements and observation opportunities.
Improves support-level AP by 4.5 points and search SPL by 4.2 points over the strongest competing memory in each metric.

papers.abstract: Existing approaches to offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) struggle with long-horizon tasks. Discounting shrinks value differences between distant states until they fall below the function approximation error, leaving the agent with no signal for ranking states. Temporal abstraction, which treats k environment steps as a single transition, restores this signal at long range, but no single fixed k suits all state-goal distances: large k preserves value differences across long temporal distances while collapsing distinctions between nearby states, and small k does the reverse. We make this trade-off explicit and introduce Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA), which conditions a single value function on k. GITA trains one policy by aggregating advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values, so scales assigning larger positive advantages to a state-goal pair contribute more strongly to its update. GITA does not need to choose between local resolution and long-range signal; it retains both without committing to a single k. On OGBench, GITA outperforms a broad range of offline GCRL baselines, raising average success rate across all tasks by 25 percentage points (73% relative improvement) over HIQL. It also improves over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA, by 7 percentage points (14% relative).
bullets: Offline GCRL struggles on long-horizon tasks because discounting weakens value differences between distant states.
A fixed temporal abstraction scale k creates a trade-off: large k helps long-range planning, while small k preserves nearby-state resolution.
GITA conditions one value function on k and trains a single policy using advantage-weighted supervision across multiple k values.
On OGBench, GITA improves average success by 25 percentage points over HIQL and 7 points over the strongest fixed-k method, OTA.
The approach avoids committing to a single temporal abstraction scale, though its reported scope is offline GCRL on OGBench tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Generalized Implicit Temporal Abstraction (GITA) for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, a key technique for long-horizon robot navigation.
papers.title: Learning Multiple Timescales for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: GITA improves offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning by learning across multiple temporal abstractions, preserving both long-range guidance and local state distinctions.

papers.abstract: This paper explores a reward-based policy to achieve zero-shot transfer between source and target environments with completely different observation spaces. While humans can demonstrate impressive adaptation capabilities, deep neural network policies often struggle to adapt to a new environment and require a considerable amount of samples for successful transfer. Instead, we propose a novel reward-based policy only conditioned on rewards and actions, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new environments with completely different observations. We discuss the challenges and feasibility of a reward-based policy and then propose a practical algorithm for training. We demonstrate that a reward policy can be trained within three different environments, Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing, and transferred to completely different observations, such as different color palettes or 3D rendering, or Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim, in a zero-shot manner. We also demonstrate that a reward-based policy can further guide the training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.
bullets: Targets the poor adaptation of observation-based deep policies when source and target observations differ substantially.
Introduces a reward-based policy that avoids dependence on environment-specific visual observations.
Presents a practical training algorithm and discusses the feasibility of reward-only conditioning.
Demonstrates zero-shot transfer across Pointmass, Cartpole, and 2D Car Racing settings, including visual changes and Stretch robot navigation in Habitat-Sim.
Shows that the reward-based policy can also guide training of an observation-based policy in the target environment.

papers.abstract: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework to enable fast adaptation of interactive policies in a multi-agent system (MAS). Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) enables agents to rapidly adapt to new tasks/environments using a bi-level optimization mechanism. However, existing meta-RL generally focuses on single-agent systems. Extending these frameworks and algorithms to multi-agent systems poses additional challenges, as tasks are characterized by not only the environment but also agents' strategic interactions. To address these challenges, we model multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems as Markov games (MGs) and develop a meta-MARL framework for rapid interactive policy adaptation across a distribution of MGs. A new concept, called meta-NE, is defined to describe the desired solution concept in a meta-MARL problem. Sufficient conditions for the equivalence between a meta-NE and a stationary point of the gradient-play-based meta-MARL algorithm are established. Our evaluation on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrates that the proposed meta-MARL method achieves faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines, validating the effectiveness of our framework.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting policies across multi-agent tasks that vary in both environments and agent interactions.
Models multi-agent reinforcement learning problems as Markov games distributed across tasks.
Introduces meta-NE as a solution concept for meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning.
Establishes sufficient conditions linking meta-NE solutions to stationary points of a gradient-play meta-MARL algorithm.
Evaluations on autonomous-driving tasks demonstrate faster adaptation than pretrained MARL baselines.

papers.abstract: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.
bullets: Targets the high cost of autoregressively generating coordinates for visual plans such as points, boxes, and trajectories.
Uses a lightweight drafter to predict each primitive in one forward pass, adapting to its type, dimensionality, and length.
Trains on annotated primitives and accepts structurally valid predictions without requiring exact autoregressive token matching.
Reduces prediction errors across evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks and reports approximately 25× faster 3D point-motion generation.
A world action model using VFlash plans reaches 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces suites, versus 62.6% for the baseline.

papers.abstract: Dense optical flow allows small drones to avoid obstacles. However, few dense optical flow networks are designed for microcontrollers (MCUs) with neural accelerators, whose on-chip SRAM limits the input resolution. We present PACE-NAS, a macro-to-micro neural architecture search framework that decouples memory from latency: a macro design fixes the backbone and its peak SRAM, and a micro design searches operators and depths to trade accuracy against compiler-estimated latency. We apply it to EdgeFlowNet on a Grove Vision AI V2 board (Ethos-U55), where profiling locates the peak SRAM at the full-resolution output head. Replacing transposed convolutions with bilinear upsampling and convolutions lowers the peak SRAM by 18%, and two lightweight context modules lower the endpoint error (EPE) without raising the peak. All searched subnets share this peak, so the search needs no memory constraint. We name the Pareto-optimal models MCUFlowNet; the fastest variant, MCUFlowNet-S, runs 1.76x faster than a retrained EdgeFlowNet at a 1.6% higher EPE and, in simulated forest flights at 2 m/s, reaches the goal without collision in 51.5% of trials, against 41.8%. PACE-NAS also applies to semantic segmentation, where a searched PIDNet-S variant runs 1.17x faster at similar accuracy. Code is available at https://gitlab.kuleuven.be/emedia-research-lab/esat-stadius/mcuflownet/mcuflownet.
bullets: Targets dense optical flow on MCUs, where limited on-chip SRAM restricts input resolution.
PACE-NAS separates macro design for peak SRAM from micro search over operators and depths for accuracy–latency trade-offs.
Replacing transposed convolutions and adding lightweight context modules reduces memory use and endpoint error without increasing peak SRAM.
MCUFlowNet-S runs 1.76× faster than retrained EdgeFlowNet with 1.6% higher EPE, and avoids collisions more often in simulated forest flights.
The framework also speeds up a PIDNet-S semantic-segmentation variant by 1.17× at similar accuracy.

papers.abstract: Frontier-based exploration systems repeatedly evaluate geodesic travel costs between robot poses and candidate viewpoints, and tour-based planners consume the full pairwise distance matrix built from them. Recomputing these matrices with one graph search per source scales with the explored map size, whereas distance caches that refresh only locally affected or newly created frontiers can retain stale costs between surviving pairs when newly discovered free space creates a global shortcut. We present H-TRIP (Hierarchical Tropical Rank-one Incremental Propagation), an exact distance index grounded in Kleene algebra over the min-plus semiring for monotonically growing occupancy grids. H-TRIP partitions the known map into a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports. Each unknown-to-free revelation is decomposed into efficient rank-one min-plus edge insertions at the affected leaf, and only decreased port-to-port summaries are propagated along its ancestor chain. A shared hierarchical lift evaluates the dense many-to-many matrix of shortest distances for all active query points on the occupancy map. We prove that sequential insertions preserve exact shortest-path distances on the grid. Benchmark experiments confirm exact agreement with reference searches on fully built maps and show that dense many-to-many queries at a few dozen viewpoints are up to two orders of magnitude faster than sequential k x BFS. On exploration runs with sixteen robots, in-loop queries on the growing occupancy graph are 2.21x-8.59x faster than co-scheduled k x BFS on maps with side 256, 512, and 1024 cells.
bullets: Addresses stale distance caches and the high cost of recomputing pairwise geodesic distances as maps expand.
Uses a spatial hierarchy with fixed boundary ports and rank-one min-plus updates for each newly revealed free-space region.
Propagates only decreased port-to-port summaries through affected ancestor nodes, then lifts them to query-point distances.
Proves exactness under sequential occupancy-grid insertions and matches reference graph searches on completed maps.
Achieves up to two orders of magnitude faster dense queries than sequential k×BFS; sixteen-robot runs are 2.21×–8.59× faster on tested map sizes.

papers.abstract: Current 4D occupancy world models use heavy cross-attention or deep recurrence to disentangle ego-motion from scene dynamics. This requires significant computational capacity. However, this effort is largely redundant since the ego-vehicle's intended future motion is provided by the downstream motion planner. We present FreeOcc, a lightweight continuous-time world model that introduces explicit $SE(2)$ geometric decoupling into a conditional flow-matching framework. By mathematically factoring out self-motion, we create a purely dynamic feature space. This space supports attention-free temporal fusion and allows physics-constrained ODEs to operate strictly on residual agent kinematics. To maximize deployment efficiency, FreeOcc introduces an uncertainty-aware blending mechanism. This routes well-observed voxels to a single-pass decoder, reserving the ODE solver exclusively for ambiguous, high-uncertainty regions. Requiring only 28.3M parameters-roughly 40% of comparable models-our optimal ensemble mode (FreeOcc-E) runs at 27 FPS. On nuScenes, FreeOcc achieves state-of-the-art forecasting performance with a 0.47 m Near Field Chamfer Distance (NFCD) and 32.1% mIoU. Furthermore, the model transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI. It also proves highly robust, retaining 92.8% of its ideal mIoU under significant sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.
bullets: Addresses the computational cost of disentangling ego-motion from scene dynamics in 4D occupancy world models.
Uses explicit SE(2) geometric decoupling to create a purely dynamic feature space with attention-free temporal fusion.
Applies physics-constrained ODEs only to residual agent motion and ambiguous, high-uncertainty voxels.
The 28.3M-parameter FreeOcc-E runs at 27 FPS and reports 0.47 m NFCD and 32.1% mIoU on nuScenes.
Transfers zero-shot to SemanticKITTI and retains 92.8% of ideal mIoU under sensor packet loss and timestamp jitter.

Figure 1: Overview of FreeOcc. Previous sweeps are encoded into BEV, fused by a continuoustime temporal aggregator, propagated to future ego frames by SE(2) warping, and decoded by the Discriminative Occupancy Decoder plus the Physics-Aware Continuous Flow Matching.
