papers.abstract: We present a progressive imitation framework that learns terrain-appropriate humanoid parkour skills and subsequently adapts their hand--knee support. Human demonstrations provide traversal behaviors, but their contact patterns need not suit a robot's proportions or the available support surfaces. Our framework changes the role of demonstrations across three stages: privileged imitation produces physically executable robot references; terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide skill acquisition; and geometric support guidance with a reduced motion-prior weight enables contact adaptation. Candidate-based precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation guide support without prescribing a contact sequence. The deployed policy selects behaviors from onboard depth, proprioception, and velocity commands without an external skill label. On the Noetix E1, the policy achieves 96.34\% hybrid success in simulation and transfers without real-world policy fine-tuning, completing 29 of 30 individual obstacle trials and four of five hybrid courses. Support-adaptation ablations show higher traversal success for the complete adaptation stage on the tested terrains, while qualitative observations show changes in contact placement. These results support acquiring skills from demonstrations before relaxing their influence to accommodate robot-specific support configurations.
bullets: Human demonstrations are converted into physically executable robot references before skill learning.
Terrain-indexed adversarial motion priors guide parkour acquisition, then reduced prior influence allows geometric support adaptation.
Candidate precontact attraction and actual-contact evaluation guide support without prescribing a fixed contact sequence.
The onboard policy uses depth, proprioception, and velocity commands without an external skill label.
On the Noetix E1, it achieves 96.34% hybrid simulation success, completes 29/30 individual obstacle trials and 4/5 hybrid courses; results are limited to the tested terrains and tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the training framework. Motion preprocessing (right) retargets human demonstrations and physically refines them into robot reference rollouts with kinematic, height-scan, and dynamic information. Terrain-indexed adversarial supervision compares reference and policy motion windows to provide a routed style reward. Geometric hand–knee candidates (bottom) guide precontact placement, while contact evaluation and state transitions determine support and retention terms. Task, style, and support rewards are combined with the weights in Eq. 1 for actor–critic training. The actor and critic use gated expert networks, distinct from the discriminator heads. At deployment, only the actor and its observation-processing modules are retained; privileged geometry, reference motions, discriminators, and the critic remain in training.

papers.abstract: We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by trans- forming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordi- nate frame. This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training. The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios. We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions. Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data. This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance. However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization. To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.
bullets: Canonicalizes obstacle configurations into a shared coordinate frame so a surrogate trained on one reference mission can support others.
The neural surrogate predicts minimum UAV–obstacle clearance and guides test generation toward critical scenarios.
On the Aerialist test bench, it achieved a 42% average critical-test-case hit rate versus about 10% for the constrained-random baseline.
The approach maintained high input diversity and competitive performance against recent UAV testing competition techniques.
Reproducibility resources include the trained surrogate and over 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.

papers.abstract: Selecting a next motion in a populated scene is not just a matter of avoiding what is currently in the way: an action can be locally feasible yet drift onto the road instead of the crosswalk, cut into a stream of crossing pedestrians, or bottleneck a narrow passage. These failure modes are invisible from the current state alone, and acting on them requires reasoning about what each candidate action will cause. World models offer exactly this, namely action-conditioned predictions of the future, but rolling them out at every decision step is a cost deployable navigation systems cannot pay, and the field has largely traded foresight for speed. We argue this is a false dichotomy. The natural place for a world model in human-aware navigation is at training time, as a preference oracle that distills foresight into a fast policy, rather than at inference time, as an online planner. We pair a discrete visual action prior with two task-aligned world models, one for nearby social dynamics and one for future scene semantics, that score candidate actions by their predicted consequences and refine the policy through group-relative preference distillation. At deployment, both world models are removed and the policy acts in a single forward pass. Across five held-out evaluation scenarios, this yields navigation that is simultaneously safer, more socially and group-coherent, and more goal-directed than strong reactive and learned baselines, with naive observers rating the resulting motion as more human-like. Taken together, our findings point to a different approach for bringing world-model foresight into deployable agents: not accelerating rollouts, but amortizing them into the policy so that the cost of looking ahead is confined to training. Project page: https://seoneun.github.io/-NeurIPS-2026-Seeing-Beyond-the-Next-Step/
bullets: Reactive navigation may choose locally feasible actions that cause unsafe, socially disruptive, or semantically inappropriate futures.
The method uses a discrete visual action prior and two task-aligned world models: one predicts nearby social dynamics, while the other predicts future scene semantics.
World models score candidate actions during training and guide group-relative preference distillation; they are removed at deployment for single-pass inference.
Across five held-out scenarios, the resulting policy is reported as safer, more socially and group-coherent, more goal-directed, and more human-like than reactive and learned baselines.
The approach confines the computational cost of foresight to training rather than performing online world-model rollouts.

papers.abstract: Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) can degrade during aerial inspection in repetitive or poorly textured environments. We propose an active environment-modification framework for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) relying on cameras and an inertial measurement unit only, without prior maps or additional localization sensors. Inspired by the fairy tale of Tom Thumb, the UAV creates visual features on demand by releasing ground markers or marking walls through physical contact. An information-based indicator triggers interventions using temporal confirmation and hysteresis. Evaluation includes three simulated environments and a 900-run factorial campaign. Lower cruise speed and active marking are associated with reduced divergence, while accuracy among non-divergent runs depends on speed-strategy interactions. Corridor experiments, with five runs per configuration, use OptiTrack for flight control while VIO-based marking decisions remain active online. The combined framework reduces the reported position root mean square error by approximately 35% relative to baseline VIO, supporting active feature creation for drift mitigation.
bullets: Addresses VIO degradation during aerial inspection without prior maps or additional localization sensors.
Uses physical ground markers or wall markings to create trackable visual features.
Triggers interventions with an information-based indicator, temporal confirmation, and hysteresis.
Simulations and corridor experiments associate active marking and lower speed with reduced divergence.
Accuracy among non-divergent runs varies with interactions between speed and intervention strategy.

papers.abstract: Legged robots equipped with manipulators have shown significant potential in the fields of daily life and industry in complex environments. However, existing methods mainly focus on global navigation or manipulation independently, while overlooking the last-mile navigation problem, where the robot must jointly determine the base placement, approach direction, and grasp execution to achieve reliable object grasping, and different manipulation stages require distinct control behaviors. To address these challenges, we propose Last-Mile Grasp-Navigation (LMGN), a unified policy learning model for Quadruped robot loco-manipulation. An Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) representation is first introduced to explicitly represent the features of grasp-compatible base placement and approach direction. We then develop a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts (HMoE) policy that models stage-aware behaviors across the stages of base adjustment, pre-grasp alignment and grasp execution, and object lift. Finally, a new optimization method that jointly aligns navigation and manipulation, stage-dependent expert routing, and action-level consistency is proposed to optimize the HMoE policy. Extensive experiments on the Habitat and Isaac Gym simulators demonstrate that LMGN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, denoting that integrating grasp-aware reachability with stage-aware policy learning significantly improves the success rates of last-mile navigation and target grasp for robots.
bullets: Targets the last-mile problem: jointly choosing base placement, approach direction, and grasp actions.
Uses Explicit Distance and Directional Reachability (ED-DR) to represent grasp-compatible robot positioning and approach directions.
Employs a semantically aligned Hierarchical Mixture-of-Experts policy for stage-specific behaviors.
Jointly optimizes navigation–manipulation alignment, expert routing, and action consistency.
Experiments in Habitat and Isaac Gym report improved last-mile navigation and grasp success over existing methods.

papers.abstract: Real-world environments are messy, with paths often blocked by everyday objects like chairs and toys, requiring robots to perform interactive navigation by manipulating obstacles to clear a path. Existing methods rely on extensive simulation-based learning or per-scene instructions specifying which objects to avoid or manipulate. They struggle to generalize across novel objects, diverse environments, and varied contexts such as a cart of fragile glassware that should be avoided while an empty one can be pushed. We formalize this problem as open-world interactive navigation and present MessyNav, a zero-shot framework based on vision-language models (VLMs). At its core, MessyNav performs explicit VLM-based affordance reasoning before task planning to decide whether to swipe, pick up, or avoid an object and produce a high-level plan. Evaluated on a mobile manipulator across real-world indoor and outdoor environments, MessyNav improves success rate by 27 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline in real-robot trials and achieves statistically significant gains in a larger-scale offline evaluation, without task-specific training.
bullets: Addresses open-world interactive navigation where obstacles may need to be moved rather than avoided.
Uses explicit VLM affordance reasoning before planning to choose actions such as swiping, picking up, or avoiding objects.
Handles context-dependent cases, such as pushing an empty cart but avoiding one carrying fragile glassware.
Evaluated on a mobile manipulator in real indoor and outdoor environments.
Improves real-robot success by 27 percentage points over the strongest baseline, without task-specific training.

figures.caption: Figure 2: MessyNav: A framework for zero-shot open-world interactive navigation. MessyNav consists of an Affordance Reasoner that infers object interactability from an RGB image using a VLM to evaluate both robot-centric physical feasibility and object-centric interaction safety. For example, it will label a cart with a laptop as non-interactive while labeling a wheeled crate with a bin as interactive. Given the object affordance labels, a Task Planner then sequences manipulation and navigation actions from an open-language skill library containing a simple set of motion primitives (pick up, swipe left, swipe right) and a LiDAR-based navigation stack (move to) that we find can tackle a wide range of interactive navigation scenarios. Finally, the generated plan is executed by grounding object references in 3D coordinates using VLM keypoint identification, semantic segmentation, and depth-based deprojection.

Figure 4: Explicit affordance reasoning improves context-dependent task planning. In this scene, a suitcase supporting a stack of books is inherently unstable, while the black cart holding a single book can be safely cleared. [Left] MessyNav reasons about affordances before planning, correctly labeling the suitcase as non-interactive and the cart as interactive, and swiping the cart aside to clear the path. [Middle] vlm-planner-only plans directly from the image without an explicit affordance stage and incorrectly decides to swipe the unstable suitcase. [Right] closed-set-planner assigns fixed category-level affordances that misclassify the suitcase as interactive, leading to an unsafe plan.

Figure 5: Qualitative Results across Environments. We deploy MessyNav in varied settings to test its zero-shot capability. The robot successfully reasons about affordances and executes interactions across different lighting conditions, environments, and object types.

MessyNav succeeds on 10/15 trials versus 6/15 for vlm-planner-only. While most of vlm-planner-only’s failures are planning failures in which vlm-planner-only decides to interact with non-interactive objects (7 of 9), MessyNav reduces these to 2, showcasing the importance of explicit affordance reasoning.

Figure 3: MessyNav reasons about context, not just object category. In this cluttered scene, closed-set-oracle assigns affordances by category alone, misclassifying the rolling cart as interactive (ignoring the glassware it carries) and the suitcase as interactive (ignoring its fragile sticker). In contrast, MessyNav reasons at the instance level. It treats the cart and the glass stemware as a single fragile unit and reads the sticker on the suitcase as a contextual cue, correctly labeling both as non-interactive.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.
bullets: Targets outdated scene knowledge caused by changes between robot visits.
Uses probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view selection near the path and uncertain or changing objects.
Integrates perception with hierarchical-task model predictive control, using arm redundancy while prioritizing base-trajectory tracking.
Real-world tests report improved map consistency, lower task-dependent map entropy, and reduced navigation risk versus passive and non-task-aware baselines.
Validated in simulation and real-world sequences with controlled semi-static scene changes.

papers.abstract: Autonomous colonoscopic navigation can reduce operator burden and the risk of loop formation or tissue trauma, but remains challenging due to deformable anatomy, weak-texture and specular endoscopic visuals, and contact-rich viscoelastic interactions. Existing methods either rely on geometry-driven pipelines, which are efficient and interpretable yet brittle due to manually engineered features and switching logic, or adopt learning-based policies, whose inferred depth/geometry can become temporally inconsistent or overly smooth under weak texture and specular highlights while simulation-trained variants (e.g., deep reinforcement learning) may further suffer from a sim-to-real gap. We propose ColoACT, an autonomous navigation system that integrates an RGB-D-E based Action Chunking Transformer policy (ColoACT policy) for a compact self-propelled Bevel-Gear-Based Endoscopic Robot (BGER). The ColoACT policy augments RGB with estimated relative depth and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to enhance fold-ridge saliency and other high-frequency geometric cues, and enables smooth continuous control of the BGER by predicting overlapping action chunks and fusing them via temporal ensembling. In different \textit{ex-vivo} porcine colons (approximately 60 cm), our system achieves success rates of 85.4\% and 72.5\% in straight and curved segments, respectively, and achieves 70\% success in 90-degree turns and 60\% in double-bend sequences, with feasibility further demonstrated in challenging triple-bend segments. The project page is available at: https://Adamhu1.github.io/ColoACT/.
bullets: Addresses weak texture, specular highlights, deformable anatomy, and contact-rich interactions that challenge conventional and learning-based navigation.
Uses an RGB-D-E Action Chunking Transformer with RGB, estimated relative depth, and a gradient-based pseudo-elevation map to emphasize fold ridges and geometric cues.
Predicts overlapping action chunks and fuses them through temporal ensembling for continuous, smooth robot control.
In ex-vivo porcine colons, success rates were 85.4% in straight segments, 72.5% in curved segments, 70% in 90-degree turns, and 60% in double-bend sequences.
Triple-bend experiments further demonstrate feasibility, though performance scope is limited to ex-vivo evaluation.

papers.abstract: Autonomous exploration demands that robots continuously evaluate candidate viewpoints based on their expected information gain and execution cost. Sampling-based planners estimate this gain by volumetric raycasting and, due to its computational cost, evaluate candidates under an assumption of mutual independence, ignoring the overlap between viewpoints along the same path. This work presents a GPU-accelerated method for computing path-dependent marginal information gain, where instead of storing and merging the observed unknown voxels along each candidate path, previous observations are represented using depth buffers. Candidate rays are projected into the depth buffers of their ancestors to identify observation overlap and exclude regions expected to be observed. The planning tree is evaluated in depth order to maintain the dependency between viewpoints and their optimized yaws, while candidate nodes and rays at each level are processed in parallel on the GPU. The proposed method stays within 5-10% of the exact marginal gain computed using voxel hash maps, with speed-ups of up to 118x on a desktop GPU and 28x on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The method was integrated into two sampling-based exploration planners and evaluated in three simulation environments, where marginal gain reduced the time to 95% coverage in five of the six evaluated planner-environment combinations. Real-world experiments also showed a 30% reduction in the time to 95% coverage, as well as earlier exploration termination times.
bullets: Addresses the cost and inaccuracy of assuming independent information gain between viewpoints on the same path.
Projects candidate rays into ancestor depth buffers to detect overlapping observations without storing voxel sets.
Processes planning-tree levels and candidate rays in parallel on GPUs while preserving viewpoint dependencies and optimized yaw choices.
Achieves gain estimates within 5–10% of exact voxel-hash-map computation, with speedups up to 118× on desktop GPUs and 28× on Jetson Orin NX.
Integrated planners reached 95% coverage faster in most simulation cases and showed a 30% real-world reduction in coverage time.

papers.abstract: We focus on legible robot motion generation in social navigation settings. Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently infer the robot's intent. While mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, social robot navigation presents a new challenge: the robot must clearly convey its intent while ensuring human safety in dynamic pedestrian environments where human attention is often divided. With the goal of enabling robots to generate legible motion in dynamic and constrained spaces, we investigate how the choice of representation and the level of human attention shape navigation performance and human impressions. Focusing on the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, we conduct two controlled user studies involving alternative legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 (N = 45) investigates the role of intent representation, showing that passing-side legibility, particularly when adaptively updated, leads to smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than destination-based and non-legible baselines. Study 2 (N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion allows for smooth human motion even under distraction, even if this is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI.
bullets: Legible motion must communicate intent while maintaining safety in dynamic, constrained pedestrian environments.
Two controlled user studies evaluated alternative legibility formulations within a shared model predictive control framework.
Passing-side intent, particularly when adaptively updated, was perceived as more competent and less demanding than destination-based and non-legible motion.
Legible motion enabled smoother human movement under distraction, although subjective ratings did not always show the same effect.
The findings support interaction-level intent representations for coordinating robot–human navigation.

papers.abstract: Knowing that a pedestrian is occluded is useful to a robot even when the detector cannot recover the hidden pixels, but occlusion estimators are normally trained on occlusion annotations that deployment settings rarely have. We show that occlusion can be read off two distance estimates a camera-only pipeline already computes. Apparent height is largely unchanged by occlusion, because the detected box still spans the whole person; monocular metric depth is pulled toward the occluder, because the nearest surface inside the box is what a depth map reports. Only their ordering matters, so no focal length, stature, or depth scale is needed, provided the depth model's error is close to a pure gain, a condition that can be checked without labels. The score detects heavy occlusion on KITTI with AUC 0.909 (0.888 over all annotated pedestrians, including those the detector misses), requires no training and no occlusion labels, and is not a proxy for range: within fixed distance bands it holds AUC 0.894-0.925 while true distance alone sits near chance. On synthetic CARLA scenes with measured visibility it reaches 0.819, against 0.644 for distance alone. We arrived here after measuring three standard architectural responses to occlusion, depth fusion, occlusion-simulating augmentation, and attention, none of which improved detection outside its training distribution in the configurations we tested, and after finding that a detector trained on German roads loses half its accuracy on self-annotated street scenes in Lagos, Nigeria. Signals that need no local annotation are worth more in settings that benchmarks do not represent.

It detects heavy occlusion with AUC 0.909 on KITTI, 0.819 in synthetic CARLA scenes, and remains effective within fixed distance ranges.
Several tested architectural approaches did not generalize beyond training distributions, highlighting the value of annotation-free signals.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a method to detect occlusion in monocular depth/height estimates without training labels, which is crucial for robust robot navigation and spatial understanding.
papers.title: Occlusion for Free: Detecting Occlusion from the Disagreement Between Two Monocular Distance Cues
papers.tldr: Occlusion can be detected without occlusion labels by comparing two monocular distance cues whose disagreement reveals when depth is pulled toward an occluder.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous air-ground teams can use aerial sensing to address the limited range and viewpoint of ground-vehicle sensors, but deciding when the UGV needs assistance and what information the UAV should collect remains a challenge. This paper presents a planner-conditioned air-ground assistance method that evaluates how uncertain map information affects the UGV's current MPPI rollouts. When navigation remains degraded, we score the same rollouts under resolved map hypotheses, select the map layer with the largest useful improvement, request the corresponding aerial measurement, fuse the returned information, and replan. Unlike approaches driven by fixed support roles, task structure, or uncertainty alone, our method conditions assistance on whether resolving uncertainty improves predicted ground navigation. Across 180 simulation trials on three off-road routes, the method achieves 98.9% goal attainment while reducing mean UAV flight time by 87.7% relative to continuous greedy aerial mapping. Aggregated across the routes, each second of estimated UAV flight time saves 2.94 s of UGV navigation time. Field experiments spanning approximately 2 km of UGV operation demonstrate uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.
authors: Pranay Samineni, Adam Thorpe, John Chubick, Anand Balakrishnan, Christian Ellis, Swarat Chaudhuri, Ufuk Topcu
bullets: Targets the challenge of deciding when a UGV needs aerial assistance and what map information the UAV should collect.
Evaluates how uncertain map layers affect the UGV’s current MPPI rollouts, then selects the most useful aerial measurement.
Fuses the returned aerial information and replans the UGV trajectory.
In 180 simulation trials, achieved 98.9% goal attainment and reduced mean UAV flight time by 87.7% versus continuous greedy mapping.
Field experiments over approximately 2 km demonstrated uncertainty resolution and successful navigation recovery.

papers.abstract: Ground robots operating in temperate forests suffer from systematic LiDAR occlusions caused by tree trunks, creating persistent blind regions that degrade traversability estimation. In this paper, we propose FOSCo-Net, a self-supervised voxel completion framework that learns to reconstruct occluded geometry from a single scan using temporally accumulated observations as automatic supervision, and we evaluate cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs. FOSCo-Net consistently improves reconstruction quality and traversal safety, with a gated skip decoder achieving the most reliable performance and significantly reducing false obstacle predictions compared to baselines.
bullets: Addresses persistent LiDAR blind regions caused by tree trunks in temperate forests.
Reconstructs occluded voxel geometry from a single scan using accumulated observations as automatic supervision.
Evaluates cylindrical and Cartesian ego-centric grids with multiple decoder designs.
A gated skip decoder provides the most reliable reconstruction and reduces false obstacle predictions versus baselines.
Scope: ground-robot LiDAR perception and traversability estimation in forest environments.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop driving benchmarks in CARLA rank agents by a driving score that multiplies route completion by an infraction penalty. This score does not distinguish an agent that stops in front of an obstacle from one that pushes past it. In a corridor closed by two parked cars, for example, one agent that drives through with contact averages 52.2 on the blocked widths, while the agents that stop average between 37.8 and 40.6. We propose failure-boundary profiles, an evaluation in which each scenario family varies one measured factor, such as corridor width or the time gap in oncoming traffic, and each variant is certified from measurement as one where the agent should proceed or one where it should stop. Along this axis we estimate two curves per agent, commitment (the probability of attempting the passage) and competence (the probability of passing without contact), and locate where each crosses one half, with intervals that account for the simulator's run-to-run variance. The certified labels also give a summary metric, decision accuracy, which credits clean passes on passable variants and stops on blocked ones. We evaluate seven driving agents on seven CARLA families. The rule-based expert reaches a decision accuracy of 0.74 and TFv6, the highest-scoring learned agent, 0.60. Agents with similar driving scores fail in different ways, and agents that reliably stop at a blocked corridor still rarely wait for a gap in oncoming traffic. We also apply the method, unchanged, to a warehouse robot in Isaac Sim. The navigation policy we test stops at blocked gaps in only one of three families, and two fine-tuned versions of it pass more gaps cleanly but no longer stop at all.
authors: Milan Bulat, Gino Ardelean, Ellington Kirby
bullets: Driving scores can reward agents that push through obstacles rather than stop safely.
The method varies one scenario factor at a time and estimates commitment, competence, and decision accuracy across certified passable or blocked cases.
Across seven CARLA agent families, the rule-based expert achieved 0.74 decision accuracy versus 0.60 for the highest-scoring learned agent.
Agents with similar driving scores showed different failure modes, including poor waiting for safe oncoming-traffic gaps.
Applied unchanged in Isaac Sim, the tested robot policy stopped at blocked gaps in only one of three families; fine-tuning improved clean passage but eliminated stopping behavior.

papers.abstract: Inspired by the coordination of global motion and local shape adaptation in snakes, elephant trunks, and octopus arms, we propose a unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots in cluttered and confined environments. Existing approaches often address high-level path planning and local motion control separately, limiting coordinated base-arm motion, kinematic consistency, and collision avoidance. Our framework integrates long-horizon trajectory planning with real-time geometric refinement under kinematic and environmental constraints. The global layer combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning to generate smooth reference trajectories. The local layer uses a geometry-consistent inverse kinematics solver and Riemannian optimization to coordinate mobile-base motion and continuum deformation while avoiding obstacles. We evaluate the framework through simulated pipe-traversal tasks with multiple baseline planners and real-world experiments involving navigation among dense obstacles and manipulation in confined spaces. Results demonstrate improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability, supporting coordinated whole-body motion of mobile continuum robots in constrained environments.
authors: Duo Tang, Ping Deng, Sophie Armanini, Yajing Shen, Toshio Fukuda, Cosimo Della Santina, Peng Lu
bullets: Addresses the limitations of separately planned base motion and local arm control, which can cause kinematic inconsistency and poor obstacle avoidance.
Combines A* search with minimum-jerk planning for smooth, long-horizon reference trajectories.
Uses geometry-consistent inverse kinematics and Riemannian optimization for real-time coordination of mobile-base motion and continuum deformation.
Evaluated in simulated pipe traversal and real-world dense-obstacle and confined-space manipulation tasks.
Reports improved motion consistency, feasibility, and adaptability compared with multiple baseline planners.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a unified planning and control framework for mobile continuum robots using Riemannian optimization to coordinate whole-body motion and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Riemannian Optimization-based Whole-body Obstacle Avoidance for Mobile Continuum Robots in Cluttered Environments
papers.tldr: A unified planner-control framework uses global trajectory planning and local Riemannian optimization to enable coordinated, collision-free whole-body motion for mobile continuum robots in cluttered spaces.

papers.abstract: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) support planning by comparing predicted latent states with an encoded goal. For this comparison to guide temporal progress, states closer in time to the goal should receive lower costs. However, training representations for prediction and distribution regularization does not directly enforce this ordering. We examine this mismatch in flat LeWorldModel (LeWM) by analyzing how its Euclidean goal cost changes with temporal separation. Our analysis identifies conditions under which states at different long offsets receive similar average costs, weakening their temporal distinction. To learn the missing ordering explicitly, we introduce Time-to-Goal (T2G), a lightweight metric trained on latent triples from offline trajectories. A margin ranking loss encourages smaller distances for temporally nearer states, requiring no rewards or policy labels. The learned metric then replaces the Euclidean planning cost while the JEPA encoder and predictor remain frozen. Diagnostics on AntMaze and FourRoom show that T2G preserves stronger temporal contrast and improves near--far ranking at long offsets. Across four navigation and manipulation benchmarks, T2G improves the average planning success rate from 32.7\% (flat LeWM) to 63.0\% and approaches or even surpasses the performance of the hierarchical H-JEPA baselines. These results show that learning temporal ordering for the goal cost can substantially improve latent planning even with a flat world model.
bullets: Flat JEPA Euclidean goal costs may fail to distinguish states by temporal proximity, especially at long offsets.
T2G trains a lightweight metric on offline trajectory latent triples using a margin-ranking loss, without rewards or policy labels.
The metric replaces Euclidean planning costs while keeping the JEPA encoder and predictor frozen.
Diagnostics show stronger temporal contrast and improved near–far ranking on AntMaze and FourRoom.
Across four benchmarks, average success rises from 32.7% to 63.0%, matching or surpassing hierarchical H-JEPA baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of T2G metric training. A latent triple (zt, zt+k, zt+k+∆) is sampled from an offline trajectory, where the near and far states are separated from the anchor by k and k+∆ steps, respectively. The three encoder blocks denote the same frozen JEPA encoder applied to the corresponding observations. T2G evaluates the learned temporal distances from the anchor to the near and far latents and optimizes the metric with a margin ranking objective, so that the near state is closer to the anchor than the far state by at least a margin m. Only the metric network and its scale are updated, and the world model remains frozen.

Figure 6: Temporal guidance of Euclidean squared and T2G costs on recorded AntMaze (top) and FourRoom (bottom) executions. Left: mean cost to the same sampled future goals, normalized by each cost’s mean over the tested offsets. Middle: normalized temporal contrast between offsets separated by one model step (five environment steps). Right: the fraction of comparisons in which the temporally nearer state receives a lower cost, with ties receiving half credit; the dashed line marks 50%. Horizontal axes report temporal separation in environment steps. At long offsets, T2G maintains a larger positive contrast and higher ranking accuracy in both environments.

The horizontal axis is the separation k from a sampled future goal in model steps, with a fixed comparison gap of ∆ = 1 model step (five environment steps). Curves show |δ∆B(k)| and |δ∆q(k)|, each divided by the environment’s mean Euclidean squared distance DE over the tested offsets. Each predicted latent is scored by its learned temporal distance to the goal, dθ(zt, zg), and the solver updates the actions to minimize the aggregated cost. The updated actions are executed and planning is repeated from new observations in a receding-horizon loop, while the encoder, predictor, and solver remain unchanged.

papers.abstract: Marine surface vehicles (MSVs) have attracted considerable attention for their commercial, scientific, and military applications. Owing to their favorable performance-to-cost ratio, shipboard cameras are widely used to detect and recognize potentially hazardous situations across diverse operational scenarios. However, visual perception is inevitably degraded by restricted conditions, including irregular motion of the imaging platform, adverse weather, and long imaging distances. To improve situational awareness and navigation capabilities, complementary sensors, such as the automatic identification system (AIS), radar, and light detection and ranging (LiDAR), etc., have become essential shipboard equipment. Multi-sensor fusion can provide richer perceptual information and help ensure navigational safety of MSVs in restricted visibility. This article reviews recent progress from intelligent vision to vision-centered multi-sensor fusion for newcomers and researchers in intelligent ship navigation and intelligent waterborne transportation system (IWTS). After introducing the generation of quality-degraded images in restricted visibility, we will review intelligent vision methods for four key issues, i.e., shipboard video stabilization, visual perception enhancement, object detection and tracking, and navigable area segmentation. We then examine vision-centered multi-sensor fusion methods, including infrared-visible image fusion, radar-vision fusion, LiDAR-vision fusion, AIS-vision fusion, and other multi-sensor fusion scenarios. Open-source datasets and safety-critical applications are also summarized and discussed. Finally, we highlight open challenges and future research directions. The collected maritime datasets are available at https://github.com/MAPGroup/Datasets and will be regularly updated.
authors: Ryan Wen Liu, Fengchuan Song, Tianxiang Wang, Guobei Peng, Youngrong Kim, Xian Zhong, Hooi-Siang Kang, Maohan Liang, Junzhi Yu, Shanliang Yao
bullets: Restricted visibility caused by platform motion, adverse weather, and long distances degrades camera-based maritime perception.
Reviews four vision tasks: video stabilization, visual enhancement, object detection and tracking, and navigable-area segmentation.
Covers fusion of vision with infrared, radar, LiDAR, AIS, and other complementary sensors.
Summarizes open-source maritime datasets, safety-critical applications, open challenges, and future research directions.
Dataset resources are provided through the MAPGroup repository and are intended to be regularly updated.

papers.abstract: Short-horizon model predictive control (MPC) is fast but myopic. ZipMPC compensates by learning a context-dependent correction of the short-horizon cost that imitates a long-horizon expert. We observe that the optimal correction is often multimodal: when a slower opponent can be passed on either side, good corrections of opposite sign coexist, and the expert's choice between them hinges on tiny cost differences. Deterministic regression then averages modes or inherits inconsistent expert tie-breaking. We propose ZipDrift, which trains a one-step drifting generator over MPC cost corrections, tilted toward low closed-loop cost and learned only from cost evaluations of candidate corrections, without differentiating through the optimiser. A few generated candidates are ranked by a learned critic, and the model-based MPC then enforces dynamics and constraints. In a kinematic overtaking benchmark derived from ZipMPC, 53% of contexts are bimodal and the manual short-horizon MPC crashes in 28.5% of test episodes. With an eight-dimensional stagewise correction, ZipDrift is collision-free in all 600 test episodes and matches the best evaluated candidate, whereas an idealised ZipMPC-style regressor crashes in 4.0% (16.0% with inconsistent expert labels) and critic-ranked random candidates with the same budget in 2.0%.
bullets: Short-horizon MPC is fast but myopic, and optimal cost corrections can be multimodal when multiple maneuvers are viable.
A deterministic regressor may average these modes or depend on inconsistent expert tie-breaking.
ZipDrift uses a one-step drifting generator trained from candidate cost evaluations, without differentiating through the optimizer.
A learned critic ranks a few generated corrections, while MPC enforces dynamics and constraints.
In the benchmark, ZipDrift had 0% collisions versus 4.0% for an idealized regressor and 2.0% for critic-ranked random candidates.

papers.abstract: Adaptive sampling can substantially improve the value of sparse ocean observations by directing mobile robots toward measurements that are most informative for an evolving environment. Recent learned generative ocean models can produce high-resolution forecasts and ensembles at substantially lower computational cost than traditional numerical models, creating an opportunity to use rich predictive forecasts directly in closed-loop robotic sampling. However, these models do not natively provide the explicit uncertainty representations assumed by classical informative-planning methods, and their forecasts often evolve in learned latent spaces rather than directly in physical ocean variables. We develop a multi-robot closed-loop adaptive sampling framework that uses a single learned generative model for forecasting, uncertainty estimation, planning, and measurement assimilation. The model forecasts an ensemble in latent space, decodes it to physical ocean states, and uses ensemble statistics to construct A- or D-optimal sampling objectives. We select sampling locations subject to robot reachability under predicted currents. The collected measurements are assimilated back into the latent state using observation-conditioned diffusion sampling. Across 120 test scenarios A- and D-optimal sampling generally outperforms static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines while adding little planning overhead. Our experiments uncover several scenarios in which model uncertainty diverges from forecast error, motivating future work in uncertainty quantification.
bullets: Addresses sparse ocean observations and the lack of explicit uncertainty estimates in generative forecasting models.
Generates latent-space ensembles, decodes them to physical states, and derives A- and D-optimal sampling objectives from ensemble statistics.
Plans reachable robot locations under predicted currents and assimilates measurements through observation-conditioned diffusion sampling.
A- and D-optimal strategies generally outperform static, random, and systematic-coverage baselines with little additional planning overhead.
Some scenarios show divergence between model uncertainty and forecast error, highlighting a limitation in uncertainty quantification.

papers.abstract: Olfaction provides critical information about airborne chemical cues, yet it remains largely underexplored in embodied AI, with limited prior machine olfaction work focusing primarily on semantic odor perception. We introduce OdorSpaces, a physics-based simulation platform and benchmark for visual-olfactory embodied navigation. OdorSpaces augments Habitat-Sim with 3D odor transport and dispersion simulated by Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS), enabling agents to navigate photorealistic indoor environments using both visual and olfactory observations. The benchmark includes two representative source-seeking scenarios: invisible gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization. We develop an initial multimodal reinforcement learning policy that integrates visual observations and olfactory measurements over time. Experiments show that the policy outperforms a diverse set of baselines, establishing a strong reference for future research on visual-olfactory embodied navigation.
authors: Changyeon Lee, Kelin Yu, Zheng Wei, Shuna Ni, Ruohan Gao
bullets: Addresses the limited study of olfactory sensing in embodied AI beyond semantic odor perception.
Extends Habitat-Sim with FDS-based 3D odor transport and dispersion in photorealistic indoor scenes.
Covers gas-leak localization and early-stage fire localization as source-seeking tasks.
Provides a multimodal reinforcement-learning policy that integrates visual and olfactory observations over time.
The policy outperforms diverse baselines, offering a reference point for future research.

papers.abstract: We propose MA-SafeDiffuser, a multi-agent extension of SafeDiffuser that equips diffusion-based trajectory planners with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees for joint-agent safety specifications. Building on the single-agent construction that embeds control barrier function (CBF) constraints into reverse-diffusion updates, we: (i) formalize joint safe sets as intersections of per-agent and pairwise barrier sets; (ii) derive centralized and decentralized (communication-aware) constrained denoising procedures with provable invariance under mild assumptions; (iii) address local-trap and deadlock phenomena via time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs; and (iv) develop a lightweight benchmarking suite including a multi-agent Maze2D domain. Empirically, MA-SafeDiffuser reduces violation counts relative to unconstrained diffusion baselines, while retaining planning quality. We provide algorithms, proofs, and reference implementations.
authors: Kiran Ravish, Ankita Kushwaha, Preeti, Pawan Kumar
bullets: Models joint safety using per-agent and pairwise control barrier-function constraints.
Provides centralized and communication-aware decentralized constrained denoising procedures with finite-time diffusion invariance guarantees under mild assumptions.
Uses time-varying specifications and liveness CBFs to mitigate local traps and deadlocks.
Introduces a lightweight benchmark suite, including a multi-agent Maze2D domain.
Experiments report fewer safety violations than unconstrained diffusion baselines while retaining planning quality.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a scalable optimal-transport-based framework for terminal distribution matching in multi-agent systems. While optimal transport provides a natural way to measure distributional mismatch and assign agents to a desired spatial distribution, global discrete transport can become computationally expensive for large-scale systems. We address this bottleneck by partitioning agents and target samples into spatially corresponding blocks and solving smaller local transport problems. Under a mass-balance condition, the resulting restricted coupling remains feasible for the global problem and provides an upper bound on the Wasserstein cost. The local assignments generate target locations for finite-horizon agent control, applicable to both linear and nonlinear dynamics. By alternating local assignment and control, we establish a cycle-to-cycle descent guarantee for the resulting transport surrogate. The proposed framework therefore enables scalable terminal distribution matching while retaining a rigorous connection to the Wasserstein objective. The technical soundness of the proposed results is validated through simulations.
bullets: Partitions agents and target samples into spatially corresponding blocks to replace one expensive global transport problem with smaller local problems.
Under a mass-balance condition, the restricted local coupling is feasible globally and upper-bounds the Wasserstein cost.
Uses local assignments to generate target locations for finite-horizon control under linear or nonlinear dynamics.
Alternating assignment and control yields a cycle-to-cycle descent guarantee for a transport surrogate.
Simulations validate the technical soundness of the framework.

papers.abstract: We propose PadLoc, a training-free localization back-end that places a moving sensor within a known floor plan. Floor plans are cheap, persistent, and robust to appearance change, but recent learned-depth methods localize against them by filtering per-frame depth through dense $(x,y,\theta)$ pose grids. PadLoc keeps the swappable depth front-end and replaces the dense grid back-end with sparse geometric matching: dominant wall orientations define a small pose-candidate set, masked normalized cross-correlation scores observed free space against the plan, and a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter plus consensus readout decodes the trajectory. Holding each competitor's depth fixed, PadLoc matches or beats UnLoc's forward filter and the F3Loc filter at every Gibson trajectory length, and UnLoc's offline refinement from $T=35$ on; it exceeds Z-FLoc's published results with a shared MapAnything front-end. On Bonn LiLocBench, PadLoc improves pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23-32 pp under wheel odometry and 35-43 pp with ground-truth motion; with full-FOV LiDAR plus wheel odometry the same readout reaches 100% SR@1m at 9-10 cm median error on the static sequence. On the Hilti-Trimble Localization Challenge PadLoc localizes a camera-only fisheye rig on construction floors hundreds of metres across at 0.90-0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions; adding learned wall isolation, applied to every session, covers all five at 0.67-0.92 with the localizer unchanged throughout. PadLoc thus matches or outperforms dense grid back-ends while preserving sensor modularity and a compact state that does not grow with trajectory length.
bullets: Uses dominant wall orientations to generate a small set of pose candidates and masked normalized cross-correlation to match observed free space to a known floor plan.
Combines a moving-pose Gaussian-mixture Bayes filter with consensus readout, while allowing the depth front-end to remain interchangeable.
Matches or exceeds competing back-ends across reported Gibson, Bonn LiLocBench, and Hilti-Trimble evaluations.
Improves Bonn pooled SR@1m over UnLoc by 23–32 percentage points with wheel odometry and 35–43 points with ground-truth motion.
On construction-floor sessions, achieves 0.90–0.98 online SR@2m on three of five sessions, extending to all five with learned wall isolation.

papers.abstract: Web services provide walking directions for nearly every city, but following them reliably over long routes remains challenging for autonomous robots. Point-goal navigation policies rely heavily on accurate GNSS, while most vision-language navigation models struggle to execute even short instructions outdoors. We present WayTrace, a hierarchical system that connects web-map directions to robot motion through language. An off-the-shelf orchestrator vision-language model reads the turn-by-turn directions, a satellite map and recent camera images, and issues one atomic language command at a time, such as "cross the road to the left". An onboard trace predictor, trained on over one million automatically labelled samples from street-level images, draws the path for this command in the image, and a reinforcement learning policy tracks it. In long-range simulated missions, WayTrace remains robust to GNSS noise and rarely leaves crosswalks or sidewalks, while point-goal baselines degrade sharply with about ten times more violations. Deployed on a wheeled-legged robot, WayTrace completes real-world missions of up to 1.37 km at about 1.1 m/s through a busy city centre, rural trails and a university campus, handling crosswalks, staircases and construction sites. Project page: https://way-trace.github.io
authors: Manthan Patel, Jonas Frey, Pascal Roth, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of reliable outdoor, long-range navigation despite GNSS noise and weak vision-language instruction execution.
Uses a vision-language orchestrator to interpret turn-by-turn maps, satellite imagery, and camera views into atomic commands.
A trace predictor converts each command into an image-space path, which a reinforcement-learning policy follows.
In simulation, it remains robust to GNSS noise and produces about ten times fewer crosswalk and sidewalk violations than point-goal baselines.
A wheeled-legged robot completed missions up to 1.37 km across urban, rural, and campus environments, including stairs and construction sites.

papers.abstract: Although existing candidate trajectory evaluators have substantially improved end-to-end planning accuracy, their underlying mechanism remains suboptimal. Model-based evaluators typically make scoring future-aware by explicitly predicting candidate-conditioned future states over the planning horizon, which we term rollout. However, rollout incurs high inference cost and accumulates prediction errors. We argue that planning does not require reconstructing a full future scene for each candidate, but only future-relevant information for reliable comparison. We therefore propose RFWorld, a Rollout-Free World model for end-to-end trajectory evaluation. RFWorld constructs a shared scene memory and shapes it into a future-readable representation via lightweight training-time temporal readout with semantic supervision, keeping training overhead low. At inference time, candidate trajectories directly query the shared memory via sparse spatial readout for scoring, reducing computation by roughly the planning horizon times the number of candidate trajectories, while avoiding recursive rollout errors. Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive show that RFWorld learns a more planning-aligned world representation and achieves state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Junzhe Wang, Jinqing Zhang, Qingjie Liu
bullets: Existing rollout-based evaluators are costly and accumulate prediction errors over the planning horizon.
RFWorld builds a shared scene memory and trains it with lightweight temporally supervised readout to encode future-relevant information.
At inference, candidate trajectories sparsely query the shared memory instead of generating candidate-specific future states.
This reduces computation by roughly the planning horizon multiplied by the number of candidates.
Experiments on NAVSIM and Bench2Drive report state-of-the-art performance and more planning-aligned representations.

papers.abstract: By harnessing the inherent commonsense capabilities of pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), current Vision-Language Action(VLA) models for legged robots excel at interpreting language-based navigation commands but lack the physical grounding and explicit safety assurance required for real-world operation. Therefore, this paper aims to cage Legged-Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) through a safety architecture that provides physical grounding and ensures navigation safety. The key idea is not to abandon the powerful capabilities of end-to-end VLA planning, but rather to augment and cage them. In particular, we integrate a high-level VLA planner with a low-level physical-grounding layer that leverages efficient state estimation, in-situ 3D spatial perception, and an Signed Distance Field (SDF) representation to generate executable trajectories. We provide a navigation planner with provable collision-avoidance guarantees under the stated assumptions by combining a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with Discrete Exponential Barrier Function (dEBF) constraints. The proposed Legged-VLN system is modular, making it compatible with various VLM/VLA models and agnostic to the robot platform. The proposed system is validated with extensive real-world experiments on humanoid and quadrupedal robots, demonstrating versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language driven navigation capabilities.
authors: Abhijeet M. Kulkarni, Saimouli Katragadda, Yuze Du, Zijun Sha, Guoquan Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between language-level VLA planning and the physical safety requirements of real-world legged-robot navigation.
Combines a high-level VLA planner with state estimation, in-situ 3D perception, and signed distance fields to produce executable trajectories.
Uses a low-dimensional Bezier-parameterized MPPI planner with discrete exponential barrier-function constraints for collision avoidance under stated assumptions.
The platform-agnostic system is compatible with different VLM/VLA models and is evaluated on both humanoid and quadrupedal robots.
Real-world experiments demonstrate versatile, efficient, and safe vision-language navigation.

papers.abstract: As embodied agents perform object-goal navigation across residential environments, they accumulate successful experiences whose semantic structure recurs across scenes even when geometric trajectories do not. Reusing such experience is challenging because differences in region naming and observation granularity produce distinct graph representations of similar approaches, while meaningful differences in anchors, branches, and endpoints must stay distinguishable. We introduce HTCE, a homeomorphism-inspired topological framework that canonicalizes and reuses navigation experience. Feature and topology subdivisions characterize representational variations, and their semantically constrained reductions produce comparable semantic sequences and structural signatures while preserving semantic anchors, branching relations, and navigation endpoints. HTCE then retrieves historical successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching as guidance for a frozen vision-language policy. Canonicalization compresses the experience index losslessly, merging 17.7--23.6\% of distinct stored route descriptions while retaining full task performance. Under a single frozen vision-language backbone shared by all compared systems, HTCE attains the best SR and SPL in every setting---59.9\%/31.8\% on HM3D v0.1, 71.0\%/31.5\% on HM3D v0.2, and 46.6\%/16.6\% on MP3D---with SR gains of up to 4.9 points and structured retrieval contributing up to 2.8 SPL points. The code is available in https://github.com/startracker0/htce.git
authors: Xiaoran Xu, Yupeng Wu, Tianyu Xue, Xuanran Dong, Yifan Xu, Xiaoshan Yang, Changsheng Xu
bullets: Addresses mismatched region naming and observation granularity while preserving meaningful anchors, branches, and endpoints.
Uses feature and topology subdivisions with semantically constrained reductions to create comparable route sequences and structural signatures.
Retrieves prior successful approaches through subdivision-aware matching to guide a frozen vision-language policy.
Losslessly merges 17.7–23.6% of distinct route descriptions while retaining full task performance.
Achieves the best reported SR and SPL across HM3D and MP3D settings, with gains of up to 4.9 SR points and 2.8 SPL points from structured retrieval.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generalize across tasks, but their autoregressive decoders need sequential forward passes in proportion to the action horizon, each bounded below on embedded aerial platforms by streaming billions of parameters from memory. We present Aero-VPA, a lightweight Vision-Predictor-Action architecture for 3D navigation on edge hardware. A compact RGB-D Vision Transformer and a five-head ensemble predictor, trained without pixel reconstruction, forecast the next latent state; a Conditional Flow Matching solver generates a velocity and yaw-rate chunk in two Euler steps, so each decision takes five sequential network evaluations; and the ensemble dispersion drives an uncertainty fallback. Version 1 specified the architecture, deployment and protocol without results. This version reports the first closed-loop evaluation: PX4 software-in-the-loop simulation of quadrotor missions in procedurally generated forests. Behaviour cloning failed on all 60 missions despite open-loop errors of 0.02-0.04 m/s: the policy copies its last command, a copycat form of causal confusion. DAgger with a privileged, safety-gated supervisor gave the first successes but plateaued at 11.1-21.1% across six checkpoints. A map-free runtime shield with a 15 s depth memory, barrier constraints, a cap on motion outside the 73-degree field of view and backoff along the flown path raised the first DAgger policy's success on 180 paired missions from 21.1% to 52.2% (95% CI [45.0, 59.4]; exact McNemar p = 1.2 x 10^-10) and cut its crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, while timeouts rose from 2.8% to 23.3%. All six checkpoints gained 30.0-34.4 percentage points, at mean speeds of 1.16-1.36 m/s. The code (https://github.com/ylee-sling/Aero-VPA), the trained policy (72.6 MB, https://huggingface.co/ylee-sling/aero-vpa) and the full benchmark dataset are public.
bullets: Addresses the sequential decoding and memory-bandwidth costs of autoregressive VLA policies on embedded aerial platforms.
Uses a compact RGB-D ViT, non-reconstructive JEPA-style latent prediction, a five-head predictor ensemble, and two-step conditional flow matching for velocity/yaw-rate chunks.
DAgger training alone achieved only 11.1–21.1% success across six checkpoints; behavior cloning failed on all 60 missions despite low open-loop error.

A map-free shield using depth memory, barrier constraints, field-of-view limits, and path backoff increased one policy’s success from 21.1% to 52.2% and reduced crashes from 72.2% to 22.2%, with more timeouts.
Code, a trained 72.6 MB policy, and the benchmark dataset are publicly released; results are limited to PX4 software-in-the-loop simulations in procedurally generated forests.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Aero-VPA deployment architecture. The inference loop (top) runs once per camera frame and produces a velocity and yaw-rate chunk Ct through five sequential network evaluations; the safety filter applies the uncertaintydependent attenuation α(σ̄), the braking envelope vsafe, and the validity horizon Ht. The executor (bottom) evaluates the newest valid chunk at its chunk-local time, converts it to NED setpoints, and streams them to PX4 over microXRCE-DDS; it engages the braking fallback when a fallback is requested or no valid chunk is available. The runtime shield (orange, added in version 2) filters every setpoint against a 15 s depth memory or flies recovery manoeuvres itself; the setpoint it dispatches is fed back as āt (dashed). In the evaluation of Section 6 the companion-computer software ran on a cloud GPU against PX4 SITL (Section 4.6).

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal agents have shown promising progress in embodied planning and web interaction. However, existing evaluations often rely on simplified tasks with limited combinatorial structure, leaving it unclear whether current agents can robustly integrate perception and reasoning for multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints. We introduce DualWorldBench, a unified benchmark for evaluating agent planning under controlled symbolic--temporal and grounded--topological complexity. Built around a shared pickup--delivery interface, DualWorldBench consists of three complementary components: TextWorld, which isolates symbolic planning under varying task compositions and release dynamics; SimWorld, which evaluates grounded path planning under controlled topological variation with text, image, or multimodal inputs; and DualWorld-VQA, a diagnostic suite spanning perception, scene understanding, and planning. Experiments reveal a common gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning. In TextWorld, agents struggle to derive optimal task sequences under interacting temporal constraints; in SimWorld, grounded observations are not reliably converted into feasible action sequences. DualWorld-VQA further confirms that perception and topology understanding do not necessarily translate into constrained planning. Together, these results identify the central challenge as composing symbolic or grounded evidence into globally feasible and efficient multi-goal plans. These findings establish DualWorldBench as a challenging testbed for agents with tighter perception--reasoning--planning integration. All datasets and code are publicly available at our project website https://dualworld.netlify.app/.
authors: Yang Chen, Bin Wen, Danyang Peng, Hong-Jie You, Zi-Qiao Shang, Lan-Zhe Guo
bullets: Targets embodied and web agents’ difficulty with multi-goal planning under temporal, physical, and multimodal constraints.
Provides TextWorld for symbolic temporal planning, SimWorld for grounded topological path planning, and DualWorld-VQA for perception, scene understanding, and planning diagnostics.
Finds a gap between local understanding and globally consistent planning: agents miss optimal task sequences and produce infeasible grounded actions.
Shows that perception and topology understanding alone do not reliably support constrained planning.
Datasets and code are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian mapping enables fast and high-fidelity novel view synthesis, with broad applications in augmented reality, robotics, and autonomous systems. However, many current methods assume static scenes or filter out dynamics as outliers. In this paper, we study in-view scene changes where objects are manipulated in front of the camera within a single online sequence, unlike prior works that detect changes outside the camera view or between separate captures. This setting entangles transient and persistent dynamics, as objects can be distractors while moving and persistent once they settle. While recent studies start to address distractors by removing them for clean static background, in-view scene changes remain underexplored. To resolve this, we present SettleSplat, a monocular mapping system that maintains up-to-date 3D Gaussian maps under such changes. Specifically, we lift coarse per-pixel uncertainty into Gaussian dynamicity field, then prune transient ones. For persistent changes, we derive geometric contradictions weighted by parameter-free rendered depth uncertainty to separate true changes from under-optimized regions. On Bonn and Co-Fusion, SettleSplat achieves consistent 3D Gaussian maps, outperforming current baselines on both full images and change regions while maintaining comparable speed.
authors: Anh Thuan Tran, Xiyun Song, Yubin Zhou, Heather Yu, Jana Kosecka, Liang Peng
bullets: Addresses in-view scene changes, where moving objects may be transient distractors or persistent changes.
Uses per-pixel uncertainty to construct a Gaussian dynamicity field and prune transient geometry.
Identifies persistent changes through geometric contradictions weighted by rendered depth uncertainty.
On Bonn and Co-Fusion, outperforms baselines on full images and changed regions while maintaining comparable speed.

figures.caption: Figure 2. System overview. Given monocular RGB frames (a), SettleSplat estimates depth, then tracks and maps with the DROID-W backbone (b) while learning per-Gaussian dynamicity field δ that prunes transient distractors. During refinement (c), geometry contradiction score g, derived from the rendered map and estimated depth and weighted by the rendered depth uncertainty, is integrated with the tracking uncertainty into reliability map r. Frames before the settlement frame K are weighted by W = r2, while later frames supervise the settled scene without masking.

Figure 3. Qualitative comparison on Bonn (rows 1–3) and Co-Fusion (rows 4–6), covering moving, adding, and removing objects. Red boxes show the change regions. At old object locations, baselines leave ghosting artifacts, while SettleSplat reconstructs the updated scene cleanly. For added and moved objects, SettleSplat preserves appearance and detail, whereas the baselines blur or miss them. For removed objects, SettleSplat is competitive with other baselines while reducing ghosting.
Table 2. Novel view synthesis results on the CoFusion dataset, evaluated on the full image and within the change region. Best and second-best results are highlighted.

papers.selection_reason: Extends Gaussian Splatting to handle in-view dynamic scene changes, a transferable technique for 3D mapping and robot navigation in dynamic environments.
papers.title: SettleSplat: Monocular Gaussian Mapping under In-View Scene Changes
papers.tldr: SettleSplat maintains accurate monocular 3D Gaussian maps when objects move and settle within the camera’s view during online mapping.

papers.abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability provides certified backward reachable tubes (BRTs) for safety-critical robotic systems, but the level-set computation scales exponentially in the state dimension and has historically been performed offline. As autonomy stacks (ADAS/AV, humanoid robotics, and vision-language-action models) increasingly rely on black-box, probabilistic policies, a deterministic safety layer with formal guarantees is an essential complement. We present a CUDA implementation of the canonical WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs level-set Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs solver for 2D, 3D, and 4D dynamics that is fast enough to run inside a robot's control loop. In 32-bit floating point (FP32) on a single workstation GPU (NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada), it computes the 3D Air3D BRT at 112 Hz, a 4D pursuit-evasion BRT at 61 Hz, and a 2D wind-affected drifter BRT at 74-147 Hz, 5.9-17.5x faster than the JAX reference hj_reachability at matched precision and 1.7-16x faster than a torch.compile reimplementation of the same scheme. In 64-bit floating point (FP64) it agrees with hj_reachability on eight benchmark cases, reproduces Mitchell's Air3D BRT to within 0.04% of the reference cell count, and runs 2.0-4.6x faster. On an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor it computes Air3D at 66 Hz (N=41) and the 2D drifter at 54 Hz, 3.8-8.9x faster than hj_reachability on the same device. As a multi-agent application, an in-kernel label-propagation extension recovers the K-agent capture-basin Voronoi tessellation from a single combined HJ solve, independent of fleet size; it runs at 4.0 ms per tick in a closed-loop wildfire-response simulation of six quadcopters under time-varying, non-uniform wind.
bullets: Targets the exponential cost and traditionally offline nature of HJ backward reachable tube (BRT) computation for safety-critical autonomy.
Implements the WENO5 + TVD-RK3 + Lax-Friedrichs HJI scheme in CUDA for 2D–4D dynamics, including an in-kernel multi-agent label-propagation extension.
Runs benchmark BRT computations at 61–147 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX 4000 Ada and at 54–66 Hz on a Jetson AGX Thor.
Matches reference results in FP64, including reproducing the Air3D BRT within 0.04% of the reference cell count.
Demonstrates a six-quadcopter wildfire-response simulation with a capture-basin Voronoi tessellation computed in 4.0 ms per control tick.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Closed-loop wildfire-response fleet under time-varying, non-uniform wind. Six homogeneous quadcopters defend a 20 × 20 km region (cruise a = 20m/s) against three fires. The joint HJ capture-basin Voronoi tessellation, computed via in-kernel label propagation from each drone’s current position, is refreshed at every 10Hz outer-loop tick. Colored basins are each drone’s 10-minute reachable region; red diagonal hatch marks cells unreachable within the horizon by any drone. White curves are basin bisectors. Triangles mark drones en route (with the MM :SS predicted-arrival countdown); inverted triangles, returning; circles, patrolling at home. Red X marks a burning fire, gray X a suppressed fire. (a) Initial state: drones at homes, basins anisotropic with the prevailing NE wind. (b) The Center drone en route to Fire #1 (NE region); its basin has followed it east through the domain. (c) Fire #2 (SW region) en route during the gust, with the wind rotated. (d) Late phase (t = 700 s), wind rotated further: a pocket in the upwind direction is unreachable in the 10-min window.

Ours is 2.0–4.6× faster than JAX and 1.3–1.4× faster than torch.compile; the largest gains over JAX appear on the drifter and 4D cases, where the fused per-stage kernels, in-kernel BRT clamping, and host-static CFL step remove the most per-step work relative to JAX/XLA’s per-stage materialization. papers.selection_reason: Fast GPU solver for reachability, relevant to safety in robot navigation and control.
papers.title: Online Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability Onboard the Robot Control Loop: A Real-Time GPU Solver for Safety-Critical Autonomy
papers.tldr: A CUDA-optimized Hamilton-Jacobi reachability solver enables formally certified safety computations to run in real time within robot control loops on GPUs and embedded hardware.

papers.abstract: Transfer learning from pretrained backbones has become standard practice in multi-sensor computer vision---yet two questions remain open: which pretrained weights transfer best to multi-sensor setups, and can in-domain pretraining outperform off-the-shelf solutions? Frameworks like MultiMAE demonstrate the utility of masked autoencoding in a multi-modal context, but rely entirely on dense, model-derived modalities. It is unclear how robustly these methods translate to real-world applications that use physical sensors, where the aggregation of diverse public datasets for large-scale pretraining inherently introduces modality sparsity. To investigate this systematically, we curate a multi-sensor autonomous driving collection of $2.82M$ images from 16 publicly available datasets, incorporating both physical hardware modalities (RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event) and model-derived modalities (Stereo Depth, Segmentation). We use this collection for in-domain pretraining based on the MultiMAE approach. We adapt MultiMAE's loss formulation to accommodate sparse samples, and study the effect of an enforced encoder bottleneck for modality alignment and of additional losses specific to dense reconstruction (SSIM and FFT). We then systematically compare against common pretrained backbones (ViT, MAE, DINO and MultiMAE) across downstream sensor fusion tasks. We find that MultiMAE is a surprisingly strong out-of-the-box baseline, transferring effectively even to modalities it has never seen, while our targeted modifications yield incremental but consistent improvements on multi-sensor transfer and overall robustness.
authors: Fabio Montello, Ronja G\"uldenring, Lucas Mogensen Sandby, Christoffer Koo {\O}hrstr{\o}m, Lazaros Nalpantidis
bullets: Curates 2.82M images from 16 public autonomous-driving datasets spanning RGB, LWIR, NIR, Event, stereo depth, and segmentation.
Pretrains on this heterogeneous collection with a MultiMAE-based approach adapted for modality-sparse data.
Studies encoder bottlenecks for modality alignment and SSIM/FFT losses for dense reconstruction.
Compares ViT, MAE, DINO, and MultiMAE backbones across downstream sensor-fusion tasks.
Finds MultiMAE transfers effectively even to unseen modalities; targeted modifications improve transfer and robustness incrementally and consistently.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our modified MultiMAE architecture designed for sparse physical sensors. Independent tokenizers process each available sensor modality before a fixed token budget is sent to a shared ViT encoder. Instead of relying on decoder-level cross-attention, an MLP bottleneck aligns and concatenates active sensor tokens along the channel dimension (zero-filling missing ones) to produce a unified spatial representation before decoding.

Our in-domain pretrained weights present steeper learning curves at early training steps, providing a stronger starting point for adapting to new sensor modalities. The performance gap narrows as training progresses, which suggests that once MultiMAE catches up to the target modality, it is able to use its strong cross attention capabilities.
