papers.selection_reason: Systematically studies multimodal initialization for multi-sensor autonomous driving, relevant to sensor fusion and pretraining strategies for navigation.
papers.title: Do Pretrained Backbones Transfer to Physical Sensors? A Systematic Study of Multimodal Initialization Across the Sensor Stack
papers.tldr: A systematic study finds that MultiMAE transfers well across physical and derived sensors, while sparse-modality adaptations provide consistent additional gains in multi-sensor robustness.

papers.abstract: Causal inference has emerged as a powerful paradigm enabling robots to make safe, efficient decisions by reasoning about the ``why'' behind events. However, its real-world application is hindered by the difficulty of collecting causal data, especially in human-populated environments where training takes time, while users expect immediate operation. To this end, we tackle the challenge of transferring simulation-learnt causal relations to the real world with minimal effort. While retaining the invariant high-level causal structure, we empirically demonstrate the system adapts efficiently to real-world situations by updating only the causal model parameters with a limited set of new observations. Our results show that the parameter update enables rapid sim-to-real transfer. The framework runs efficiently onboard of a mobile robot and significantly outperforms a non-causal baselines navigating successfully and safely in complex human-shared scenarios.
authors: Luca Castri, Gloria Beraldo, Nicola Bellotto
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting causal data and training robots directly in human-populated environments.
Preserves the high-level causal structure learned in simulation while adapting its parameters to real-world observations.
Runs efficiently onboard a mobile robot for navigation in shared human environments.
Reportedly enables rapid sim-to-real transfer and significantly outperforms non-causal baselines in successful and safe navigation.
Scope: adaptation relies on an invariant causal structure and a limited set of new real-world observations.

papers.abstract: A substantial line of work builds rotation invariance directly into point cloud architectures. We benchmark 10 architectures (PointNet, PointNet++, DGCNN, RIConv, RIConv++, RISurConv, PointMLP, PointTransformer, and the equivariant VN-PointNet and VN-DGCNN) across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion, and analyze the results with confirmatory hypothesis tests rather than point estimates. The three rotation-invariant (RI) architectures achieve the best pose robustness but rank among the lowest on noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains. We ask whether this cost is intrinsic to invariance or specific to how invariance is obtained. We retrain all 10 architectures unchanged, with a simple invariance loss on the embedding and three training seeds each, and evaluate all models on the independently designed ModelNet40-C. Invariance training transfers narrowly but reliably. It improves exactly the corruption families its perturbations target wherever the baseline has headroom (mean occlusion +10.5, lidar +13.4 percentage points of accuracy). At matched training budget the best standard backbone and the best RI architecture end on par on unseen corruptions (within 2.5 percentage points in every seed), and invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model. Once rotation augmentation is widened, standard backbones concede only a flat, angle-independent accuracy offset under full-sphere rotation. We release the benchmark along with a package for analyzing point cloud robustness and reproducing our results.
authors: Abdulla Nasir Chowdhury, Gulpi Qorik Oktagalu Pratamasunu, Kazuhiro Fukui
bullets: Benchmarks 10 point-cloud classifiers across 5 domains under pose, noise, and occlusion using confirmatory hypothesis tests.
Rotation-invariant models provide the strongest pose robustness but rank near the bottom for noise robustness in 4 of 5 domains.
A simple embedding-level invariance loss transfers narrowly, improving targeted corruption families when baseline headroom exists.
On independently designed corruptions, the best standard and rotation-invariant models perform similarly; invariance-trained RIConv++ is the most seed-stable top model.
Wider rotation augmentation leaves standard backbones with a consistent, angle-independent accuracy gap under full-sphere rotations; the benchmark and analysis tools are released.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a statistical benchmark for rotation-invariant point cloud architectures, relevant to robust 3D perception for robotic navigation and manipulation.
papers.title: Do We Still Need Rotation-Invariant Architectures? A Statistical Robustness Benchmark for Point Cloud Classification
papers.tldr: Rotation-invariant architectures excel under pose changes but sacrifice noise robustness; targeted invariance training can narrow this gap without a clear overall winner.

papers.abstract: Computing distances between sets is important in many robotic applications, such as motion planning and control. In many applications, derivatives of the distance are needed as well. It is well known that the Euclidean distance is not always differentiable, which create issues to algorithms that need a derivative. In this paper, we introduce NESDF, the Normal Euclidean Signed Distance Function between two general (with mild regularity assumptions but possibly non-convex) sets. This metric is still not differentiable, but it allows us to introduce a generalization, $h$-NESDF, which has a smoothing parameter $h$ such that the metric is infinitely differentiable for all $h>0$ and that reduces to the NESDF when $h$ goes to $0$. The metric is amenable to GPU parallelization, and thus can be computed efficiently. We show extensive simulation results to evaluate its viability in motion planning.
authors: Vinicius Mariano Gon\c{c}alves, Pedro Antonio de Souza Campos Rodrigues
bullets: Addresses the nondifferentiability of Euclidean set distances, which can hinder derivative-based robotics algorithms.
Introduces NESDF, a normal Euclidean signed distance for general, possibly non-convex sets under mild regularity assumptions.
Generalizes NESDF to h-NESDF with smoothing parameter h>0, yielding infinite differentiability and recovering NESDF as h approaches zero.
Designed for efficient GPU-parallel computation.
Extensive simulations evaluate its viability for motion planning.

papers.selection_reason: Provides a differentiable distance function useful for motion planning and control, transferable to learning-based navigation.
papers.title: h-NESDF: An Infinitely Differentiable Signed Distance Between Two Sets with Robotic Applications
papers.tldr: h-NESDF provides an infinitely differentiable, GPU-friendly signed distance between general sets for gradient-based robotic motion planning and control.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the V2X-Real track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR from an Ouster OS1-64 unit, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.7457 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.4382 and a realism score of 0.9251. Three findings account for most of our result, and all three were diagnostic rather than architectural. First, a coordinate frame mismatch between our predictions and the evaluation ground truth was suppressing detection AP entirely; recovering it took our score from 0.3520 to 0.5147 in a single submission. Second, a single global non maximum suppression threshold was destroying genuine pedestrian detections, because pedestrians occur in groups and a 0.3 IoU threshold applied to a 0.7 m box suppresses distinct neighbouring people; correcting this per class raised overall mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295. Third, approximately 31 percent of the real reference point cloud consists of null returns encoded as the literal point (0, 0, 0), a format feature entirely absent from our synthetic clouds, which pinned Earth Mover's Distance near its floor until we modelled it. Negative results are reported at equal length, and Section 9 gives a full account of data provenance and compliance. That section also accounts for every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: The challenge requires training only on synthetic LiDAR while evaluating on unseen real roadside LiDAR and synthetic-cloud realism.
Recovering the correct coordinate frame increased the combined score from 0.3520 to 0.5147.
Per-class NMS prevented suppression of closely grouped pedestrians, raising detection mAP from 0.0751 to 0.4295.
Modelling real-cloud null returns at (0, 0, 0), absent from synthetic data, improved distributional realism.
The final entry achieved a combined score of 0.7457, with detection mAP 0.4382 and realism score 0.9251.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on Sim2Real V2X LiDAR detection for autonomous driving, addressing specific sensor alignment and post-processing issues for real-world navigation.
papers.title: Coordinate Frame Recovery, Per Class NMS and Null Return Modelling for Sim2Real V2X LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A diagnostic-focused Sim2Real V2X LiDAR pipeline substantially improved detection and realism by fixing coordinate-frame errors, using class-specific NMS, and modelling null returns.

papers.abstract: We describe our approach to the LUMPI track of the UrbanTwin Sim2Real LiDAR Challenge, in which a 3D object detector must be trained exclusively on synthetic data and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, while the synthetic point clouds are simultaneously scored for distributional realism. Our final entry scores 0.4793 combined, from a detection mAP of 0.1333 and a realism score of 0.9126. Our contribution is not a new architecture. Working from a PointPillars baseline, we obtained most of our gains from three sources. First, a diagnosis that small object failure in roadside LiDAR is a localisation problem rather than a detection problem, which led to a parameter free geometric refinement worth 86 percent relative on pedestrian AP. Second, an audit of our own post processing which revealed that a shipped rule was destroying valid predictions, the repair of which produced our single largest detection gain at 335 percent relative on the Van class. Third, treating the realism metrics analytically rather than as a black box, which showed that one of the four components is a closed form function of nine summary statistics. We also report an experimental methodology that we believe is the more transferable result. Because mean AP decomposes into independent per class terms, a single submission can carry several mutually controlled experiments, and a submission assembled entirely from previously measured components has a score that is known before it is sent. We predicted our final score to four decimal places prior to submission. We report negative results at equal length, and give a full account of data provenance and compliance in Section 8, including a full account of every mechanism contributing to the submitted score.
bullets: Targets detection trained only on synthetic LiDAR and evaluated on unseen real roadside LiDAR, alongside synthetic-data realism scoring.
A parameter-free geometric refinement addressed small-object localization, yielding a reported 86% relative pedestrian AP gain.
Fixing a post-processing rule that removed valid predictions produced the largest detection improvement: 335% relative on the Van class.
Analytical examination of realism metrics identified one component as a closed-form function of nine summary statistics.

The proposed submission methodology combines independently controlled class-wise experiments, enabling pre-submission score prediction and transparent reporting of negative results and data provenance.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses Sim2Real LiDAR detection for roadside navigation, focusing on geometric refinement and distributional alignment for real-world deployment.
papers.title: Geometric Refinement and Distributional Alignment for Sim2Real Roadside LiDAR Detection
papers.tldr: A PointPillars-based Sim2Real roadside LiDAR system improves challenge performance through geometric localization refinement, post-processing repair, and analytical realism optimization rather than a new detector architecture.

papers.abstract: Extracting semantically meaningful staypoints from raw trajectory streams is a foundational prerequisite for mobility analytics. However, real-world trajectory data is frequently degraded by severe spatial noise and protracted temporal dropouts. Classic threshold-based extraction methods, such as the widely adopted sliding-window algorithm, are highly sensitive to these anomalies, routinely fracturing continuous stationary episodes into disjointed fragments. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Sequential Staypoint Extraction (SSPE) algorithm. SSPE employs a resilient, state-driven architecture that replaces static spatial anchors with a dynamic centroid and introduces an $n$-step lookahead heuristic to structurally tolerate transient coordinate drift. Concurrently, it utilizes temporal bridging mechanisms to prevent artificial fragmentation during prolonged signal loss. Since optimal extraction parameters vary significantly across datasets, we further introduce a fully unsupervised, consensus-based parameter estimation framework. This framework derives baseline statistical scales directly from the raw trajectory data and identifies the optimal parameter configuration by maximizing structural agreement, thereby eliminating the reliance on annotated ground truth. We evaluate SSPE on the ExtraSensory dataset, a real-world mobility corpus with manually verified ground-truth staypoints, against the sliding-window implementation of Trackintel, one of the most widely adopted extraction baselines in the field. Empirical results demonstrate that SSPE achieves superior accuracy, yielding higher F1-scores while simultaneously improving computational efficiency over this standard.
authors: Yueyang Liu, Lance Kennedy, Andreas Z\"ufle
bullets: Addresses staypoint fragmentation caused by spatial noise and prolonged signal dropouts.
Uses a dynamic centroid, an n-step lookahead heuristic, and temporal bridging to tolerate drift and missing observations.
Estimates parameters without annotated ground truth through consensus-based structural agreement.
Evaluated on the ExtraSensory dataset against Trackintel’s sliding-window baseline.
Reports higher F1-scores and improved computational efficiency than the baseline.

figures.caption: Table 1: F1, precision, and recall on the ExtraSensory dataset.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a robust algorithm for staypoint extraction in trajectory data, a foundational task for mobility analytics and agent localization/navigation relevant to embodied agents.
papers.title: SSPE: Robust Sequential Staypoint Extraction in Degraded Trajectory Data
papers.tldr: SSPE robustly extracts meaningful staypoints from noisy, temporally incomplete trajectories using dynamic state tracking, lookahead, temporal bridging, and unsupervised parameter selection.

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in congested environments requires both collision avoidance and coordinated passage. We introduce neuromorphic decision dynamics (NDD), a decentralized, event-based controller, that provides navigation in congested spaces with guarantees on safety, liveness, robustness, and scalability. NDD makes safe-and-live deconfliction a controllable, locally tunable emergent property of local agent interactions, without requiring communication, preassigned priorities, models of neighbors' objectives or future actions, or estimates of group size or global network properties. By design, NDD couples the dynamics of internal decision and attention states with changing physical states and locally observed relative motion. Each agent continuously modulates its speed along its prescribed path, responding as soon and as much as conflict resolution requires. Agents self-organize into disjoint, locally engaged groups that resolve conflicts concurrently. When any group's conflict becomes safety-critical, decision-action feedback destabilizes collective indecision, and coordinated conflict-resolution emerges that stabilizes a safe traversal order within the group. Order persists as conflicts clear, but groups may split or merge as agents autonomously adapt to new conflicts and those with resolved conflicts resume their nominal motion. We derive explicit conditions on sensing range, feedback gains, response time scales, and actuation limits that guarantee collision avoidance and traversal-order formation in finite time with no deadlock or livelock for finite, heterogeneous agent populations of arbitrary, changing size. Computational cost scales with the number of local interactions sensed by each agent. Large-scale simulations, comparisons with existing approaches, and hardware experiments demonstrate NDD in complex congested scenarios and validate its scalability.
bullets: Addresses collision avoidance and coordinated passage without communication, priorities, neighbor-intent models, or global population estimates.
Couples internal decision and attention dynamics with physical state and locally observed relative motion, allowing agents to modulate speed along prescribed paths.
Agents self-organize into local conflict groups that resolve interactions concurrently; feedback breaks indecision and establishes a safe traversal order in finite time.
Provides explicit conditions for sensing, feedback, response times, and actuation that guarantee safety, liveness, and no deadlock or livelock for finite heterogeneous populations.
Simulations, comparisons, and hardware experiments demonstrate operation in complex congested scenarios and support scalability; computational cost depends on sensed local interactions.

Fig. 6: NDD remains safe and on-path as congestion increases. Methods are compared using homogeneous Dubins-car agents in the same 50 randomized start–goal scenarios per population size, 𝑁 ∈ {4, 8, 12, 24, 32} (minimum crossing angle 𝛼𝑒 = 70◦). (A) Safe-agent success is the percentage of agents reaching their goals without a safety violation. NDD maintains 100% success, whereas the success rate of LivePoint, the strongest baseline by this measure, remains below 100% and declines as congestion increases. (B) Mean minimum pairwise separation versus mean time per agent to reach its goal. Marker size denotes population size; the dotted line marks the 𝑑safe = 0.7 m safety threshold. NDD retains a safe separation margin across all group sizes, although its completion time increases with population size. Shorter baseline times should not be interpreted as faster safe-and-live deconfliction when separation falls below the safety threshold. (C) Mean deviation from prescribed paths. NDD maintains zero deviation, resolving conflicts through speed modulation rather than spatial detours. The panels distinguish safe completion from goal attainment alone and show that baseline path deviation does not ensure safety in these tests.

Fig. 7: NDD enables safe-and-live deconfliction through shared crossing regions. Panels show Dubins-car agents with unlimited sensing range and nominal speed 1 m/s. (A to D) Near-antipodal exchange, with agents starting around a circle and moving toward roughly opposite goals. (E to H) Intersecting groups of approximately parallel paths. Columns compare NDD (A and E), ORCA (B and F), LivePoint (C and G), and decentralized CBF-QP (D and H) using the same start–goal configuration within each row. Crossed circles mark pairs whose separation fell below the 𝑑safe = 0.7 m safety distance; insets enlarge the corresponding regions. In contrast, ORCA, LivePoint, and decentralized CBF-QP record 9, 6, and 16 colliding pairs in the top row and 20, 15, and 41 in the bottom row, respectively.

Fig. 3: Contested-region construction from instantaneous local kinematics. (A) The dashed rays extend the currently measured velocity directions and are instantaneous heading projections; the physical paths may subsequently smoothly curve. The intersection of the rays defines the geometric crossing point 𝒒𝑒c and crossing angle 𝛼𝑒. Conflict evidence depends on possible temporal overlap of these intervals and does not require equal arrival at 𝒒𝑒c . (B) The right-triangle constructions locate the upstream segment boundaries. papers.selection_reason: Decentralized safe navigation controller for congested environments; fits robot navigation.
papers.title: Neuromorphic Decision Dynamics for Deadlock-free Safe Navigation in Congested Environments
papers.tldr: NDD is a decentralized, event-based navigation controller that enables heterogeneous agents to safely and deadlock-free resolve conflicts in congested environments using only local sensing and motion adaptation.

papers.abstract: Open-world robotic mobile manipulation requires acting in physical environments with only partial information. While recent Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM) agents show strong open-world reasoning capabilities, existing architectures that rely on direct tool calling struggle with geometric uncertainty and thus are limited to fully-observable tabletop environments. In contrast, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems can solve long-horizon tasks under partial observability but incur high computational costs and require closed worlds. We propose \textbf{TAMPAgent}, an agentic planning framework that unifies the reasoning of LVLMs with the structured constraint satisfaction of TAMP systems. We endow an LVLM agent with a belief-space planning model operating over an extensible API of perception, planning, and control tools. The agent formulates a partial task plan composed of parameterized observation and execution actions, which is subsequently completed using classical search algorithms. After extracting the plan's geometric constraints, the agent leverages its tool API to bind valid parameter values, satisfying feasibility requirements and producing an executable motion plan. Upon execution, the agent continuously updates its belief history and repeats this closed-loop process by interleaving observation and manipulation actions. Evaluated across complex household mobile manipulation tasks on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 platforms, TAMPAgent significantly outperforms direct tool-calling agentic baselines, demonstrating that integrating TAMP constraint satisfaction into agentic planning loops is essential for unstructured, partially observable environments.
bullets: Targets open-world mobile manipulation, where geometric uncertainty challenges direct tool-calling agents.
Uses an LVLM to create partial plans with parameterized observation and execution actions.
Completes plans through classical search, geometric constraint extraction, and tool-based parameter binding.
Continuously updates belief history by interleaving perception and manipulation in a closed loop.
Evaluated on Rainbow Y1 and Unitree G1 household tasks, it outperforms direct tool-calling baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Integrating agents with planning. We compare four systems that maps a history of observations to whole body control for long-horizon mobile-manipulation tasks: (a) TAMP [14, 7] solves hand-authored problems with a task planner that orchestrates tools. (b) VLM-TAMP [9, 10] uses the agent to write the problem from open-world understanding but keeps the planning pipeline fixed. (c) CaP [3, 15, 5, 6] lets the agent write programs that orchestrate tools directly to find solutions. (d) TAMPAgent (ours) lets the agent orchestrate both the task planner and the tools to find certified solutions that satisfy the planner derived constraints.

papers.abstract: This work investigates human-swarm interaction (HSI) for steering large collectives through an intermediary robot helper. While prior robot-swarm control and HSI techniques commonly assume swarm members are addressable, these assumptions often fail for ``ungovernable'' swarms such as wildlife flocks and schools of fish. Motivated by pastoral shepherding, we compare low-level teleoperation to a higher-autonomy motion-primitives interface in a virtual reality (VR) shepherding task under varied swarm cohesion dynamics. Results indicate that motion primitives that operate on collective shape (e.g., boundary-based control) improve task performance and reduce perceived workload.

papers.abstract: Navigating crowded urban environments requires robots to avoid pedestrians while adhering to social norms such as remaining on sidewalks. Existing approaches typically address either crowd avoidance or semantic path planning in isolation. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL) navigation policy that jointly reasons about semantic terrain and dynamic obstacles from a single semantically annotated bird's-eye-view (BEV) map, without relying on explicit human-state estimation. Our policy outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines and transfers zero-shot to a legged robot, demonstrating socially compliant navigation in highly dynamic real-world scenarios.
bullets: Targets both pedestrian avoidance and semantic constraints such as staying on sidewalks.
Combines semantic terrain and dynamic-obstacle reasoning in one navigation policy.

Outperforms established crowd-navigation and semantic-aware baselines.
Transfers zero-shot to a legged robot in dynamic real-world scenarios.

papers.abstract: Mechanical thrombectomy (MT) is an effective treatment for acute ischemic stroke, yet access remains limited by the availability of neurointerventional expertise. Telerobotic and AI-assisted systems may help address this challenge, but it remains unclear how clinicians interact with different levels of autonomy and how autonomous navigation systems perform in realistic environments. This work introduces Copilot Assistance Modes (CAMs), a framework for clinician-AI collaboration in robotic endovascular navigation spanning the autonomy spectrum from manual operation to full autonomy. In the first in-vitro user study comparing clinician-AI collaboration strategies, 11 experts and two students evaluated six navigation modes in a patient-specific vascular phantom. Objective performance metrics were combined with subjective assessments, including workload and usability. Autonomous performance was additionally evaluated both in silico and in vitro to investigate sim-to-real transfer. Hands-on manual navigation achieved the strongest overall performance (100% success). While fully autonomous navigation achieved 81% success in simulation, performance dropped to 23% in vitro. In contrast, several clinician-AI shared-autonomy modes achieved success rates of 92-97%, approximately four times higher than full autonomy and comparable to direct robotic control (95%), demonstrating mitigation of sim-to-real domain shift through clinician-AI collaboration. Among the evaluated AI-driven approaches, user-directed task delegation and rotational shared control demonstrated the most favorable balance between performance and clinician acceptance. These findings suggest that effective clinician-AI collaboration and allocation of control authority may currently be more important for reliable robotic neurointerventional navigation than increasing autonomy alone.
bullets: Evaluated six Copilot Assistance Modes spanning manual control to full autonomy in a patient-specific vascular phantom with 11 experts and two students.
Combined navigation success metrics with clinician workload and usability assessments.

Several shared-autonomy modes achieved 92–97% success, comparable to direct robotic control at 95%.
User-directed task delegation and rotational shared control offered the best balance of performance and clinician acceptance.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobility is essential for sustained lunar surface operations, as communication delays and line-of-sight occlusions limit continuous teleoperation. Although recent traversability estimation methods increasingly rely on deep learning, the domain gap between terrestrial analogue environments and real lunar terrain can limit their generalisation, and real lunar traversability labels are scarce, making fully supervised training difficult. To address these challenges, we build a weakly supervised framework trained on sparse pairwise annotations and study whether augmenting visual features with depth-derived geometric information: depth, surface normals, and combined geometric descriptors. We evaluate the models in both in-domain and cross-domain settings using two terrestrial analogue datasets and the real lunar Chang'E PCAM dataset. Contrary to expectations, we find that naive geometric augmentation yields no consistent improvement over a strong visual-only baseline in either setting, with effects small relative to seed-to-seed variance. Instead, the choice of training source emerges as the dominant factor in transfer quality: models trained on domain-relevant sources transfer substantially better to real lunar imagery than the geometric fusion strategy improves any single model. Our evaluation runs onboard a resource-constrained edge device and provides a controlled baseline for designing more expressive multimodal fusion architectures in future lunar perception systems.
bullets: Addresses limited real lunar labels and the domain gap between terrestrial analogues and lunar terrain.
Uses a weakly supervised framework trained from sparse pairwise annotations.
Compares visual-only models with depth, surface-normal, and combined geometric feature augmentation.
Evaluates in-domain and cross-domain transfer across two terrestrial analogue datasets and the real lunar Chang’E PCAM dataset.
Runs on a resource-constrained edge device; results motivate more expressive multimodal fusion methods.

papers.abstract: Ball-balancing robots (ballbots) must lean to accelerate, and the lean is limited by the wheel torques and by safety. Planners that use the full robot model are expensive, while planners that ignore the balance dynamics produce references that cannot be followed. This paper presents a two-layer navigation scheme for a three-omni-wheel ballbot. The upper layer is a model predictive controller on a \emph{jerk model} of the ball position, with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating and concave obstacles. The lower layer is a hierarchical sliding mode controller with an extended state observer and a robust exponential control barrier function on the tilt (HSMC-ESO-ECBF). The layers are linked by an acceleration bound derived in closed form from the largest steady tilt that the barrier function admits, so that the plan never asks for a lean the tracker refuses. For obstacles whose motion is only predicted, the obstacles are inflated by conformal prediction radii that bound the prediction error with a prescribed probability. In MuJoCo, with omni-wheel roller contacts and torque saturation, the scheme keeps at least $10$\,cm of clearance, tracks the plan within $2$\,cm RMS, keeps the tilt below the limit and plans in $9$--$12$\,ms, $10$--$15$ times faster than a full-model nonlinear MPC that enters the inflated obstacles; with predicted obstacles, the conformal inflation removes the collisions of a constant-velocity predictor in $30$ random crossing scenarios and reduces them in an endless run on a closed path.The source code and video illustrations are available at https://safe-ballbot.github.io
bullets: Uses an upper-layer MPC with discrete-time control barrier functions for static, moving, rotating, and concave obstacles.
Uses a lower-layer hierarchical sliding-mode controller with state estimation and a tilt barrier function to enforce balance limits.
Derives an acceleration bound from the allowable steady tilt, linking planning and tracking so references remain feasible.
Inflates predicted obstacles using conformal prediction radii to account for motion-prediction errors.
In MuJoCo, maintains at least 10 cm clearance, 2 cm RMS plan-tracking error, tilt limits, and 9–12 ms planning times; conformal inflation reduces collisions with predicted obstacles.

papers.abstract: Real-world driving requires context-aware decision-making. Existing end-to-end driving benchmarks primarily assess trajectory quality through safety, compliance, comfort, and driving progress, leaving context-dependent decision-making insufficiently characterized. To fill this gap, we present PlanContext, a benchmark for evaluating in-context driving decision-making. PlanContext constructs paired evaluations by varying high-level driving intentions while keeping the observed scene fixed, enabling a natural and controllable assessment of context-dependent decision-making. We further define six representative driving contexts and jointly evaluate contextual decision correctness, road compliance, and dynamic safety with class-balanced metrics. Experiments on 9,561 scene-condition instances from NAVSIM and 23 public end-to-end driving models show that high conventional driving-quality scores do not consistently correspond to strong route-level in-context driving decision-making. Further analysis shows that model behavior varies with decision timing, road structure, and traffic interaction depending on the decision required by the current context. Our results highlight in-context driving decision-making as an important complementary dimension for evaluating end-to-end driving systems.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a decentralized guiding vector field framework for rigid formation path following in multi- UAV systems based on the superposition of simple rule-driven vector fields. Each control objective is encoded as a dedicated vector-field component: a normalized tangential term to ensure progression along a prescribed geometric path at a desired speed, a convergence term driving the formation toward the path, a local coordination term that preserves the desired formation shape through a pseudo-path parameter, and a local separation term for inter-agent collision avoidance. The coordination mechanism requires the exchange of only a single scalar per agent, resulting in low communication bandwidth. Partial theoretical results establish convergence of the swarm to the desired path and formation in the absence of the sepa- ration term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed. The approach is experimentally validated using a swarm of five quadrotors executing two 3D choreographies. The first experiment involves tracking a helical path while maintaining a rigid V-shaped formation. The second demonstrates a spiral- like motion obtained by a rotating circular formation tracking a vertical line. The experimental results support the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed framework.
bullets: Combines tangential, path-convergence, formation-coordination, and inter-agent-separation vector fields.
Each agent exchanges only one scalar, reducing communication requirements.
Provides partial convergence guarantees for path and formation tracking without the separation term, while collision avoidance is formally guaranteed.
Validated with five quadrotors on helical and spiral-like 3D choreographies.
Experiments support the framework’s practical effectiveness for rigid formation path following.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robots are gaining traction in off-road environments, driven by their rising demand in agriculture, defense, and search-and-rescue operations. However, these environments are inherently unpredictable and navigation remains a formidable challenge given the complex environmental conditions including challenging terrain and varying illumination. Off-road autonomy requires robust perception across multiple spatial scales and imaging modalities, yet most sensing setups struggle to capture both far-field environmental context and near-field terrain detail simultaneously across various illumination conditions. To facilitate development of robust off-road perception and traversability estimation systems, we propose MS-DOTT (Multi-Sensor Dataset for Off-road Terrain Traversability) a comprehensive multi-modal off-road dataset with long-range 3D sensing and short-range, fine-grained perception to facilitate high-fidelity terrain understanding by combining proprioceptive signals for tracking vehicle dynamics with exteroceptive imaging and pointcloud data. The dataset includes trajectories recorded across nominal lighting, low-light, and no-light conditions with diverse 2D and 3D sensing for both long-range large-scale and short-range high-resolution sensing, as well as 4D RADAR measurements that provide velocity estimates for detected pointclouds. We demonstrate the utility of the dataset by adapting a SOTA multi-sensor fusion method for the purpose of traversability estimation. This dataset will aid the robotics community in advancing research and development of methods for traversability estimation, off-road perception and multi-sensor fusion in unstructured environments.
bullets: Targets the challenges of off-road autonomy, including complex terrain, unpredictable environments, and changing illumination.
Combines long-range 3D sensing with short-range, fine-grained 2D/3D perception for multi-scale terrain understanding.
Includes proprioceptive vehicle-dynamics signals, exteroceptive images and point clouds, and 4D RADAR with pointwise velocity estimates.
Covers nominal-light, low-light, and no-light trajectories using diverse sensing modalities.
Demonstrates the dataset’s utility by adapting a state-of-the-art multi-sensor fusion method for traversability estimation.

papers.abstract: Collision-free reaching is central to manipulation, yet real cells often leave the size and exact position of an obstacle unobserved, which excludes reinforcement learning controllers that take obstacle geometry as input. A reward limited to a collision penalty does not depend on the clearance outside the obstacle, so under a step cost its learned policy skims the obstacle surface and fails once the obstacle radius exceeds its training value. We investigate whether a single analytic reward term can induce a safety margin without exposing the obstacle to the policy. We augment the reward of a simulated Franka Emika Panda reaching task with a horizontal artificial potential field that penalizes proximity within a safety margin around each of two pillars (fixed nominal layout, random drift). Under hidden observation, policies trained with this term maintain a safe success rate above 88% across a radius sweep from 0.03 m to 0.055 m (30 seeds), while policies without it fall below 10% at the maximum tested radius; the term induces a minimum clearance of 47.9 mm against 9.6 mm without it and eliminates training collisions at least eight times earlier (median steps). The advantage is statistically significant at all out-of-distribution radii and holds across three reinforcement learning solvers and under full observation. Its safe success rate is comparable to that of a classical potential-field planner given the pillar positions. The margin is a fixed buffer rather than an adaptation to the radius, and it lengthens the path by about 19%.
bullets: Without clearance-aware rewards, policies skim obstacle surfaces and fail when obstacles are larger than during training.
The method adds a horizontal potential-field penalty around two pillars without revealing their size or exact position to the policy.
Across obstacle radii of 0.03–0.055 m, augmented policies maintain over 88% safe success, versus under 10% without augmentation at the largest radius.
The method increases minimum clearance to 47.9 mm from 9.6 mm and works across three reinforcement-learning solvers and full observation.
The induced margin is fixed rather than radius-adaptive and increases path length by about 19%.

papers.abstract: Social navigation is essential for autonomous service robots operating in human environments, but progress remains constrained by the lack of extensive real-world benchmarks. This paper presents the Real Social Navigation Testbed (RESONATE), a reproducible benchmark for human-aware navigation based on a unified robotic platform, a shared ROS 2 software stack, precise trajectory ground truth, and structured social interaction scenarios. We evaluate eight controller configurations, combining classical and predictive local planners with different social modeling strategies, over eight representative scenarios with five repetitions each, yielding 320 physical experiments. The benchmark combines quantitative navigation and social metrics with participant-based qualitative assessments to jointly measure efficiency, safety, comfort, and perceived social behavior. Results reveal scenario-dependent trade-offs among the tested methods. The algorithms that stands out for their performance are the DWA with Gaussian social costmaps for its reliability, and the SFM-MPPI to provide the best balance between robustness, navigation efficiency, and social acceptance. Overall, RESONATE supports the robotics community with a real-world benchmark, reusable baselines, data, and testbed, and a consistent evaluation protocol for advancing socially aware navigation research.
bullets: Addresses the lack of extensive, standardized real-world benchmarks for social navigation.
Provides a unified robot platform, ROS 2 stack, trajectory ground truth, structured scenarios, reusable data, and baselines.
Evaluates eight controller configurations across eight scenarios and 320 physical experiments using quantitative and participant-based qualitative measures.
Measures navigation efficiency, safety, comfort, and perceived social behavior together.
Finds scenario-dependent trade-offs; DWA with Gaussian social costmaps is reliable, while SFM-MPPI offers a strong balance of robustness, efficiency, and social acceptance.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving policies require effective visual representations that capture both spatial scene structure and temporal dynamics. Video latent prediction has emerged as an effective paradigm for learning spatiotemporal visual representations, yet it remains unclear whether scaling this objective with action-free driving videos can yield representations that benefit end-to-end planning. We study action-free video latent prediction as a scalable pretraining objective and introduce ScaleDrive, a driving-oriented framework pretrained exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action annotations or benchmark-specific data. We keep the pretrained video encoder frozen during downstream end-to-end planning training to isolate the transferability of representations learned from internet driving videos. Ego-motion and depth probes show that scaling action-free video pretraining progressively strengthens the temporal and geometric information encoded in the frozen representation. We systematically study the visual representation transfer across different end-to-end driving policies and closed-loop benchmarks, where ScaleDrive consistently improves downstream performance and demonstrates that scaling action-free video latent prediction yields representations that generalize across both planning policy architectures and evaluation scenarios and protocols.
bullets: Addresses whether action-free video pretraining can learn representations useful for downstream driving.
Pretrains a video encoder exclusively on large-scale internet open-world driving videos, without action labels or benchmark-specific data.
Freezes the encoder during downstream planning training to isolate representation transferability.
Probes indicate that scaling strengthens encoded temporal and geometric information, including ego-motion and depth cues.
Improves performance consistently across driving policy architectures, closed-loop benchmarks, and evaluation protocols.

papers.abstract: Control barrier functions (CBFs) are a standard way to keep a planner inside a safe set, but they assume control affine dynamics, a barrier function given in closed form, and a known nominal controller. Integral control barrier functions (ICBFs) remove the first assumption and absorb input constraints, yet they still assume a given nominal controller and a barrier function. In this work, we present an approach to learn all three from data, using neural ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for the dynamics, imitation for the nominal controller, and supervised regression for the barrier function. The learned dynamics, nominal controller, and the barrier function are used to build the ICBF filter constraint analytically. Furthermore, the barrier is trained on viability rather than geometry, meaning that a state counts as safe only if some emergency maneuver can still avoid the constraint under the actuator limits, a correction that geometric labels miss entirely and that grows with speed. Actuator limits then enter the online program as hard bounds while the learned barrier rows may be relaxed, which keeps the program solvable at every state and the actuator limits exact, and we bound how far the input it returns can drift from the one the true models would give. On agile racing with a 6-D dynamic bicycle, the filter removes all 12 unsafe episodes from 200 held out layouts at an unchanged success rate and above 100 Hz on one CPU core, holds the input constraint on every episode of a benchmark where a jointly trained baseline holds it on 53.38%, and keeps that advantage under large errors in the plant friction.
bullets: Addresses CBF limitations requiring control-affine dynamics, known barriers, and a nominal controller.
Learns dynamics with neural ODEs, the nominal controller by imitation, and the barrier through supervised viability regression.
Uses emergency-maneuver viability labels, capturing speed-dependent safety that geometric labels miss.
Keeps actuator limits hard, allows learned barrier constraints to relax for solvability, and bounds deviation from the true-model input.
On agile racing tasks, removed all 12 unsafe held-out episodes, ran above 100 Hz on one CPU core, and maintained actuator constraints under friction-model errors.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous driving requires more than recognizing the current scene: the ego vehicle must anticipate how surrounding traffic participants will evolve under its own motion. However, existing end-to-end driving models typically encode scenes into dense visual or BEV features, leaving object-level interactions implicit. We propose (INTERACT INTERaction-aware Action-Conditioned Trajectory learning), a three-stage framework that learns a slot-based object-centric world model from unlabeled driving videos and transfers it to trajectory planning. INTERACT first learns recurrent slots that group dense visual features into temporally structured scene-entity representations without object annotations. It then infers latent ego actions from slot context and video transitions, and uses them to condition future slot prediction, capturing how ego motion and surrounding entities co-evolve. Finally, the learned slots, latent actions, and future slot predictions are distilled into a trajectory planner to guide trajectory generation and selection. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM and nuScenes validate the effectiveness of INTERACT. In particular, it achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM, with improvements in safety-critical collision metrics.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of predicting how surrounding traffic evolves in response to the ego vehicle’s motion.
Uses recurrent slots to discover temporally structured scene entities without object annotations.
Infers latent ego actions and conditions future slot prediction on those actions to model interaction dynamics.
Distills learned slots, actions, and future predictions into a trajectory planner.
Validated on NAVSIM and nuScenes, achieving state-of-the-art NAVSIM performance with improved collision-related metrics.

papers.abstract: No algorithm is best on all problems, but a real warehouse is a narrow problem: its layout and processes rarely change. Operators still run one general multi-robot planner at many sites, because experts cannot tune it for each one. In this work, which we call Late Autumn, we explore whether LLM coding agents running autonomous research can specialize a general planner for one site, trading generality for throughput, much as post-training adapts a pretrained LLM to one task. We study six campaigns on a lifelong planner that combines task assignment with multi-agent path finding, on a floor modeled on an existing automated warehouse. We find that (1) the agents raise throughput by 22--60%, and the gains hold on unseen seeds; (2) they rediscover known MAPF mechanisms, such as corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and rollouts, and independent campaigns find the same bottleneck; (3) the gains largely carry over to another layout, a larger fleet, and other service times, shrink with a smaller fleet, and mostly vanish under an outbound-heavy demand mix; and (4) each final patch (0.7k--2.4k lines) is a chain of scored commits with a median step of 27 lines, so experts can review it, and review finds problems that the score misses; some patches multiply planner compute by over 100x. LLM agents can therefore turn each site's bias into extra throughput at little engineering cost, with reviewable patches; we expect experts to shift toward designing insightful metrics and fast simulators that mirror the real problem.
bullets: Specialization targets fixed warehouse layouts and processes, where site-specific tuning can trade generality for throughput.
Across six autonomous campaigns, agents improved throughput by 22–60% and retained gains on unseen seeds.
Agents rediscovered MAPF techniques including corridor-exit priorities, local guidance, and rollouts, with campaigns identifying similar bottlenecks.
Benefits mostly transferred across layouts, fleet sizes, and service times, but weakened with smaller fleets and largely disappeared for outbound-heavy demand.
Final patches were reviewable chains of small scored commits, but review exposed issues missed by scoring and some patches increased planner compute by over 100×.

papers.abstract: Navigation world models predict future observations conditioned on navigation actions to support planning, but their generalization across real-world environments remains constrained by the limited coverage of action-labeled data. Action-free navigation videos provide diverse visual experience, yet lack the recorded actions required for action-conditioned training. We introduce OpenNWM, a generalist navigation world model with latent action pretraining. It learns universal latent actions from large-scale action-free videos through visual prediction pretraining, and further aligns them with physical motions via action-conditioned post-training. To support video pretraining, we curate NavAnywhere, a large-scale action-free navigation video dataset comprising 17.5 million visual observations from 15 heterogeneous sources. It captures navigation by ground robots, humans, and drones, with diverse viewpoints and motion patterns across five broad scene types: residential areas, public and commercial spaces, urban settings, parks, and natural landscapes. Experiments demonstrate improved visual prediction on in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, together with improved navigation performance. These results show that latent-action pretraining enables diverse, action-free videos to improve dynamics learning and generalization for open-world navigation.
bullets: Addresses limited action-labeled data and poor cross-environment generalization in navigation world models.
Pretrains universal latent actions through visual prediction on action-free navigation videos.
Post-trains the latent actions with action-conditioned data to align them with physical motion.

papers.abstract: We present Xiaomi Auto World Model 2.0, a unified streaming causal world model for Physical AI. It models and generates causal physical evolution in the real world, and unifies heterogeneous conditioning inputs for view-consistent generation. The architecture integrates View-Temporal Attention (VTA) to capture cross-view spatial dependencies and temporal dynamics, together with Multi-view Rotary Position Encoding (RoPE) to encode positional relationships across views and time. WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view, multi-temporal observations in a single forward pass and uses their renderings as explicit scene context to preserve geometry and appearance during long-horizon generation. Conditioning inputs are fused through VAE latent concatenation in a shared representation space. We incorporate Gated Linear Attention (GLA) into the temporal layers of VTA for efficient streaming inference, reducing computation and KV-cache memory during multi-view rollouts. A physical-interaction data pipeline covers diverse interactions and long-tailed events. From Pre-train onward, these data are combined with large-scale videos and heterogeneous visual modalities to learn visual, geometric, and dynamic priors. During Mid-train, training across diverse view configurations further improves the model's ability to capture how actions and object states shape subsequent scene evolution. After distillation-based Post-train, we apply the model to closed-loop simulation, closed-loop training, and World Action Model (WAM) applications. These applications generate physically consistent future states and support world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation for Physical AI.
bullets: Addresses the need to model real-world physical evolution and long-horizon, view-consistent scene generation.
Combines View-Temporal Attention, multi-view RoPE, and Gated Linear Attention for spatial-temporal modeling and efficient streaming inference.
WorldRec 2.0 reconstructs static and dynamic 3D Gaussians from multi-view observations and uses rendered geometry and appearance as scene context.
Fuses heterogeneous conditioning through shared VAE latent representations and trains on interaction data, videos, and diverse view configurations.
Supports closed-loop simulation and training, world-state prediction, policy learning, and action generation through World Action Model applications.

Overall, the model is trained in three stages to achieve efficient and controllable streaming generation.

papers.abstract: Registering intraoperative Ultrasound (US) bone-surface point clouds to preoperative Computed Tomography (CT) models can support radiation-free orthopedic navigation. Differences in imaging physics produce distinct surface sampling patterns, complicating cross-modal feature matching. Bone strongly reflects ultrasound and casts an acoustic shadow, so US captures only the probe-facing bone surface and leaves most CT points unmatched. This partial coverage makes correspondences ambiguous on near-symmetric bones. We propose CUFormer, a modality-aware registration framework. We introduce a Modality-Aware Transformer (MAT) that encodes input modality through identity embeddings and updates features through modality-specific adapters within a shared geometric matcher. We model imaging visibility and use predicted reference-side visibility to weight coarse and fine correspondences. CUFormer achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods on two CT-US datasets, UltraBones100k and UltraBonesHip, and the CT-RGB-D dataset SpineDepth. On UltraBones100k, it reaches mean rotation error 4.53$^\circ$, translation error 3.19\,mm, and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) 2.54\,mm, reducing RMSE by 65.8\% relative to the best-performing baseline by this metric. These results demonstrate CUFormer's effectiveness in aligning partial bone surfaces with preoperative CT across anatomical sites.
bullets: Addresses mismatched CT and ultrasound surface sampling, including partial US coverage and ambiguous correspondences on near-symmetric bones.
Uses a Modality-Aware Transformer with identity embeddings and modality-specific adapters in a shared geometric matcher.
Predicts reference-side visibility to weight both coarse and fine point correspondences.
Achieves the lowest mean registration errors among evaluated methods across UltraBones100k, UltraBonesHip, and SpineDepth.
On UltraBones100k, reports 4.53° rotation error, 3.19 mm translation error, and 2.54 mm RMSE; RMSE is 65.8% lower than the strongest baseline by that metric.

papers.abstract: Surface cleaning requires robots to adapt both where they clean and how they interact with contamination whose response to cleaning may vary spatially and remain unobservable prior to interaction. We formulate adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process and propose a belief-aware planning framework that uses observed cleaning outcomes to update a latent local cleaning-response model and adapt subsequent cleaning motions, forces, and passes. Preliminary grid-world simulations demonstrate the resulting closed-loop planner adapting its spatial decomposition and cleaning actions as the surface evolves.
bullets: Models adaptive surface cleaning as a partially observable Markov decision process.
Updates a latent, spatially varying cleaning-response model from observed outcomes.
Adapts cleaning motions, forces, passes, and spatial decomposition in closed loop.
Preliminary grid-world simulations show adaptation as the surface evolves.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the adaptive cleaning pipeline. At each iteration, the sensor input is converted into a scalar contamination observation to update the surface belief. Contaminated regions are grouped by spatial connectivity or alternative k-means clusterings (illustrated for k = 1, 3, and 5). For each cluster, the planner generates a candidate plan and evaluates J(P ; bt) under the current belief. The highest-scoring plan is executed and then the updated surface is observed to begin the next cycle. Red shading indicates contamination (darker = higher xj ); shaded orange circles denote spiral actions, while green and blue line segments denote wipe and move actions, respectively.

Fig. 2. Evolution of the simulated surface and cleaning actions over planning iterations. Red shading indicates remaining contamination; orange circles denote spiral actions, while green outlines and line segments denote wipe actions and their trajectories. Panels (b)–(d) illustrate the planner’s spatial decompositions: nearby contamination is grouped together in (b), split into clusters with separate actions in (c), and regrouped as the residual geometry changes in (d). In later iterations, sparse contamination leads the planner to favor local wipe actions over broad spiral actions to avoid unnecessary coverage of clean areas.

papers.abstract: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.
bullets: Characterizes 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes spanning 1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks on H800 GPUs.
Brain contexts grow to 215k tokens; repeated long-context prefills can displace generation as robot concurrency increases.
A single VLA GPU supports one robot under a 0.25-second action deadline and at least 32 robots under a 1.0-second deadline.
Increasing sustained brain concurrency from 20 to 32 robots cuts throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/second.
A static active-episode cap restores roughly 2.24–2.25 requests/second and increases completed episodes to 5.00–5.55 per minute.

papers.selection_reason: Characterizes the resource constraints (KV-cache thrashing) of serving fleets of agentic robots, providing insights into system-level efficiency for embodied AI agents.
papers.title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
papers.tldr: Agentic robot fleets face competing VLA action deadlines and brain KV-cache demands, but workload-aware admission control can prevent KV thrashing and sustain much higher throughput.

papers.abstract: End-to-end planners decode the ego trajectory either by coordinate regression, which is fast but blends plausible maneuvers into one trajectory that may follow none of them, or by diffusion and flow matching, which model the trajectory distribution but need several inference steps. Drifting models move this iteration into training: a one-step generator learns to follow an attraction--repulsion field between generated and ground-truth samples. Drifting was developed for class-conditional image generation, where every class supplies many positive samples. In planning, every scene is its own condition. Pooling scenes would attract the generated trajectories of one scene to the ground truth of unrelated scenes, whereas computing the field per scene leaves a single positive, the expert trajectory. Mutual repulsion then holds the generated trajectories on a shell around it, so any single generated trajectory deviates from the ground truth. We present DriftingPlanner, a trajectory planner trained with the drifting loss alone, without any coordinate regression term. It computes the field per scene and removes the shell at inference: it decodes every noise vector together with its negation in one batched pass, and averaging each antithetic pair cancels the linear part of the displacement from the shell center. On NAVSIM navtest, DriftingPlanner reaches a state-of-the-art 93.75 PDMS, and with single-step inference its drifting decoder comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best diffusion or flow matching setting, which needs ten inference steps.
bullets: Coordinate regression can merge plausible maneuvers, while diffusion and flow-matching planners require multiple inference steps.
The method computes an attraction–repulsion field separately for each scene, avoiding attraction to unrelated scenes’ trajectories.
Training uses the drifting loss alone, without a coordinate-regression objective.
At inference, noise–negation pairs are decoded in one batch and averaged to cancel displacement around the expert trajectory.
On NAVSIM navtest, it achieves 93.75 PDMS and comes within 0.13 PDMS of the best ten-step diffusion or flow-matching setting.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of DriftingPlanner. The perception backbone and the condition encoder map the sensor input and the ego status e to a condition c. The generator gθ maps c and a latent zi ∼ N (0,I) to a trajectory xi in a single forward pass, and N latents give N generated trajectories x1, . . . ,xN of the same scene. During training (dashed boxes), each generated trajectory xi has one positive, the ground-truth (GT) trajectory y, and N−1 negatives, the other generated trajectories Jx jK of the same scene; generated trajectories of different scenes never form pairs. Attraction toward the positive (green arrow) and repulsion from the negatives (red arrow) sum to the drifting field Vi (black arrow), and gθ is trained to move xi toward the stop-gradient target Jxi +ηViK. The field is computed on the scaled trajectories and summed over several kernel temperatures (Sec. 3.3). The GT trajectory enters training only as the positive of the field; unlike regression planners, no L1 or L2 loss directly compares xi with y.

Figure 2. Generated trajectories of a single trajectory query on three NAVSIM navtest scenes. Blue: 16 trajectories generated from independent noise; dashed: deployed output, i.e., the antithetic mean with M = 8; dotted: expert trajectory. (a) Left turn. (b) Right turn. (c) Straight driving.

Best per column in bold.

papers.selection_reason: Learning-based one-step trajectory planning for autonomous driving; directly fits learned planners and navigation policies.
papers.title: DriftingPlanner: Drifting Generative Models for One-Step Trajectory Planning in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriftingPlanner enables one-step trajectory generation for end-to-end autonomous driving by training a drifting model and averaging antithetic outputs to remove sampling bias.

papers.abstract: An AI can find a safe action faster than any human, but it must never decide what counts as safe. We present GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical digital engineering and operations, built on one partition of authority: learned models propose, rank, and accelerate; a symbolic rules engine checks every consequential action against hard limits before it executes; and validated physics confirms and decides. GURU runs a workflow as a closed control loop, with Navigation, Action, and Planning agents sharing one Common Internal Language and one training factory. Nuclear, aviation, and national-security guidance now requires this pattern; a harnessed language model keeps the model at the center, GURU puts a validated reference there. In computational fluid dynamics, the workflow raised the converged-simulation rate on unseen aircraft geometries from under 1 percent to 74 percent over 100 single-attempt cases, ran 54 live cases to Mach 6 on three facilities, and an ablation put the symbolic layer at 13 points of boundary-layer capture. Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters raised ParaView control success from 55 to 75 percent. In space domain awareness, where a language model cannot be trusted to decide, a frozen self-supervised world model under validated propagation scored highest of five methods at conjunction risk, including fully fine-tuned language models, with several-times-lower seed variance: the trustworthy design gives up nothing in accuracy, and the recipe transferred to reactor anomaly detection. A radar-to-avoidance debris pipeline was demonstrated in stages on a 2026 reentry; the hierarchy coordinates simulated teams of 200 aircraft. Training scaled near-linearly past 1,000 Aurora nodes and ran at 8,000. The approach extends to a control-grade microreactor digital twin with validated physics, not a learned model, as the safety basis.
bullets: Uses Navigation, Action, and Planning agents connected by a shared internal language and training factory in a closed-loop workflow.
Applies symbolic verification before consequential actions execute, with validated physics serving as the safety basis rather than learned models.
Improved unseen-aircraft CFD convergence from under 1% to 74% across 100 single-attempt cases; also demonstrated live Mach 6 cases on three facilities.
Knowledge-graph retrieval and role adapters increased ParaView control success from 55% to 75%; validated world modeling achieved the best conjunction-risk score among five methods.
Demonstrations span space-domain awareness, reactor anomaly detection, debris avoidance, large simulated aircraft teams, and a control-grade microreactor digital twin.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Data Factory outputs feed multiple automated-machine-learning frameworks trained in parallel. Candidate models are evaluated, compared, and ranked under Monte Carlo cross-validation, and the best predictor for each target is registered for downstream use in the workflow.

Figure 1: The GURU hierarchy. The Planning layer performs long-horizon forecasting and planning with JEPA world models and model predictive control. The Action layer turns plans into bounded decisions through optimization, parameter prediction, and anomaly detection. The Navigation layer executes and monitors operations across software and physical systems. Feedback flows bidirectionally, so plans constrain low-level action while observations update the planner. The middle layer, labeled Discrete actions in the figure, is the Action layer.

Figure 8: Knowledge-graph construction pipeline. Heterogeneous software sources are converted into a common, provenance-preserving observation representation, using vision-language models and automatic speech recognition (ASR) for video and deterministic or vision-language extraction for PDF documents, before being transformed into candidate claims and merged into a canonical knowledge graph. The shared intermediate schema allows document and video evidence to contribute to the same reusable representation.

Figure 21: The horizon-aware forecaster that produces the forward tracks. The extended model takes a look-ahead interval, up to 72 hours (at most 7 days), from as much as 28 days of history, and predicts the embedding of the whole future trajectory rather than a single point. Sweeping the look-ahead forward and backward turns the same model into a scanner across the historical archive for behavior staggered in time to avoid notice. The forecaster is a joint-embedding predictive architecture (LeCun, 2022; Assran et al., 2023).

Figure 17: Software-control architecture and knowledge-learning loop for ParaView. The Planning agent decomposes a user goal into structured actions; the Grounding agent maps each action and the current application state to executable code or GUI operations; and the Execution agent applies the selected operation and returns the resulting state. Tutorials, documents, and interaction trajectories provide knowledge for retrieval and role-specific training.

Figure 2: The GURU platform. The Learning Engine trains Navigation, Action, and Planning agents. The rules engine validates schemas, ontologies, constraints, and execution state. The agent society coordinates specialized agents through message pools and a shared workspace for auditable execution. Inputs span sensor streams, simulation outputs, documents, and direct user interaction, and the same platform drives applications in digital engineering, space operations, and reactor operations.

Figure 4: The Common Internal Language unifies agents through a shared semantic substrate for concepts, values, rules, and procedures, a uniform message format for the global workspace, and hierarchical task structures ready for planning and execution. Inset: a natural-language and geometry request is translated into typed, unit-aware attribute records with explicit provenance and uncertainty fields.

Figure 3: Lightweight clients capture multimodal input and workflow intent. Structured representations and high-dimensional embeddings are routed to backend services for reasoning, orchestration, and execution across local, cloud, and high-performance computing environments. Remote applications can be driven and viewed through a streamed display.

Figure 45: CFD simulation outcomes by grid generator and parameter selection. Stacked outcome shares for the earlier Pentagrow pipeline with predicted parameters, the extrusion-based generator with random parameters, and the extrusion-based generator with learned parameter selection. Outcomes are failed grid generation, failed initial solve, failed during adaptation, not finished, not converged, and converged. The rightmost configuration is the headline result in the text: 100 cases, one attempt each, of which 92 completed and 74 converged.

Figure 6: Current and target states are encoded into latent embeddings. The predictor learns action-conditioned transitions in that latent space, which lets agents forecast the behavior of an interface or environment without reconstructing raw observations.

Figure 7: Multimodal sources for software-knowledge acquisition. Document and video tutorials provide procedural demonstrations and application knowledge, while autonomous ParaView exploration produces state-action-outcome trajectories. The exploration examples show before-and-after application states; several attempts did not achieve the requested goal, which is why execution without an error is never treated as achievement. Both sources are transformed into reusable observations for knowledge extraction and agent training.

Figure 49: Quantitative comparison of anomaly-detection methods and JEPA scoring rules. (Top left) Balanced accuracy at the warning threshold by method. (Top right) Correct-classification rate per fault group. (Bottom left) Temporal anomaly scores for four JEPA scoring variants. (Bottom right) Balanced accuracy and average precision for each scoring rule. Embedding kNN gives the best and most consistent balance across fault families.

Figure 46: Frozen JEPA matches or exceeds configuration-matched baselines on conjunction risk, with seed-stable performance. Mean binary F1-score over 10 seeds on the shared test split, with every method trained under the same budget (batch size 96, 1,000 training steps); labels show mean ± standard deviation. The frozen JEPA encoder with a small MLP head scores highest, and its low seed-to-seed variance shows the result does not depend on a lucky seed, even though none of its backbone weights are trained.

Figure 11: GURU CFD Suite workflow for high-speed aerial vehicles. The figure shows one representative airframe from the live run described above, the Fury: from a natural-language prompt, GURU configured an aerodynamic sweep at Mach 2 to 4, 40 to 50 km, plus or minus 5 degrees angle of attack, about 1M cells, and autonomously submitted it to HPC. Post-processed output for the Fury airframe shows Mach contours and surface pressure-coefficient distribution, the computational mesh, converged residual histories, and axial surface pressure and heat-flux profiles. Video: https://youtu.be/GQIJjjVolNY

Figure 13: The generation model maps image embeddings and augmented renderings into meshable vehicle geometries. Representative outputs span 11 aerial vehicle classes, from fixed-wing subsonic and transonic to supersonic and hypersonic, eVTOL, flying-wing and blended-wing-body, delta-wing and canard, high-lift, rotorcraft, lighter-than-air, and unconventional configurations, with 673 geometries reaching successful volume-grid generation.

Figure 36: Historical traffic replay with modeled hazard bands and candidate reroutes. The dashboard combines recorded aircraft tracks, event evidence, illustrative debris bands, and proposed route alternatives. The evidence panel distinguishes published predictions, event confirmation, and traffic records; the decision panel summarizes modeled intersections and rerouting costs. The displayed alternatives are simulation outputs, not aircraft actions that occurred during the event. Also identified in the dashboard - limits on route completion, cost estimation, and multi-aircraft conflict assessment. Video: https://youtu.be/Jtyf78QsXlE

Figure 20: Two-phase design. In pre-training, the world model learns from context and target windows split from up to 28 days of state-vector history, with a slow exponential-moving-average target encoder and a Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer optimized under an MSE objective in embedding space. In the conjunction stage, the frozen encoder produces embeddings for the history of two objects, which are combined into a symmetric pair representation and read by a conjunction head trained on public conjunction-message labels to output a collision risk score.

Explicit program state, API information, and capability catalogs improve base-model performance, while graph retrieval is most valuable when supplied context is limited. papers.selection_reason: Presents GURU, a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system for mission-critical operations, combining learned models with symbolic rules and validated physics, relevant to embodied agents and interactive world models.
papers.title: GURU: A Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Multi-Agent System for Verification-Aware Automation of Mission-Critical Digital Engineering and Operations
papers.tldr: GURU is a hierarchical neuro-symbolic multi-agent system in which learned models propose actions, symbolic rules enforce hard safety limits, and validated physics makes final decisions for mission-critical operations.

papers.abstract: Two groups of pedestrians face avoidable risk on the city sidewalk: people living with visual impairment, who reach an obstacle before anything warns them, and people walking with divided attention, who register a hazard late or not at all. A vision system can warn them only about obstacles it has learned to recognize, so its training data limits the protection it offers. No suitable training set exists: public benchmarks are recorded from vehicles, aerial platforms, or fixed rigs, general-purpose detectors omit the street furniture that causes trips, and pedestrian-focused collections are confined to single regions with incompatible class schemes. This paper introduces the Real-time Obstacle Detection (ROD) dataset: more than 24,000 images and 40,000 annotated obstacles across 25 classes, from vehicles and people to the stairs, manholes, traffic cones, and benches that general-purpose detectors overlook. Because street furniture differs between cities, ROD unifies twenty-nine public collections onto one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from two contrasting cities on two continents, Tehran and Toronto. Every label is human-verified, and each capture campaign is admitted only after a compact detector shows it can learn the class. Six lightweight YOLO detectors (nano and tiny variants) benchmarked on ROD all exceed 0.86 recall; YOLO12n attains the highest recall (0.889), YOLO26n the highest precision (0.925), and YOLOv9t the best mAP@0.50 (0.882) with the fewest parameters. Because the recall and mAP rankings disagree, selecting a model by mAP does not minimize missed obstacles, so per-class recall is reported for all 25 classes.
bullets: Addresses safety risks for visually impaired pedestrians and people walking while distracted.
Combines 29 public collections under one taxonomy and adds eye-level imagery from Tehran and Toronto.
Contains over 24,000 images and 40,000 human-verified obstacle annotations across 25 classes, including stairs, manholes, cones, and benches.
Benchmarks six lightweight YOLO detectors; all achieve recall above 0.86, with different models leading in recall, precision, and mAP@0.50.
Reports per-class recall because mAP rankings do not necessarily identify the model that minimizes missed obstacles.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 End-to-end construction pipeline for the ROD dataset.
