Track 2 normalizes fieldcaptured imagery from Tehran and Toronto, then annotates it either automatically, through the AnnotationFlow pipeline running SAM 3 inside a Roboflow Workflow, or manually in CVAT where no reliable concept prompt exists; every label from both routes is verified by a human. papers.abstract: When searching for an object, humans naturally combine semantic intuition - reasoning about where the object is likely to be stored - with geometric awareness of what parts of the space are visible, occluded, or unexplored. Effective robot object search requires the same joint reasoning, yet existing methods rely on only one: geometric methods maintain principled spatial beliefs but lack deep semantic understanding, while language-model based methods leverage commonsense knowledge but maintain no explicit belief over space. We argue that jointly reasoning over semantic and geometric evidence in an explicit 3D belief enables human-like interactive object search that outperforms either modality alone. To test this claim, we build a system that accumulates per-object VLM plausibility scores and geometric occupancy evidence via Bayesian log-odds filtering into a unified 3D voxel belief field. High-belief regions in the combined belief field drive action selection at each step: taking a closer look from a different viewpoint, navigating toward an unexplored region of the workspace, or physically interacting with a closed cabinet. We deploy this system end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid and find that it outperforms geometry-only search and LLM-based planning methods. Project website - https://skymanaditya1.github.io/objsearch-website/
bullets: Addresses the gap between geometry-only methods and language-based planners that lack spatial beliefs.
Combines VLM object-likelihood scores with geometric occupancy evidence using Bayesian log-odds filtering.
Uses high-belief voxel regions to choose viewpoints, explore unseen areas, or interact with closed cabinets.
Evaluated end-to-end on a bimanual mobile humanoid, outperforming geometry-only and LLM-based search methods.

papers.abstract: Before foraging, desert ants perform learning walks (LWs) to acquire visual memories around their nest. With experience, these walks expand, become straighter, and contain fewer visual scans. We previously proposed a model in which these behaviours emerge from the angular mismatch between path integration (PI) and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass (VC). Here, we test whether this mechanism can generate learning walks on a physical robot, despite the sensory and motor noise inherent to real-world conditions. We implement the model on a four-wheeled robot equipped with a panoramic camera, an IMU and wheel encoders providing compass and stride information for PI, and test it outdoors using a replicated desert-ant experimental setup. The PI--VC mismatch regulates walking speed, turning, pirouettes, and returns to the nest, while PI provides a teaching signal for visual learning. The robot autonomously decides when to acquire visual memories, while its behaviour gradually shifts from exploration towards foraging as visual learning progresses. The robot reproduces desert-ant LW features, including expanding and straightening trajectories, decreasing pirouette frequency, and improved visual homing. These results demonstrate that a simple error-driven mechanism can generate key features of learning walks under real-world conditions, supporting its plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants. More broadly, this work illustrates how physical robots can be used to test biological models.
bullets: Learning walks emerge from angular mismatch between path integration and a mushroom-body-inspired visual compass.
The mechanism controls speed, turning, pirouettes, nest returns, and visual-memory acquisition.
Implemented on an outdoor four-wheeled robot with a panoramic camera, IMU, and wheel encoders despite real-world noise.
The robot reproduced expanding and straightening paths, fewer pirouettes, and improved visual homing as learning progressed.
Results support the mechanism’s plausibility as an explanation for active visual learning in desert ants and demonstrate physical robots as tools for testing biological models.

papers.abstract: Autonomous systems that navigate their environment need methods to quickly assess the feasibility and safety of desired trajectories. Traditional solutions that rely on numerical integration can be computationally heavy, while fast data-driven surrogates lack the formal guarantees that numerical approaches provide. This work demonstrates a framework that uses (1) a neural network with a spectral backbone to learn trajectories and quantile bands with built-in constraints (initial conditions and stability); (2) a modified conformal quantile regression to provide calibrated, joint trajectory-level coverage; and (3) interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points. After refactoring the network for inference, the trajectory inference time for a quadrotor under a closed-loop linear quadratic regulator is 3.45~ms on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. The total pipeline time, including trajectory inference time, is 9.81~ms, or approximately 100~Hz, consistent with typical control rates.
bullets: Targets the computational cost of numerical trajectory integration while retaining formal coverage guarantees.
Learns trajectories and quantile bands with built-in initial-condition and stability constraints.
Uses modified conformal quantile regression for calibrated joint coverage over entire trajectories.
Applies interval arithmetic to extend noise-free coverage guarantees to control points.
On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, inference takes 3.45 ms and the full pipeline runs in 9.81 ms, approximately 100 Hz.

papers.abstract: Planning with world models enables test-time adaptation for embodied agents, offering superior generalization over direct policy learning. However, long-horizon tasks remain hindered by cumulative errors and search complexity. Existing hierarchical methods often use rigid macro-actions or latent skills, leading to brittle representations and limited fine-grained control. We introduce ID-WM (Implicit Dynamics World Models), a hierarchical world model that decouples state-space reachability from local control. Our framework utilizes a high-level model to sample feasible transitions across the state manifold and a low-level world model as an inverse dynamics solver to ground these transitions into precise actions. This allows the planner to identify reachable subgoals without being constrained by low-level execution details. By prioritizing local physical feasibility over global behavioral patterns, ID-WM synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, transcending the specific behavioral modes seen during training. We demonstrate its effectiveness across three navigation and manipulation suites, achieving a 38.5% improvement over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion-based planners. Crucially, by leveraging this hierarchical structure to mitigate compounding errors, our approach yields a 135% performance gain over single-level world model MPC, particularly in complex, unseen configurations for long-horizon tasks. Videos can be viewed at https://id-wm.github.io
authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Yvonne Wu, Zichen Jeff Cui, Nicolas Ballas, Mido Assran, Lerrel Pinto, Yann LeCun
bullets: Addresses compounding prediction errors and search complexity in long-horizon planning.

Synthesizes novel long-horizon plans from short segments, including in unseen configurations.
Improves performance by 38.5% over state-of-the-art policy and diffusion planners and by 135% over single-level world-model MPC across three navigation and manipulation suites.

papers.abstract: Autonomous wheelchairs can improve the quality of life for individuals with mobility impairments by providing greater independence. However, reliable navigation especially in human environments is a major challenge due to factors such as dynamic obstacles, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, and the users' need to complete multiple stops along the way before reaching their final destination. This paper presents a hybrid path planning framework for multi-goal navigation in dynamic environments. The framework integrates the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) for global task ordering with the Potential Field (PF) method and heuristic local planners such as Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT) and A-star (A*) to achieve collision-free navigation. Within this hybrid framework, TSP determines the visiting order of intermediate stations, PF transfers global path information, and local planners avoid obstacles while guiding the robot to the stations. The local planners generate feasible paths that allow the robot to follow the global trajectory and reroute to avoid static and dynamic obstacles. For this purpose, two algorithms have been developed: (i) TSP-PF-RRT and (ii) TSP-PF-A*. The performance of the proposed algorithms are evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded scenarios that contain heterogeneous dynamic and static obstacles. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid framework enables efficient multi-goal navigation while maintaining safe operation in dynamic environments with humans, with TSP-PF-RRT achieving fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances.
authors: Damla Leblebicio\u{g}lu, Rachel Barume, Ta\c{s}k{\i}n Pad{\i}r
bullets: Addresses wheelchair navigation challenges involving unpredictable pedestrians, dynamic obstacles, and multiple intermediate stops.
Uses TSP to order destinations, potential fields to transfer global path guidance, and RRT or A* to generate collision-free local routes.
Introduces two planners: TSP-PF-RRT and TSP-PF-A*.
Monte Carlo simulations in crowded and extra-crowded environments evaluate performance with heterogeneous static and dynamic obstacles.
TSP-PF-RRT achieves fewer or no collisions and shorter travel distances in the reported experiments.

papers.abstract: Spline representations provide a compact way to approximate continuous trajectories using a finite number of parameters. When approximating trajectories generated by dynamical systems, the efficiency of a spline representation depends strongly on the placement of knot points. Uniform knot distributions often lead to inefficient representations, requiring either unnecessary control points or producing poor approximations in regions where the trajectory varies rapidly. In this work we propose a learning-based method for adaptive knot placement in B-spline approximations of trajectories generated by ordinary differential equations. A neural network learns a mapping from the initial condition of the system to quantities that characterize the local variation of the resulting trajectory. These estimates are used to construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator, reducing the number of control points needed to meet a prescribed accuracy.
authors: Jasmine Ratchford, Raffaele Romagnoli, Mark H. Klein
bullets: Uniform knot placement can waste control points or poorly capture rapidly varying trajectory regions.
The method learns local trajectory-variation characteristics directly from the system’s initial condition.
These predictions construct nonuniform knot distributions that approximately equidistribute a local error indicator.
The goal is to meet a prescribed approximation accuracy with fewer control points.
The abstract describes the approach and objective but does not report specific experimental results or limitations.

papers.abstract: This paper extends an existing framework for the coordination of mobile agents in unknown worlds, by considering the possibility of dynamic instability. In the original problem, known as the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) (arXiv:2512.09495), the multi-agent system must establish a communication network which completely covers an initially unknown constrained space. However, the POCGAGP fails to account for the unpredictability often seen in real-world deployment. To address this, the dynamic case (DPOCGAGP) introduces two settings which can influence the mobile network during deployment: Agent Loss and World Change, which represent dynamic changes to the world. Within this study, we present advancements to two state-of-the-art algorithms, the Centralized Agent-Directed Exploration for Network Coverage (CADENCE), and its decentralized analogue, DADENCE, to provide solutions in these cases. We then compare their performance against another state-of-the-art benchmark algorithm, and show that the adapted algorithms outperform across our benchmark test set, which comprises over 4500 test cases of varied size and structure.
authors: Hugo Gandhi, Edwin Meriaux, Antonio Lor\'ia
bullets: Extends the POCGAGP framework to dynamic settings called DPOCGAGP.
Models two disruptions: Agent Loss and World Change.
Adapts CADENCE and DADENCE for dynamic network coverage.
Evaluates the methods on more than 4,500 varied benchmark cases.
Reports that both adapted algorithms outperform a state-of-the-art benchmark across the test set.

papers.abstract: Accurate BEV map prediction is a critical component of autonomous driving systems, enabling downstream planning and control. Recent approaches such as Mask2Map achieve strong performance by predicting vectorized, instance-level map elements directly from multi-view images. However, existing BEV map prediction models operate largely independently of object-level scene understanding, despite the fact that traffic participants frequently occlude or implicitly encode information about road geometry. In this work, we propose a multitask architecture that jointly predicts BEV maps and 3D objects, explicitly enabling information exchange between the two tasks. Building upon Mask2Map, we introduce an object detection branch and incorporate cross-task feature fusion at both the BEV feature level and the instance-query level via deformable attention and cross-attention mechanisms. This design allows map instances to leverage object context while remaining robust to occlusions caused by traffic participants. Experimental results on the nuScenes and Argoverse 2 datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently improves BEV map prediction accuracy, with particularly significant gains of 21% mAP in scenes containing heavy object occlusion.
authors: Christian Bohn, Harsh Yadav, Klaus Friedrichs, Hasan Tercan, Tobias Meisen
bullets: Targets the limited object-level scene understanding of existing BEV map prediction methods.
Extends Mask2Map with a multitask architecture that predicts vectorized maps and 3D objects.
Exchanges information through BEV-level deformable-attention fusion and instance-query cross-attention.
Improves map prediction on nuScenes and Argoverse 2, with a reported 21% mAP gain under heavy object occlusion.

papers.abstract: Ultra-wideband (UWB) enables high-accuracy distance estimation (ranging), but performance degrades in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions. When UWB tags are worn, the human body inevitably causes a wearer-induced NLOS (WNLOS), yielding significant errors; still, despite its relevance, WNLOS remains understudied. Moreover, WNLOS detection typically must occur on-device at the tag, requiring classification accuracy to be balanced against tight runtime and energy constraints often hard to meet with machine learning (ML) -- the dominating NLOS classification approach. Meanwhile, UWB radio link indicators (LI) offer a faster and lightweight alternative that has rarely been explored. We study existing on-device ML and LI classifiers when applied to WNLOS, and propose novel hybrid ones exploiting their complementarity. We focus on chest-worn tags and analyze 21 classifiers on a dataset of 1.5 million samples across channels, PHY settings, environments, subjects, and orientations. Results show that while all of them achieve good classification accuracy, relative performance, including ranging errors due to misclassification, depends heavily on channel and PHY configuration. Runtime and energy efficiency also vary dramatically; some techniques offer marginal accuracy gains while consuming up to 39.6x more energy. Therefore, we also introduce a recommender tool to identify optimal classifiers under user-defined constraints, publicly released with our dataset.
authors: Markus Gallacher, Vu Anh Minh Le, Matteo Trobinger, Davide Vecchia, Carlo Alberto Boano, Gian Pietro Picco
bullets: Wearer-induced NLOS from the human body can substantially degrade UWB ranging but remains understudied.
The work evaluates machine-learning and lightweight radio link-indicator classifiers, and proposes hybrid methods combining both.
Performance—including ranging impact from misclassification—varies substantially across channels and PHY settings.
Energy costs differ sharply: some methods provide only marginal accuracy gains while using up to 39.6× more energy.
A recommender tool helps select classifiers under user-defined accuracy, runtime, and energy constraints; the dataset and tool are publicly released.

papers.abstract: Highway work zones are critical edge cases for autonomous vehicles (AVs), combining atypical geometries and jurisdiction-specific regulations that existing benchmarks fail to capture: real-world datasets lack 360{\deg} multi-modal, full-scene 3D work zone annotation, and no single recorded site can span the layouts and regulatory variants needed for generalizable models. We present WorkIng, a dual-domain benchmark and training resource. WorkIng-Highway provides a 360{\deg} multi-modal work zone benchmark with synchronized 128-channel LiDAR, six RGB cameras, and RTK-GPS across 32 km, yielding 12,000+ annotated frames and 227,399 tracked 3D bounding boxes. WorkIng-CARLA complements this with procedural simulation spanning 24 regulation-aware scenarios across six canonical topologies and six international traffic standards, populated by 100+ custom 3D assets. Benchmarking representative 3D detection and end-to-end planning architectures shows that real-world data remains the primary performance driver, and that scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves architectures across 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning. Resources: https://github.com/cvims/WorkIng
authors: Xujun Xie, Dominik R\"o{\ss}le, Adithya Mohan, Daniel Cremers, Torsten Sch\"on
bullets: WorkIng-Highway provides 360° multimodal sensing with LiDAR, six cameras, RTK-GPS, and extensive 3D annotations across 32 km.

Evaluations span 2D recognition, 3D detection, and trajectory planning architectures.
Results indicate real-world data is the main performance driver, while scenario-stratified synthetic augmentation improves performance across tasks.
The benchmark targets work-zone geometry and regulatory diversity missing from existing datasets.

papers.abstract: Achieving safe navigation in confined dynamic environments remains a challenging problem, as robots must balance navigation efficiency with safety. Existing actor--critic MPC architectures typically employ differentiable MPC layers, but this way cannot readily accommodate explicit state constraints, making it intractable to involve collision avoidance within learning-based planning. To address this issue, we propose an actor--critic model predictive control framework with state constraints. We first use vertices to represent the robot and obstacles, and half-spaces to represent the workspace. Based on these, the nonlinear robot dynamics is locally linearized and the hyperplane-based collision avoidance constraints are convexified into the differentiable MPC layer, and then the actor exploits closed-loop feedback to adjust the MPC objective parameters that shape local motion behavior, while the critic evaluates long-term task performance. We further relax the convexified constraints with bounded and penalized slack variables to form an elastic quadratic program, accommodating cases where the local constraint approximations cannot be satisfied simultaneously. Simulation tests and experiments, involving dynamic collision avoidance for multi-robot in narrow cases, illustrate the advantages of the proposed framework in adaptively adjusting the learned policy and improving navigation efficiency over existing approaches while maintaining the motion safety.
authors: Chaoran Wu, Jiayu Fan, Qichen Tan, Yuyi Liu, Jin Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of incorporating explicit collision-avoidance state constraints into differentiable actor–critic MPC.
Represents robots and obstacles with vertices and the workspace with half-spaces, then locally linearizes dynamics and convexifies collision constraints.
Uses an actor to adapt MPC objective parameters through closed-loop feedback and a critic to assess long-term task performance.
Introduces bounded, penalized slack variables in an elastic quadratic program for locally infeasible constraints.
Simulations and experiments on dynamic multi-robot collision avoidance in narrow spaces show improved navigation efficiency while maintaining safety over existing approaches.

papers.abstract: Robotic exploration can reduce human exposure to hazardous environments by autonomously searching unknown areas for objects of interest while constructing a complete, risk-aware map. However, existing autonomous exploration approaches typically prioritize geometric coverage or information gain, without explicitly coupling semantic object detection and the risk associated with operating near potentially hazardous objects. Moreover, many systems have been demonstrated primarily in simulation or controlled environments, leaving limited validation of risk-aware semantic exploration in complex, unstructured field settings. To address this gap, we propose SAFARI, a framework that treats object detection as a native channel of a unified probabilistic map, thereby jointly informing exploration and planning with both geometric and semantic evidence. We evaluated SAFARI in 11 missions across three field sites on a quadruped platform. The framework achieved an average coverage of 98.7% of the accessible mission area, without operator intervention for 97.6% of mission time, and detected objects with characteristic dimensions as small as 15cm. Lastly, through ablation studies and a detailed analysis of system behavior, we show that object-size awareness and safety-aware path planning are crucial for effective hazardous-object search.

papers.abstract: Motion planning in clutter is embodiment-specific: the feasible free space and reachable commands depend on each robot's geometry and dynamics. Existing cross-embodiment policies output normalized commands that disregard these differences, or compensate through per-robot training and distillation. World models can in principle pool cross-embodiment data, yet command-conditioned models bind their latent dynamics to a single action space, while pose-conditioned models omit the mapping from commands to body-specific motion. On flat ground, however, embodiment affects the planner's observations only through the camera ego-motion. This letter proposes Hourglass, an hourglass-shaped architecture that factorizes cross-embodiment motion planning at this interface: a body-agnostic world model and each robot's differentiable ego-dynamics, which map commands to that ego-motion, are coupled only through it. The world model is trained on data pooled across embodiments and camera mounts; each robot's ego-dynamics is a reduced-order template with identified physical parameters. A generalist parameter-conditioned policy is learned once at this junction: each imagined step rolls out the template and then the world model, and imagination training through each robot's template makes the policy body-aware. On seven simulated robots of five locomotion types, the generalist policy outperforms imitation-learning and diffusion-policy baselines on the same world model by 3.8--10.6 percentage points in success rate and matches per-robot specialists without dedicated training, while approaching its parameter-conditioned MPPI teacher within 1.4--2.8 points without an online map. After three minutes of teleoperated driving for identification, the synthetic-data-trained model transfers zero-shot to a real skid-steer robot unseen in training, navigating unseen indoor scenes.

papers.abstract: Centralized multi-agent path planning with cooperative localization in GPS-denied environments is generally computationally intractable when formulated in full belief space due to tightly coupled uncertainty dynamics. Prior work typically approximates belief dynamics or restricts inter-agent coupling. This work examines a multi-agent planning problem in which a primary agent must reach a goal in minimum time subject to a chance-constrained collision-avoidance requirement and a terminal bound on localization uncertainty. We obtain a tractable surrogate of the underlying belief-space problem by optimizing over the mean-state trajectories of all agents and propagating covariance for terminal constraint evaluation only. We propose CONSORT (Cooperative Navigation with Support-Optimized Routing and Trajectories), a discrete-to-continuous pipeline combining hexagonal-grid joint search with spline-based trajectory refinement. Across 50 randomized scenarios, the planners separate as the terminal uncertainty bound tightens, with CONSORT solving 80% of scenarios where the strongest baseline solves 54%, at comparable path length. In marine simulations, with the plans executed under feedback control on an independently developed factor-graph estimate, the trajectories remain collision-free and their terminal uncertainty falls within 6% of the planner's prediction.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems are increasingly deployed as heterogeneous fleets with diverse kinematic and actuation capabilities. While graph control barrier function (GCBF) methods provide a scalable framework for decentralized safe control, existing approaches typically assume homogeneous robot dynamics. Methods that directly encode robot classes can distinguish known types, but do not represent state-dependent motion capabilities or naturally transfer to unseen robot models. To address this challenge, we propose the Capability-Conditioned Heterogeneous Graph Control Barrier Function (CC-HGCBF), defined in a shared second-order reference-point operational space. This formulation provides a common geometric representation of safety across heterogeneous robots while retaining their model-specific dynamics and admissible control constraints. To enable zero-shot transfer, we introduce the Radial Capability Field (RCF), a compact, fixed-dimensional representation of each robot's state-dependent finite-horizon reachable velocity set. Conditioning the shared graph barrier and decentralized policy on the RCF enables them to adapt to changes in robot state, kinematic constraints, and control limits without relying on predefined robot identities. We jointly train the barrier and policy using proactive safety labeling and neural CBF-QP supervision, and evaluate them on mixed teams containing both seen and unseen robot models. Experiments demonstrate scalable safe coordination and zero-shot transfer to robot models and capability variations withheld during training. Physical-robot experiments further demonstrate zero-shot deployment to unseen kinematic models without retraining.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Janghyun Cho, Jeehyun Lee, Changjoo Nam, Yiwei Lyu

papers.abstract: Safe navigation in heterogeneous multi-robot teams faces two coupled challenges: differences in robots' braking and turning capabilities limit how each robot can respond to an approaching neighbor, while simultaneous interactions require a single control action to satisfy multiple collision-avoidance constraints. Together, these challenges can make local safety constraints incompatible with a robot's admissible controls, leaving a decentralized safety controller without a feasible action. We propose a Capability-Aware Backup-Recoverability Filter (CA-BRF), based on the insight that navigation actions should preserve access to a certified recovery maneuver. First, we construct a backup-recoverable set in a shared Cartesian operational space by evaluating whether prescribed backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until the robots come to rest. Each maneuver respects the corresponding robot's kinematic and actuation constraints, making the recovery certificate capability-dependent. Second, CA-BRF filters candidate controls by selecting admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions while coordinating the selection across simultaneous interactions. This preserves backup recoverability while retaining as much of the candidate action as possible and ensures that all pairwise recovery conditions are satisfied by a single executable control for each robot. Together, we establish recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed-loop system even when the nominal safety-constrained optimization becomes infeasible. The validity and effectiveness of the proposed CA-BRF are validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments of robots with five different kinematic classes.
authors: Joonkyung Kim, Yanze Zhang, Wenhao Luo, Yiwei Lyu
bullets: Addresses infeasibility caused by differing braking/turning capabilities and multiple concurrent collision-avoidance constraints.
Builds a shared-space backup-recoverable set by checking whether constrained backup maneuvers maintain pairwise safety until stopping.
Coordinates admissible interpolations between candidate and backup actions across simultaneous interactions.
Establishes recursive feasibility and safety for the discrete-time closed loop, including cases where nominal safety optimization is infeasible.
Validated in simulations with up to 30 heterogeneous robots and experiments spanning five kinematic classes.

papers.abstract: End-to-end policies, from task-specific controllers to robot foundation models, learn complex behavior from raw observations but are not guaranteed to remain safe, so they are often wrapped in a safety filter. The resulting system operates under two domains: the filter's operational design domain (ODD), where its assumptions hold and safety is certified, and the policy's competence domain, where it is reliable. Filters typically fix their conservativeness regardless of the policy's competence, trading performance inside the ODD against margin beyond it. We ask whether the policy's confidence should set that level, and propose a filter-agnostic pipeline that modulates it at runtime: inside the ODD, where every setting is safe, confidence buys performance; beyond it, low confidence adds margin, which helps when it flags where the filter's model fails. Preliminary F1TENTH simulations, where this holds, show the modulated filter combining the strengths of permissive and conservative filters.
bullets: Fixed-conservativeness filters trade performance inside their operational design domain (ODD) against safety margin outside it.
The proposed filter-agnostic pipeline uses policy confidence to modulate filtering at runtime.
High confidence permits better performance where filter assumptions are valid; low confidence adds margin beyond the ODD.
Preliminary F1TENTH simulations show the approach combines strengths of permissive and conservative filters.

papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share residential spaces with companion animals, yet navigation behavior is rarely designed with animal welfare in mind. This paper presents a pilot study evaluating a curve-out maneuver, a laterally arcing pass-by trajectory triggered at the dog's alert distance, proposed as a candidate welfare-informed navigation intervention grounded in canine social communication research and legible motion theory. Following a research through design approach, we developed and evaluated a first design iteration of the artifact in a naturalistic home environment with a companion dog. Contrary to our hypothesis, the curve-out produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline. We argue that discontinuous execution limitation, the robot stopping and reorienting multiple times to approximate the arc, undermined legibility, which in itself became a stressor. The pilot surfaces the legibility of robot behavior to non-humans' eyes and proxy stimulus validity as structural challenges for AMI and repositions the design problem for future work.
bullets: Autonomous delivery robots increasingly share spaces with companion animals, motivating welfare-informed navigation.
Researchers designed a laterally arcing pass-by maneuver triggered at the dog’s alert distance, based on canine communication and legible-motion theory.
In a naturalistic home evaluation with one companion dog, the maneuver produced a more acute stress response than the straight-line baseline.
Repeated stopping and reorienting made the maneuver discontinuous and potentially less legible, becoming a stressor itself.
The pilot reframes cross-species navigation around animal legibility and the validity of proxy stimuli.

papers.abstract: Teams that cannot communicate seem stuck with what each member sees. We show that their opponent can tell them the rest. Silent hunters, jammed robots and traders who never meet all face an adversary that reacts to the group as a whole; every member can read that reaction, a tell, and learn what no member knows alone. One tell can do the work of a message from every member. The adversary would rather hide, but hiding interferes with its own task, and a team that commits in advance to how it will respond decides how much hiding is worth. A committed team never loses when its opponent cares more about its own goals, and does as well as a fully informed team exactly when the opponent's stake outweighs any gain from lying. Below that point the team learns more by trusting less: in a solved Gaussian model it obtains the truth by promising not to use all of it and keeps the cost the opponent would have paid to conceal; an exact test decides when this holds in finite games. How a team spreads its trust matters too. A lone uninformed member with a full-support prior needs a private coin, but with additive squared-error losses two interchangeable members who respond differently replace it, and a small discount on trust insures against misjudging the enemy. Information, on this view, is not only gathered or aggregated; it is produced by how a team commits to respond.
bullets: An opponent’s group-level response can serve as a shared “tell,” revealing information unavailable to individual members.
Precommitting to response rules determines how much the opponent can hide and can prevent losses when the opponent prioritizes its own objectives.
In a solved Gaussian setting, deliberately limiting how much information the team uses can recover the truth while preserving the opponent’s concealment cost.
An exact test characterizes when this information-recovery result holds in finite games.
Trust allocation matters: private randomization, differentiated responses, or a small trust discount can protect against deception.

papers.tldr: A noncommunicating team can learn hidden information from how an opponent reacts to its precommitted decisions.

papers.abstract: Giving embodied agents the freedom to act autonomously, initiate interactions, and understand their surroundings through experience is a step toward bringing them to life in the physical world. Realizing this vision requires action, interaction, and memory to work together, so that each encounter can inform current decisions and contribute experience for future tasks. We present EvoLife, a unified navigation harness that enables a multimodal embodied agent to choose how to move, when to ask, and what experience to carry forward. Its hybrid action space supports waypoint navigation, local discrete adjustments, pixel-based navigation, and object-directed navigation. Active interaction allows the agent to seek clarification or assistance when it encounters ambiguity or difficulty, while persistent spatial memory binds observations and dialogue to places, retaining useful experience to guide subsequent visits. We evaluate eight benchmarks across four task families: vision-language navigation, object navigation, interactive instance navigation, and continuous multi-task navigation. With an average of only 1.87 active interactions per episode, our method achieves a first-visit success rate (SR) of 100% across four 100-episode sets spanning vision-language navigation and object navigation. Complete-sequence SR reaches 98% on 50 LHPR-VLN sequences and 94% on 50 GOAT-Bench sequences. In the R2R revisit setting, success weighted by path length (SPL) increases from 82.23% to 93.31% with retained experience. Multi-day physical navigation further demonstrates exploration, proactive help-seeking, and revisiting remembered places. Together, these results advance the vision of bringing embodied agents to life through autonomous action, proactive interaction, and the accumulation and reuse of experience.

papers.abstract: Object goal navigation requires an embodied agent to locate and reach target objects in complex environments. Humans often rely on low-cost yet informative schematic maps, such as rough sketches or directional annotations. We develop a workflow for schematic-guided embodied navigation with two components: a training-data generation pipeline and ScheNav, a closed-loop navigation framework. Our lightweight data-generation pipeline turns 2D floorplans into navigation training environments, yielding Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with paired navigation episodes and noise-controllable schematic maps. ScheNav turns rough schematic guidance into exploration and stopping decisions by using SchemaField, a learned spatial module that fuses the guidance with accumulated observations and predicts spatial value fields. The framework updates these fields as exploration proceeds, with trajectory-based training and a cross-frame consistency objective supporting coherent guidance across changing viewpoints. ScheNav learns to use schematic guidance entirely from simulated floorplans and transfers this ability to unseen embodied environments. Experiments show improved navigation success and path efficiency across schematic maps, goal ellipses, and pointed directions, together with tolerance to the tested schematic perturbations and omissions. Together, these results demonstrate that rough schematic guidance offers a practical way to improve embodied navigation.
bullets: Addresses object-goal navigation in complex environments using low-cost schematic maps such as sketches, goal ellipses, and directional pointers.
Introduces Furnished-RPLAN, a dataset of over 33k furnished layouts with navigation episodes and controllable schematic-map noise.
Uses SchemaField to fuse schematic guidance with accumulated visual observations and predict spatial value fields for exploration and stopping.
Trains with trajectory-based learning and cross-frame consistency to maintain coherent guidance across viewpoints.
Experiments report improved navigation success and path efficiency, with tolerance to tested schematic perturbations and omissions.

figures.caption: Figure 2. The ScheNav framework. Schematic guidance at any level, a schematic map, ellipses, a pointed direction, or none, is encoded by SchemaField, the only learned component our framework introduces: a schematic-fusion transformer fuses the guidance with the observed map from the map memory, and a distance decoder and a corridor decoder predict the two value fields from the fused embedding in a single forward pass. Two rule-based components read the fields. The Goal Verification module compares the distance-field value at goal instances detected in the map memory against a threshold τstop, and the decision transformation scores frontier candidates with the corridor field and gates stopping, emitting a waypoint or a stop. Map memory, frontier extraction, and execution are supplied by the host navigation system, and each new observation closes the loop.

Figure 3. Furnished-RPLAN construction pipeline. Starting from an RPLAN vector floorplan, a vision-language pipeline proposes and extracts a machine-readable furniture layout. The resulting furnished environment is used to generate navigation episodes, paired schematic guidance, and the local observations consumed by ScheNav.

Figure 1. Overview of schematic-guided navigation. A human provides imperfect schematic guidance, such as a rough sketch or a pointed direction. ScheNav grounds the guidance in the agent’s observations and predicts a value field that rises toward the goal. Guided by the predicted field, the agent reaches the goal along an efficient route in an environment it has barely explored.

Figure 4. Closed-loop trajectories on one episode under decreasing guidance. The five panels show our four input conditions and unmodified UniGoal on the same episode, rendered on a textured top-down view of the scene. The dashed inset in each panel shows the schematic input the agent receives, and is blank for the no-guidance condition and the baseline; in the direction panel the floorplan behind the arrow is drawn only for illustration, and the model receives the direction vector alone. Orange curves trace the agent from start to stop, a green check marks a successful stop, and the red cross marks a failed stop. The path lengthens gracefully as guidance weakens, from the schematic map through the ellipse and direction conditions to no guidance at all, while the host stops incorrectly after prolonged, tangled exploration.

papers.abstract: Vehicle-infrastructure cooperation can complement onboard sensing with broader and more informative observations of the traffic environment, providing valuable support for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing cooperative driving methods mainly exploit roadside information to enhance the representation of the current scene, while the future consequences of prospective driving actions are rarely modeled explicitly. This limits the ability of the planner to anticipate how its decisions may interact with the evolving traffic environment. To address this issue, we propose V2X-WAM, a cooperative world action model that tightly couples cooperative scene understanding, action generation, and future-world reasoning. V2X-WAM constructs a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle- and infrastructure-side observations, while compressing infrastructure information into a compact quantized message for efficient communication. Based on the resulting cooperative representation, a multimodal planner generates prospective trajectories, which explicitly condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow prediction. The predicted world consequences are then fed back to refine the planned trajectory, forming a closed interaction between action and future-world evolution. Experiments on a large-scale real-world cooperative driving dataset demonstrate that V2X-WAM consistently improves planning accuracy and safety over representative end-to-end cooperative driving methods, while achieving stronger future-world prediction and substantially lower communication overhead. Ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed design.
bullets: Addresses the limitation that existing V2X methods mainly represent the current scene without explicitly modeling action consequences.
Builds a reliability-aware spatiotemporal representation from vehicle and infrastructure observations, with infrastructure data compressed into a quantized message.
Uses a multimodal planner whose candidate trajectories condition future occupancy and dynamic-flow predictions.
Feeds predicted future-world consequences back into trajectory planning, creating a closed action–world interaction loop.
Experiments show improved planning accuracy and safety, stronger future-world prediction, and substantially lower communication overhead; ablations support the design.

papers.abstract: We study a constrained sequential decision problem for detecting regions of interest from noisy online measurements collected by a team of energy-constrained mobile sensors. The sensor motion is restricted to a precomputed set of feasible paths that satisfy mobility constraints, limited available energy by requiring return to charging stations, and avoidance of known obstacles. We cast the resulting active path selection as a multi-armed bandit problem and propose an iterative search algorithm that adaptively assigns paths using confidence bounds computed from the collected data. We also propose a graph-based method to construct low-cardinality path covers under the team's constraints. We establish finite-time and anytime probabilistic correctness guarantees for the proposed algorithm, derive non-asymptotic upper bounds on the times required to detect all regions of interest and to label all nodes, and show that these bounds match algorithm-independent lower bounds up to constant factors for a broad class of problem instances. Using numerical simulations, we illustrate the behavior of the proposed approach and the effect of path redundancy and team size on search performance.
bullets: Models constrained path selection from noisy online measurements as a multi-armed bandit problem.
Uses confidence-bound updates to adaptively assign feasible sensor paths.
Constructs low-cardinality path covers while respecting mobility, energy, charging, and obstacle constraints.
Provides finite-time and anytime correctness guarantees plus non-asymptotic detection and labeling bounds.
Simulations examine how path redundancy and team size affect search performance.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has predominantly relied on open-loop imitation learning for training, which presents two limitations. First, expert demonstrations show only one behavior per scenario, so the model cannot learn alternative valid behaviors and, in turn, cannot adapt to user-specified preferences at test time. Second, noise or ambiguity in these demonstrations can produce inconsistent, unreliable supervision for the end-to-end models. Driving is inherently multi-modal: multiple different behaviors can be valid responses to the same scene, and this diversity arises largely from speed rather than path. We introduce a planning paradigm that learns the path through imitation while scoring a set of candidate speeds across multiple criteria with a learned function supervised by physically grounded safety constraints. We realize this paradigm as Closed-Loop Aware Planning for Autonomous Driving (CLAP-AD), a plug-in planning head that integrates with existing end-to-end driving models and, to our knowledge, is the first to enable explicit test-time control over their speed selection without speed-conditioned training. On Bench2Drive-Speed, CLAP-AD sets a new state of the art Speed-Adherence Score of 82.53, topping TFv6, the strongest baseline on this metric, by 12.9 points while retaining strong closed-loop driving performance. On Bench2Drive, it improves driving score by +28.5 and +32.7 over UniAD and VAD, and on NAVSIM v2, built on real-world driving data, EPDMS by +6.1 over its backbone. Project page: https://clap-ad.github.io
bullets: Addresses limited behavioral diversity and noisy supervision in open-loop imitation learning.
Learns paths through imitation while scoring candidate speeds using multiple criteria and physically grounded safety constraints.
Works as a plug-in planning head for existing end-to-end driving models without speed-conditioned training.
Achieves state-of-the-art speed adherence on Bench2Drive-Speed and improves driving performance on Bench2Drive and NAVSIM v2.
Scope: the approach focuses on behavioral multimodality arising primarily from speed rather than path.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the CLAP-AD planning head. The architecture consists of an Ego-Path block that takes ego detection and motion queries as input and predicts a feasible driving path. The Collision block encodes surrounding agents’ detection and motion queries, fuses them with the predicted path representation, and uses learned collision queries to produce collision scores. Similarly, the Traffic Light and Stop Sign blocks employ dedicated queries that attend to their respective detection features together with the path embedding to generate their speed scores.

Figure 5. Driving Score versus Comfort on the 220 Bench2Drive routes. Comfort falls as Driving Score rises; the dashed line is a least-squares fit over the methods shown. This is not evidence that competent driving is uncomfortable: every quantity the metric monitors is an amplitude of motion, so policies that stall or creep satisfy all of them trivially.

Figure 1. CLAP-AD improves speed-adherence across three different end-to-end driving models. (a) CLAP-AD consistently improves Speed-Adherence across all three backbones; only on TFv6 does this cost a small amount of Driving Score. (b) An example of how CLAPAD respects the user’s requested target speed.
Figure 4. Front camera images of different driving scenarios with predicted speed scores. Collision, traffic light, and stop sign branches individually predict scores for every speed class.

Figure 3. Speed-profile variability across two experts on a repeated HardBrake scenario. Lines show the mean speed over three re-runs of the same route; shaded bands show ±1 standard deviation. PDM-Lite and Think2Drive brake at markedly different points along the route, showing that even expert-level speed behavior is inherently multi-modal. Within each expert, PDM-Lite (rule-based) reproduces an identical profile across all three runs (avg. std = 0.00 m/s), while Think2Drive (RL-based) diverges substantially between runs (avg. std = 3.02 m/s).

papers.abstract: Autonomous micro-mobility vehicles (MMVs) such as wheelchairs, scooters, and bicycles have the potential to improve mobility access and support safe low-speed transportation in pedestrian-shared spaces. Achieving MMV autonomy will require realistic, predictable MMV motion. However, many existing autonomous vehicle stacks rely on simplified kinematic models that fail to capture key MMV characteristics such as tire slip, friction, and wheel layouts, limiting realism and gradient-based optimization. In this paper, we explore differentiable formulations of dynamics models for autonomous micro-mobility systems. We first construct DiffKBM, a differentiable version of the kinematic bicycle model (KBM). Then, we introduce DiffGM3, a differentiable formulation of the General Micro-Mobility Model (GM3), a unified tire-based dynamics formulation for micro-mobility vehicles that supports a wide range of MMV configurations. DiffKBM and DiffGM3 enable end-to-end differentiable optimization through MMV dynamics, making them suitable for integration into differentiable autonomy stacks. We evaluate these dynamics models in both open-loop and closed-loop settings: (1) open-loop trajectory matching, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are integrated as a dynamics layer within DiffStack and optimized to reproduce real-world MMV trajectories, and (2) closed-loop autonomous navigation, where DiffKBM and DiffGM3 are paired with a differentiable MPC controller in CrowdNav pedestrian scenarios. In the open-loop setting, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in reproducing trajectories with improvements in ADE and NLL across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle modes, and reductions in planning loss for bicycle and motorcycle trajectories. We also find that, in closed-loop settings, DiffGM3 improves on DiffKBM's CrowdNav performance by producing 55\% fewer collisions and a 75\% lower discomfort frequency for the bicycle mode.
bullets: Targets limitations of simplified vehicle models that omit tire slip, friction, and diverse wheel layouts.
Constructs DiffKBM, a differentiable kinematic bicycle model, and DiffGM3, a differentiable general micro-mobility dynamics model.
Evaluates both models in open-loop trajectory matching and closed-loop navigation with differentiable MPC in pedestrian scenarios.
DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM across bicycle, scooter, and motorcycle trajectory evaluations.
For bicycle navigation, DiffGM3 yields 55% fewer collisions and 75% lower discomfort frequency than DiffKBM.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Overview of the DiffMPC pipeline integrated with DiffKBM or DiffGM3. At each timestep, the environment provides a state estimate xt , which is passed to the optimizer with the goal position and surrounding pedestrian states pedst . The optimizer proposes a control sequence u0:T−1 and uses either DiffKBM or DiffGM3 parameterized by learnable parameters ρKBM or ρGM3 to roll out predicted future states x0:T . A cost function is defined with learnable cost weights ρC. Because both the dynamics and the cost function are differentiable, gradients can be back-propagated through the prediction and cost modules to enable end-to-end learning of MMV dynamics parameters. The first control action u0 is applied to the environment, and the process repeats in a receding-horizon loop.

Fig. 2: DiffGM3 contains several differentiable components with sets of learnable parameters ρlean,ρtire, and ρVI. First, the steering control input δ is converted into tire-specific steering angles δi. This, along with the MMV’s previous longitudinal velocity vx, lateral velocity vy, and yaw rate r, is used to calculate tire velocities. Meanwhile, longitudinal and lateral accelerations, ax and ay, are used to transfer load among the tires, and the previous lean angle γ and roll rate γ̇ are used to determine the next lean angle. In addition to wheel angular velocity Ω, the results from these modules are inputs to the tire brush model, where forces and moments are computed. The outputs for each tire are integrated into the vehicle dynamics to obtain longitudinal, lateral, and yaw acceleration. Finally, the resulting position is calculated with Euler integration. This fully differentiable formulation allows gradients to backpropagate to each module so parameters can be tuned on MMV trajectory data.

Fig. 5: Closed-loop Navigation in Pedestrian Crowds Comparison between DiffGM3 Bicycle and DiffKBM: We show two unique scenarios each for DiffGM3 and DiffKBM. Longer pedestrian paths reflect the longer navigation time taken by the MMV to avoid moving pedestrians to reach its goal. Scenario 1: DiffGM3’s route reflects its ability to use real-world kinematics to avoid pedestrians when necessary, while DiffKBM’s simple kinematics forces it to attempt to fit right in between two pedestrians, resulting in a collision. Scenario 2: While both models reach the goal, DiffGM3’s longer route demonstrates less discomfort and higher minimum distance from pedestrians relative to DiffKBM’s direct route.

Fig. 3: Open-loop Trajectory Matching Comparison between the DiffKBM and DiffGM3: (a) On bicycle trajectories, DiffGM3 is able to stay on path because it has learnable parameters to prevent overturning. However, in some cases, it stops before the goal as shown by the red arrow, leading to a higher goal cost in the planning loss function. (b) On the other hand, the DiffKBM reaches its goal but veers off the ground-truth straight path, as indicated by the red arrow. This is due to the DiffKBM’s lack of support for realignment in its formula for yaw. (c) For a scooter, DiffGM3 is able to steer the scooter to its goal while avoiding other agents. (d) On the same trajectory, the DiffKBM causes the ego agent to turn towards another agent and slow down, preventing it from reaching its goal.

Fig. 1: DiffKBM implements wheelbase L as a learnable parameter in the steering component. The resulting turning rate θ̇ along with velocity are used in Euler integration to obtain the position. By making KBM end-to-end differentiable, we are able to tune L for an MMV with unknown wheelbase length.

TABLE V: Closed-loop Pedestrian Crowd Navigation Performance Comparison between DiffGM3 and DiffKBM: DiffGM3 prioritizes safety and demonstrates significantly fewer collisions across all vehicle configurations relative to DiffKBM. Specifically, in the baseline comparison between the two bicycle models, DiffGM3 produces 55% fewer collisions, with a 3% better success rate. DiffGM3’s incomplete rate and slower navigation time can be explained by its tendency to avoid collisions by veering away from the goal, resulting in situations where the vehicle is unable to arrive at the goal within the time limit. This also explains why DiffGM3’s discomfort frequency is 50%-75% better than DiffKBM’s across all modes. Moreover, DiffKBM’s faster navigation times are primarily the result of collisions ending the scenario early.

TABLE IV: Open-loop Trajectory Matching Evaluation Results: DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM in ADE (Bicycle: - 1.16%, Scooter -9.84%, Motorcycle: -2.37%) and NLL (Bicycle: -3.02%, Scooter -2.05%, Motorcycle: -4.75%) on all modes. For planning loss, DiffGM3 outperforms DiffKBM on bicycle (-4.16%) and motorcycle (-28.9%) trajectories, but performs worse on scooters (19.39%).

TABLE III: DiffGM3 parameters optimized using IMPTC trajectories. Align gain kalign and damping coefficients dyaw,droll help to stabilize the MMV and reduce oversteering. Moments of inertia Iz, Ix, and tire parameters are tuned because they are not easily measurable.

papers.abstract: Autonomous highway driving for heavy-duty trucks is a challenging control problem. The greater mass, dimensions and intricate dynamics increase the requirements for cooperation from surrounding traffic in critical maneuvers, requiring a careful balance between safety constraints and efficient long-horizon decision making. Model Predictive Control (MPC) provides rigorous constraint satisfaction but relies on terminal cost which can limit its effectiveness at short, computationally affordable horizons. Reinforcement Learning (RL) captures long-term driving behavior but offers no constraint guarantees and tends toward overly conservative policies when trained under sparse collision penalties. In this paper, we propose a hybrid MPC and RL framework for highway driving in autonomous trucks, where a finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, uses a pre-trained RL model for terminal cost estimation. We evaluate the framework in a simulation environment with reactive surrounding traffic and compare it against pure MPC with zero terminal cost, rollout with terminal cost estimation using a base policy, and pure RL. Results show that the hybrid approach achieves zero collisions with the lowest cost of any configuration.
authors: Hooman Hamze, Benjamin Houshmand, Deepthi Pathare, Erik B\"orve, Morteza Haghir Chehreghani, Nikolce Murgovski
bullets: Targets the challenge of balancing safety constraints with efficient long-horizon decisions for heavy-duty trucks.
Combines finite-horizon MPC, solved via dynamic programming, with a pre-trained RL model that estimates terminal costs.
Evaluated in simulation with reactive surrounding traffic against zero-terminal-cost MPC, base-policy rollouts, and pure RL.
The hybrid approach achieved zero collisions and the lowest cost among the evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: Monocular RGB tracking is useful for robots operating near people, but perception errors affect binary stop/proceed decisions in ways that geometric accuracy metrics do not capture. We examine how much decision error arises from the safety rule versus perception. We prove that lateral-only distance is a lower bound on planar distance: with accurate positions, it cannot miss dangers identified by the planar rule, but it produces unnecessary stops. We introduce a two-factor Shapley attribution separating rule and perception contributions, and further distinguish missed detections from localization errors. Experiments use ETH and UCY pedestrian videos with simulated stationary robots, disjoint calibration and evaluation pedestrians, and time-block bootstrap intervals. Across 898 pedestrians in three scenes, the lateral rule missed no dangers on annotated positions but achieved only 5.6-31.9% stop precision. In two scenes with RGB perception, calibrated ground-plane localization achieved 0.59 m and 0.51 m planar RMSE, compared with 1.72 m and 1.39 m for a geometric baseline and 0.81 m and 0.68 m for calibrated Depth Anything V2. Detection recall of 0.43 and 0.26 made missed detections the leading source of missed danger. A two-standard-deviation safety margin with ground-plane localization matched or improved on the lateral rule's missed-danger rate in all eight scene-threshold settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven. All robot interactions are simulated, and outcomes are offline decision classifications, not demonstrations of collision avoidance.
bullets: Lateral-only distance is a conservative lower bound on planar distance: it missed no dangers with accurate positions but caused many unnecessary stops.
A two-factor Shapley framework attributes decision errors to the safety rule versus perception, separating missed detections from localization errors.
Ground-plane localization outperformed the geometric baseline and calibrated Depth Anything V2 in the reported scenes.
Low detection recall was the leading contributor to missed dangers in RGB-perception experiments.
A two-standard-deviation safety margin matched or improved missed-danger rates in all tested settings and reduced unnecessary stops in seven of eight.

papers.abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning remains challenging in stochastic long-horizon settings, where compounding value estimation errors hinder reliable goal reaching. While prior methods have sought to address this challenge through various approaches, a key challenge remains path mirage, where agents overcommit to spuriously successful trajectories in offline datasets induced by stochasticity, often leading to failure on difficult tasks. To address this issue, we propose Branch-aware Graph Planning (BGP), which captures stochastic branching structures by identifying high-variability points as graph nodes and designing goal-conditioned edges with segmented learning to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity along paths. As a result, BGP enables reliable goal reaching even in highly stochastic long-horizon environments, and experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show that it substantially outperforms prior state-of-the-art offline goal-conditioned RL methods. Our implementation is available at https://umlic.github.io/papers/BGP/.
authors: Junhyeon Bae, Jaebak Hwang, Gwanwoo Choi, Minung Kim, Seungyul Han
bullets: Targets path mirages: spurious successes in offline data that cause agents to commit to unreliable routes.
Represents high-variability points as nodes in a branching graph.
Learns goal-conditioned graph edges with segmentation to avoid unreliable branches and reduce unnecessary stochasticity.
Experiments on diverse OGBench tasks show reliable goal reaching and substantial improvements over prior methods.
Scope: designed for stochastic, long-horizon offline goal-conditioned environments.

papers.abstract: Efficient crowd navigation requires anticipating dynamic collision-free space without relying on fragile object tracking. We propose the Don't Risk It Planner (DRIP), an end-to-end LiDAR-only planning framework that couples occupancy forecasting with trajectory-conditioned clearance and uncertainty estimation. Operating directly on LiDAR-derived occupancy grid histories, DRIP predicts a distribution over minimum robot-obstacle clearance for candidate control sequences to evaluate collision risk. The model is trained using a risk cost that grounds predictive uncertainty directly in empirical collision outcomes rather than geometric regression alone. In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, DRIP achieves higher success rates with fewer collisions and reduced freezing behavior compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Mathai Mathew Pulicken, Laksh Nanwani, Basant Sharma, Phani Teja Singamaneni, Arun Kumar Singh, K. Madhava Krishna
bullets: Addresses safe, efficient navigation in dynamic crowds without relying on fragile object tracking.
Uses LiDAR-derived occupancy-grid histories to forecast occupancy and estimate clearance and uncertainty for candidate control sequences.
Trains risk predictions against empirical collision outcomes, rather than geometric clearance regression alone.
In closed-loop experiments with up to 45 pedestrians, it improves success rates while reducing collisions and freezing versus state-of-the-art baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of DRIP’s LiDAR-only prediction and trajectory-conditioned risk architecture. A history H of pose-warped BEV occupancy maps is encoded independently by a shared-weight spatial CNN, conditioned on ego velocity V through FiLM. Spatiotemporal Transformer blocks then reason over the temporal history and spatial BEV tokens to produce a shared scene representation zscene. Two branches use this representation: the occupancy decoder predicts the future evolution of the scene (Ôk) over a 20-step horizon, while the trajectory-conditioned Distance Head combines scene features with candidate trajectory queries qk to predict a stepwise clearance distribution (µk, σ 2 k) and a trajectory-specific kernel width λ. These predictions are subsequently used to compute the distributional MMD2 risk r̂θ(u) for each candidate trajectory u.

Fig. 3: Box plot of best-of-K clearance residuals relative to privileged ground truth across dynamic evaluation episodes. The risk-calibrated model ((18)) yields a lower median error and narrower spread than the NLL-only baseline without Lrisk , Lhaz), demonstrating well-calibrated predictive variance that tightly bounds actual obstacle encounters.

papers.abstract: Humanoids have become increasingly agile and capable in real-world environments. To operate safely in dynamic scenarios, they must rapidly evade fast-moving obstacles while maintaining stability and physically feasible whole-body motion. Learning such behaviors remains challenging due to the high-dimensional dynamics of humanoid systems and the need to jointly balance reactive obstacle avoidance, motion naturalness, and control robustness. In this work, we present Humanoid Dodgeball, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework for agile dynamic obstacle avoidance in humanoids. Our method enables highly dynamic whole-body evasive maneuvers against incoming projectiles through threat-aware reward shaping, while multiple direction-specific adversarial motion priors regularize the learned behaviors toward stable and diverse human-like motions. Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves dynamic obstacle avoidance performance across diverse obstacle speeds and launch distances, while preserving robust and physically plausible humanoid motions.
authors: Aoqian Zhang, Chunzheng Wang, Haoran Chen, Annan Tang, Cheng Xiang, Fan Shi, Shuzhi Sam Ge
bullets: Targets dynamic obstacle avoidance while preserving balance, physical feasibility, and natural motion.
Uses threat-aware reward shaping to encourage agile evasive responses.
Employs direction-specific adversarial motion priors to regularize behavior toward diverse, stable human-like motions.
Simulation and hardware experiments show improved avoidance across varied obstacle speeds and launch distances.
The abstract focuses on projectile evasion and does not specify broader obstacle types or quantitative results.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of Humanoid Dodgeball. During simulation training, predictive and near-field threat for key bodies are computed to characterize incoming projectile hazards and guide threat-aware reward shaping for whole-body evasion. Direction-specific adversarial motion priors, selected according to the root escape direction, regularize the learned behaviors toward diverse and natural human-like dodge motions. When the threat subsides, recovery rewards, including orientation and capture-point objectives, encourage rapid stabilization. During hardware deployment, the trained actor is executed using obstacle positions estimated from the motion-capture system.

(b) A projectile directed toward the head is avoided through a coordinated forward step and ducking motion. (c) A ball aimed at the right shoulder is avoided by stepping laterally to the left. (d) A projectile targeting the head is avoided through a rightward step combined with a ducking maneuver. These examples demonstrate that the learned policy produces diverse whole-body evasive strategies in response to different obstacle trajectories and incoming directions.

papers.abstract: Pretrained generative models, such as diffusion and flow matching models, have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in synthesizing high-quality data. However, steering their generative trajectories to satisfy strict constraints--such as identity preservation in image editing or obstacle avoidance in robotics--remains fundamentally challenging. While recent training-free guidance methods enforce path-safety, they rely heavily on min-norm controllers that only account for immediate constraint satisfaction. These myopic approaches often yield suboptimal trajectories that hover dangerously close to the boundary, severely restricting the model's ability to optimize toward its target. In this paper, we propose AegisFlow, a training-free, non-myopic path-safe guidance framework that recasts guided generation as a safety-critical optimal control problem with global scope. By integrating a time-varying barrier function directly into the global cost functional, AegisFlow naturally enforces constraints along the entire generative path. To compute the global optimal control, we derive a tractable, mathematically grounded approximation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that AegisFlow outperforms state-of-the-art methods across text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning, establishing a significantly better trade-off between target alignment and constraint satisfaction. Code is available at https://github.com/LiuKunpeng03/AegisFlow.
authors: Kunpeng Liu, Boshi Zhang, Keyou You
bullets: Addresses the myopic behavior of existing path-safe guidance methods, which may stay near constraint boundaries and limit target optimization.
Recasts guided generation as a globally scoped safety-critical optimal control problem.
Integrates a time-varying barrier function into the global cost to enforce safety throughout the full generative path.
Uses a tractable approximation to the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation to compute global guidance.
Experiments on text-guided image manipulation and robotic planning show improved target-alignment/safety trade-offs over prior methods.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots commonly pair a global planner with a local model predictive controller (MPC), but nonconvex obstacle avoidance and a limited horizon can make the robot freeze in complex layouts. Deciding whether to replan, wait, or call for help is a supervisory decision. Recent work queries a large language model (LLM) supervisor on every anomaly, which is slow and costly. We instead distill the LLM online into a decision tree. After each training episode, counterfactual replay labels recoveries as needed, unnecessary, or harmful. These labels retire unhelpful rules. In simulation, on 20 unseen layouts where the MPC alone freezes, the tree handles at least 18 correctly across all seeds, either by reaching the goal or by calling for help when no feasible path exists. The tree matches both an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules, while issuing no LLM queries at test time. Handwritten rules cannot anticipate the long tail of situations a physical robot will encounter. Online distillation is a promising remedy: the tree handles familiar cases, and the LLM is consulted only for new ones, whose validated recoveries become new rules. Language models can thus also serve as designers of supervisors rather than only as runtime supervisors.
bullets: Targets MPC failures where limited horizons and nonconvex obstacles cause autonomous robots to freeze.
After each episode, counterfactual replay labels recovery actions as needed, unnecessary, or harmful, pruning ineffective rules.
In simulation across 20 unseen freezing layouts, the tree handled at least 18 correctly across all seeds.
It matched an always-query LLM supervisor and expert-designed rules while making no test-time LLM queries.
The proposed scope is hybrid operation: use the tree for familiar cases and consult the LLM only for novel situations.

papers.title: Teaching a Tree to Recover: Online Distillation of an LLM Supervisor with Counterfactual Replay
papers.tldr: An online-trained decision tree distills an LLM supervisor into reusable recovery rules, handling complex robot-navigation failures without querying the LLM at test time.

papers.abstract: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.
authors: Maonan Wang, Yuxin Cai, Junming Liu, Zhengyan Huang, Yi Yu, Ding Wang, Yifeng Zhang, Yirong Chen
bullets: Addresses the dependence of existing visual traffic signal controllers on fixed cameras and specific intersection layouts.
Maps visual features to lanes, movements, and phases, then uses a shared policy to rank candidate signal phases across layouts and plans.
Trains with over 5K human control decisions, simulator traffic-state supervision, and appearance-diverse trajectory re-rendering.
Closed-loop tests show 7–9% lower average waiting time than visual baselines and the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios.

papers.abstract: Legged robots have demonstrated advanced capabilities across a wide range of real-world tasks, yet much of this progress concerns the robot controlling only itself. Once the robot is coupled to an external object -- particularly an underactuated one -- the dynamics of the combined assembly become more complex. Towing a wagon is a common practical scenario, where coupled dynamics make reliable navigation challenging. This difficulty is amplified in confined spaces, where collision-free navigation requires finding a narrow set of feasible paths under strict real-time constraints. To address this, we propose a navigation framework that combines Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control over a learned Forward Dynamics Model (FDM). The CFM model mitigates the initialization problem of MPPI and accelerates its convergence, while MPPI with the FDM recovers feasible solutions beyond the CFM model's training distribution by iterative refinement. We integrate the framework into a full-stack navigation system for RAIBO-Wagon, a quadruped towing a custom wagon, and validate it in real-world outdoor experiments on 15 m-long courses through confined spaces, with all sensing and computation performed fully onboard. The system achieves an 85% success rate across 40 trials, towing a total load of up to 40 kg -- nearly 100% of RAIBO's body weight.
authors: Insung Yang, Eunchae Kim, Jungwoo Hur, Seunghun Jeon, Donghyuk Choi, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Addresses the coupled, underactuated dynamics and narrow feasible paths that make wagon towing difficult for legged robots.
Combines Conditional Flow Matching for efficient trajectory initialization with MPPI control using a learned Forward Dynamics Model.
MPPI iteratively refines solutions and can recover feasible behavior beyond the flow model’s training distribution.
Validated fully onboard on 15 m outdoor courses through confined spaces, achieving an 85% success rate over 40 trials.
Towed loads up to 40 kg, approximately the robot’s body weight.
