papers.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
authors: Peitong Duan, Khashayar Gatmiry, Jeffrey Nichols, Samy Bengio, Emmanuel Abbe
bullets: Addresses brittle trajectory memorization and high inference costs in UI navigation.
Decouples navigation into a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model.
Uses LLM-based dense step rewards plus terminal task-completion rewards, optimized with PPO and step-level advantages.
Introduces GiGPPO, which stabilizes value estimation using rewards from visually similar states in concurrent trajectories.

Evaluations across UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld show stronger performance than SFT and terminal-only RL baselines, including nearly sevenfold OOD improvement for 8B agents on Android and competitive results on real iOS apps.

Because the Apple Maps workflow requires selecting the destination before the starting location, the agents are easily confused by the task prompt’s phrasing, which mentions the starting point first. The GiGPPO agent initially sets the destination as Apple Park, but it corrects itself by exiting the directions search and restarting with the Santa Clara Caltrain Station as the destination, demonstrating strong error recovery. papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) sensing enables robot ego-motion estimation in darkness, smoke, and fog, yet RF odometry remains challenging because multipath and moving reflectors make cross-frame matching highly ambiguous. Existing methods often rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision. We present RFWalk, a self-supervised, RF-only odometry framework that models dense correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph and learns them from unlabeled sequences through temporal cycle consistency. To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.
authors: Kunzhe Song, Jialuo Du, Jingkai Lin, Huacheng Zeng
bullets: Addresses ambiguous RF frame matching caused by multipath and moving reflectors.
Models dense range-azimuth correspondences as random walks on a space-time graph.
Uses temporal cycle consistency and a Doppler consistency loss without pose labels or auxiliary sensors.

Remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic pedestrian scenes.

papers.abstract: Anticipating the motion of nearby objects is critical for safe and efficient robot navigation. Without a proper understanding of what may move, a robot may plan overly conservative, inefficient trajectories to guarantee safety, or it may be overly risky, resulting in unacceptable collisions. While tracking and predicting the motion of known objects has seen significant progress, little research addresses how a robot should adapt online to novel objects, including anticipating how one object may move another (e.g., a person operating a forklift to move a pallet). To enable this capability, we propose a meta-learned graph neural network that leverages a semantic, geometric, and relational history of objects to accurately predict, from a few online observations, when objects will begin to move in new environments. We demonstrate that our method, which is trained only in simulation, accurately anticipates the motion of objects unseen at training time, transfers to hardware without any fine-tuning, and outperforms a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline in both simulation and hardware experiments. Our method's accurate prediction enables collision-free traversals in a closed-loop navigation simulation, while remaining within four seconds of the fastest, collision-prone planner.
authors: Mason Peterson, Gage MacLin, Camilla Tabasso, Jonathan P. How, Joshua Migdal, Tye Brady, Taskin Padir

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe quadrotor flight in unknown environments, yet conventional frame-based cameras remain challenged by motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency under fast motion. Event cameras, with sub-millisecond latency, high dynamic range, and negligible motion blur, offer a promising alternative, but leveraging them for closed-loop control remains difficult. Existing approaches either adopt cascaded architectures that first estimate depth and then map it to control commands, introducing error propagation, or achieve end-to-end control through costly offline pretraining before online fine-tuning can even begin. We address these challenges with a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to render events efficiently within the training loop, integrated into a differentiable simulation pipeline that enables direct gradient backpropagation through the differentiable physics model, improving sample efficiency. This allows us to train an end-to-end policy that maps event frames directly to control commands, without intermediate depth estimation. We validate our approach through zero-shot real-world deployment on a quadrotor, achieving robust obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including under low-light conditions where conventional cameras typically fail.
authors: Chenlu Shou, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency in frame-based obstacle avoidance for fast quadrotor flight.
Uses a CUDA-based event simulator integrated with differentiable physics to backpropagate through the training loop.
Learns an end-to-end policy mapping event frames directly to control commands, avoiding cascaded depth estimation.
Demonstrates zero-shot real-world deployment in odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including low light.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System Framework Overview. The simulator renders a grayscale frame from each quadrotor state, and two consecutive frames are used to compute the event frame. The event frame is fed into a differentiable policy consisting of a CNN and a GRU, which predicts an action. The differentiable point-mass dynamics model then propagates the current state forward using this action. A loss is computed based on the resulting state and action, and the corresponding gradients are propagated backward through the entire differentiable pipeline to update the policy.

papers.abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a B\'ezier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
authors: Yuanxiang Yang, Yu Liu, Fabricio Oliveira, Yu Han, Claudio Roncoli

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in off-road terrain is commonly achieved using hierarchical control and planning architectures that rely on explicit cost maps and one-way information flow from a high-level planner to a low-level controller, decoupling planning from the true execution cost experienced during control. We propose a hierarchical planning and control framework in which information flows bidirectionally, allowing the low-level controller to guide trajectory selection at the planning level. The highest level of the hierarchy is a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control-style planner that determines optimal trajectories and passes these waypoints to a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Rather than drawing from an explicit cost map, our MPPI planner leverages the value function of the RL controller as an implicit cost representation. In this formulation, MPPI serves as a trajectory exploration mechanism, while the low-level controller's value function guides the search. To account for the distribution shift seen by the value function between training and evaluation, we propose an online policy evaluation process that adapts the value function to unseen driving experiences, and we demonstrate this adaptation in unseen off-road simulation environments. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator across a range of challenging terrain conditions and compare its performance against a baseline MPPI controller. The results demonstrate that our method achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations while eliminating the need for explicit cost maps and enabling tighter coupling between planning and control.
authors: Anoushka Alavilli, Raymond Song, Guanya Shi, Jeff Schneider
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level planning and low-level execution in hierarchical off-road navigation.
Uses MPPI to explore trajectories, with the pretrained controller’s value function guiding trajectory selection.
Applies online policy evaluation to adapt the value function to unseen driving experiences and distribution shift.
Evaluated in a high-fidelity off-road simulator across challenging terrains against a baseline MPPI controller.
Reports safer, more effective goal-directed navigation while removing the need for explicit cost maps.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of our value-guided planning framework. We pre-train RL policies to provide both an actor πθ(s) and a value function Vϕ(s). MPPI samples candidate trajectories and evaluates them using a cost that combines goal progress with the negative value estimate, treating −Vϕ(s) as a control-aware cost. The selected trajectory is executed by the policy, and the resulting experience can be used to update the value function online. This enables planning to be guided by the expected performance of the controller without requiring an explicit cost map.

Fig. 3: Comparison of pitch and vertical jerk violations across all 64 evaluation trajectories for the MPPI baseline ((A), (B)), our algorithm ((C), (D)), and our algorithm with online adaptation ((E), (F)). Panels (A), (C), and (E) show pitch violations exceeding 0.4 rad (22.9◦), while (B), (D), and (F) show vertical jerk violations exceeding 10e−2 m/s3. The violations are colored by their severity and are no more than 0.7 rad. and 2 m/s3 for pitch and jerk respectively. The MPPI baseline includes an explicit pitch cost term, whereas our method is trained with a jerk penalty in the reward function. When divided into equally-spaced buckets of low, medium, and high violation severity, the MPPI baseline recorded 317, 51, and 19 jerk violations and 84, 0, and 0 pitch violations, respectively; ours recorded 22, 1, and 0 jerk violations and 11, 1, and 0 pitch violations; and ours with online adaptation recorded 31, 0, and 0 jerk violations and 1, 1, and 3 pitch violations.

Fig. 2: Comparison between baseline MPPI, our algorithm, and our algorithm with online adaptation. All trajectories were unseen during training. In (A), our method incurs damage midway through the trajectory, while the online adaptation variant avoids this region through online updates alone, without any prior knowledge that this region would cause damage. In (A), (B), and (E), the baseline MPPI algorithm becomes stuck and is unable to complete its planned route. In (C), our algorithm demonstrates its ability to follow existing trails, which provide safer traversal than off-trail terrain. In (D), our algorithm with online adaptation reaches the maximum time limit and does not complete the trajectory.

Fig. 4: (A) Visualization of training data coverage and evaluation start–goal waypoints. (B) Trajectories traversed by the online adaptation variant of our algorithm, colored by the incurred reward as defined in Eq. 1. (C) and (D) show value estimates of the traversed terrain during execution for our algorithm without and with online adaptation, respectively. These value maps can be interpreted as implicit cost maps over the visited regions. After online adaptation, regions associated with lower reward decrease in value (i.e., appear lighter), reflecting updated terrain estimates. Despite this, the algorithm continues to favor on-trail paths, as they are predicted to have higher value than off-trail terrain. All colorbars are scaled between the 10th and 90th percentiles of the plotted values.

TABLE I: Comparison of navigation performance and terrain interaction metrics across methods. Each algorithm is evaluated on 64 randomly sampled start–goal pairs, all unseen during training. Episodes terminate after a maximum of 50 seconds (250 control steps) and are marked as failures if the goal is not reached within this budget (denoted “timeout”). Other episodes terminate with the vehicle stuck (on a steep slope, for example), and these failures are denoted “stuck.” Reported values reflect trajectory statistics aggregated over all trials; lower values in Z-axis motion and orientation indicate smoother traversal. papers.abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io
authors: Jacob Levy, Arthur Bouton, Tristan D. Hassler, Hari Nayar, David Fridovich-Keil
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps from unmodeled slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation while limiting costly trial-and-error.
Uses a reward-weighted loss to adapt a simulation-trained world model online.
Trains a loss predictor to identify likely future performance-relevant errors and guides MPC exploration toward them.
In simulation, reaches about 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution conditions.
On the ERNEST rover, restores coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five trials.

papers.abstract: Smart wheelchairs are robotic devices that gather information from the surroundings and allow people to safely drive through various environments. They usually rely on the interpretation of high-level user's intentions, typically decoded through human-robot interface (HRI) or brain-machine interface (BMI). However, navigating in an unknown environment and accurately understanding user commands remain significant challenges. Misinterpretation of commands or the environment can lead to user frustration, distrust of the system, or even unsafe situations. In this paper, we present a novel Multi-Layer Navigation System (MLNS) for a smart wheelchair that enables navigation in unknown environments while interpreting and safely contextualizing user's intentions even in the case of limited and faulty commands. The stack relies on a Virtual Sensors-Driven Potential Fields (ViSPF) method for obstacle detection that accounts for the wheelchair's actual size, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) module for trajectory generation, and an open-vocabulary computer vision algorithm for target identification. Finally, a system based on Priority Queue (PQ) was implemented for target selection. We validated our system on a real smart wheelchair with experiments involving 10 participants without disabilities, including scenarios with faulty input interfaces. The results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our system in real-world environments, proving its potential for practical applications in assistive technologies.
authors: Piero Simonetto, Anna Polato, Francesco Pasti, Muhammad Rameez ur Rahman, Sebastiano Vascon, Nicola Bellotto, Emanuele Menegatti, Stefano Tortora, Luca Tonin
bullets: Addresses unsafe navigation and command misinterpretation in smart wheelchairs with restricted input interfaces.

Uses a priority-queue mechanism to select navigation targets and contextualize user intentions.
Validated on a real smart wheelchair with 10 participants, including faulty-interface scenarios, demonstrating robust real-world operation.
Scope: experiments involved participants without disabilities; broader clinical validation is not described.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.
authors: Yuhang Peng, Zhikai Wang, Ziyi Wang, Jiaru Zhong, Xiaoji Zheng, Jingzhi Huang, Yi Wang, Jiangtao Gong

On R2R-CE val-unseen, the full system outperforms evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines; removing temporal memory greatly lengthens paths and lowers SR.
Real-world tests on Unitree Go2 show higher success than a post-trained baseline in evaluated corridor and office settings; LAW2 probes instruction-following behavior beyond endpoint success.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners have demonstrated remarkable success on long-horizon diffusion planning by sampling short trajectories, namely chunks, and composing them into a long trajectory. However, averaging overlapping chunks can induce the mode-averaging problem, resulting in discontinuous trajectories. Several works aim to address this problem, whereas a non-negligible portion of plans remains infeasible. In this work, we propose Selective Compositional Diffuser (SCD), handling this problem by measuring reachability. To this end, we present a self-supervised learning method for the reachability classifier. This is trained on offline data and generated chunks jointly to address potential distributional mismatch, while reducing the bias inherited from the generated data. Based on this, we construct a graph whose edge costs represent whether consecutive chunks are reachable, and traverse the graph to find effective yet efficient routes. Lastly, we generate bridging trajectories and refine the composed trajectory for smooth transitions. We evaluate our method on OGBench stitching tasks. It practically reduces incompatible mode compositions and the mode-averaging problem compared to the studied baselines. Across tasks, SCD improves success rates, reaching state-of-the-art results on HumanoidMaze-Large and Giant tasks.
authors: Chanyoung Park, Youngjoong Kim, Jaesik Park
bullets: Addresses discontinuities from averaging overlapping chunks and infeasible plans in compositional diffusion planners.

On OGBench stitching tasks, reduces incompatible mode compositions and mode averaging compared with studied baselines.
Improves success rates and achieves state-of-the-art results on HumanoidMaze-Large and Giant.

papers.abstract: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360{\deg} cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180{\deg} and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180{\deg}, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200{\deg} FIORD and 205{\deg} FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.
authors: Allen Tu, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Shifan Zhu, Hailing Wang, Yen-Liang Lin, David Held, Matthias Zwicker, Tom Goldstein
bullets: Addresses fisheye reconstruction beyond 180° while producing collision-ready geometry.
Uses calibrated densification for full-FoV surface recovery.
Applies calibrated mip filtering and wide-angle appearance modeling to separate blur and lens falloff from the scene and mesh.
Improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 dB on FIORD and 1.97 dB on FullCircle.
Achieves the highest reported mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set, while supporting real-time rendering and full-FoV ray tracing.

papers.abstract: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/TACOS.
authors: Jean-Michel Fortin, William Larriv\'ee-Hardy, Gabriel Jeanson, Olivier Gamache, Daniele De Martini, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere
bullets: Defines a consistent footstep instability score from the residual of a legged-robot factor graph.
Projects the score into preceding camera images to train a dense visual instability predictor.
Provides a hindsight-based hard score and an immediately available causal soft score.
Both variants outperform evaluated alternatives for detecting and ranking contact instability; the best predictor improves rank correlation further with onboard context.
In a 50 m forest test, the predictor responds to mud and vegetation while avoiding geometric obstacles such as fallen branches.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) are becoming increasingly important and useful for embodied intelligence, as they enable robots to anticipate the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with the physical environment. However, underwater robots are usually subject to passive dynamics, such as inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift, which can continue to affect the vehicle even after an action is completed. Existing WAMs, which primarily predict action-conditioned visual observations, are not explicitly designed to capture such passive motion dynamics. In this paper, we present AquaWAM, the first World Action Model designed for underwater embodied agents. Instead of predicting future images, AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including the thruster dead band, the inertial glide that outlasts each command, and ambient currents. Specifically, it senses through the DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for understanding goals and target pose. By modeling compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations, AquaWAM substantially reduces the model size and computational cost compared with conventional WAMs. Experimentally, AquaWAM achieves a 72.6% task success rate across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods while making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Our model also remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable. For example, without DVL velocity measurements, our method still achieves a 61.6% success rate, compared with 39.4% for U0.
bullets: Addresses inertia, buoyancy, drag, thruster dead bands, drift, and currents that conventional visual WAMs do not explicitly capture.
Uses DVL, IMU, pressure, and joint-encoder data for compact navigation-state prediction, while cameras provide semantic and target-pose information.
Achieves 72.6% success across 20 USIM underwater tasks and makes decisions 2.7× faster than U0 on a Jetson AGX Orin.
Maintains robustness under missing DVL velocity measurements, achieving 61.6% success versus 39.4% for U0.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in previously unseen environments requires effective perception, persistent environmental representation, and collision avoidance while maintaining progress toward a goal. Existing perception-based methods often rely on prior maps or short-horizon observations, limiting their ability to exploit previously observed structure. We propose a memory-aware multi-sensor navigation framework that integrates LiDAR and RGB perception, online distance-field representation learning, and a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (MCBF-QP). The framework persistently represents static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles, enabling the MCBF-QP controller to exploit previously observed geometry for obstacle circumvention and adapt its safety constraints and guidance to local conditions. Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate improved navigation efficiency and goal-reaching performance while maintaining collision avoidance in narrow passages and around dynamic obstacles.
bullets: Targets limitations of prior-map dependence and short-horizon perception in unseen environments.
Fuses LiDAR and RGB data with online distance-field representation learning.
Separately preserves static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles.
Uses a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program for safe, context-aware control.
Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor settings show improved efficiency and goal reaching while avoiding collisions in narrow and dynamic scenarios.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed memory-aware multi-sensory perception and navigation framework, integrating onboard state estimation, dynamic obstacle detection, online environment representation learning, and stage-adaptive MCBF control for safe and live navigation in previously unmapped environments.

papers.selection_reason: Memory-aware multi-sensor navigation with persistent environment representation and adaptive safety control for robots in dynamic scenes.
papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Sensor Perception for Efficient and Safe Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: A memory-aware LiDAR–RGB navigation framework persistently models environments and adapts safety control to navigate efficiently and collision-free around static and dynamic obstacles.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.27--0.50m in bipedal locomotion and 0.50--0.20m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/REACH/.
authors: Shengzhang Xu, Yuning Guo, Weiyi Hu, Yifeng Xu, Zhongyu Li, He Kong
bullets: Addresses the limitation of bipedal systems that cannot traverse spaces below crouched-walking clearance.
Uses hierarchical reinforcement learning with history-conditioned latent representations for contact-rich crawling.
Employs a bidirectional transition policy to connect crouched walking and crawling despite major kinematic and contact changes.
Combines learned locomotion skills with LiDAR-based 3D planning and proactive body-height commands.
Real-world experiments show accurate tracking, terrain robustness, reliable mode transitions, and confined-space traversal.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based humanoid locomotion with height adaptation and LiDAR planning; fits embodied AI navigation and robot learning.
papers.title: REACH: An RL-based Hierarchical Humanoid Crawling Framework for Adaptable Confined Space Traversal
papers.tldr: REACH enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to adaptively switch between variable-height walking and crawling for robust traversal of confined spaces.

papers.abstract: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.
authors: Riccardo Bianco, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses precise timing, alignment, and collision avoidance when flying through moving narrow gaps.
Uses signed-distance gating to turn sparse traversal success into dense, differentiable pathwise losses.
Trains a visual-feature-to-thrust/body-rate policy in one stage without privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation.
Pathwise gradients outperform score-function gradients in controlled precision-critical benchmarks.
Achieves 99.3% simulation success and 80% success across 10 real-world trials from varied initial conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Differentiable simulation for visuomotor quadrotor navigation through dynamic gaps; fits learned robot navigation and planning.
papers.title: Learning Visuomotor Quadrotor Flight Through Dynamic Narrow Gaps via Differentiable Simulation
papers.tldr: A differentiable pathwise objective enables a vision-and-inertial policy to learn dynamic narrow-gap quadrotor flight from scratch and transfer to real hardware.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure - moving contrast edges - to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64x64 event observation in 17 microseconds on a single GPU - over 400x faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline - enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes - three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty, traversability probability approx. 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. Code: https://github.com/tudelft/rendering-free-event-nav
authors: Dequan Ou, Austin Lopez, Quentin Missinne, Christophe De Wagter, Guido C. H. E. de Croon
bullets: Generates event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion, avoiding photorealistic image rendering.
Produces 64×64 event observations in 17 μs on a single GPU, over 400× faster than a rendering-based pipeline.
Enables obstacle-avoidance policies to converge in under 30 minutes and transfer zero-shot to ray-traced simulation.
Achieves 83% success in unseen cluttered simulated courses and 70% in a texture-dense indoor hall.
A quantized 1.2 MB policy runs onboard a 56 g Crazyflie, reaching an average 82% success rate across three real-world courses.
papers.selection_reason: Rendering-free event simulation enables fast reinforcement learning for obstacle-avoidance navigation; directly relevant to learned robot navigation.
papers.title: Rendering-Free Event Frame Simulation for Fast Reinforcement Learning of Autonomous Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: A rendering-free event simulator enables dramatically faster reinforcement learning for agile robot navigation and transfers effectively to both simulated and real-world drones.

papers.abstract: In smart factory environments, passive entities such as humans and movable obstacles may interfere with autonomous robot operations, posing significant safety risks. Detecting potential conflicts between robots and entities outside their field-of-view (FoV) is therefore of paramount importance. However, conventional passive object detection systems rely on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, or cameras, which operate under direct line-of-sight (LoS) and are limited by obstacles and occlusions. To overcome these limitations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception via the communication infrastructure thanks to cooperation among distributed wireless devices. In this paper, we propose a framework for passive entity sensing beyond the robot's FoV that relies solely on distributed channel measurements from the communication infrastructure to perform risk-aware classification. These measurements are embedded into high-dimensional representations using hyperdimensional computing (HDC), enabling robust and scalable learning without explicit channel reconstruction. Numerical simulations based on a commercial ray tracer and ROS-based validation in realistic smart factory scenarios demonstrate improved safety and enhanced path planning with up to 89% accuracy under severe occlusions, while maintaining low computational complexity.
authors: Placido Mursia, Marco Rossanese, Francesco Devoti, Adrian Lendinez Ibanez, Lanfranco Zanzi, Xi Li, Xavier Costa-Perez
bullets: Addresses robot safety risks from humans and obstacles hidden by occlusions in smart factories.
Uses distributed communication-channel measurements rather than direct line-of-sight LiDAR, radar, or camera sensing.
Maps measurements to high-dimensional representations with hyperdimensional computing for risk-aware classification without reconstructing channels.
Validated through ray-tracing simulations and ROS-based smart-factory scenarios.
Supports safer path planning under severe occlusions, with scope demonstrated in simulated and realistic validation environments.
papers.selection_reason: Distributed RF perception with hyperdimensional computing for non-line-of-sight obstacle awareness and safer robot path planning.
papers.title: Leveraging Distributed Sensing and Hyperdimensional Computing for Non-Line-of-Sight Passive Object Sensing
papers.tldr: A distributed wireless sensing framework using hyperdimensional computing detects passive objects outside a robot’s field of view, achieving up to 89% accuracy under severe occlusions with low computational complexity.

papers.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
authors: Daan van Hamersveld, Ewoud Smeur, Iurii Kriachko
bullets: Addresses the need for lower-cost, longer-range interception of medium-altitude, long-endurance drones.
Uses a neural network to map filtered monocular-vision observations directly to actuator commands.
Trains the policy with proximal policy optimization in a custom Python environment.
Outperforms two classical guidance controllers under most simulated conditions.
Successfully intercepts maneuvering fixed-wing targets in real-flight tests.
papers.selection_reason: Learned visuomotor policy for autonomous fixed-wing interception, relevant to robot navigation and RL-based robotic control.
papers.title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
papers.tldr: A reinforcement-learning controller enables a fixed-wing drone to autonomously intercept maneuvering aerial targets in simulation and real flight.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies form structured internal representations of traffic, ego behavior, and road constraints. These representations offer a monitoring interface for anticipating failures, complementing risk signals from trajectories, controls, and manually designed features. We introduce the Structured Representation Probe (SRP), a lightweight monitor that reads actor, ego, and map representations from a frozen policy. SRP learns a separate linear risk direction for each source and aggregates element scores through cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling, retaining sensitivity to salient evidence while reducing dependence on token count. Event-window supervision links the readout to upcoming hard failures, and auxiliary event type heads jointly train the source directions across failure modes. Online alerting uses a single generic score without modifying the driving policy. Bench2Drive experiments on DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD show higher frame-level PR-AUC and ROC-AUC than the evaluated runtime baselines. On DriveTransformer at a horizon of 2 seconds, ROC-AUC reaches 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency, with 2.67% readout runtime overhead. The trained probes also retain the ability to distinguish impending failures on new routes.
authors: Jiawei Liang, Tianrui Lou, Le Yang, Xianghao Jiao, Wei Wang, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Addresses the need for risk monitoring that complements trajectory-, control-, and hand-crafted-feature-based signals.
Reads actor, ego, and map representations, learning source-specific linear risk directions and combining element scores with cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling.
Uses event-window supervision and auxiliary event-type heads to train a single generic online alert score without changing the driving policy.
On Bench2Drive with DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD, SRP outperforms evaluated runtime baselines; for DriveTransformer at a 2-second horizon, ROC-AUC is 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency.
Adds 2.67% readout runtime overhead and retains failure-discrimination ability on new routes.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a Structured Representation Probe (SRP) for risk anticipation in end-to-end autonomous driving policies. This addresses safety and monitoring in robot navigation systems.
papers.title: Structured Representation Probing for Risk Anticipation in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: SRP monitors frozen end-to-end driving policies by probing structured internal representations to anticipate imminent failures with low runtime overhead.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles in enclosed spaces such as tunnels and mines rely on range maps that smoke, dust and fog make inaccurate. Conformal prediction calibrates a keepout around the mapped walls that covers the true unsafe set at a chosen probability. Typically an unmodified planner treats the keepout as an inflated obstacle, and nothing ensures that the vehicle can stop before the keepout as it moves when sensing degrades. In narrow passages this margin and the planner's buffer close the route, and existing remedies recover reach by relaxing the coverage level. This paper conditions the conformal margin on a label-free severity estimate to hold coverage near its target as degradation varies. A planning and control layer enforces one braking-distance condition on the keepout at plan time and at every command, takes the measured tracking residual as its only margin and never alters the keepout. The keepout is validated on ground-robot smoke recordings and the closed loop in simulated quadrotor flights in a foggy tunnel against the standard deployment. In closed-loop simulation the proposed system substantially reduces entries into the calibrated keepout and reaches numerically more goals than the deployment pattern in both calibration regimes, an observed gain of 3.2 percentage points pooled whose per-regime confidence intervals include zero. The per-class keepout holds its coverage near the target on held-out recordings.
bullets: Problem: Inaccurate range maps and planner buffers can make narrow passages impassable, while standard deployment does not ensure stopping before moving keepouts.
Method: Condition the conformal keepout margin on a label-free severity estimate and enforce a braking-distance constraint during planning and every control command.
Design: Use measured tracking residuals as the only additional margin and never modify the calibrated keepout.
Evaluation: Validate keepout coverage on ground-robot smoke recordings and test closed-loop navigation in simulated quadrotor flights through a foggy tunnel.

Result and scope: The system reduced keepout entries and reached numerically more goals than the standard deployment; the pooled gain was 3.2 percentage points, but per-regime confidence intervals included zero.
papers.selection_reason: Conformal keepout planning for enclosed-space navigation; fits learned navigation planning.
papers.title: KEPT: Conformal Keepouts Kept in Planning for Enclosed-Space Navigation in Degraded Sensing
papers.tldr: KEPT combines degradation-aware conformal keepouts with braking-aware planning to improve safe navigation in smoke-, dust-, and fog-obscured enclosed spaces without relaxing coverage targets.

papers.abstract: Humanoids and other legged robots operating in complex environments must remember information that leaves their field of view and only becomes relevant much later. Reinforcement learning policies address this using memory networks such as LSTMs that are trained end-to-end with the policy to memorize such task-relevant aspects. Yet, such architectures often fail to preserve sufficient information over long horizons. In this work, we propose a network architecture based on Hadamard memory that specifically targets robot navigation. Our Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) enables RL agents to store generic task-relevant information at specific, position-based memory cells, enabling flexible and spatially grounded memorization. We evaluate LSMM on the task of autonomous maze exploration, where it matches the maze coverage of strong recurrent and finite-history baselines while being the only architecture that remembers the maze layout, reducing the reconstruction error threefold.
authors: Leon Magnus, Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Long-horizon navigation requires remembering information beyond the robot’s current field of view.
The proposed Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) stores task-relevant information in position-based memory cells.
LSMM is evaluated for autonomous maze exploration against recurrent and finite-history baselines.
It matches baseline maze coverage and is the only evaluated architecture to remember maze layout, reducing reconstruction error threefold.
papers.selection_reason: Spatial memory for legged robot exploration; fits robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Remember Where You Walk: Learning Spatial Memory for End-to-End Legged Robot Exploration
papers.tldr: LSMM gives legged-robot RL agents spatially grounded memory, enabling them to retain and reconstruct maze layouts over long exploration horizons.

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time 3D object detection based on LiDAR and camera data is critical for safety in autonomous driving, where systems must accurately perceive their surroundings with minimal latency. Many state-of-the-art systems achieve high-quality detection results but fail to meet real-time constraints, limiting their practical use. To address this challenge, we propose FastBEVFusion, a simple, fast, and robust fusion system for 3D object detection. Based on modality-specific features, FastBEVFusion projects these features into semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces, without relying on a computationally intensive and potentially error-prone depth estimation. Given these BEV spaces, we propose a light-weight, soft, and dynamic fusion module based on cross-attention, which adapts dynamically to the scene context and enables feature fusion across the entire BEV spaces. Experiments on the complex nuScenes dataset show that FastBEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems, and achieves over 50 FPS without deployment libraries. Additionally, our system shows strong robustness to calibration errors, making FastBEVFusion a powerful 3D object detection system for real-world applications.
authors: Tom Sanitz, Emre G\"ulsoylu, Simone Frintrop, Christian Wilms
bullets: Targets the latency and reliability challenges of real-time multimodal 3D detection for autonomous driving.
Projects modality-specific features into semi-aligned BEV spaces without computationally expensive depth estimation.
Uses lightweight cross-attention for scene-adaptive fusion across the full BEV representation.
Evaluated on nuScenes, it outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems and exceeds 50 FPS without deployment libraries.
Shows strong robustness to calibration errors, supporting practical real-world use.
papers.selection_reason: Real-time LiDAR-camera BEV fusion for 3D object detection; directly applicable as perception for robot navigation and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: FastBEVFusion: Simple Multi-Modal Fusion for 3D Object Detection at 50 FPS
papers.tldr: FastBEVFusion enables robust LiDAR-camera 3D detection at over 50 FPS using depth-free BEV projection and lightweight dynamic fusion.

papers.abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.
authors: Sahar Nasirihaghighi, Tianyuan Wang, Kenan Niu, Stefano Stramigioli
bullets: Addresses the need for structured, continuous coronary-scene understanding beyond separate vessel segmentation or device localization.
Uses simulated fluoroscopy generated from 3D coronary CT angiography, including vessels, guidewires, stenoses, and varied geometries.
Jointly predicts vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip location, and stenosis location from a single X-ray frame.
Transforms predictions into a vascular graph with centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and angles.
Generates an interpretable roadmap from a selected graph root to the target lesion; evaluation is demonstrated in simulation.
papers.selection_reason: Simulation-driven coronary perception network with graph-based roadmap generation for robotic guidewire navigation; fits robot navigation and embodied perception.
papers.title: MCP-Net: Real-Time Coronary Perception Network and Topological Analysis for Robotic Guidewire Navigation
papers.tldr: MCP-Net jointly interprets fluoroscopic coronary scenes and converts them into a topological roadmap for robotic guidewire navigation.

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation (ImageNav) requires an agent to reach a location specified by a goal image in an unknown environment. For drones, this task demands exploration, goal- directed navigation, and collision avoidance under limited onboard computing resources. Existing aerial ImageNav methods are built on single-view observations, requiring additional rotation and exploration to search for goal-relevant cues outside the field of view. In this paper, we present Omni-IGN, a fully onboard ImageNav system that integrates quad-fisheye perception, an attention-based reinforcement learning (RL) policy, and a collision-aware safety layer. The policy adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views to provide directional guidance for continuous navigation. The quad-fisheye RGB images support both ImageNav and obstacle avoidance without a dedicated depth sensor. On Habitat benchmarks, Omni-IGN achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines. Moreover, flight tests in IsaacSim validate the effectiveness of integrating learning-based depth estimation with the action safety layer for collision avoidance. Finally, real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without any fine-tuning or external localization. The code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zichen Yan, Rui Huang, Shenao Wang, Yucong Wang, Nuthasith Gerdpratoom, Lin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limited field of view, exploration, and collision-avoidance challenges in aerial ImageNav.
Combines quad-fisheye RGB perception, attention-based reinforcement learning, and a collision-aware safety layer.
Adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views for continuous directional navigation.
Achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines on Habitat benchmarks.
Demonstrates collision avoidance in IsaacSim and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in real-world experiments.
papers.selection_reason: Onboard image-goal navigation for drones with RL policy and obstacle avoidance; directly fits embodied visual navigation.
papers.title: Omni-IGN: Onboard Image-Goal Navigation for Drones with Omnidirectional Vision
papers.tldr: Omni-IGN enables drones to navigate toward image goals using omnidirectional vision, onboard reinforcement learning, and collision-aware safety without external localization or depth sensors.

papers.abstract: Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution and subsequent replanning.
authors: Shuo Pei, Bosun Liang, Saihui Zha, Chen Sun, Huachun Tan, Yong Wang
bullets: Identifies a sample-to-execution gap: better generated proposals can still lead to worse committed actions.
Combines intent-guided diffusion proposals with execution-grounded candidate selection.
Feeds the committed trajectory back into subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics.
Reports leading closed-loop performance across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, including an average score of 85.62 and 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM.
Counterfactual and prefix analyses indicate more reliable conversion of strong candidates into executed decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based closed-loop planning with execution-grounded selection for autonomous driving, fitting learned navigation.
papers.title: ExecDiffuser: Closing the Sample-to-Execution Gap in Diffusion Planning
papers.tldr: ExecDiffuser narrows the gap between high-quality diffusion proposals and the single trajectory actually executed in closed-loop driving.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an approach to achieve side-by-side autonomous motion with a pair of personal mobility vehicles (PMVs). Given a global path, two PMVs plan cooperatively so as to hold a social formation that lets the passengers hold a conversation, while keeping the ride safe and smooth. Each vehicle runs its own sampling-based model-predictive planner; the planners exchange nothing but the odometry each vehicle could observe of the other, and the joint decision is expressed as a pair of utility matrices over pairs of candidate trajectories, resolved by a common rule. The behavioural parameters are fitted by inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by ten pairs of people in human-driven PMVs in an indoor environment, and the lanes the pair can use are derived offline from the corridor itself rather than fixed by hand. A safety layer the cost cannot override executes a move only if the vehicle can still brake clear, measured from its whole body, and a vehicle that is stuck reverses along its own path and continues. In closed-loop simulation over 24 runs in the conditions the drivers were recorded in and 24 in four generated obstacle layouts, no vehicle entered a wall or a cone. The pair holds conversational formation for 60.5 and 68.9 percent of the time among obstacles (anticlockwise and clockwise) and 81.2 and 91.5 percent in a clear aisle, against the drivers' 34.0 and 36.0 percent, and 52.9 and 56.0 percent, and it matches their speed. It keeps one lateral formation where the drivers alternated between a close diagonal and a wide abreast one, and it varies far less. Experimental results are based on a differential drive kinematic simulator running on ROS 2.
bullets: Uses inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by 10 human pairs to fit cooperative behavioral parameters.
Each vehicle runs a sampling-based model-predictive planner and exchanges only observable odometry with its partner.
A common utility-matrix rule coordinates trajectory choices, while corridor-derived lanes and a non-overridable braking-based safety layer support navigation.
In simulation, no vehicle collided with walls or cones across 48 closed-loop runs, and conversational formation was maintained more often than by human drivers.
The system matched driver speed but used a more consistent lateral formation; evaluation was limited to a differential-drive kinematic simulator in ROS 2.
papers.selection_reason: Learns cooperative side-by-side navigation policies for personal mobility vehicles from human driving data.
papers.title: Learning Side-by-Side Navigation for Personal Mobility Vehicles from Human Drivers
papers.tldr: A learned, decentralized planner enables two personal mobility vehicles to move safely side-by-side while maintaining a conversational formation.

papers.abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Ziang Guo, Didar Seyidov, Yixiao Zhou, Xuefeng Zhang, Ali Alridha Abdulkarim, Chen Min, Zufeng Zhang, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Addresses cascading map degradation caused by absorbing monocular tracking errors into the map.
Uses chunk-level streaming spatial geometry as a metric prior to supervise both tracking and mapping.
Introduces a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel that models viewpoint-dependent information.
Jointly optimizes geometry and poses to produce globally consistent maps and trajectories.
Outperforms per-frame association baselines on KITTI and Waymo Open datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Monocular 3DGS SLAM for outdoor navigation with joint geometry-pose optimization; directly relevant to embodied visual navigation.
papers.title: SG^2SLAM: Spatial Geometry-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Monocular Outdoor Navigation
papers.tldr: SG^2SLAM improves monocular outdoor SLAM by jointly optimizing streaming spatial geometry, camera poses, and ray-conditioned 3D Gaussian primitives for more consistent trajectories and maps.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining long-range navigation with precision vertical landing under nonlinear dynamics and uncertainty.
Uses a three-stage curriculum, critic warm-up, rehearsal to limit catastrophic forgetting, and observations containing a full 3×3 rotation matrix.
Introduces a bounded, computationally simpler reward function whose progress term tracks cumulative distance closed.
Under the reported evaluation, the policy achieved 99.98% success versus 68.31% for the baseline.
The proposed policy retained 69.1% initial fuel and had 7.07 units mean final pad-distance, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Curriculum-driven deep RL for autonomous far-range navigation and precision landing; directly relevant to learned embodied navigation and control.
papers.title: Curriculum-Driven Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Far-Range Rocket Landing
papers.tldr: A curriculum-driven deep RL framework enables autonomous rocket landing from far greater initial distances while achieving high success and precise touchdowns in simulation.

papers.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
bullets: Direct-policy world action models typically need tens of denoising steps, limiting real-time deployment.
OSWAM uses imagination tokens to provide physical priors and action-conditioned representations at diffusion initialization.
Privileged information distillation with future conditioning improves future-aware action generation.
Experiments report comparable or better performance than multi-step direct-policy and Joint-WAM baselines, with about 3× speedup and latency as low as 40 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.
The abstract evaluates autonomous driving and embodied control, without specifying broader domains or limitations.
papers.selection_reason: OSWAM reduces world action model inference to a single diffusion step using imagination tokens, enabling real-time autonomous driving and embodied control.
papers.title: OSWAM: An Effective World Action Model with One-Step Action Generation
papers.tldr: OSWAM enables high-quality one-step action generation for autonomous driving and embodied control by initializing diffusion with structured action priors and distilling future-aware information.

papers.abstract: Robotic missions involving spatially distributed tasks often require jointly selecting rewarding locations and planning feasible motions under limited travel budgets. This paper proposes Reward-Guided RRT*, a new sampling-based framework that constructs a budget-feasible mission through a sequence of locally joint task-selection-and-motion-planning stages, evaluated directly in the continuous state space, without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph. The method incrementally builds a mission using reward-guided RRT* searches, while a return-feasibility procedure ensures that each selected task can be visited without violating the mission budget. Experiments with increasing obstacle complexity and number of tasks show solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* while requiring substantially fewer sampled states. We also extend the framework to Dubins steering and evaluate it in CoppeliaSim with a scaled car-like robotic platform, demonstrating its ability to incorporate vehicle kinematic constraints.
bullets: Builds missions incrementally through locally joint task-selection and motion-planning stages.
Uses reward-guided RRT* without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph.
Applies return-feasibility checks to ensure selected tasks remain within the mission budget.
Achieves solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* with substantially fewer sampled states in experiments.
Extends to Dubins steering and demonstrates operation with a car-like robot in CoppeliaSim.
papers.selection_reason: Extends RRT* for budgeted task and motion planning, incorporating reward guidance to efficiently select tasks and plan motions.
papers.title: Reward-Guided RRT* for Budgeted Task and Motion Planning
papers.tldr: Reward-Guided RRT* jointly selects rewarding tasks and plans feasible motions under a travel budget directly in continuous space.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.
bullets: A matched 12-candidate tuning protocol changed the baseline RMSE ranking, moving BL-SMC from last to first; this ordering persisted on fresh realizations and with 48 candidates.
Reference preview substantially improved MPC tracking and eliminated fallback activity on the figure-eight task.
On abrupt steps, performance depended on the interaction among fallback policy, actuator prediction, and actuator authority.
Measured command delays caused most or all tested nominal MPC configurations to miss deadlines, while a 100-iteration solver cap removed deadline misses in tested profiles.
The study recommends reporting tracking accuracy alongside tuning effort, completion/failure rates, fallback activity, input variation, and timing.
papers.selection_reason: A reproducible simulation study analyzing how tuning and fallback policies affect quadrotor controller comparisons, providing a reporting checklist.
papers.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
papers.tldr: Quadrotor controller rankings can change substantially with tuning, reference preview, fallback design, actuator modeling, and command timing—not tracking error alone.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems.
