Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.
bullets: Targets inefficient exploration in sampling-based drone planning for complex 3D environments.
Converts natural-language instructions into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints.
Uses command-aligned subset sampling to structure exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness.
Simulations produce collision-free, consistent trajectories with reduced sampling effort versus uniform RRT-based planners.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a language-aided subset sampling motion planner for drone navigation, combining LLM grounding with sampling-based planning.
papers.title: Extended LASMP: Language Aided Subset Sampling Based Motion Planner for Drone Navigation
papers.tldr: Extended LASMP uses language-grounded navigation commands to guide 3D sampling for more efficient quadcopter motion planning.

papers.abstract: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds have matured into a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC, but they remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, we contribute a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators through a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of the software stack we build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, and a controller that exploits these added degrees of freedom, letting classical optimal controllers and learned policies be swapped on the same hardware without modification. We validate the integrated system, PINGU, across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The results show that these additions extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of thruster-only planar spacecraft testbeds for inertia-coupled manipulation and contact-rich operations.
Integrates a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms with interchangeable end-effectors through a unified ROS 2 interface.
Provides a reinforcement-learning environment and digital twin supporting interchangeable classical optimal controllers and learned policies.
Validates the system on navigation, disturbance rejection, momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking tasks.
Demonstrates an ATMOS-class emulator extended into the contact-rich regime on a single reproducible platform.
papers.selection_reason: Open-source spacecraft emulator with learned RL control and contact-rich manipulation; directly relevant to embodied robot learning and navigation.
papers.title: PINGU: Extending Air-Bearing Spacecraft Emulators with Open-Source Actuators and Learned Control for Contact-Rich Proximity Operations
papers.tldr: PINGU upgrades an open-source air-bearing spacecraft emulator with reaction-wheel and force-sensing arm actuators, enabling reproducible contact-rich proximity-operation experiments with both classical and learned control.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving maps current observations directly to future trajectories, yet those trajectories must remain valid as the scene evolves. Future state modeling aims to address this temporal mismatch, but general representations often contain information unrelated to ego planning and affect trajectory generation only through auxiliary supervision, static conditioning, or proposal evaluation. We propose FeasibleFlow, a one-step end-to-end generative framework that jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories. Our Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow uses the pathwise Jacobian-vector product in the MeanFlow identity to incorporate field evolution into trajectory transport. Because safety feedback is sparser than progress feedback, we further introduce the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) and Pareto-ReinFlow to balance safety and progress in candidate selection and generation, respectively. Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate the strong performance of FeasibleFlow and validate both the joint transport of feasibility and trajectories and the proposed safety-first mechanisms.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static observations and trajectories that must remain valid as scenes evolve.
Introduces Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow to couple feasibility-field evolution with trajectory transport via a pathwise Jacobian-vector product.
Uses Anchor-relative ranker and Pareto-ReinFlow to prioritize sparse safety feedback while balancing safety and progress.
NAVSIM experiments demonstrate strong performance and support the value of joint feasibility–trajectory transport and safety-first mechanisms.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end driving framework for trajectory generation and feasibility, directly relevant to embodied navigation.
papers.title: FeasibleFlow: One-Step Joint Transport of Configuration Feasibility and Trajectories for End-to-End Driving
papers.tldr: FeasibleFlow jointly generates evolving scene-feasibility fields and multimodal driving trajectories in one step, using safety-focused mechanisms to improve trajectory selection and generation.

papers.abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$
bullets: Introduces 16 database–query datasets from terrestrial Space Analog Domains, covering environmental, viewpoint, and illumination variation.
Defines matches by whether a relative pose estimator can produce a useful pose for downstream SLAM, rather than by fixed pose thresholds.
Provides ground-truth matrices derived from an ensemble of state-of-the-art relative pose estimators.
Evaluates nine state-of-the-art VPR methods and finds substantial room for improvement.
Offers a pre-release dataset and evaluation resources via GitHub.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for visual place recognition in space analog environments, relevant to robot navigation and SLAM loop closure.
papers.title: VPR-Space: A Benchmark for Visual Place Recognition in Space Analog Domains
papers.tldr: VPR-Space benchmarks visual place recognition for challenging, feature-poor Moon- and Mars-like environments with SLAM-relevant ground truth.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.
authors: Khaled M. Seyam (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Julian Wiederer (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Samar Fathalah (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Markus Braun (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Bin Yang (University of Stuttgart, Germany)
bullets: NeuroNCAP analysis attributes 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions to planning failures rather than perception.
The method attacks each planner through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its planning head, avoiding video rendering during search.
Automated quality-diversity search generates 50 attack scenes per planner, each paired with a safe escape trajectory for fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning roughly halves collision rates for SparseDrive and DiffusionDrive on NeuroNCAP, from 28.0% to 12.2% and 37.5% to 19.2%, respectively.
Cross-planner transfer is limited, indicating that targeting the specific planner is important; scope is demonstrated on two planners and NeuroNCAP.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses safety-critical scene generation and fine-tuning for end-to-end driving planners, directly relevant to learned robot navigation and policy learning.
papers.title: Model-Aware Generation of Safety-Critical Scenes for Robust End-to-End Driving via Distilled Planner Surrogates
papers.tldr: A planner-specific, model-aware scene-generation framework uses distilled BEV planner surrogates to create safety-critical training scenes that substantially reduce collisions while preserving normal driving.

papers.abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Hanchao Leng, JiaHui Huang, Hanbing Li, Jingwei Zhao, Kuiyuan Yang, Chen Gao, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses information loss and cross-modal inconsistency caused by modeling driving modalities separately.
Encodes appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories into a shared continuous latent.
Uses a frozen tokenizer with a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents.
On NAVSIM, the unified design improves future prediction and planning while reducing downstream computational cost.
With reinforcement-learning post-training, DriveUniWAM reaches a PDMS of 91.54 and state-of-the-art performance among evaluated WAM planners.
papers.selection_reason: Unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models; directly relevant to interactive world models and learned planning.
papers.title: DriveUniTok: A Unified Multimodal Tokenizer for Driving World-Action Models
papers.tldr: DriveUniTok unifies visual appearance, LiDAR depth, and ego motion into one decodable latent, improving driving world-model prediction and planning efficiency.

papers.abstract: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1--31.2\% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.
authors: Bing Sun, Yue Lin, Canhui Wen, Xin Chen, Yang Liu, Dong Wang, Huchuan Lu
bullets: Targets visibility-preserving navigation around obstacles with smooth, feasible motion.
Predicts control sequences and differentiably converts them into trajectories so trajectory-level objectives train the policy directly.
Uses decaying expert guidance to transition from effective initial behavior toward task-driven learning.
Adds a predictive safety lock that switches to classical planning and control when motion is unsafe or target prediction fails.

Across simulated settings, it achieves the highest tracking success, reduces RMS linear jerk by 14.1–31.2% versus the best competing method on that metric, and runs in 4.25–5.63 ms per cycle; robot tests cover indoor passages and outdoor forests.
papers.selection_reason: Learns direct-control policy from optimization for dynamic target tracking with obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Learning Direct Control from Optimization for Dynamic Target Tracking
papers.tldr: LECO learns smooth, direct control for dynamic target tracking by transferring trajectory-optimization objectives into an offline neural policy with a safety fallback.

papers.abstract: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. The source code is publicly available.
authors: Siyuan Yang, Junning Lyu, Xiaoyu He, Lakmal Seneviratne, Shaoming He
bullets: Addresses cascading inter-UAV localization uncertainty in multi-hop GNSS-denied swarm operations.
Uses Fisher-information-based covariance approximation to model uncertainty propagation along reference chains.
Tightens control barrier function constraints for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with graceful-degradation guarantees.
Combines hierarchical Voronoi targeting with formation keeping for forward-looking coverage.
Demonstrations with 6–30 UAVs, Monte Carlo deployments, and MBZIRC runs show feasible control and robust search containment; source code is available.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-aware CBF for multi-UAV swarm search; relevant to embodied robot navigation and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Localization-Uncertainty-Aware UAV Swarm Search for GNSS-Denied Maritime Surveillance
papers.tldr: An uncertainty-aware control framework enables UAV swarms to maintain localization, connectivity, and collision safety while efficiently searching GNSS-denied maritime areas.

papers.abstract: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
authors: Hyunwoong Bae, Jisu Han, Jiyeon Choi, Dohoon Kim, Taesup Moon
bullets: Introduces OSMA-Bench, using spatially matched scenarios that vary only by obstacle type.
Proposes the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure obstacle-conditioned clearance, speed, and smoothness.
VLM and VLA policies inconsistently adapt motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts.
Policies distinguish obstacles semantically but fail to reflect that distinction in motion parameters or actions.
For VLM-based systems, inserting an explicit parameter-inference step improves motion adaptation.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for obstacle-conditioned safe motion adaptation in household robot navigation directly fits learned robot navigation.
papers.title: Benchmarking Obstacle-Conditioned Safety in Household Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: OSMA-Bench reveals that current VLM and VLA navigation policies often recognize obstacle risk without translating it into appropriately cautious motion.

papers.abstract: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons's hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29 m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.
authors: Basheer Al-Tawil, Magnus Jung, Ayoub Al-Hamadi
bullets: Addresses the train-deploy gap caused by idealized training trajectories versus noisy RGB-D pose and depth estimates at inference.
Uses a shared pipeline for pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing during both training and deployment.
Encodes recent hip-center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and predicts future velocities using a GRU head.
Achieves 0.29 m average ADE and 0.51 m FDE on ETH/UCY.
Has 262K parameters and runs in real time on modest hardware, including deployment on a TIAGo robot with a Jetson Orin.
papers.selection_reason: Real-time human trajectory prediction for mobile robot navigation in dynamic environments.
papers.title: Real-Time Human Trajectory Prediction from RGB-D for Mobile Robots Using Bi-Mamba
papers.tldr: TrajMamba enables real-time short-term human trajectory prediction for mobile robots by aligning training and deployment inputs with a lightweight bidirectional state space model.

papers.abstract: Floor traction influences wheel-slip behavior, dead-reckoning accuracy, and the navigation performance of wheeled mobile robots that rely on wheel odometry. As these robots become increasingly common in GNSS-denied indoor environments, including automated manufacturing and retail facilities, their onboard measurements could also be used to characterize floor conditions and improve localization. In this study, a skid-steer robot was driven over five floor surfaces with distinct traction characteristics using commanded velocity profiles designed to induce wheel slip through repeated acceleration and direction reversal. Differences between the body velocity estimated from inertial sensing and the velocity obtained from wheel odometry were evaluated using the integrated relative-velocity error, phase-derived wheel-to-body response delay, and velocity-reversal response delay. Welch power spectral density analysis was additionally applied to characterize the frequency distribution of the velocity mismatch during positive and negative acceleration. Band-integrated spectral power, spectral centroid, and spectral decay rate were extracted from each recording and evaluated using linear discriminant analysis and multiclass classification. The response-delay measurements produced consistent surface-dependent trends, with the longest delays observed on soap and the shortest delays observed on carpet. The spectral features also provided clear separation among the tested surfaces, achieving a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These results demonstrate that both the magnitude and frequency domain characteristics of wheel-to-body velocity mismatch contain useful information about tire-surface interactions. Such information could support surface recognition and the development of slip-aware wheel-odometry weighting within robot state-estimation frameworks.
authors: Kulbhushan Komarraju, Nathaniel Pearson, Yu Gu, Jason Gross
bullets: Floor traction affects wheel slip, wheel-odometry accuracy, and indoor robot navigation.
The robot was driven with acceleration and reversal maneuvers designed to induce slip on five distinct surfaces.
Researchers compared inertial body velocity with wheel odometry using integrated error, response delays, and Welch power-spectral features.
Response delays varied by surface, with the longest on soap and shortest on carpet.
Time- and frequency-domain mismatch features separated the surfaces and could support slip-aware localization and odometry weighting.
papers.selection_reason: Wheel-slip-based surface classification supports slip-aware odometry and localization for wheeled robot navigation.
papers.title: Floor Friction Assessment from Robot Tire-Surface Interaction
papers.tldr: A skid-steer robot can identify floor traction conditions from wheel–body velocity mismatch, achieving 97.1% balanced classification accuracy across five tested surfaces.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating in dynamic, challenging conditions such as intersections and roundabouts must guarantee collision avoidance under uncertainty while maintaining real-time feasibility. Most existing planners struggle to simultaneously guarantee both requirements. Chance-constrained formulations embed safety constraints directly in the optimization but become infeasible as uncertainty compounds; deterministic planners provide feasible solutions but fail to address the uncertainty that causes collisions; end-to-end learned policies provide neither guarantee in an interpretable form. We present a modular perception-prediction-planning pipeline that closes this gap by propagating uncertainty as structured, interpretable quantities across module boundaries. Rather than embedding probabilistic risk directly in the optimization, our pipeline resolves collision probabilities upstream and constructs convex safe sets within which the planner provides a guaranteed feasible solution at every cycle -- decoupling the safety guarantee from solver feasibility. Across Monte Carlo trials in a four-way unsignalized intersection, our pipeline achieves 0% collisions and 0% solver infeasibility at 12.7ms per cycle, compared to 36% and 10% collision rates for deterministic and chance-constrained baselines respectively. The ablation study confirms the necessity of each uncertainty source and the hardware deployment on Clearpath Jackal UGVs validates the pipeline's real-time viability on physical platforms.
authors: Doris Xu, Jin Hyun Park, Guadalupe Alvarado Fernandez, Adhyan Prasad, Mark Campbell
bullets: Targets safe, feasible autonomous driving in uncertain dynamic scenarios such as intersections and roundabouts.
Propagates structured uncertainty through modular perception, prediction, and planning components.
Resolves collision probabilities upstream and builds convex safe sets for a guaranteed feasible planner solution each cycle.
In four-way unsignalized-intersection Monte Carlo trials, it reported 0% collisions, 0% solver infeasibility, and 12.7 ms per cycle.
Ablations and Clearpath Jackal UGV deployment support the importance of the uncertainty sources and real-time physical viability.
papers.selection_reason: Uncertainty-aware perception-prediction-planning pipeline for collision avoidance in autonomous vehicles; directly relevant to robot navigation and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Interpretable Collision Avoidance and Feasibility Guarantees through an Uncertainty Aware Pipeline
papers.tldr: An interpretable uncertainty-aware AV pipeline separates collision-risk handling from planning to guarantee both collision avoidance and feasible real-time solutions.

papers.abstract: In a decentralized multi-robot team under partial observability, the fact that decides a robot's next action is often visible only to a teammate. Existing decentralized methods communicate kinematic information, such as position or planned trajectory, which cannot convey what the teammate perceives. Learned communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) can carry perceptual content, but the resulting messages are task-coupled and opaque. We propose Latent Telepathy. Each robot broadcasts the perceptual latent vector it already computes for its own use, the output of an encoder trained with a self-supervised joint-embedding predictive objective, frozen, and shared across the team. A teammate learns to act on it from task reward alone. Because the encoder already runs for perception, the message costs no additional computation and a single compact vector of bandwidth. Because the encoder is frozen before any policy is trained, the message means the same thing to every robot, and the receiving robot is never told what it means. We evaluate Latent Telepathy with a content-controlled protocol in which bandwidth, latency, topology and receiver are held fixed and only the message content varies. Broadcasting the latent lets a navigator avoid an occluded hazard in 99.7% of episodes, matching a noiseless hand-designed message. Position and trajectory messages remain at chance, and the raw camera image, 186 times wider, is less reliable than the compressed latent. The result holds from a discrete gridworld to rendered pixels under continuous velocity control, and the encoder decodes the hazard from a physical robot's camera in 102 of 102 live decisions. We also identify a requirement for porting MARL communication results to continuous control, that the decision a message informs must remain reachable by exploration, and show how to restore it.
bullets: Addresses partial observability where critical perceptual information is visible only to another robot.
Broadcasts each robot’s existing frozen perceptual latent, avoiding extra computation and using one compact message vector.
The shared encoder gives messages consistent meaning across robots while receivers learn to use them from task reward alone.
Latent messages enabled hazard avoidance in 99.7% of episodes, matched a noiseless hand-designed signal, and outperformed position, trajectory, and raw-image messages.
Results span gridworld, rendered pixels with continuous control, and 102/102 live physical-robot decisions; successful transfer requires the informed action to remain reachable through exploration.
papers.selection_reason: Decentralized multi-robot navigation using self-supervised perceptual latent communication to avoid occluded hazards.
papers.title: Latent Telepathy: Multi-Robot Communication with Self-Supervised Perceptual Latents
papers.tldr: Latent Telepathy enables robots to share actionable visual information through compact, shared self-supervised perceptual latents, allowing teammates to avoid occluded hazards without task-specific message semantics.

papers.abstract: Self-play in high-throughput simulators yields driving policies with robust closed-loop performance, but improvement per unit of simulation diminishes as training scales. Policies learn to handle common situations early, while further rollouts repeatedly encounter unresolved failures. Post-training offers an opportunity to target these failures, but existing methods primarily evaluate alternative actions or continuations at visited states, although successful recovery may require changing driving style earlier. We propose CounterPlay, a counterfactual self-play post-training approach that backtracks from failed tasks and retries them under alternate driving styles. CounterPlay rests on three key components. First, failure-driven backtracking uses the policy's value estimates to select an earlier stored state from which to retry the task. Second, reward conditioning enables a single policy to retry the task from this state using candidate styles ranging from cautious to aggressive. Third, CounterPlay retains task-completing retries only if no other vehicle incurs a new or earlier collision or off-road event relative to the factual branch. Retries that pass verification with fresh randomness are then distilled into the policy under its deployment condition. On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both the Interactive and Random splits across all eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions, which is just 1% of the anchor's 100B self-play training budget. Improvements over the anchor hold across all three evaluated driving styles. CounterPlay resolves a substantial fraction of the anchor's timeout cases on BehaviorBench and achieves a balance between task completion and safety that neither continued self-play nor adopting a more aggressive driving style attains.
bullets: Targets diminishing self-play gains by focusing on unresolved failures rather than repeatedly sampling common situations.
Backtracks from failures to an earlier state selected using value estimates, then retries with styles from cautious to aggressive via reward conditioning.
Keeps only verified retries that complete the task without introducing earlier or additional collisions or off-road events.
Distills successful retries into the policy under its normal deployment condition.
On BehaviorBench, reaches state-of-the-art scores across eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions—1% of the anchor’s 100B self-play budget—and resolves many timeout cases.
papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual post-training for self-play driving policies improves learned navigation and planning policies, directly relevant to embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: CounterPlay: Counterfactual Post-Training for Self-Play Driving Policies
papers.tldr: CounterPlay improves self-play driving policies by replaying failed tasks from earlier states with alternative driving styles, achieving strong results with far less post-training simulation.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.
Reports higher success and modestly better path efficiency than WMNav on HM3D v0.1 and MP3D.
On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.
papers.selection_reason: The paper presents HGWM, a hierarchical system for zero-shot object navigation that integrates LLM-generated priors with persistent spatial-semantic memory. It uses a graph-matching approach to combine visual observations with language instructions, directly fitting the Vision-Language Navigation and Robot Navigation subtopics, and utilizes persistent memory for the Embodied Memory subtopic.
papers.title: HGWM: Hierarchical Graph-Guided World Model for Zero-Shot Object Navigation via Graph Matching
papers.tldr: HGWM improves zero-shot object navigation by combining an LLM-derived room prior with persistent graph-based spatial-semantic memory and hierarchical graph matching.

papers.abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multimodal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird's eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
authors: Samuel Triest, Amirreza Shaban, David D. Fan, Wenshan Wang, Sebastian Scherer
bullets: Addresses robust traversability estimation under limited sensing, complex terrain, and high-speed motion.
Builds a geometric-semantic voxel map from onboard multimodal sensors using visual foundation models.
Jointly predicts BEV geometry, semantics, speed, and cost with annotation-free self-supervised learning, including map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning.
Ablations show that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting improve planning quality, with their combination needed for state-of-the-art off-road planning.
Real-world experiments report 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal when combining inpainting with uncertainty-based risk estimation.
papers.selection_reason: Presents self-supervised IRL-based traversability learning and terrain estimation for off-road robot navigation, relevant to learned planning and control.
papers.title: TravSUITE: Traversability via Self-Supervised, Uncertainty-Aware IRL and Terrain Estimation
papers.tldr: TravSUITE enables faster, safer off-road robot navigation by combining VFM-based mapping, self-supervised traversability learning, and uncertainty-aware risk adaptation.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.
authors: Yan Shi, Kehua Chen, Jiarui Qi, Yihong Tang, Haichen Liao, Yinhai Wang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in MLLM-based driving, where committing to one interpretation can cause premature errors.
Uses particle-filter-inspired belief tracking: a VLM propagates, scores, and resamples diverse scene hypotheses as observations arrive.
On Bench2Drive, improves Driving Score from 68.50 to 81.37 and Success Rate from 41.36% to 54.09%.
Shows the largest gains in ambiguous situations, including unsignalized intersections and oncoming-traffic interactions.
Also improves interactive behaviors such as merging, emergency braking, and giving way.
papers.selection_reason: Closed-loop MLLM-based autonomous driving with belief tracking directly fits embodied navigation and vision-language-action.
papers.title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriveMind improves closed-loop autonomous driving by maintaining and updating multiple scene hypotheses across frames instead of reasoning from scratch each time.

papers.abstract: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.
authors: Carson Kohlbrenner, Niraj Pudasaini, William Xie, Naren Sivagnanadasan, Nikolaus Correll, Alessandro Roncone
bullets: Whole-body proximity sensors provide useful inductive biases for reflexive collision avoidance.
Lossy, low-resolution sensing outperformed high-resolution coverage as a learning bias.
Anticipating future contact location and timing unexpectedly reduced sample efficiency.
Eight sensor representations were evaluated in reinforcement-learning simulations with over 200 humanoid robots.
The study focuses on end-to-end dodgeball behavior under intentionally constrained resources.
papers.selection_reason: Studies learned collision avoidance and sensor representations for humanoid robots under an RL setting, relevant to obstacle avoidance and robot learning.
papers.title: Move, don't think: sample-efficient collision avoidance with lossy proximity sensors
papers.tldr: Low-resolution, lossy proximity sensing can help robots learn collision avoidance more efficiently than richer sensing under tight data and compute limits.

papers.abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read-decide-execute-check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision-language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator-selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.
authors: Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Weizhe Tang, Bofeng Cao, Sikai Chen, Xiaopeng Li, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the correct path among multiple geometrically plausible work-zone routes.
Generates candidate paths geometrically, then fuses geometric scores with agreement to a VLM-predicted trajectory.
Trains the VLM to identify lane status and hazard side before making a passage decision, with rule-based intervention for control compliance.
On 2,306 ROADWork episodes, SAGE reduces average displacement error by 8.3%, final displacement error by 12.0%, and hard-constraint violations by 37% versus the geometric ranker.
The approach improves all tested generator-selector combinations and is competitive with or better than adapted driving VLMs on reported accuracy and safety measures.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-grounded pathway prediction for work-zone driving, combining geometric candidate generation with spatial/control reasoning; relevant to robot navigation and spatial VLM grounding.
papers.title: SAGE: A hybrid vision-language and geometry framework for work-zone pathway prediction under temporary traffic control
papers.tldr: SAGE combines geometric candidate paths with vision-language reasoning to select safer, MUTCD-compliant routes through temporary work zones.

papers.abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
authors: Jiawei Chen, Yinxi Wang, Zihan Yang, Meijun Gao, Yaowei Liu, Shuming Zhang, Zecheng Li, Xiangju Mi, Yuxuan Liu, Runzhong Huang, Tianlin Li, Xun Zhang, Zhengyang Wang, Xu Miao, Tong Yang
bullets: Addresses the limitation of relying directly on representations shaped by generic vision pretraining.
Uses Representation Residuals, a compact transformer over multilevel features from multiple vision foundation models.
Jointly trains navigation with a JEPA-style latent “dream” that predicts the next scene representation before each action.
Reports new state-of-the-art results across VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and point-goal benchmarks, with gains transferring to a physical robot.
The learned latent predicts future depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy without direct occupancy supervision; its scope is navigation-focused and evaluated on the stated benchmarks and robot setting.
papers.selection_reason: Navigation foundation model with self-constructed visual representations and latent next-state prediction; state-of-the-art on VLN and robot navigation benchmarks.
papers.title: See What I Need, Dream What I Want: A Navigation Foundation Model on a Self-Constructed Representation Space
papers.tldr: RepresentNav learns a task-specific visual representation and predicts future scene states in latent space, substantially improving navigation and reducing collisions across simulated and real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion over complex terrain requires anticipating footholds that may no longer be visible at touchdown. Limited camera coverage and self-occlusion make it necessary to retrieve relevant terrain information from earlier observations. We present FootQuery, a perceptive locomotion framework that queries depth history using each foot's predicted next touchdown. The policy predicts touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception and uses these distributions, together with per-foot features, to query sparsely sampled historical depth frames. During training, realized contacts are projected into historical images to supervise retrieval at the regions where those contacts were visible. The retrieved per-foot features are fused with global visual memory to generate control actions. A progressive force-assistance curriculum supports early exploration, while event-consistent tread-midline shaping encourages coordinated stair contacts. Deployment requires only proprioception and onboard depth images. In simulation, the complete framework outperforms its component ablations on the most challenging tested stairs, gaps, and platforms. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate continuous traversal with a single policy across outdoor stairs and indoor routes combining stair ascent and descent, platforms, and gaps. These results support organizing visual history around anticipated contacts for perceptive humanoid locomotion.
bullets: Addresses limited camera coverage and self-occlusion that can hide footholds before touchdown.
Predicts per-foot touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception, then queries relevant regions in sparsely sampled historical depth frames.
Supervises retrieval using projected realized contacts and fuses retrieved per-foot features with global visual memory for control.
Uses force-assistance curriculum training and tread-midline shaping to support exploration and coordinated stair contacts.
Outperforms component ablations in challenging simulated terrain and enables real-world traversal of stairs, platforms, and gaps with one policy.
papers.selection_reason: Future-touchdown-guided depth history retrieval for humanoid locomotion fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: FootQuery: Future-Touchdown-Guided Retrieval from Depth History for Perceptive Humanoid Locomotion
papers.tldr: FootQuery improves humanoid locomotion on complex terrain by retrieving historical depth information around each foot’s predicted future touchdown location.

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context. A bearing-sector interface provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status. It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle. Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m), including night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone. On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff: RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails. This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.
bullets: Targets reflections, glare, motion-induced waterline shifts, and darkness that undermine RGB-based obstacle detection.
Fuses RGB, LWIR, FMCW mmWave radar, and inertial context, exposing calibrated bearing-sector obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status to navigation.
Distinguishes sensor dropout from valid obstacle-free observations, supporting predictable degradation during multimodal failures.
In eight held-out low-light recordings, calibrated fusion reached AP 0.869 and ECE 0.108; RGB alone had higher AP (0.903) when usable, while fusion preserved sensing when RGB failed.
A 24-leg, 351 m lake pilot included night operation using LWIR and radar without usable RGB; scope is limited to the reported lake recordings and pilot conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Context-aware multimodal obstacle perception and sensor-status modeling support autonomous surface vessel navigation.
papers.title: Context-Aware RGB-Thermal-Radar Obstacle Perception for Resource-Constrained ASVs
papers.tldr: A context-aware RGB-LWIR-radar fusion system helps resource-constrained ASVs maintain calibrated obstacle perception when RGB cameras degrade or fail, including at night.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.
bullets: Addresses safe aerial navigation when accurate ground-truth obstacle data is unavailable.
Uses a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to encode detailed scene geometry.
Introduces a reachability-based planner exploiting quadrotor differential flatness.
Computes continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate vehicle occupancy.
Finds paths in 81.2% of challenging test cases, compared with 51.2% for the nearest baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Risk-aware quadrotor motion planning using a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting scene representation; relevant to robot navigation and 3D scene modeling.
papers.title: AirSplan: Risk-Aware Motion Planning for Quadrotors in Cluttered 3D Gaussian Splats
papers.tldr: AirSplan combines high-fidelity 3D Gaussian Splatting with risk-aware reachability planning to find collision-free quadrotor paths in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Collision-free motion planning requires reliable collision models from sensed environments and validation of states along a continuous trajectory. To make this tractable, most planners check for collision at discrete states along continuous trajectories against a single determinized model of the environment, introducing a trade-off between safety and computational efficiency. While continuous collision checking approaches that approximate the swept volume of the robot exist, they are computationally expensive or overly conservative. Data-driven approaches can learn the swept volume; however, these neural models are susceptible to approximation errors and are therefore often limited to serving as coarse filters for downstream collision checkers. In this work, we propose to learn a signed distance function of the swept volume as a probabilistic field, enabling quantification of epistemic uncertainty, incorporation of perception noise, and eventual integration into a chance-constrained trajectory optimization framework. We demonstrate our approach on challenging high-dimensional manipulation problems with significant sensor noise, both in simulation and on real hardware.
bullets: Addresses the safety–efficiency trade-off of discrete collision checks and costly or conservative continuous swept-volume approximations.
Learns the swept volume as a probabilistic signed distance field rather than a deterministic neural approximation.
Models epistemic uncertainty and incorporates perception noise for more reliable collision reasoning.
Targets integration with chance-constrained trajectory optimization.
Demonstrated on high-dimensional manipulation tasks in simulation and on real hardware with significant sensor noise.
papers.selection_reason: Learned probabilistic swept-volume signed distance field for chance-constrained trajectory optimization; relevant to learned planning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Stochastic Neural Signed Swept Volume for Real-time Chance-Constrained Trajectory Optimization
papers.tldr: A probabilistic neural signed-distance model of robot swept volumes enables uncertainty-aware, chance-constrained trajectory optimization under noisy perception.

papers.abstract: Temporary obstacles that may block a robot's planned route create a sequential navigation problem: a robot must decide whether to wait for a blockage to clear, reroute, or acquire more information about the obstacle before acting. We formulate graph navigation among temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process and introduce SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). SPARROW searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Class-conditioned survival models are learned online from both clearance observations and right-censored encounters where the robot reroutes before clearance is observed. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances as each action unfolds, so the planner can account for blockages that may occur along alternative routes. We further introduce a value-of-learning criterion that trades the immediate cost of collecting labelled survival data against its expected reduction in future navigation regret. Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR, a recent survival-based method for the same problem. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.
bullets: Models navigation with temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process.
Uses POMCP to search over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions.
Learns obstacle survival and clearance behavior online, including from right-censored rerouting encounters.
Selects information-gathering actions using a value-of-learning criterion.
Reduces mean time-to-goal by 12–26% in simulation and 20.5% on a physical robot versus OSCAR.
papers.selection_reason: POMCP-based robot routing with learned survival models and adaptive waiting/rerouting directly fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: SPARROW: Survival-POMCP for Adaptive Robot Routing, Observation, and Waiting
papers.tldr: SPARROW uses belief-space planning to help robots decide when to reroute, observe, or wait around temporary obstacles, reducing travel time in simulation and on a physical robot.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the search of each robot's tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.
authors: Shashank A. Deshpande, Blake T. Edwards, Jonathan P. How
bullets: Addresses the gap between centralized offline joint optimization and decentralized real-time navigation that lacks joint-optimality objectives.
Extends dispersive-tree search for differentially flat systems to multi-robot coordination by replacing inter-robot coupling with local constraints.
Uses decentralized column generation to negotiate shared-space “rents” and guide each robot’s tree search.
Simulation shows up to 22% lower total travel time than centralized offline planners and up to 37% lower than a decentralized real-time baseline; hardware tests use six robots.
The approach remains effective when real-time deadlines interrupt negotiation, though certification requires quiescence.
papers.selection_reason: Develops WarpWeaver, a decentralized, real-time planner for multi-robot coordination that approaches joint optimality.
papers.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
papers.tldr: WarpWeaver is a decentralized, asynchronous planner that coordinates multiple robots toward near-optimal joint motion in real time, with solutions certified at negotiation quiescence.

papers.abstract: A conventional embodied agent in an indoor environment builds a map by accumulating noisy real-world measurements and results from heavy inference to guide navigation. While the detailed measurements may differ due to scene changes or sensor settings, the unique topological structure of navigable passages or the connectivity between rooms may provide training-free guidance that complements local observations. We propose a sparse topometric graph as an efficient structural representation for robust indoor navigation, alleviating the need for fine-grained matching, which is computationally expensive, memory-intensive, and prone to real-world variations. The map consists of nodes that encode local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges that capture traversable connectivity. A learned graph-matching network finds consistent subgraph structures across sessions by considering both node-level geometric descriptors and neighborhood connectivity. The holistic contextual matching is robust to local ambiguities caused by weak distinctiveness or repetitive structure, and establishes stable correspondences despite local scene changes, different sensor modalities, or limited spatial overlap. We analyze the practicality of the graph through cross-session point-goal navigation, where a goal specified in a prior reference map must be reached from an unknown initial pose in a later session. Experiments show that our method achieves the highest success rates (77.1% on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes), while reducing memory by more than two orders of magnitude compared to point-level representations. The proposed approach further supports cross-session alignment and goal-directed navigation with strong scalability and robust real-world transfer.
authors: Eun Sun Lee, Minkyun Seo, Gwangtak Bae, Junho Kim, Seunggu Kang, Jaesik Park, Young Min Kim
bullets: Represents indoor maps with nodes for local 3D geometry and distance-weighted edges for traversable connectivity.
Uses learned graph matching over geometric descriptors and neighborhood structure to establish correspondences across sessions.
Handles local ambiguities, scene changes, different sensor modalities, and limited spatial overlap without training-specific fine-grained matching.
In cross-session point-goal navigation, achieves 77.1% success on Gibson and 40.0% under 3D-FRONT scene changes.
Reduces memory use by more than two orders of magnitude versus point-level representations.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse topometric graph memory and graph-matching for cross-session indoor navigation, fitting robot navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: A Sparse Topometric Graph for Scalable Cross-Session Indoor Navigation
papers.tldr: A sparse topometric graph enables scalable, robust cross-session indoor navigation by matching room connectivity and local geometry instead of fine-grained measurements.

papers.abstract: Robotic swarms must coordinate across diverse missions, yet existing controllers often require redesign, retuning, or retraining when objectives change. Here we show that probabilistic energy modeling provides a unifying representation for versatile swarm control, in which diverse missions emerge from compositions of shared interaction principles rather than task-specific control formulations. By exploiting the correspondence between Gibbs random field energy minimization and structured reward maximization, we encode fundamental swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms within a unified probabilistic objective. Decentralized policies trained within this representation are composed into a single controller through lightweight policy gating, without retraining. An interpretable action-attention mechanism captures non-uniform local interactions, while dimensionless normalization supports transfer across swarm scales and platforms. Demonstrated on aerial swarms, the unified policy generalizes zero-shot across six mission classes, 10-100 agents, two hardware platforms, and indoor cluttered and GPS-denied woodland environments. Large-scale simulations achieve 0.96-1.00 task success rates with 1-10 ms per-agent inference latency, while physical deployments confirm zero-shot transfer to real platforms and unstructured environments. These results establish probabilistic energy modeling as a scalable and transferable framework for decentralized swarm control.
authors: Xiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhu, Xintong Wang, Qingyuan Yang, Rui Huang, Feng Xue, Lin Li, Qingrui Zhang
bullets: Represents diverse swarm behaviors as reusable energy terms combined in a unified probabilistic objective.
Uses Gibbs energy minimization, structured reward maximization, policy gating, and interpretable action attention.
Supports zero-shot generalization across six mission classes, 10–100 agents, two aerial platforms, and challenging environments.
Reports 0.96–1.00 simulated task success with 1–10 ms per-agent inference latency; physical tests confirm transfer.
Scope: demonstrated for aerial swarms and the evaluated missions, scales, platforms, and environments.
papers.selection_reason: Unified probabilistic energy model for decentralized swarm navigation and control; fits learned navigation policies.
papers.title: Probabilistic Energy Modeling Unifies Versatile Swarm Control
papers.tldr: Probabilistic energy modeling enables one decentralized swarm controller to transfer across missions, swarm sizes, platforms, and environments without retraining.

papers.abstract: Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts face a practical question in unseen regions: can they rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the planner itself adapt? We study this question using a planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none of eight test-time routing schemes improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default, which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an oracle that selects the best expert for each scene reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 m. In contrast, reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 target-region scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean offset of 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 m for the static default. Comparisons under the same target-region training budget show that target-region training drives the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning across training cities also improves open-loop offsets, although closed-loop performance deteriorates. Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate trajectories. These results show the limited headroom for selecting among existing experts and the greater open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
authors: Yun Li, Ehsan Javanmardi, Simon Thompson, Jiachen Gong, Qunli Zhang, Zifan Zeng, Shiming Liu, Peng Wang, Yidu Zhang, Manabu Tsukada
bullets: Across three held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes beats the static default in fleet-mean lateral offset.
Even oracle expert selection improves mean offset by only 0.9 m.
Reward-based fine-tuning on 20 target-region scenes reduces matched offset from 12.4 m to 6.9 m with joint replay.
Target-region training drives the gains, while replay helps limit forgetting on original operating domains.
Some adaptation baselines achieve low offsets through degenerate trajectories; nuPlan results show open-loop gains but closed-loop deterioration.
papers.selection_reason: Studies routing versus adaptation for diffusion planners, with test-time adaptation and target-domain fine-tuning for navigation planning.
papers.title: To Route or to Adapt? Multi-Expert Diffusion Planners in Unseen Regions
papers.tldr: Adapting a diffusion planner with limited target-region training substantially outperforms routing among existing domain experts in unseen regions, though closed-loop performance may worsen.

papers.abstract: Flexible robotic endoscopes provide access through tortuous anatomy, where friction, deformation, and wall interaction separate commanded insertion from useful distal progress. Operators interpret this mismatch and retreat to recover a navigable configuration. Recognizing the approach to that decision requires relating motor intent to distal response and the local visual scene. We introduce Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion (MPRF), a causal model that anticipates operator retreat from commands, electromagnetic (EM) tracking, and endoscopic video. A nominal-progress model predicts the response expected in normal or successful navigation; a temporal predictor combines its EM residual with all three observed modalities. In a 150-episode colon-phantom collection, MPRF achieves 0.580 +/- 0.007 AUPRC across three seeds, compared with 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control. Complete multimodal histories provide the principal ranking advantage, while the residual adds an explicit intent-response representation with a small, uncertain increment over raw fusion. Analysis of frozen alarms relates warning timing to the behavioral label and explains the increase in event recall under a longer matching window. These results establish a basis for behavioral assistance during operator-controlled navigation.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Tianchun Wu, Jiatan Sun, Yuming Sun, Jianru Zhang, Hongliang Ren
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between commanded insertion and useful distal progress caused by friction, deformation, and wall interaction.
Uses a nominal-progress model to estimate expected navigation response, then combines its EM residual with commands, tracking, and video in a causal temporal predictor.
Evaluated on 150 colon-phantom episodes, achieving 0.580 ± 0.007 AUPRC versus 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control.
Complete multimodal histories provide the main ranking benefit; the residual representation adds only a small, uncertain improvement over raw fusion.
Frozen-alarm analysis links warning timing to retreat labels and explains improved event recall with a longer matching window.
papers.selection_reason: Causal multimodal prediction of navigation retreat in robotic endoscopy; relevant to learned navigation and shared control.
papers.title: Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion for Anticipating Navigation Retreat in Robotic Flexible Endoscopy
papers.tldr: MPRF anticipates when operators will retreat during robotic flexible endoscopy by fusing commands, EM-tracked motion residuals, and endoscopic video.

papers.abstract: This paper presents TRACE, a traversability-aware reactive navigation framework designed for the autonomous operation of ground robots in unstructured forest environments. Unlike traditional approaches, TRACE leverages VLM-based confidence maps from positive and negative natural-language prompt sets and combines them through evidential fusion to produce a dense traversability map that prioritizes the terrain based on signs of previously traversed paths. Traversability-annotated points are then extracted and used to derive the left and right boundaries of the traversable path via percentile binning followed by spline or regularized polynomial fitting. These boundaries are then incorporated as soft barrier constraints within an NMPC formulation, enabling safe and adaptive path following in complex natural environments. Rigorous experimental trials carried out in real-life forest environments demonstrate TRACE ability for smooth navigation in cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrains.
authors: Mario A. V. Saucedo, Midhun Edatharam Kunnath, Elias Small, Akash Patel, Shruti Kotpalliwar, Christoforos Kanellakis, George Nikolakopoulos
bullets: Builds dense traversability maps by fusing VLM confidence from positive and negative natural-language prompts.
Prioritizes terrain showing signs of previously traversed paths.
Estimates traversable-path boundaries using percentile binning and spline or regularized polynomial fitting.
Injects the estimated boundaries as soft barrier constraints into an NMPC controller.
Real-world forest trials demonstrate smooth navigation through cluttered, deformable, and visually ambiguous terrain.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-driven traversability constraints for reactive navigation in unstructured terrain.
papers.title: TRACE: Traversability-aware Reactive Navigation via VLM-driven Adaptive Constraints Estimation
