papers.title: LynxScenes: A Large-Scale Real-World Benchmark for Outdoor Wheel-Legged Robot Perception, Navigation, Imagination and Reconstruction
papers.tldr: LynxScenes is a large-scale real-world benchmark for evaluating outdoor wheel-legged robot perception, navigation, future-scene reasoning, and reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Unknown payloads alter robot dynamics and make precise contact execution difficult when foothold margins are small. We present LOAD, a perceptive locomotion framework that combines explicit inertial estimates with implicit dynamics features for narrow-beam traversal. Separate recurrent modules infer torso inertial changes and task-relevant history from proprioception, while a height-map teacher is distilled into a depth-based student. We extensively evaluate LOAD and its variants in simulation and on hardware across beam widths and payload configurations. The results show that implicit dynamics features accelerate training, while explicit inertial estimation further improves traversal success; combining both enables LOAD to approach the performance of a privileged policy supplied with ground-truth inertial parameters. Hardware experiments demonstrate traversal with unilateral payloads of 6 kg on a 10 cm beam and 9 kg on a 15 cm beam, and an evenly distributed 11 kg payload on a 15 cm beam. These results support combining physical estimates and history features for precision locomotion under unknown loads.
authors: Kunzhao Ren, Zhishuo Zhu, Xiaobin Xiong
bullets: Targets precision footholds when payload changes make robot dynamics uncertain.
Uses recurrent proprioceptive modules for explicit inertial estimation and implicit task-history features.
Distills a height-map teacher into a depth-based student for perceptive locomotion.
Combining both feature types approaches a privileged policy with ground-truth inertial parameters.
Hardware tests demonstrate loaded traversal on narrow beams, including unilateral and distributed payloads.
papers.selection_reason: Learned perceptive locomotion with online dynamics awareness for precision footholds, relevant to robot navigation and learning.
papers.title: Locomotion with Online Awareness of Dynamics for Precision Footholds
papers.tldr: LOAD combines estimated inertial changes and learned dynamics history to help robots traverse narrow beams precisely under unknown payloads.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in real-world environments often requires long-horizon operation under partial observability and evolving goals. Existing mapless navigation approaches predominantly assume fixed goals throughout an episode, limiting applicability to practical scenarios where goals change online during execution. We study online chained-goal navigation, where goals evolve through existing-goal redirection or new-goal emergence without explicit transition signals. Under this setting, we find navigation may require either continued exploration or strategic revisitation, creating conflicting memory requirements. We propose Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Belief Learning (GLST), a memory-decomposition framework that separates latent beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations for long-horizon reasoning. We further introduce goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation under evolving goals. Extensive experiments in simulation across diverse terrains demonstrate improved chained-goal navigation performance over baselines. Real-robot experiments using the Spot quadruped further validate our memory decomposition framework.
authors: Yousef Liang, Ryan Ardalan, Yarden Goraly, Chenhao Zhu, Yue Yin, Jonas Frey, Claire Tomlin, Marco Pavone, Shankar Sastry
bullets: Targets chained-goal navigation under partial observability, where goals may be redirected or newly introduced without explicit transition signals.
Separates latent beliefs into global/local spatial and long/short temporal representations to support exploration and strategic revisitation.
Uses goal-conditioned rewards to balance exploration and exploitation as goals evolve.
Experiments in simulated diverse terrains and on a Spot quadruped show improved chained-goal navigation over baselines.
The approach is evaluated in simulation and real-robot settings; broader scope beyond these settings is not established in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a memory decomposition framework (GLST) for online chained-goal navigation that separates beliefs into global-local spatial and long-short temporal representations, directly addressing long-horizon reasoning and memory requirements in embodied agents.
papers.title: GLST: Global-Local Spatio-Temporal Memory Decomposition Framework for Online Chained-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: GLST enables mapless robots to navigate long-horizon environments with goals that change online by decomposing memory across spatial and temporal scales.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.
authors: Shuzheng Wang, Haoxuan Li, Shengzhen Li, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Uses a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture with separate World, Language, and Action experts.
Introduces Cross-Expert Attention to align semantic and dynamic representations through controlled information exchange.
Applies Flow-GRPO reinforcement-learning post-training to improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning.
Reports 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, with strong open- and closed-loop performance.
Shows zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive without specific fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Unified world-language-action model for autonomous driving, directly covering trajectory generation, future dynamics, and semantic understanding.
papers.title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: DriveWLA unifies scene semantics, future dynamics, and trajectory generation in one World-Language-Action model for autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Collision rate remains a dominant metric for evaluating autonomous driving trajectory safety, but its binary nature obscures substantial safety differences among collision-free trajectories. Existing surrogate-safety metrics provide finer-grained assessments, yet often trade off physical interpretability against adaptivity to interaction context. We introduce FutureRisk, a continuous metric that quantifies the latent future risk of a trajectory by how closely and persistently its realized interactions approach unsafe states. At its core, our Context-Adaptive Risk Model (CARM) combines a context-dependent safety-time distribution with an independently supervised critical-event-time distribution. Its safety criterion is bounded around a closed-form physical prior, while a bounded residual provides additional adaptation without abandoning this physical anchor. Experiments on DeepAccident and Bench2Drive show that FutureRisk achieves stronger agreement with native collision labels than existing surrogate-safety measures, discriminates risk among collision-free trajectories, and transfers zero-shot across datasets. Comparisons across four planners further show that FutureRisk reveals safety differences hidden by binary collision outcomes. Together, these results establish FutureRisk as a fine-grained, interpretable, and context-adaptive metric for trajectory safety evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/Xuewen2025/safety-evaluation.
authors: Xuewen Luo, Linlian Jiang, Bo Yu, Fan Ding, Xinxin Zuo, Yang Wang
bullets: Collision rate cannot distinguish safety differences between collision-free trajectories.
FutureRisk estimates risk from how closely and persistently interactions approach unsafe states.
Its Context-Adaptive Risk Model combines context-dependent safety-time and supervised critical-event-time distributions.
A bounded physical prior and residual preserve interpretability while enabling interaction-aware adaptation.
On DeepAccident and Bench2Drive, it better agrees with collision labels, separates collision-free risks, and transfers zero-shot across datasets.
papers.selection_reason: Learned context-adaptive trajectory safety metric for autonomous driving, transferable to navigation planning evaluation.
papers.title: Which Trajectory Is Safer? Combining Rule and Learning for Safety Evaluation
papers.tldr: FutureRisk combines physical safety rules with learned context adaptation to provide a continuous, interpretable measure of autonomous-driving trajectory risk.

papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables driving policies to adapt to changing deployment conditions, but requires safe exploration throughout training. Safety filtering alone does not ensure stable policy improvement or reduced dependence on corrections. We propose Safe Online Adaptive Refinement (SOAR-Flow), a framework for safe and stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized Flow-based driving policies. A control barrier function (CBF)--model predictive control (MPC) filter corrects potentially unsafe actions before execution. To support stable policy updates, we introduce Gaussian-return-aware value calibration based on calibrated Q-learning (Cal-QL), using recorded behavior returns and predicted return variability to smooth conservative critic updates and mitigate policy degradation. Paired corrective learning teaches feasible action adjustments, while an intervention-to-go predictor encourages decisions requiring fewer future corrections. Its predictions also regulate guidance strength, allowing recovery supervision to weaken as predicted dependence decreases. Together with gradually reduced calibration regularization, this supports continued task improvement while preserving hard execution constraints. We analyze conditions for safe execution at control steps and diminishing auxiliary learning influences. We evaluate SOAR-Flow in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV). The results demonstrate improved driving performance and reduced reliance on safety corrections during protected online fine-tuning. The demonstration video and project overview are available at https://lzqw.github.io/SOAR-Flow/.
authors: Zeqiao Li, Yijing Wang, Haoyu Wang, Zheng Li, Zhiqiang Zuo
bullets: Addresses unstable policy improvement and persistent safety-correction dependence during online RL for autonomous driving.
Combines a CBF–MPC safety filter with Gaussian-return-aware value calibration to enforce safe actions and mitigate policy degradation.
Uses paired corrective learning and an intervention-to-go predictor to guide feasible actions and adaptively reduce recovery supervision.
Evaluated in simulation and on an uncrewed ground vehicle, showing improved driving performance and fewer safety corrections during protected fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Safe online RL fine-tuning of driving policies with CBF-MPC filtering, relevant to learned navigation and robot RL.
papers.title: Beyond Safe Execution: Safe Online Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving with Value Calibration and Adaptive Guidance
papers.tldr: SOAR-Flow enables safer, more stable online fine-tuning of offline-initialized driving policies while reducing reliance on corrective interventions.

papers.abstract: Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world-action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world-action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world-action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.
authors: Qihang Huang, Wenhui Huang, Collister Chua, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Songyan Zhang, Zhidong Wang, Daiying Tian, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses limited reciprocal interaction in hierarchical and parallel occupancy-aware planning methods.
Generates dense scene occupancy and continuous ego trajectories jointly from scene representations.
First predicts scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory, then refines ego-centric occupancy and motion in future ego frames.
Uses explicit semantic geometry rather than pixel synthesis for direct planning reasoning.
Reports state-of-the-art results in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction on Bench2Drive and nuScenes.
papers.selection_reason: OccWAM proposes a joint occupancy and trajectory generation model via flow matching for autonomous driving, preserving semantic geometry for planning.
papers.title: OccWAM: Occupancy World-Action Models with Joint Scene-to-Ego Flow Matching
papers.tldr: OccWAM jointly predicts future occupancy and ego trajectories through two-stage scene-to-ego flow matching for geometry-aware autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.
authors: Bowen Feng, Keqin Wang, Yulong Yang, Amogh Joshi, Christine Allen-Blanchette, Dhruv Shah, Felix Heide
bullets: Addresses the cost of manually annotating language-conditioned robotic navigation and reasoning.
Uses an open-source VLM as both a self-teacher and student policy; the teacher infers navigation goals and reasoning from privileged trajectory feedback.
The student uses onboard observations to predict future ego-frame trajectories and describe scene semantics, plans, and reasoning.
Evaluated on 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks.
Reports 30% higher success than the strongest baseline indoors and on multi-stage tasks, plus 95% success on outdoor tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Language-conditioned navigation policy via action self-distillation; directly fits embodied navigation and VLA.
papers.title: Training Generalist Navigation Policies via Action Self-Distillation
papers.tldr: Action Self-Distillation trains language-conditioned generalist navigation policies without human language or reasoning annotations by distilling privileged trajectory feedback from a vision-language model.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot exploration under communication and mobility constraints requires balancing information gain with reachability. We present a distributed semantic exploration framework that combines Dirichlet mapping, budget-constrained trajectory selection, and Resource-Aware distributed Greedy (RAG) coordination. Each robot clusters frontiers, computes terrain- and heading-aware least-cost paths with a single budget-limited Dijkstra search, and selects feasible paths by marginal information gain, represented by the expected reduction in Dirichlet entropy. Each robot's per-round selection is exact, the team's joint per-round information gain is at least half the centralized optimum, and the bound degrades gracefully under limited communication. Ten-run gridworld ablations show improved coverage, semantic mIoU, and map certainty with lower entropy and traversal cost per unit distance than shortest-distance frontier selection. Budget-sensitivity experiments show that an intermediate budget best balances path reach and receding-horizon execution. In photorealistic full-system simulation against five coordination rules run in their native published forms, the proposed method attains the highest mean coverage and semantic accuracy while being the only one that respects the per-trajectory mobility budget.
authors: Changxuan Yao, Sandilya Sai Garimella, Lu Gan, Panagiotis Tsiotras
bullets: Uses Dirichlet mapping, semantic frontier clustering, and terrain- and heading-aware budget-limited path planning.
Coordinates robot choices with Resource-Aware distributed Greedy (RAG) using expected Dirichlet-entropy reduction as marginal information gain.
Each robot selects exactly per round; the team achieves at least half the centralized per-round information gain, with graceful degradation under limited communication.
Gridworld ablations report improved coverage, semantic mIoU, and map certainty, alongside lower entropy and traversal cost per unit distance than shortest-distance selection.
Photorealistic simulation reports the highest mean coverage and semantic accuracy among five native coordination baselines while uniquely satisfying mobility budgets.
papers.selection_reason: Distributed semantic multi-robot exploration framework that optimizes trajectory selection under mobility and communication constraints.
papers.title: Mobility-Budget-Constrained Submodular Maximization for Distributed Semantic Multi-Robot Exploration
papers.tldr: A distributed multi-robot exploration method jointly optimizes semantic information gain and mobility-limited reachability, achieving strong coverage and semantic mapping while respecting trajectory budgets.

papers.abstract: We propose ATOM (Abstract Transition and Option Modeling), a hierarchical navigation framework that combines higher-level graph planning with reusable lower-level option policies for efficient repeated navigation in large-scale 3D environments represented by hierarchical structures such as 3D scene graphs (3DSGs). ATOM operates on a hierarchical graph representation, implemented using, for instance, the Rooms and Places layers of a 3DSG, where each directed abstract transition is associated with a navigation option. For each transition, ATOM computes and stores a reusable option policy along with its state-dependent cost-to-go. Across repeated navigation tasks, ATOM maintains a smoothed empirical distribution over option initiation states and uses it to progressively refine the corresponding abstract transition cost. Ablation studies show that ATOM reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% relative to a monolithic MDP baseline while maintaining trajectories within approximately 7% of a Global Places A* shortest-path reference. Experience-informed refinement further reduces abstract transition-cost estimation error by 10.3%. Physical experiments validate ATOM on an F1Tenth vehicle, successfully completing all five navigation queries with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing previously generated solutions.
bullets: Uses hierarchical scene-graph transitions for high-level planning and option policies for low-level navigation.
Stores each option’s policy and state-dependent cost-to-go for reuse across tasks.
Refines abstract transition costs using a smoothed distribution of observed option initiation states.
Reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% versus a monolithic MDP baseline while keeping trajectories within approximately 7% of a shortest-path reference.
Physical F1Tenth experiments completed all five queries, with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing prior solutions.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical navigation framework combining graph planning with reusable option policies for efficient large-scale 3D navigation.
papers.title: ATOM: Abstract Transition and Option Modeling - Experience-Informed Hierarchical Navigation
papers.tldr: ATOM accelerates repeated navigation in large 3D environments by combining hierarchical graph planning with reusable, experience-informed navigation options.

papers.abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.
authors: Mariko Storey-Matsutani, Anatoly Zlotnik, Lee Holguin, Zigfried Hampel-Arias, Richard Linares
bullets: Addresses RPO missions spanning multiple dynamics, objectives, and constraints across mission phases.
Trains five specialized policies for orbit matching, far-range, mid-range, close-range approach, and docking.
Uses a learned high-level manager to select controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state.
Evaluates end-to-end trajectories and phase transitions against a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic.
Also analyzes training and inference metrics for individual policies and the complete hierarchy.
papers.selection_reason: Hierarchical RL for multiphase spacecraft rendezvous planning; transferable to embodied navigation and control.
papers.title: From Orbit Matching to Docking: A Hierarchical Reinforcement-Learning Approach to Multiphase Rendezvous Trajectory Design
papers.tldr: A hierarchical reinforcement-learning system autonomously manages the full spacecraft rendezvous sequence from orbit matching through docking by selecting among specialized phase controllers.

papers.abstract: Autonomous quadrotor flight in cluttered environment is an key capability for tasks like inspection and search. Navigation policies trained in simulation and transferred to hardware can fly at high speed in open space, but they can still collide as obstacle clearance shrinks. We attribute most of these collisions to a single mechanism, namely motion in directions the onboard camera does not observe. Heading that is not aligned with the direction of travel and lateral excursion during obstacle avoidance both carry the vehicle toward obstacles outside its field of view. We introduce ClearNav, a navigation policy trained with two reward terms that constrain motion to the observed direction, a forward-looking heading target and a penalty on lateral velocity. A third term penalizes speed near obstacles so that an obstacle entering the field of view remains avoidable. In simulation, across 18 held-out scenarios with 2304 paired flights per policy unseen in training, ClearNav improves success by 6.8 points, cuts the collision rate by 65% relative to the state of the arts, and flies at maximum 5m/s. For the proximity term alone under matched commanded speeds, the collision reduction still holds at 70%. The effect is significant on static scenes and consistent in direction on moving obstacles, though not significant there at the suite level, showing that safer flight in clutter is possible even on the limited sensors and compute of small drones. We also validate our navigation policy in a real-world cluttered environment, showing that it enables the quadrotor to navigate through the cluttered environment successfully and safely.
authors: Aditya Azad, Arthur Huang, Guanrui Li
bullets: Targets a key failure mode in simulation-to-hardware flight: moving toward obstacles outside the onboard camera’s field of view.
Uses rewards for forward-looking heading, low lateral velocity, and reduced speed near obstacles.
Across 18 held-out simulated scenarios, improves success by 6.8 points and reduces collisions by 65% versus prior methods.
Collision reduction remains 70% under matched commanded speeds when using the proximity term alone.
Validated in a real-world cluttered environment, with consistent benefits on static scenes but no suite-level significance on moving obstacles.
papers.selection_reason: Learned quadrotor navigation policy with obstacle avoidance and perception-aligned control, directly matching robot navigation.
papers.title: ClearNav: Perception-Aligned Quadrotor Flight Using Differential-Physics
papers.tldr: ClearNav reduces quadrotor collisions in clutter by aligning motion with the camera’s observed direction and slowing near obstacles.

papers.abstract: Robots sharing walkways need to know where people will be, yet semantic occupancy maps show only where they are. We present ReForesight, an open-source ROS 2 toolkit that adds instance-level future occupancy and re-identification after occlusion to a particle-based semantic mapping pipeline. A 36.6k-parameter MLP predicts each tracked person or vehicle up to 3 s ahead, guarded by a Kalman fallback and a stationary gate, and the object's own points are moved to the forecast pose, forming a "ghost" point cloud in the map frame without an occupancy decoder. An optional tracker re-associates objects after occlusion using keypoint descriptors the pipeline already computes and a metric 3D gate. On four held-out CODa sequences, the MLP lowers the mean 3 s final displacement error from 0.728 m (Kalman) to 0.662 m and beats a similar-size GRU (0.692 m) on every sequence, at 0.04 ms per instance on one CPU core. Code, all models, and a ROS-free demo are released; field demonstrations use an outdoor cleaning robot.
authors: Didar Seyidov, Faith Ogunwoye, Hajira Amjad, Danil Tolkachev, Yuri Sarkisov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Extends particle-based semantic mapping with instance-level future occupancy and post-occlusion re-identification.
Uses a 36.6k-parameter MLP, with Kalman fallback and a stationary-object gate, to forecast motion up to 3 seconds.
Moves tracked objects’ point clouds to predicted poses to create map-frame “ghost” occupancy without an occupancy decoder.
Optional re-association combines existing keypoint descriptors with a metric 3D gate.

On four held-out CODa sequences, the MLP achieves 0.662 m mean 3-second final displacement error versus 0.728 m for Kalman and 0.692 m for a similar-size GRU; runtime is 0.04 ms per instance on one CPU core.
papers.selection_reason: Provides learned future occupancy forecasting and re-identification for robots navigating shared dynamic environments, relevant to robot navigation.
papers.title: ReForesight: Occlusion-Robust Re-Identification and Future Occupancy Forecasting for Dynamic Semantic Mapping
papers.tldr: ReForesight enables semantic maps to forecast and re-identify people and vehicles through occlusions, improving 3-second position accuracy with minimal computation.

papers.abstract: Navigating humanoid robots through dynamic, non-convex environments requires tightly coupling onboard perception with footstep planning and dynamic locomotion control. Existing methods frequently discard complex free space through simplified convex obstacle bounds and fail to account for real-time dynamic occupancy predictions. This paper presents a real-time framework for humanoid navigation that directly constructs spatio-temporal safe corridors from LiDAR-based particle representations and couples them with Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP)-based planning and Whole Body Control (WBC) to enable navigation around and within moving non-convex structures without restrictive geometric assumptions. Simulations on the Digit humanoid yield a 96% success rate in navigating around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 by 24 m^2 arena. Ablation studies confirm that the proposed iterative polytope generation significantly outperforms single-iteration baselines in narrow corridors, while evaluations demonstrate robustness to clutter, sensor noise, control delays, and force perturbations.
bullets: Addresses the loss of usable free space and poor handling of dynamic occupancy in existing navigation methods.
Builds spatio-temporal safe corridors directly from LiDAR-based particle representations without restrictive convex obstacle assumptions.
Couples corridor generation with Linear Inverted Pendulum planning and Whole Body Control for dynamic locomotion.
In Digit simulations, achieves a 96% success rate around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 × 24 m² arena.
Shows improved narrow-corridor performance with iterative polytope generation and robustness to clutter, sensor noise, delays, and force perturbations.
papers.selection_reason: Presents real-time humanoid navigation with spatio-temporal safe corridors in dynamic non-convex environments, directly relevant to embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: LiDAR-based Humanoid Navigation in Dynamic, Non-Convex Environments via Spatio-Temporal Safe Corridors
papers.tldr: A real-time LiDAR-driven framework enables Digit humanoid navigation through moving, non-convex environments using spatio-temporal safe corridors coupled with footstep and whole-body control.

papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
authors: Delun Li, Xueyao Wei, Rui Chen, Yifei Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Models navigation where interactions change spatial connectivity, target visibility, or both sequentially.
Introduces MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark covering channel, container, and mixed tasks with interaction-necessity annotations.
Evaluates navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and interaction cost separately.
Proposes MultINav-Agent with interactive perception, expected-change action selection, and post-interaction graph verification.
Reports consistent improvements over adapted baselines across all task types.
papers.selection_reason: Interactive embodied navigation benchmark and agentic framework with persistent state-conditioned interaction graph; fits robot navigation, VLA, and embodied memory.
papers.title: Interactive Navigation Beyond Reachability: Benchmark and Agentic Framework
papers.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and agent framework for navigation tasks requiring interactions such as opening doors and containers to reach or reveal goals.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.
authors: Shengzhen Li, Yongkang Li, Hao Gao, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited representation quality and high latency caused by generic visual pretraining and dense patch processing.
Distills complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models.
Adapts the encoder to multi-frame driving and stores spatiotemporal context in register tokens for planning.
Uses register-guided token compression to reduce redundant patch computation while improving planning performance.
Reports 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Builds a knowledge-dense, token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving, improving planning and achieving 2x speedup via register-guided token compression.
papers.title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ConDenseDrive distills diverse visual knowledge into a token-sparse encoder that improves planning while delivering 2.0× faster inference for end-to-end autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.
authors: Ke Gui, Chenghao Shi, Ziyue Wang, Longwen Chen, Xieyuanli Chen, Huimin Lu
bullets: Addresses image-goal navigation when targets are outside the current view and persistent spatial memory is required.
Uses learned scene-coordinate localization to anchor current, goal, and history frames in a shared reference frame.
Jointly predicts future states and actions in latent space, avoiding pixel reconstruction and CEM-style planning.
Reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2% across four trajectory prediction benchmarks.
Improves closed-loop success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and SPL from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Geometry-grounded world action model for image-goal navigation with latent state-action prediction and persistent spatial memory.
papers.title: G$^2$WAM: World Action Models for Efficient and Geometry Grounded Image-Goal Navigation
papers.tldr: G$^2$WAM enables efficient image-goal navigation by combining geometry-grounded spatial memory with latent world-action modeling, improving trajectory prediction and navigation success without explicit 3D reconstruction or costly planning.

papers.abstract: Safe robot navigation in unknown, dynamic environments requires more than geometric collision checking: a robot still far from an obstacle may be unable to avoid it because of its speed, orientation, or the obstacle's motion. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis captures this in a value function whose sign separates states that admit a safe continuation from those where collision is unavoidable, but computing it online for every newly observed environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions to give optimization-based controllers this information in real time. Since the value function never exceeds the constraint, it equals a directly computed constraint, such as a signed distance, minus a nonnegative dynamics correction. Learning only this correction keeps represented obstacles outside the predicted safe set despite approximation errors. The first two of five methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control, for static local environments and predicted obstacle motion. The next two use it as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static environments and, through pairwise barriers in relative coordinates, for a varying number of moving obstacles. Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. The fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver, which limits the first four to low-dimensional models. For control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, the HJ Hamiltonian is maximized at a vertex, so a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs can generate training labels. With a loss from the HJ variational inequality, these labels yield barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.
bullets: HJ reachability identifies states where collision is unavoidable, but online computation is too expensive for newly observed environments.
Neural implicit models learn the nonnegative dynamics correction to signed-distance constraints, preserving conservative safety under approximation error.
The learned representations support model predictive control and control-barrier-function filters for static environments and moving obstacles.
Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show improved collision avoidance, particularly with short planning horizons and moving obstacles.
A tree-search labeling method avoids grid-based solvers and extends barrier-candidate generation to control-affine systems with up to 13 states.
papers.selection_reason: Learned reachability safety representations for real-time robot navigation in unknown dynamic environments directly fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Learning Reachability-Based Safety Representations for Real-Time Robot Navigation in Unknown and Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: The dissertation learns reachability-based safety representations offline so robots can perform real-time, dynamics-aware collision avoidance in unknown and dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.
authors: Wei Yao, Chuyao Wang, Ziwei Wang, Nabil Aouf
bullets: Addresses severe sim-to-real degradation in vision-based autonomous-driving reinforcement learning.
Uses simulated-observation attribution maps to identify and perturb appearance-sensitive Fourier components while preserving task-relevant structure.
Optimises policies to focus on task-critical features and reduce reliance on irrelevant visual cues.
Simulation and zero-shot real-world experiments show improved travel distance and reward, particularly on unseen cluttered maps.
Attribution analysis indicates more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and reality.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real RL for vision-based autonomous driving; transfers policies to real-world navigation.
papers.title: XAI-Guided Fourier Domain Generalisation for Pure-Simulation Sim-to-Real Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: XFD uses explainability-guided Fourier perturbations and robust policy optimisation to improve zero-shot sim-to-real visual driving without real-world training data.

papers.abstract: Deploying robots in human-shared environments requires deciding not only how to navigate, but also when dedicated social signals are worth emitting. Classic observation-based inference can be misleading in such settings: confounding factors may bias the estimated relationship between a signal and the task outcome, leading to incorrect decisions. Causal inference provides a framework for disentangling these relationships by modelling the mechanisms linking observations, actions, and outcomes, and by estimating interventional effects after accounting for confounding paths. We study a human-robot interaction scenario in a corridor and use a causal model to estimate whether a social navigation signal causally improves transit success. We represent the interaction as a causal DAG involving robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles). We compare the interventional estimate with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning only on the robot action, which does not explicitly model interventions. Our results show that accounting for confounding variables can reverse the conclusions drawn from naive observational analysis: the observational estimate wrongly suggests that the social signal is detrimental, whereas the causal estimate shows that it is beneficial. This discrepancy highlights how failing to account for confounding can lead to incorrect conclusions and demonstrates the importance of causal models for context-aware signalling decisions in social robot navigation.
authors: Francesco Baldo, Luca Castri, Gloria Beraldo, Nicola Bellotto
bullets: Studies when social signals are worth emitting in human-shared corridor navigation.
Models robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and static obstacles in a causal DAG.
Compares an interventional causal estimate with an observational estimate conditioned only on robot action.
Accounting for confounding reverses the conclusion: the signal appears detrimental observationally but beneficial causally.
Highlights causal modeling as important for context-aware signalling decisions.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses robot navigation decision-making by estimating the causal impact of social signals, distinguishing between observational and interventional effects.
papers.title: Estimating the Causal Impact of Social Navigation Signals in Corridor Scenarios
papers.tldr: Causal analysis shows that social navigation signals improve corridor transit, while naive observational analysis can misleadingly suggest the opposite.

papers.abstract: Multimodal model predictive control (MM-MPC) avoids local minima among moving obstacles by solving one optimal control problem (OCP) per combination of avoidance sides, so its computational cost grows exponentially with the number of decision-critical obstacles. We propose SideNet-MPC, which replaces this enumeration with a mode decision learned by imitating MM-MPC as an expert. A graph neural network is trained to predict the expert's minimum-cost mode, one avoidance side per obstacle. Its edges encode, for each obstacle pair, the gap predicted for the moment the vehicle first reaches either obstacle, so a neighbor that blocks a preferred passage can reverse the proposed side. The expert's selection rule compares its minimum-cost mode with the previously executed mode; SideNet-MPC keeps this rule and substitutes the network proposal for the minimum-cost mode. Hence at most two OCPs are solved per control period, and every applied input still comes from an OCP with control barrier function constraints rather than from the network. In $100$ seed-matched closed-loop Monte Carlo runs of mixed traffic, SideNet-MPC reaches $93\%$ of the expert's success rate and needs \SI{18.6}{ms} per control period on a single thread, 48\% less than the expert's \SI{35.5}{ms} on sixteen parallel threads. In a controlled gap sweep, its proposed side reverses in the same gap interval as the expert's, whereas proposers without pairwise edges, trained on the same data, never reverse and all deadlock at the blocked gates of a deterministic scene.
authors: Changyu Lee, Byung-Kwan Lee, Kanghoon Yoon
bullets: MM-MPC avoids local minima by enumerating avoidance-side combinations, but this cost grows exponentially with decision-critical obstacles.
A graph neural network predicts one avoidance side per obstacle, using pairwise gap information to account for blocked passages.
The controller preserves the expert’s mode-selection rule and solves at most two optimal control problems per control period.
In 100 seed-matched mixed-traffic runs, it achieved 93% of the expert’s success rate and reduced reported control time from 35.5 ms to 18.6 ms.
Pairwise graph edges enabled side reversals in the same gap interval as the expert; models without them deadlocked in the tested deterministic scene.
papers.selection_reason: Learned mode selection for efficient multimodal MPC in obstacle avoidance navigation.
papers.title: Imitation Learning of Avoidance Modes for Efficient Multimodal Model Predictive Control
papers.tldr: SideNet-MPC imitates multimodal MPC’s obstacle-avoidance choices to reduce planning cost while retaining OCP- and barrier-function-based safety constraints.

papers.abstract: Differentiable simulation enables efficient policy optimization through analytic gradients, yet safety is commonly incorporated as a weighted penalty, requiring manual tuning of the trade-off between task performance and constraint satisfaction. We instead formulate obstacle avoidance as an explicit constraint and train quadrotor policies using primal--dual gradient descent--ascent through a differentiable simulator. We introduce two key components to enable effective constrained training. First, we propose a bounded clearance-based constraint function that provides informative gradients around the safety boundary while preventing large violations from destabilizing primal--dual optimization. Second, we introduce log-mean-exp (LME) aggregation to smoothly emphasize critical per-step safety violations across a trajectory and training batch within a single constraint governed by one dual variable. Together, these components enable the desired safety level to be specified directly while balancing constraint satisfaction and task completion. We theoretically prove that the proposed optimization with differentiable simulation converges to feasible policy under mild assumptions. Experiments demonstrate improved safety--performance trade-offs over fixed-penalty and existing policy-learning baselines, as well as generalization to denser out-of-distribution environments. Finally, the learned policy transfers zero-shot to Gazebo/PX4 and a physical quadrotor without additional fine-tuning.
authors: Yan Rui Tan, Praveen Krishnapur, Zeyu Feng, Han Bao, Yew-Soon Ong, Fan Shi
bullets: Models obstacle avoidance as an explicit constraint rather than a weighted penalty.
Uses a bounded clearance constraint for stable, informative safety gradients.
Applies log-mean-exp aggregation to focus one dual constraint on critical trajectory and batch violations.
Experiments show improved safety–performance trade-offs, denser-environment generalization, and zero-shot transfer to Gazebo/PX4 and a physical quadrotor.
papers.selection_reason: Constrained policy learning via differentiable simulation for safe quadrotor navigation; fits learned navigation and robot learning.
papers.title: Constrained Differentiable Policy Learning for Safe Quadrotor Navigation
papers.tldr: A constrained policy-learning approach uses differentiable simulation and primal–dual optimization to train quadrotors for safer navigation without manually tuning penalty weights.

papers.abstract: Generalist visual-navigation policies tell a robot which direction to go but not how far. A separate lifting step is needed at deployment to convert their unitless trajectory into a metric path that a controller can track; existing scalar lifters apply uniform scaling that misses per-waypoint corrections, while in-policy approaches that inject monocular depth into the policy inherit the prediction errors of the depth model near obstacles and at close range. We present PathLift, a per-waypoint depth-conditioned adapter that lifts a pre-trained visual-navigation policy by consuming an explicit, sensor-grade depth source (RGB-D, stereo, or projected LiDAR) and fitting per-waypoint magnitude and lateral residuals to a canonicalized prior. PathLift consistently improves closed-loop navigation across diverse visual-navigation policies in simulation and on a real wheeled robot under both stereo and LiDAR depth. By turning the policy's unitless intent into a depth-feasible metric path in a single feed-forward pass, the adapter lifts real-world success without test-time optimization.
authors: Gwanjun Shin, Hyeongseok Suh, Hongmo Jung, Jongwoo Lim
bullets: Addresses the need to determine how far a robot should travel, not just which direction.
Uses a depth-conditioned adapter that predicts per-waypoint magnitude and lateral residuals relative to a canonicalized prior.
Supports RGB-D, stereo, and projected LiDAR depth while avoiding monocular-depth errors near obstacles and at close range.
Improves closed-loop navigation across diverse policies in simulation and on a real wheeled robot with stereo and LiDAR.
Runs in a single feed-forward pass without test-time optimization.
papers.selection_reason: Depth-conditioned adapter for visual-navigation policies; directly improves learned robot navigation.
papers.title: PathLift: Depth-Conditioned Metric Lifting for Visual-Navigation Priors
papers.tldr: PathLift converts unitless visual-navigation trajectories into depth-feasible metric paths using per-waypoint corrections from explicit sensor depth.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models for embodied navigation typically rely on RGB observations, limiting their applicability in lights-out industrial environments where visible illumination may be unavailable. We study illumination-independent navigation using spatial audio for target localization and depth for obstacle-aware geometry. To support this setting, we introduce DarkNav-Bench, a benchmark with 24 industrial scenes and four progressively challenging acoustic conditions. We further propose ADAPT, an audio-depth action-planning framework equipped with spatial-audio perception and optimized for closed-loop navigation through reinforcement learning (RL). Our key RL contribution, transition-aware reward shaping (TARS), defines a pose-aware shortest-action potential over a position-heading graph. Unlike conventional geodesic-progress rewards, TARS accounts for both feasible movements and in-place rotations, providing action-consistent feedback for policy optimization. Experiments show that ADAPT consistently outperforms training-based navigation baselines and zero-shot multimodal models on both seen and unseen scenes. On unseen environments, it achieves 90.6% success under Clean conditions and retains 60.0% success under the most challenging Localized Noise setting. These results demonstrate the potential of spatial audio and depth as complementary modalities for reliable RGB-free navigation in lights-out industrial environments.
authors: Wenjun Huang, Shenghao Fu, Yian Jin, Yang Ni, Yifan Li, Lichi Li, Xingjian Diao, Pengfei Zhang, Yutong Song, Hanning Chen, Jiarui Cui, Tianyu Yang, Shilong Li, Yu Kong, Mohsen Imani
bullets: Targets lights-out navigation, where RGB observations may be unavailable.
Introduces DarkNav-Bench with 24 industrial scenes and four acoustic conditions.
Uses spatial-audio perception, depth-based obstacle geometry, and closed-loop RL planning.
TARS provides pose-aware rewards for both movement and in-place rotation.
On unseen scenes, achieves 90.6% success in Clean conditions and 60.0% under Localized Noise.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based audio-depth navigation policy for industrial environments; directly fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: ADAPT: Audio-Depth Action Planning with Transition-Aware Rewards for Lights-Out Industrial Navigation
papers.tldr: ADAPT enables reliable RGB-free industrial navigation by combining spatial audio, depth, and transition-aware reinforcement-learning rewards.

papers.abstract: A deterministic method for the problem of distributed area coverage path planning subject to the inclusion of a headland path is presented. Given a, in general, non-convex area to be covered that may, in general, include obstacle areas, multiple robots, at least one robot depot, and constraints on each machinery such as a working width, work capacity limits, travel capacity limits, nonholonomic dynamical constraints and, possibly, a robot start and end depot assignment, distributed paths for each machinery are calculated that collectively enable full area coverage. Variations are discussed, in particular, a scenario where unconstrained depots assignment can attain a global optimal solution to the problem. The importance of inclusion of a headland path for area coverage, as well as the benefits in comparison to an alternative Boustrophedon-pattern based approach are highlighted.
bullets: Addresses coverage of generally non-convex areas with obstacles using multiple robots and depots.
Accounts for machinery-specific working width, capacity limits, travel limits, nonholonomic dynamics, and depot assignments.
Discusses variations, including unconstrained depot assignment that can achieve a globally optimal solution.
Highlights the importance of headland paths and benefits over a Boustrophedon-pattern approach.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses distributed area coverage path planning with headland path inclusion for non-convex areas, relevant to multi-robot navigation strategies.
papers.title: Distributed area coverage path planning subject to the inclusion of a headland path
papers.tldr: A deterministic distributed planner computes full-coverage robot paths in complex areas while explicitly incorporating a headland path and vehicle constraints.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a geometry-aware predictive control framework for bipedal obstacle crossing across walking and running regimes. The proposed approach integrates a phase-structured trajectory generator with a constrained model predictive control (MPC) tracking layer to generate coordinated pelvis and swing-foot motions during obstacle traversal. The crossing process is represented through five interpretable phases: pre-crossing, leading-leg clearance, straddle, trailing-leg clearance, and recovery. Within this structure, swing-foot elevation is adapted as a function of obstacle height, while lateral stance widening and pelvis repositioning are introduced as functions of obstacle depth to improve transverse clearance and body alignment. A continuous gait-parameter evolution enables smooth walk-to-run transition without discrete controller switching. The generated references are tracked using MPC to regulate motion smoothness, clearance feasibility, touchdown behavior, and lateral admissibility. The framework is evaluated in reduced-order simulation over five progressively difficult obstacles under walking and running conditions. The robot successfully crosses the first four obstacles, achieving minimum body-obstacle clearances of 0.036, 0.036, 0.059, and 0.017 m, respectively. The fifth and most demanding obstacle leads to collision, identifying the current operating boundary of the proposed reduced-order formulation. Overall, the method provides a compact, interpretable, and computationally efficient basis for intelligent obstacle-aware bipedal locomotion.
bullets: Models crossing with five interpretable phases: pre-crossing, leading-leg clearance, straddle, trailing-leg clearance, and recovery.
Adapts swing-foot height to obstacle height and stance width/pelvis position to obstacle depth for improved clearance and alignment.
Uses continuous gait-parameter evolution to transition between walking and running without switching controllers.
MPC tracks generated references while regulating smoothness, clearance, touchdown, and lateral admissibility.
In reduced-order simulations, the robot crossed the first four obstacles; the most demanding fifth obstacle caused a collision, marking the method’s current operating boundary.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a geometry-aware predictive control framework for bipedal obstacle crossing, integrating phase-structured trajectory generation with MPC for local planning and obstacle avoidance.
papers.title: Geometry-Aware Predictive Control for Walk-to-Run Bipedal Obstacle Crossing
papers.tldr: A geometry-aware phase-structured planner with MPC enables smooth walk-to-run bipedal obstacle crossing, successfully handling four of five increasingly difficult simulated obstacles.

papers.abstract: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
authors: Zide Fan, Jiahui Yuan, Kaixin Zhang, Junhao Fan, Xiaohe Li, Yiru Wang
bullets: Reconstructs receiver-specific traffic graphs from local ego and peer-state information.
Uses shared graph attention to generate Stop/Go intentions augmented with predicted human-vehicle intent.
Exchanges timestamped CAV intentions and applies local conflict-aware arbitration to produce safe executable actions.
In SUMO evaluation, reports 97.53% completion, 0.10% collision, and 35.28 s mean traversal time.
Remains robust across tested communication delays and packet-loss conditions, but safety margins narrow with compound unpredictable human behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-agent RL for cooperative driving at intersections.
papers.title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X
papers.tldr: SIGN-MAPPO enables safer, more coordinated CAV navigation at unsignalized intersections despite imperfect V2X and unpredictable human-driver intentions.

papers.abstract: Existing navigation systems commonly rely on dedicated depth sensors or explicit depth reconstruction, while learning to generate trajectories directly from RGB images remains challenging due to the sim-to-real domain gap. In this work, we propose Stereo-Planner, an end-to-end vision-to-trajectory framework that enables zero-shot sim-to-real planning from stereo RGB observations. The key idea is to formulate trajectory generation as state- and scale-conditioned querying of latent stereo geometry. A Scene Representor incorporates a pretrained vision grounding foundation model to extract geometric cues shared across simulated and real-world environments, supporting generalization across visual domains. A lightweight Trajectory Decoder then translates these representations into trajectories through interleaved attention, separating trajectory-state interaction from scene-feature retrieval and incorporating the stereo baseline as a metric-scale cue. With these designs, Stereo-Planner is trained entirely on simulated data by minimizing differentiable trajectory costs and deployed directly in real-world environments without fine-tuning. Benchmark results demonstrate strong cross-scene generalization, with a 95% success rate in simulation environments at a commanded speed of 8 m/s, and competitive performance against depth-based planners using only stereo RGB observations for scene perception. Furthermore, deployment on a compact quadrotor equipped with an NVIDIA Orin NX enables autonomous flight at speeds of up to 7 m/s, with a mean onboard vision-to-action inference time of 24.27 ms. The software, simulation environments, and hardware designs will be open-sourced at https://github.com/Stereo-Planner/Stereo-Planner.
authors: Hongming Shen, Junjie Lu, Xun Chen, Wei Wang, Xinhang Xu, Bailing Tian, Lihua Xie
bullets: Addresses the challenge of RGB-based trajectory planning and the sim-to-real domain gap without dedicated depth sensors.
Uses a scene representor with pretrained vision-grounding features to extract transferable stereo geometric cues.
A lightweight trajectory decoder conditions predictions on trajectory state, retrieved scene features, and stereo baseline for metric scale.
Trained entirely in simulation with differentiable trajectory costs, then deployed directly in real environments.
Reports 95% simulation success at 8 m/s and real-world autonomous flight up to 7 m/s with 24.27 ms mean onboard inference time.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end stereo-to-trajectory planning for quadrotor navigation.
papers.title: Stereo-Planner: Learning Stereo-to-Trajectory Planning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Quadrotor Navigation
papers.tldr: Stereo-Planner learns to convert stereo RGB images directly into quadrotor trajectories, achieving zero-shot sim-to-real navigation without explicit depth reconstruction or real-world fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.
authors: Reem Abdel-Salam, Rana Mostafa, Ahmed H. Abdel-Gawad
bullets: Targets traffic signs degraded by environmental conditions and the slow execution of existing deep-learning methods.
Evaluated on GTSRB, BTSC, and Croatian rMASTIF benchmarks.
Reports accuracies of 99.75%, 99.25%, and 99.55%, respectively.
Combined preprocessing and inference take no more than 1.3 ms per image.
Demonstrates robustness to brightness and contrast variations.
papers.selection_reason: Focuses on real-time traffic sign recognition for autonomous cars, a core component of visual navigation and robot navigation in embodied AI.
papers.title: RIECNN: Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN for Traffic Sign Recognition
papers.tldr: RIECNN is a real-time CNN-based traffic sign recognizer that achieves high accuracy and robustness across diverse benchmarks under environmental variations.

papers.abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.
authors: Christopher Solinas, Radovan Halu\v{s}ka, Martin Schmid, Michael Buro, Nathan R. Sturtevant, Michael Bowling
bullets: POMDP beliefs are continuous posterior distributions, making exact planning generally intractable.
BETS represents each search-tree node’s belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE).
The embedding is propagated through POMDP dynamics and supports sampling for Monte Carlo search.
Belief, policy, and value models are trained jointly from experience using the realized hidden state as the belief target.
Across six RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan configurations, BETS is competitive or leading and performs especially well in high-dimensional beliefs, including without search.
papers.selection_reason: Learned Monte Carlo belief-space planner for POMDP navigation and control benchmarks.
papers.title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
papers.tldr: BETS improves POMDP planning by learning generative belief embeddings that are updated through environment dynamics and jointly trained with policy and value networks.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal Thermal Geo-localization (TG) provides an illumination-robust positioning solution for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied environments. However, existing thermal geo-localization methods mainly focus on near-nadir observations or depend on map-side elevation priors, limiting their applicability to continuous oblique thermal localization with only geo-referenced 2D satellite maps. To address this problem, we propose ScalLoc, a scale-aligned local-to-map localization framework for continuous oblique thermal UAV geo-localization. ScalLoc follows a reconstruction--refinement--anchoring--propagation design: it reconstructs local window geometry from thermal sequences, refines camera poses using track-based pose optimization, adaptively anchors each window to the satellite map, and propagates validated states to recover frame-level global trajectories. To support systematic evaluation, we construct Thermal-Oblique, a real thermal UAV sequence dataset containing 216 urban and rural day--night trajectories and 28,112 thermal frames with frame-level annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScalLoc reduces the mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m compared with the VGGT-only configuration, corresponding to a 76.07% reduction, and achieves the lowest frame-weighted mean position error among the compared methods. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous oblique thermal geo-localization using only lightweight 2D satellite maps, without requiring digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/FloralHercules/ScalLoc.

bullets: Addresses the limited applicability of existing thermal geo-localization methods to continuous oblique views in GNSS-denied environments.
Uses a reconstruction–refinement–anchoring–propagation pipeline to recover and globally align frame-level UAV trajectories.
Introduces Thermal-Oblique, a dataset of 216 urban and rural day–night trajectories containing 28,112 annotated thermal frames.

papers.title: ScalLoc: Continuous Oblique Thermal UAV Geo-Localization with a 2D Satellite Map

papers.abstract: Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change. Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state. TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes. From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion. In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.
authors: Hao Zhang, Yuping Yan, Yitian Hong, Luying Feng, Tianhong Wang, Fengqi Dai, Wei Chen, Yaochu Jin
bullets: Fixed temporal visual histories can become spatially mismatched as speed, posture, and gait phase change.
TempoLoco learns multiple temporal views from a long depth buffer in a shared feature space.
