It achieves a 78.4% success rate versus 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.
The system completes 41/45 simulated trials and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 across diverse terrains.
papers.selection_reason: Motion-adaptive temporal visual memory for quadruped locomotion; fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: Beyond Fixed Visual History: Learning Motion-Adaptive Temporal Receptive Fields for Complex-Terrain Quadruped Locomotion
papers.tldr: TempoLoco dynamically adapts visual-history timescales to a quadruped’s motion state, improving locomotion across complex terrains.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), single Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) search-and-rescue in outdoor scenarios remains challenging due to partial observability, making cross-altitude collaboration a promising direction. However, existing collaborative navigation methods rely on precise target localization and rigid goal-dispatching paradigms, ignoring high-altitude observation uncertainty and suppressing low-altitude exploration autonomy. To address these issues, we introduce BGC-Nav, a training-free cross-altitude collaboration framework that enables robust navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling (BGC). Specifically, the high-altitude UAV maintains a Global Belief Memory encoding task-conditioned priors, which the low-altitude agent incorporates into decision-making via Local Exhaustion Memory (LEM), Local Attraction Augmentation (LAA), and Directional Belief Prior (DBP) as an advisory bias rather than a rigid command. Extensive experiments on ESARBench show that BGC-Nav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-agent and collaborative methods. Code is available at https://github.com/uestchjw/BGC-Nav.
authors: Jiuwu Hao, Yueyang Wu, Liguo Sun, Haolin Song, Zao Zhang, Pin Lv
bullets: Addresses outdoor UAV search-and-rescue challenges caused by partial observability and uncertain high-altitude observations.
Uses a Global Belief Memory on the high-altitude UAV to provide task-conditioned priors.
The low-altitude UAV integrates this guidance through Local Exhaustion Memory, Local Attraction Augmentation, and Directional Belief Prior.
Treats high-altitude information as an advisory bias rather than a rigid goal assignment, preserving low-altitude autonomy.
Experiments on ESARBench report consistent improvements over existing single-agent and collaborative methods.ﬁ

papers.title: BGC-Nav: Cross-Altitude Multi-UAV Collaborative Navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling
papers.tldr: BGC-Nav enables training-free cross-altitude multi-UAV navigation by using high-altitude beliefs as flexible guidance for low-altitude exploration under partial observability.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.
authors: Hieu D. Pham, Quoc-An Luong, Dung D. Le
bullets: Introduces VLN-Safe, a benchmark comparing sliding evaluation with blocking evaluation that prevents motion after collisions.

papers.title: Successful but Unsafe: An Analytical Benchmark for Revealing Collisions in Vision-and-Language Navigation
papers.tldr: VLN agents can succeed while frequently colliding, but a lightweight collision guard substantially improves safety and often navigation success.

papers.abstract: Continuous indoor-outdoor navigation connects destination-level reasoning with motion decisions that must respond to current observations. We present VbotNav-0, a cloud-edge dual-policy framework that links these processes through asynchronous policy-to-policy conditioning. The cloud policy produces subgoal guidance from visual history, navigation instructions, and route tokens; the edge policy combines available guidance with current RGB and LiDAR observations to generate local trajectories. This formulation allows the local perception-action loop to continue between cloud updates. A common route representation connects indoor paths and outdoor map routes, and the training recipe combines navigation demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded visual question answering (VQA). In the reported closed-loop evaluation of 258 episodes across 145 scenes, VbotNav-0 achieves 55.04% success rate and 55.03% success weighted by path length.
authors: Shiqi Tan, Yujun Zhang, Keyu Li, Shuaixi Pan, Siyu Zhou, Hailong Qin, Yinan Yu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking destination-level reasoning with observation-driven motion across indoor and outdoor environments.
Uses a cloud policy for subgoal guidance from visual history, instructions, and route tokens, while an edge policy generates trajectories from guidance, RGB, and LiDAR.
Asynchronous policy conditioning lets local perception and action continue between cloud updates.
A shared route representation connects indoor paths with outdoor map routes; training combines demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded VQA.
In closed-loop evaluation across 258 episodes and 145 scenes, it reports 55.04% success and 55.03% success weighted by path length.

papers.title: VbotNav-0: Asynchronous Cloud-Edge Dual-Policy Navigation across Indoor and Outdoor Environments
papers.tldr: VbotNav-0 enables continuous indoor–outdoor navigation by asynchronously combining cloud-based subgoal planning with edge-based local control.

papers.abstract: Navigating cluttered environments while carrying objects remains a challenging problem for quadruped robots. Compared with works that focused on load-aware locomotion adaptation to maintain gait stability, existing autonomous navigation systems generally ignore the influence of carried objects' geometries and use fixed footprint inflation, leading to overly conservative navigation. To fill this knowledge gap, we propose a two-phase load-aware navigation learning framework. In Phase 1, we train LOADNav, a load-aware navigation policy via reinforcement learning, enabling the robot to adapt its trajectory and clearance behavior according to the geometric size of the carried object. In Phase 2, we train CoGE, an online geometry predictor via imitation learning, which estimates unknown payload geometry from occasional contact events. We evaluate the framework in cluttered environments with loads of varying sizes and shapes. The results show that our navigation policy exhibits clear load-aware behaviors, and the online geometry predictor estimates object geometry from occasional contact events, refining its estimate and adapting the navigation behavior accordingly. Without requiring any prior knowledge of the payload, it narrows the gap to geometry-aware policies.
authors: Qi Yin, XiaoLi Zhang, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets overly conservative navigation caused by fixed footprint inflation and ignored payload geometry.
LOADNav uses reinforcement learning to adapt trajectory and clearance behavior to the carried object's size.
CoGE uses imitation learning to infer unknown payload geometry from occasional robot–object contacts.
Experiments with varied load sizes and shapes show adaptive navigation and progressively refined geometry estimates.
Without prior payload knowledge, the method narrows the gap to geometry-aware policies.
papers.selection_reason: Load-aware quadruped navigation with RL and online geometry estimation, directly fitting learning-based robot navigation.
papers.title: Load-Aware Quadruped Navigation with Online Contact-based Geometry Estimation
papers.tldr: A two-phase system lets quadruped robots navigate clutter while carrying unknown-shaped objects by learning load-aware motion and estimating payload geometry from contact events.

papers.abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation-to-Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal-related evidence; and (ii) Evidence-to-Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG-Nav outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence-missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG-Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero-shot generalization capability in unseen real-world environments.
authors: Shaohao Zhu, Wensi Huang, Siqi Zhang, Yuqiang Yang, Meng Wei, Chenyang Wan, Tianle Liu, Tai Wang, Jinming Xu
bullets: Identifies insufficient use of intermediate observations and imprecise target localization as key navigation challenges.
Uses supervised fine-tuning to learn a two-stage reasoning process: Observation-to-Evidence and Evidence-to-Decision.
Accumulates goal-relevant evidence across frames, then combines it with current observations to select actions or ask clarification questions.
Reports higher success rates on HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN, with gains of 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively.
Ablations link evidence accumulation to fewer evidence-missing failures and explicit grounding to fewer stopping errors; robot deployment demonstrates zero-shot real-world generalization.
papers.selection_reason: Goal-oriented navigation foundation model with VLM grounding chain-of-thought, evaluated on navigation benchmarks and a real robot.
papers.title: GG-Nav: Goal-oriented Grounding Chain-of-Thought Elicits Reasoning in Navigation Foundation Models
papers.tldr: GG-Nav improves goal-oriented navigation by using structured grounding chains of thought to accumulate evidence from streaming observations and localize targets more reliably.

papers.abstract: Autonomous Aerial Vehicle (AAV) trajectory planning requires real-time and accurate safety gradient guidance, especially in dynamic environments. Existing methods typically rely on static maps and dynamic obstacle tracking to construct gradient fields, imposing heavy computational burdens and yielding conservative trajectories. To address these limitations, we propose a two-stage Field-to-Planning (F2P) learning framework to provide accurate and efficient safety gradients for trajectory planning in dynamic environments. In the first stage, we introduce an Ego-centric Polar Occupancy (EPO) representation that naturally matches the geometry of the onboard camera frustum, while supporting unstructured scene modeling. Subsequently, we formulate a Temporal Polar Gradient Field (TPGF) via multi-kernel separable Gaussian convolution to provide unified safety gradients, without explicitly distinguishing between static and dynamic obstacles. To mitigate the inherent spatial ambiguity introduced by applying convolutions within the polar grid, we propose an ESDF-guided offline learning strategy that incorporates geometric priors into TPGF. In the second stage, we employ the calibrated TPGF to guide the trajectory planning policy in a self-supervised learning manner. Comparative results with other approaches demonstrate the superiority of our method. Extensive real-world experiments within various cluttered dynamic environments validate the real-time performance and robustness on resource-constrained onboard systems.
authors: Haowen Gao, Zhan Chen, Yinuo Xu, Yifeng Niu, Mengyun Wang, Chao Yan
bullets: Targets the computational cost and conservatism of methods relying on static maps and explicit dynamic-obstacle tracking.
Represents scenes with an ego-centric polar occupancy grid matched to the camera frustum and suitable for unstructured environments.
Builds a unified Temporal Polar Gradient Field using separable Gaussian convolution, without separating static and dynamic obstacles.
Uses ESDF-guided offline learning to reduce spatial ambiguity, then applies the calibrated field to self-supervised trajectory-policy learning.
Comparative and real-world experiments report superior performance, real-time operation, and robustness on resource-constrained onboard systems.
papers.selection_reason: Learned temporal polar gradient fields for vision-based AAV trajectory planning in dynamic environments.
papers.title: From Field to Planning: Learning Temporal Polar Gradient Fields for Vision-based AAV Trajectory Planning in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: F2P learns temporal polar safety-gradient fields from onboard camera data to enable real-time, robust AAV trajectory planning in cluttered dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
bullets: Dense task representations can diffuse inferred rewards across the state space, weakening goal-state contrast.
An L1 penalty concentrates reward-predictive information in a smaller latent subspace without changing the architecture or test-time closed-form inference.
Across 65 DMC Suite and OGBench tasks, Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons.

papers.title: Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations
papers.tldr: Sparse-TD-JEPA adds an L1 sparsity penalty to TD-JEPA’s task representations, producing sharper inferred rewards and substantially improving zero-shot reinforcement learning.

papers.abstract: Position tracking is a well-studied problem in Euclidean navigation, yet comparatively little attention has been given to navigation on general manifolds, where motion is governed by the underlying geometry of the space. In this work, we formalize the problem of manifold navigation as a velocity-driven tracking task and propose a coordinate-chart-based learning framework in which learning models operate entirely in a Euclidean representation. Predicted trajectories are mapped to the manifold via an immersion function prior to error computation, allowing geometric consistency to be evaluated without explicitly enforcing manifold constraints during learning. Within this framework, we focus on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) for sequential position prediction on curved manifolds after comparisons with alternative recurrent architectures. We evaluate our GRU models, trained with pertinent custom loss functions, against both a standard MSE loss function and a naive vector-addition baseline. We evaluate our approach on both analytically (and numerically) defined manifolds, as well as a surface reconstructed from a LiDAR point cloud. Our results show that recurrent models can learn to approximate manifold-constrained dynamics from velocity sequences and consistently outperform Euclidean baselines. Our results demonstrate that certain custom loss functions significantly improve long-horizon prediction accuracy compared to conventional point-wise loss functions.
authors: Sarah Harkins Dayton, Sathya Rengaswami, Vasileios Maroulas, David L. Boothe, Ioannis D. Schizas
bullets: Formulates manifold navigation as velocity-driven position tracking on general geometries.
Trains recurrent models in Euclidean coordinates, then maps predictions to the manifold for geometry-aware error evaluation.
Focuses on GRUs and compares custom geometric losses with standard MSE and naive vector addition.
Evaluates on analytic/numerical manifolds and a LiDAR-reconstructed surface.
Custom loss functions improve long-horizon accuracy, while recurrent models outperform Euclidean baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based manifold navigation with recurrent networks is transferable to learned robot navigation and position tracking.
papers.title: Manifold Navigation Learning Using Recurrent Networks: Efficient Training Techniques
papers.tldr: A coordinate-chart framework with GRUs learns velocity-driven navigation on curved manifolds and improves long-horizon tracking over Euclidean baselines.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive trajectory priors for multi-robot motion planning (MRMP), but scaling them to large teams requires coordinating individual motions without expensive joint computation. We introduce Akule, a sparse interaction diffusion framework that augments a frozen single-robot prior with three learned modules: a reusable pairwise correction model $R_{\phi}$, a contextual selector $U_{\psi}$ that determines which corrections to evaluate, and a composer $G_{\omega}$ that combines their effects through context-dependent signed weights. This decomposition separates which interactions merit computation from how their effects should be combined into coordinated denoising updates. We train $R_{\phi}$ using matched pairwise trajectory optimizations, then learn $G_{\omega}$ and $U_{\psi}$ from physically optimized joint trajectories without requiring a prescribed ground-truth interaction graph. The resulting joint proposals are passed to a downstream search-based planner for validation and repair. Across diverse MRMP benchmarks, Akule achieves competitive planning success, complete-planner speedups of up to $25\times$, zero-shot population transfer, and successful planning with up to $256$ robots. Ablations further demonstrate that learned selection and composition reduce pre-repair conflicts and downstream repair effort relative to heuristic selection and uniform summation.
authors: Manav Vora, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Aditya Penumarti, Jane Shin, Melkior Ornik
bullets: Addresses the costly joint coordination problem in diffusion-based multi-robot motion planning.
Uses a frozen single-robot prior plus learned pairwise correction, interaction selection, and context-dependent composition modules.
Trains corrections from pairwise optimized trajectories and selection/composition from optimized joint trajectories without a predefined interaction graph.
Feeds generated joint proposals to a search-based planner for validation and repair.
Reports competitive success, up to 25× complete-planner speedups, zero-shot population transfer, and reduced conflicts and repair effort.
papers.selection_reason: Sparse interaction diffusion for multi-robot motion planning, fits learned planning under robot navigation.
papers.title: Akule: Fast and Scalable Multi-Robot Motion Planning via Sparse Interaction Diffusion
papers.tldr: Akule scales multi-robot motion planning by sparsely selecting and composing pairwise diffusion corrections, enabling fast coordination for teams of up to 256 robots.

papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.
bullets: Addresses Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation, where agents must find moving sound sources using visual and auditory cues.
Introduces ICGE to learn category-agnostic spatial correspondence through physics-informed sound-intensity and visual-geometry alignment.
Uses Transformer-based CMSA to dynamically combine multimodal features into a state representation for navigation policy learning.
Experiments on Replica and Matterport3D report state-of-the-art success rates with improved generalization and navigation efficiency, including unheard sounds.
papers.selection_reason: Embodied audio-visual navigation with physical alignment and scene aggregation, directly fits robot navigation.
papers.title: Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning for Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation: From Physical Alignment to Scene Aggregation
papers.tldr: A two-stage framework improves dynamic audio-visual navigation by aligning sound intensity with visual geometry and aggregating multimodal scene information.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art perceptive humanoid locomotion is mostly built on retargeted motion capture, a generative motion prior, and a distillation stage. We report a complete system that does not require this pipeline for a humanoid to cross varied terrain. In its place, we provide a five-expert mixture routed by a terrain classifier over a sensed elevation grid, and target every foothold with a model-based planner, refined by six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field instead of picked from a fixed grid. Driven through the same perception-to-actuation software a robot would run, inside a second, deployment-fidelity simulator, it crosses an $85$\,m five-segment waypoint course $18$ of $20$ times end-to-end ($90\%$, Wilson $95\%$ CI $70$--$97$) and succeeds $20/20$ on four of five segments scored alone, where an ablated configuration without the mixture and without refinement reaches $0\%$ on both the stair and the hurdle segment. The continuous refinement moves $72.4\%$ of foot placements across at least one grid-cell boundary, which produces real sub-grid correction. We also ran matched component studies to report what does not account for it: one expert equals five on the training distribution, four label-free routers collapse to near-uniform activation, and a self-supervised terrain embedding loses to the privileged label.
authors: Thanh Ly, Chien Le, Truong-Duy Dang, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Duy-Dung Le, Vien Anh Ngo, An T. Le
bullets: Replaces retargeted motion capture, generative priors, and distillation with five terrain-routed experts and model-based foothold planning.
Refines each foothold using six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field, enabling sub-grid corrections.
Completes an 85 m, five-segment course in 18/20 trials (90%; Wilson 95% CI: 70–97%).
An ablated system without expert mixture or refinement achieves 0% on both stair and hurdle segments.
Component studies find that label-free routers and a self-supervised terrain embedding underperform the privileged terrain label.
papers.selection_reason: Terrain traversal humanoid locomotion with terrain classifier and foothold planning fits embodied navigation and planning.
papers.title: Terrain Traversal Without Motion Priors: Expert-Routed Humanoid Locomotion at Deployment Fidelity
papers.tldr: A deployment-faithful humanoid system crosses varied terrain without motion priors by routing among terrain-specialized experts and continuously refining planned footholds.

papers.abstract: Zero-Shot Object Navigation (ZSON) in unknown multi-floor environments presents a significant challenge. Recent methods, mostly based on semantic value greedy waypoint selection, spatial topology-enhanced memory, and Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as a decision-making framework, have led to improvements. However, these architectures struggle to balance exploration and exploitation for ZSON when encountering unseen environments, especially in multi-floor settings, such as robots getting stuck at narrow intersections, endlessly wandering, or failing to find stair entrances. To overcome these challenges, we propose AERR-Nav, a Zero-Shot Object Navigation framework that dynamically adjusts its state based on the robot's environment. Specifically, AERR-Nav has the following two key advantages: (1) An Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy, enables robots to dynamically transition between three states, facilitating specialized responses to diverse navigation scenarios. (2) An Adaptive Exploration State featuring Fast and Slow-Thinking modes helps robots better balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning based on evolving environmental information. Extensive experiments on the HM3D and MP3D benchmarks demonstrate that our AERR-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the efficacy of our proposed strategy and modules.
authors: Jingzhi Huang, Junkai Huang, Haoyang Yang, Haoang Li, Yi Wang
bullets: Targets common failures such as getting stuck at narrow intersections, wandering indefinitely, and missing stair entrances.
Uses an Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy to select navigation states based on environmental conditions.
Its exploration state combines Fast- and Slow-Thinking modes to balance exploration, exploitation, and higher-level reasoning.
Experiments on HM3D and MP3D report state-of-the-art performance among zero-shot methods, with ablations supporting the proposed components.
papers.selection_reason: Zero-shot object navigation with adaptive exploration-recovery-reminiscing and MLLM-based decision-making; directly fits embodied navigation and embodied memory.
papers.title: AERR-Nav: Adaptive Exploration-Recovery-Reminiscing Strategy for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
papers.tldr: AERR-Nav improves zero-shot object navigation in unseen multi-floor environments by adaptively switching among exploration, recovery, and reminiscing behaviors.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound (US) acquisition depends on the operator's ability to interpret anatomy and anticipate how the view will change with probe motion. Many robotic US navigation methods select actions without explicitly predicting these anatomical changes. We propose SonoGraph-WM, an action- and goal-conditioned world model for anticipatory probe navigation. The model represents anatomy as scene graphs (SGs), capturing visible structures, their geometry, and spatial relationships without synthesizing US images. Given a history of SGs and probe poses, a unified Transformer jointly predicts future SGs and poses. A receding-horizon planner recursively imagines candidate trajectories, selects the shortest predicted path reaching a goal graph, and follows it over a short execution horizon before replanning from new observations. To reduce reliance on tracked and anatomically annotated US sequences, we generate aligned SG--pose training data from computed tomography (CT) label maps along surface-constrained probe trajectories. On four held-out CT cases, spatial relation F1 remains above 93% over 20 prediction steps, and closed-loop navigation achieves 77.50% and 75.00% success for the gallbladder and pancreas, respectively, using annotation-derived SGs. In robot--phantom navigation experiments with label-map-derived SGs, the planner reached the target view in 73.7% of trials. These findings support CT-supervised anatomical world modeling for probe planning and highlight the importance of frequent observation updates for reliable navigation. Project Page: https://noseefood.github.io/us-sonograph-wm/
bullets: Represents ultrasound anatomy as scene graphs of visible structures, geometry, and spatial relationships instead of synthesizing images.
A unified Transformer predicts future scene graphs and probe poses from observation histories; receding-horizon planning selects and repeatedly updates trajectories toward a goal graph.
CT label maps generate aligned scene-graph/pose training data, reducing dependence on tracked and anatomically annotated ultrasound sequences.
On held-out CT cases, spatial-relation F1 stayed above 93% for 20 prediction steps; navigation success was 77.50% for the gallbladder and 75.00% for the pancreas.
Robot–phantom trials reached target views in 73.7% of cases, with results emphasizing frequent observation updates for reliable navigation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned scene-graph world model for anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation; aligns with interactive world models and robot navigation.
papers.title: Scanning While Imagining: A Scene-Graph World Model for Robotic Ultrasound Navigation
papers.tldr: SonoGraph-WM enables anticipatory robotic ultrasound navigation by predicting future anatomical scene graphs and probe poses, then planning through imagined trajectories.

papers.abstract: Active exploration and semantic navigation require an embodied agent to build memory from partial observations, predict how the evolution of observed spatial memory may support future motion, and convert that prediction into actionable plans. We present GLAM, a goal-conditioned latent world model trained over global spatiotemporal memory, and GLAM NAV, the complete navigation system built around it. Given historical map tokens, a navigation goal, and the current robot pose, GLAM jointly predicts future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents, allowing future spatial context and navigation intent to be inferred in a shared representation space. The model follows a JEPA-like latent prediction paradigm, operates directly on map-level latent tokens rather than RGB reconstruction, and uses a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to supervise and decode navigation plans within GLAM NAV. Training data are collected by replaying ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat over HM3D v0.2 scene assets and slicing them into multi-timescale prediction samples. On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav subset reproduction setting, GLAM NAV improves over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline in both success rate and success weighted by path length.
bullets: Uses historical map tokens, the navigation goal, and robot pose to jointly predict future map representations and robot-centric waypoint latents.
Applies JEPA-like latent prediction directly to map-level tokens instead of reconstructing RGB observations.
GLAM NAV combines the world model with a pretrained waypoint encoder-decoder to generate actionable navigation plans.
Trained on replayed ObjectNav expert trajectories in Habitat using HM3D v0.2 scenes and multi-timescale prediction samples.
On a controlled HM3D-ObjectNav reproduction subset, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length over a reproduced BSC-Nav baseline.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation.
papers.title: GLAM: Training a latent world model over global spatiotemporal memory for active exploration and navigation
papers.tldr: GLAM learns a goal-conditioned latent world model that predicts future spatial memory and navigation waypoints for active exploration and semantic navigation.

papers.abstract: Mobile robots typically rely on geometric maps for obstacle avoidance and path planning, but the resulting obstacle representation does not always match how an object should affect navigation. A low lying cable may be missed, a flexible curtain may create spurious blockage, and a traffic cone may require an exclusion region larger than its observed footprint. We present NavPatch, an object level correction layer that assigns ADD, REMOVE, or EXTEND to navigation relevant object categories through periodic scene understanding with a vision-language model. Open vocabulary grounding localizes object instances, and LiDAR and RGB-D observations provide 3D support. Observation quality filtering and cross frame maintenance determine when each correction patch is committed, replaced, or revoked. In 50 real robot trials across five layouts, NavPatch achieves an overall success rate of 86.0%. An ablation study of four configurations with 200 runs in total shows that NavPatch improves the success rate from 70.0% to 86.0% and reduces the false commit rate from 68.4% to 40.7% compared with updates based only on the current observation.
bullets: Addresses mismatches between geometric obstacle maps and how objects should affect navigation.
Assigns object-level ADD, REMOVE, or EXTEND corrections using open-vocabulary grounding with LiDAR and RGB-D support.
Filters observation quality and maintains corrections across frames before committing, replacing, or revoking patches.
In 50 real-robot trials across five layouts, achieved an 86.0% overall success rate.
Across 200 ablation runs, improved success from 70.0% to 86.0% and reduced false commits from 68.4% to 40.7% versus current-observation-only updates.
papers.selection_reason: VLM-grounded object-level costmap correction for mobile robot obstacle avoidance and navigation.
papers.title: NavPatch: Evidence-Guided Object-Level Costmap Correction with Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: NavPatch uses vision-language scene understanding and 3D sensing to dynamically correct object-level navigation costmaps, improving robot navigation success and reducing erroneous map updates.

papers.abstract: We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar. Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
authors: Hajira Amjad, Valerii Serpiva, Viacheslav Liubimov, Didar Seyidov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Generates plausible future views from one RGB observation plus a textual reconstruction objective.
Uses a vision-language model to guide prompts for video diffusion, then applies ORB-SLAM3 and Video Depth Anything.
Aligns dense depth with camera poses and triangulated landmarks to improve multi-view geometric consistency.
In a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes rose from 13/19 to 15/19, and successful RRT trials from 62/90 to 75/90.
The approach remains subject to reconstruction and free-space failures; matched-landmark error was approximately 0.30 m across 15 corridor reconstructions.
papers.selection_reason: Video diffusion world model for anticipatory robot navigation with geometry-guided depth alignment.
papers.title: HorizonNav: Geometry-Guided Video Diffusion for Anticipatory 3D Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: HorizonNav uses text-guided video diffusion and geometry-based depth alignment to imagine and reconstruct navigable 3D surroundings from a single RGB image.

papers.abstract: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is widely used for real-time localization and mapping, but its reliability can degrade substantially in subterranean environments affected by smoke, dust, and other airborne obscurants, whereas radar remains comparatively robust. This article presents a one-class temporal learning framework for LiDAR degradation detection and reliability-aware localization under such conditions. A broad set of degradation-sensitive cues, including spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and measurement-recency features, is evaluated to characterize changes in LiDAR sensing quality. Their temporal evolution is modelled over sliding windows using an LSTM autoencoder trained exclusively on nominal operation, enabling deviations from healthy sensor behaviour to be detected without requiring labelled degradation data. The resulting LiDAR reliability estimate governs adaptive selection between LIO and radar inertial odometry (RIO), retaining LIO during reliable sensing and transferring localization authority to RIO when degradation is detected. The framework is evaluated using real-world ground robot data collected in GNSS-denied subterranean tunnels under nominal and dense-smoke conditions. Experimental results demonstrate degradation detection, adaptive modality switching, and continued localization output under severe LiDAR degradation. A feature family ablation study further shows that a reduced feature representation can improve degradation-aware localization performance in the evaluated dense-smoke scenarios, highlighting the importance of feature parsimony in one-class sensor degradation detection. The code will be released as open source to support reproducibility and further research.
authors: Moumita Mukherjee, Avijit Banerjee, Anton Koval, George Nikolakopoulo
bullets: Targets LiDAR reliability loss caused by airborne obscurants in GNSS-denied underground settings.
Uses spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and recency cues modeled over time.
Trains an LSTM autoencoder only on nominal data, avoiding labeled degradation examples.
Controls switching between LIO and RIO, preserving LIO when healthy and transferring authority to radar when degraded.
Real-world tunnel experiments show degradation detection, adaptive switching, and continued localization under dense smoke; a reduced feature set improved performance in the evaluated scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Reliability-aware localization for robots under LiDAR degradation using one-class temporal learning.
papers.title: When LiDAR Fades, Radar Takes Over: LiDAR Reliability-Aware Adaptive Localization Under Airborne Obscurants
papers.tldr: A one-class LSTM-based system detects LiDAR degradation and adaptively switches from LIO to radar-inertial odometry to maintain localization in smoke- and dust-obscured subterranean environments.

papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.
authors: Hongrui Zheng, Aditya Singh, Rahul Mangharam
bullets: Addresses joint constraints whose team-level violation costs do not reveal which agents caused them.
Uses Signal Temporal Logic robustness with running-maximum cost increments to measure episode-level violations.
Applies differentiable dynamics and full-episode sensitivities to allocate delayed constraint effects among agents.
Evaluated on payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control.
Reports 1.6–5.1× higher safe-success in transport, 11.1% better navigation safe-success, and 50–68% higher traffic throughput than constrained baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Safe multi-agent RL with constraint decomposition applies to embodied navigation, transport, and traffic-control policies.
papers.title: SafeDiSTL: Decomposing Joint Constraints for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: SafeDiSTL assigns multi-agent credit for shared safety violations using STL robustness and action sensitivities, improving safety and task performance across cooperative control tasks.

papers.abstract: Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance. The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.
bullets: Addresses vessel trajectory prediction in confined waters to support navigation and collision avoidance.
Combines historical AIS positions with local-vessel positional heat maps generated by KDE and encoded by a CNN.
Evaluates Transformer and Performer architectures trained with quantile loss to estimate model-aware prediction intervals.
Reports substantially better performance than previous work.
Local heat maps help predict movements not evident from an agent’s own past positions.
papers.selection_reason: Learning-based vessel trajectory forecasting for autonomous navigation and collision avoidance.
papers.title: Probabilistic Ship Trajectory Forecasting using Transformer Models on AIS Data
papers.tldr: Transformer- and Performer-based models use AIS histories plus CNN-encoded KDE heat maps of nearby vessel movements to produce probabilistic ship trajectory forecasts for collision avoidance.

papers.abstract: Collective Autonomous Vehicle (AV) route choices in real-world traffic networks can create externalities for Human-Driven Vehicles (HDVs), as routes that benefit AVs may increase travel times for other road users. To address this, we introduce a social component, the marginal cost, to the selfish travel time AV reward. Marginal cost captures an AV's impact on other road users by comparing their travel times with those in a counterfactual simulation in which the AV is removed. We study AV route choice in mixed-autonomy traffic settings using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), where AVs learn routing policies through repeated interactions with the traffic environment. Experiments on the real-world networks of Ingolstadt and Provins show that incorporating marginal cost into the AV reward not only limits the increase in HDV travel times and shortens AV travel times relative to selfish AV routing, but also improves overall system performance. In Ingolstadt, selfish routing of 40\% AVs increases the travel times of other vehicles by 1.7\%, and this drops to 1.1\% when the social reward is included. Interestingly, not only does overall system performance improve, but the AVs are also better off when acting socially.This effect is consistent across tested cities, penetration rates, and replications, yet when the weight of the social component in the reward increases, the system fails to reach the desired performance. For a more scalable approach to social AV routing in mixed-autonomy traffic, we compute the marginal cost only for the AVs whose route choices most affect the traffic system. This reduces the number of counterfactual simulations and achieves similar performance at a significantly lower computational cost. Our results suggest that AV routing should go beyond selfish rewards and, for the benefit of all traffic participants, include a social component in its objective.
authors: Anastasia Psarou, Mikolaj Rams, Blazej Torbus, Rafal Kucharski
bullets: Selfish AV route choices can increase travel times for human-driven vehicles in mixed-autonomy traffic.
The method estimates each AV’s impact by comparing traffic with and without that AV in a counterfactual simulation.
Experiments on Ingolstadt and Provins show lower human-driver delays, shorter AV travel times, and better system performance with social rewards.
For 40% AV penetration in Ingolstadt, the human-driver travel-time increase falls from 1.7% to 1.1%.
Computing marginal costs only for the most influential AVs preserves similar performance at lower computational cost; excessive social-reward weighting can hurt performance.
papers.selection_reason: Learned multi-agent AV routing policies in mixed traffic; directly relevant to autonomous navigation and planning.
papers.title: Collective Autonomous Vehicle Routing Needs Social Awareness for Coexistence with Human Drivers
papers.tldr: Adding a social marginal-cost reward to multi-agent AV routing reduces harm to human drivers while improving AV and overall traffic performance.

papers.abstract: End-to-end planning in complex scenes must model diverse driving intentions and select the most appropriate trajectory using scene context and future risks. However, multi-query regression may collapse to one mode, while anchor-based and generative planners share a scaling bottleneck: small candidate sets limit maneuver coverage or discovery of high-quality trajectories, whereas large sets increase generation and scoring costs. We propose ManeuverFlow to generate trajectories for distinct intentions in one step and evaluate and refine them using current and future evidence. The model selects relevant maneuver modes, draws corresponding noise from the Gaussian mixture prior, and maps it to intention-specific trajectories through a maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow field. Current features and future features predicted by the world model are aggregated along each candidate path into trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-factor prediction. Using the same evidence, the refiner predicts local Frenet residuals for selected candidates; refined and retained candidates are then jointly re-scored for selection. With a lightweight TransFuser-style ResNet-34 backbone, ManeuverFlow achieves 90.6 PDMS and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest, respectively. On WorldEngine's recent 3DGS closed-loop benchmark, it attains the highest listed PDMS$^\ast$ scores of 75.19 and 74.58 under logged and IDM-controlled traffic, respectively. Code: https://github.com/wyh-autonomy/maneuverflow.
authors: Yuhao Wei, Yong Chen, Chen Yang, Yingchen Wang, Delin Ouyang, Lingfeng Qi, Qi Lan, Zhanhua Zhang, Jie Li, Guofa Li
bullets: Addresses mode collapse and the cost–coverage trade-off of small versus large candidate sets.
Uses maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow to map maneuver-specific Gaussian-mixture noise to trajectories.
Aggregates present and world-model-predicted future features along each path for trajectory-specific scoring.
Refines selected candidates with local Frenet residuals before joint re-scoring.
Reports strong performance on NAVSIM v1/v2 and the WorldEngine 3DGS closed-loop benchmark.
papers.selection_reason: End-to-end trajectory generation and evaluation for autonomous driving with future evidence.
papers.title: ManeuverFlow: Maneuver Hypothesis Generation with Future Evidence for Trajectory Evaluation and Refinement in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: ManeuverFlow generates diverse intention-specific trajectories in one step, then uses current and predicted future evidence to evaluate, refine, and select the best plan for end-to-end autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.
authors: Kaizhen Li, Xi Zhou, Dan Zhang, Xiaowei Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of UAV–USV landing under high sea states and rapidly varying motion.
Uses a pretrained model to predict USV attitude during high-level landing decisions.
Selects suitable landing windows and touchdown times based on predicted motion.
Combines high-level planning with a conventional low-level flight controller for UAV stability and command tracking.
Real-sea motion data transferred to a MuJoCo USV provide real-sim validation, demonstrating feasibility in realistic disturbances.
papers.selection_reason: Learned attitude prediction for UAV landing-window planning on a USV; embodied navigation/planning.
papers.title: Prediction-Informed Landing Window Planning for UAV Landing on USV in High Sea States
papers.tldr: A prediction-informed hierarchical controller uses explicit USV attitude forecasts to select landing windows and touchdown timing for UAV landing on USVs in rough, rapidly changing seas.

papers.abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.
authors: Chen Yu, Sudarshan S Harithas, Juan Borbon, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between disruptive full replanning and continuing along invalidated plans.
Combines online object-property estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control.
Partially inverts the old plan only where old and new beliefs disagree, then reconstructs the remainder under the new belief.
Across 18 simulated goals, reduced pooled final position error by roughly 33% and yaw error by 47% versus fixed-depth replanning.
Hardware experiments demonstrated translation and turning of a non-holonomic cart.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) for flow-based replanning in humanoid loco-manipulation, combining online estimation with flow-based planning to handle unknown object dynamics.
papers.title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.tldr: BOPI enables humanoids to adaptively push carts with unknown dynamics by partially revising motion plans as beliefs change.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing the direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor $\rho$. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of $[\max(1-\nu_f(\mathcal{I}),h(N,\beta))]^2 \rho \frac{1}{\kappa_f}(1-e^{-\kappa_f})$ of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
authors: Yoonjae Hwang, Hojune Kim, Ellen Novoseller, Guangyao Shi, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the risk that robot loss disconnects the surviving communication network, halting coordination.
Introduces Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, jointly modeling task performance, failure resilience, and communication connectivity.
Uses a Menger-based connectivity reduction, connectivity-aware greedy selection, and a feasibility-preserving fallback.
Provides curvature-based worst-case guarantees that account for connectivity costs through a factor $\rho$ and recover classical guarantees in limiting cases.
Experiments on multi-robot target tracking evaluate the method and the practical effects of connectivity constraints.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a resilient multi-robot coordination framework using submodular maximization with $k$-connectivity constraints, offering a technically meaningful optimization approach for multi-agent navigation.
papers.title: Failure-Resilient Multi-Robot Coordination with $k$-Connectivity Constrained Submodular Maximization
papers.tldr: A connectivity-aware submodular optimization framework enables multi-robot teams to remain coordinated and effective despite robot failures or adversarial removals.

papers.abstract: Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Xinming Zhang, Yiwei Qian, Siwei Cheng, Shanze Wang, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the embodiment mismatch that makes source-robot demonstrations invalid for target-robot supervision.
Uses geometry-consistent scaling and per-demonstration validity checks to recast source data for each target embodiment.
Trains a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy to produce feasible collision-avoidance maneuvers.
Validated in simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms.
Reports a 13.8-percentage-point average success-rate gain over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations, with training completed within seconds.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses cross-embodiment mapless navigation by recasting offline demonstrations into target-specific policies using geometry-consistent scaling, a significant contribution to transferable navigation policies.
papers.title: CeDR-Nav: Cross-Embodiment Mapless Navigation via Offline Demonstration Recasting
papers.tldr: CeDR-Nav repurposes demonstrations from one robot embodiment to train effective mapless navigation policies for different robots without online data collection.

papers.abstract: Agile and reliable navigation is a core capability for embodied robots navigating complex spatial constraints and dynamic interactions. However, a single policy often struggles to accommodate the distinct decision-making demands of diverse scenarios. We present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher-Student navigation framework built around a temporal soft mixture of experts (Soft-MoE). The Teacher combines clean observations with causally maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks to construct privileged representations, while the Student learns complementary navigation features from corrupted observation histories through temporal encoding, soft expert routing, and latent distillation. Procedural scenario generation and parallel task-level simulation broaden training coverage, while deployment-informed asymmetric domain randomization supports sim-to-real transfer. Across in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, TAME-Nav achieves higher success rates, lower collision rates, and higher navigation scores than representative baselines. On a real quadruped robot, it completes all twenty trials across local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with sudden dynamic obstacles, with only one minor contact.
authors: Lingjie Zhang, Jun Xue, Shanze Wang, Haoyu Xi, Xinming Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of using one navigation policy across varied spatial constraints and dynamic interactions.
Uses an asymmetric Teacher–Student framework with temporal soft mixture-of-experts routing and latent distillation.
The Teacher uses clean observations and maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks; the Student learns from corrupted observation histories.
Procedural scenario generation, parallel simulation, and deployment-informed domain randomization support broad training and sim-to-real transfer.
Outperforms representative baselines in success, collision, and navigation scores; a real quadruped completed 20 trials with one minor contact.
papers.selection_reason: Asymmetric teacher-student navigation with temporal mixture-of-experts distillation and sim-to-real transfer.
papers.title: TAME-Nav: Temporal Asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts Distillation for Agile and Versatile Robot Navigation
papers.tldr: TAME-Nav distills privileged temporal obstacle information into a robust mixture-of-experts student policy for agile robot navigation in diverse and dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
authors: Vivek Khatana, Zijian Song, Naira Hovakimyan, Petros Voulgaris
bullets: Addresses the gap between independently generated symbolic plans and jointly feasible robot trajectories.
Compares centralized joint planning with decentralized, per-robot LLM planning.
Uses geometric grounding to detect inter-robot spatial and temporal conflicts.
Feeds structured conflict information back to LLM planners for iterative coordination.
Evaluates increasing task complexity in CARLA and with Crazyflie aerial robots, including physical executability trade-offs.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-robot path planning with LLM planners coordinated by a geometric verifier for execution-aware feasibility.
papers.title: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning
papers.tldr: A geometric verifier helps coordinate centralized or decentralized LLM planners by detecting trajectory conflicts and guiding replanning for feasible multi-robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.
authors: Shuo Zhang, Aman Sunesh, Semiha Ergan, Kaan Ozbay
bullets: Work zones introduce temporary lane changes and altered road connectivity, making vehicle-trajectory prediction difficult and underexplored.
The WZDrive-Data dataset contains 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, including vehicle, scene, control, and gaze signals.
The WZDrive predictor uses multimodal human-driving and scene information to forecast multiple possible ego trajectories.
It achieves minADE@6 of 1.09 m and minFDE@6 of 2.12 m, improving on the strongest benchmark baselines by 7.18% and 13.18%, respectively.
The study focuses on urban roadway work zones and relies on human-in-the-loop simulator data.
papers.selection_reason: Learned ego-trajectory prediction for autonomous driving in work zones, fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
papers.tldr: WZDrive combines human-in-the-loop work-zone driving data with multimodal prediction to improve autonomous-vehicle ego-trajectory forecasting in complex construction zones.

papers.abstract: Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct. Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue. We study visual-Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure. Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot. We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts. On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined. Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
authors: Lihao Wang, Tianjian Xu, Tianmin Shu, Renjie Zhao
bullets: Addresses navigation to small, occluded, or visually indistinct devices using Wi-Fi signals as a spatial cue.
Introduces WiFiSpaces, a Habitat extension that simulates pose-dependent, ray-traced Wi-Fi observations during policy rollouts.
Uses robot motion to aggregate noisy multi-view bearing measurements into a confidence-aware source estimate.
A learned policy fuses the evolving Wi-Fi estimate with depth observations for closed-loop navigation.
Improves with ray-traced Wi-Fi fine-tuning, transfers zero-shot to unseen scenes, and runs on a real robot without real-world training.
papers.selection_reason: Learned robot navigation to signal-emitting devices using visual and Wi-Fi observations, with online source localization and policy learning.
papers.title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
papers.tldr: ViFiNav enables robots to navigate unmapped indoor environments to Wi-Fi-emitting devices by combining motion-based source localization, depth vision, and Wi-Fi sensing without infrastructure changes.

papers.abstract: Recently, soft robotic procedures are being developed aiming at achieving targeted minimally invasive operations or drug administration in specific locations in the human body. Accordingly, specialized path-planning algorithms need to be investigated for the estimation of efficient paths that would protect the delicate tissue structures and simultaneously satisfy a set of requirements for the efficient navigation of the robot. In this context, we propose an image-based 3D pathplanning algorithm, which is an extension of the A* algorithm, for the navigation of a soft-growing robot inside the spinal subarachnoid space (SSS). The proposed algorithm is capable of estimating a safe pathway towards the goal location, while ensuring the establishment of anchor points that facilitate the efficient steering of the soft robot. The algorithm is evaluated using a highly detailed model of the SSS with respect to its capacity to satisfy the robot movement requirements and path efficiency.
authors: George Dimas, Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis, Panagiotis Vartholomeos, Dimitris K. Iakovidis
bullets: Targets minimally invasive procedures and drug delivery in delicate anatomical environments.
Plans paths while accounting for tissue protection and soft-robot navigation requirements.
Establishes anchor points to support effective steering of the growing robot.
Evaluated in a highly detailed spinal subarachnoid space model for movement feasibility and path efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes image-based 3D path planning for soft-growing robot navigation, directly relevant to robot navigation/planning.
papers.title: Image-Based Path-Planning for Navigation of Soft-Growing Robots in the Spinal Sub-Arachnoid Space
papers.tldr: An image-based 3D extension of A* plans safe, efficient routes for soft-growing robots navigating the spinal subarachnoid space.

papers.abstract: Humanoid and service robots operating in clut- tered human environments may encounter motion planning problems that are infeasible when all surrounding objects are treated as fixed obstacles. The Minimum Constraint Removal problem, which we refer to as MCR, addresses this situation by identifying the minimum number of constraints, such as movable objects, whose removal enables a collision-free path. However, computing an optimal MCR solution is NP-hard. In this work, we propose a graph-based heuristic pipeline that combines bidirectional feasible-set generation with fixed- length searches over reduced MCR graphs. We further derive an extended feasible-set generator for instances in which the candidates produced by the first generator do not contain a complete optimal removal set. Across six benchmarks, the evaluated pipeline matches the exact solution in three cases and, in the remaining cases, selects at most 31.25% more obstacles than the optimum, while being between 3.4 and 33.7 times faster than exact search. In one of the benchmarks, involving a manipulation task amidst clutter, selecting two rather than seven obstructing objects reduces the combined MCR, inverse- kinematics, and motion planning time from 84.72 s to 30.59 s. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a practical compromise between computational efficiency and solution quality for motion planning among movable obstacles.
authors: Antony Thomas, Fulvio Mastrogiovanni, Marco Baglietto
bullets: Targets Minimum Constraint Removal (MCR), which is NP-hard in cluttered environments with movable obstacles.
Combines bidirectional feasible-set generation, fixed-length searches, and an extended generator for difficult instances.
Matches the exact solution on three of six benchmarks; other solutions remove at most 31.25% more obstacles than optimal.
Runs 3.4–33.7× faster than exact search and substantially reduces planning time in a cluttered manipulation example.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses motion planning among movable obstacles for humanoid/service robots, fitting learned/planning navigation in cluttered environments.
papers.title: Graph-Based Heuristics for Minimum Constraint Removal in Cluttered Robot Motion Planning
papers.tldr: A graph-based heuristic efficiently finds near-minimal obstacle removals to make otherwise infeasible robot motion plans possible.

papers.abstract: As the number of autonomous robots continues to grow, safety becomes increasingly important. Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a theoretically grounded framework for ensuring safety, but existing design methods often face limitations in effectiveness, scalability, or interpretability, and may result in overly conservative safe sets. In this paper, we propose \emph{VertexCBF}, a framework for learning neural CBFs in a scalable, systematic, and explainable way. We approximate the stationary Hamilton--Jacobi value function using a neural network trained via a combination of physics-informed and sparsely supervised learning. By exploiting control-affine dynamics and a convex polytope control set, under which the Hamiltonian is maximized at the control vertices, we efficiently generate supervision points via GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, while a residual architecture guarantees that the learned CBF is never larger than the specified constraint function. We evaluate the method on 15 systems and compare it against relevant baselines, showing that it reliably recovers large safe sets where the baselines are conservative or fail completely. In addition, we perform a hardware experiment in which a mobile robot safely avoids pedestrians using a neural CBF trained with our method.
bullets: Addresses conservative, ineffective, or poorly scalable existing methods for designing control barrier functions.
Approximates the stationary Hamilton–Jacobi value function with a neural network using physics-informed and sparse supervision.
Uses GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, enabled by control-affine dynamics and convex-polytope controls, to generate supervision efficiently.
A residual architecture ensures the learned CBF does not exceed the specified constraint function.
Across 15 systems and a mobile-robot pedestrian-avoidance experiment, the method recovers large safe sets and achieves safe hardware operation.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes VertexCBF for learning neural control barrier functions to ensure safety in mobile robot navigation.
papers.title: VertexCBF: Improving Neural Control Barrier Functions via Vertex-Restricted Control Search
papers.tldr: VertexCBF learns scalable, interpretable neural control barrier functions by restricting safety-related control search to polytope vertices, enabling larger safe sets and demonstrated hardware safety.

papers.abstract: This work evaluates the direct transfer of a co-evolved communication protocol from a 2D simulation to a 3D physical environment, without retraining the network weights. Two e-puck-type robots, controlled by a GRU network with residual connection, were evaluated in a food-seeking task with social signaling.
